div.p: To Eustathius the philosopher

I had already given up in the face of the assaults of what men call fortune, which has always thrown some obstacle in the way of my joining you; and now, in a way I find marvellous, you have recalled and consoled me by your letter. For indeed I had by now begun to turn the thought over within myself, wondering whether what most people are forever repeating might not be true: that there is some necessity and fate which governs both the small and the greater of our affairs, while we men are masters of nothing at all; or else, if not this, then that some fortune altogether drives the life of man. You will grant me much pardon for these reflections once you have learned the reasons that led me to them.

I left Athens for the report of your philosophy, passing over the schools there. I ran past the city on the Hellespont as no Odysseus ever ran past the songs of the Sirens. Asia I admired, but I was hurrying toward the mother-city of the fine things in it. When I reached my own country, and looked for you in it—you, that great benefit—and did not find you, from that point on the many and varied occasions of unexpected hindrances came upon me. For either I had necessarily to fall ill, and on that account be left behind, or, when you were travelling to the East, I was unable to set out with you; and when at last, with countless toils, I had reached Syria, I found I could not be with the philosopher, for he had departed for Egypt. So once again I had to go to Egypt, a long and grievous road, and not even there did I obtain what I sought. But fortune was so perverse a lover that I had to journey either toward Persia, going forward into the farthest reaches of the barbarian lands—for you went even there, so great was the contentiousness of my evil genius—or else to sit here in Alexandria, which is in fact what came to pass. For it seems to me that, had I not given up, following you like some beast led on by a branch held out before it, you would have drawn me on even beyond Indian Nyssa, and, if there is any remotest spot in our inhabited world, you would have led me wandering there as well.

And why need I say much more? In the end, even now, while I am living in my own country, it has not been granted me to be with you, since I am kept off by long illnesses; and unless these grow somewhat milder for the time to come, not even in the winter shall we be with your eloquence. Are these not the works of fate, as you yourself would say? Are these not the works of necessity? Have they not very nearly outdone the poets' tales about Tantalus? But, as I said, I have grown easier by your letter, and I am no longer of the same mind. I hold that one ought, when God gives good things, to be thankful, and when He keeps them in store, not to be vexed. And so, if it should be granted us to be with you, we shall count this at once the best and the most pleasant of things; but if He should defer it, we shall bear the loss gently. For He surely orders our affairs better, in every case, than we ourselves would have chosen.
Basil to Gregory

I recognized your letter, as men recognize the children of their friends by the likeness that appears in them to those who begot them. For your saying that the situation of the place is not enough to instil in your soul any impulse toward the life we lead, until you have learned something of our way and manner of living—this was indeed a thought truly your own and worthy of your soul, which reckons all things here as nothing in comparison with the blessedness laid up for us in the promises. As for myself, I am ashamed to write what I do here in this remote retreat, night and day. For I have left the busy life of the city as the source of countless evils, but I have not yet been able to leave myself behind. Rather, I am like those who, from inexperience of sailing, are at a loss and seasick upon the sea: they are distressed by the size of the ship as causing them much tossing, and crossing over from it to the skiff or the boat, they are seasick and at a loss everywhere, for their nausea and bile go along with them. Such, then, is our case too. For carrying our indwelling passions about with us, we are everywhere amid the same disturbances, so that we have gained nothing very great from this solitude. But what we ought to do, and the way by which we might keep close to the footsteps of Him who has led us toward salvation—for He says, "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me"—is this.

We must try to keep the mind in stillness. For just as the eye, when it is continually shifted about—now turned to the sides, now repeatedly turned up and down—cannot clearly see what lies before it, but the sight must be fixed firmly upon the object seen if it is to make its view of it distinct; so too the mind of man, when it is dragged about by the countless cares of the world, cannot clearly fix its gaze upon the truth. The man not yet yoked in the bonds of marriage is shaken by raging desires, by impulses hard to restrain, and by certain ill-starred loves; while he who is already bound to a wife is beset by another tumult of cares: when childless, the longing for children; when in possession of children, anxiety over their rearing, the keeping of a wife, the management of a household, the oversight of servants, losses in contracts, quarrels with neighbours, entanglements in the law-courts, the hazards of trade, the toils of farming. Every day comes bringing its own darkening of the soul; and the nights, taking up the cares of the day, deceive the mind with the same imaginings.

From these there is one escape: separation from the whole world. But withdrawal from the world is not to be outside it in body, but to tear the soul away from sympathy with the body, and to become without city, without home, without property, without society, without possessions, without livelihood, free of business, free of dealings, unschooled in the teachings of men, ready to receive in the heart the impressions engraved upon it by divine teaching. And the preparation of the heart is the unlearning of the teachings that have taken prior hold of it through evil habit. For one cannot write on wax without first smoothing away the characters already there; nor can one set divine doctrines in a soul without first removing the prejudices it has acquired from custom. To this end solitude offers us the greatest benefit, lulling our passions and giving reason leisure to cut them away from the soul altogether. For just as wild beasts are easily mastered when they have been stroked into calm, so desires, angers, fears, and griefs, the venomous evils of the soul, when they have been lulled by stillness and not made savage by continual provocation, become more easily mastered by the power of reason. Let the place, then, be such as ours is, free from the company of men, so that the continuity of our discipline may be broken by nothing from outside.

The discipline of godliness nourishes the soul with divine thoughts. What, then, is more blessed than to imitate on earth the choir of the angels? At the very beginning of the day, to hasten to prayer, and to honour the Creator with hymns and songs; then, when the sun shines clearly forth, to turn to work, prayer accompanying it everywhere, and to season one's labours with hymns as with salt? For the consolations of hymns bestow upon the soul a cheerful and untroubled state.

Stillness, then, is the beginning of the soul's purification, when the tongue does not speak the things of men, nor the eyes scan the good complexion and proportion of bodies, nor the hearing slacken the soul's tone in songs composed for pleasure, nor in the words of witty and jesting men—which above all are apt to loosen the soul's tone. For the mind, when not scattered upon outward things nor diffused by the senses into the world, returns to itself, and through itself ascends to the thought of God; and shone round and illumined by that beauty, it forgets even its own nature. Drawn down neither to anxiety over food nor to concern for clothing, but keeping leisure from earthly cares, it transfers its whole zeal to the acquisition of eternal goods—how temperance and courage may be rightly achieved in it, how justice and prudence, and the other virtues which, ranged as subdivisions under these general ones, prompt the earnest man to perform fittingly each of the duties of life.

A very great road toward the discovery of one's duty is also the study of the inspired Scriptures. For in these are found both the precepts for action and the lives of blessed men, recorded and handed down, set before us like living images of life lived according to God, for the imitation of their good works. And so, in whatever each man perceives himself to be deficient, by attending to that and as it were from a common dispensary, he finds the medicine suited to his ailment. The lover of temperance continually unrolls the story of Joseph, and learns from him the deeds of temperance, finding him not only self-controlled against pleasures but settled in a fixed disposition toward virtue. He is schooled in courage by Job, who not only, when his life turned to its opposite—becoming poor from rich and childless from a father of fine children in a single moment of time—remained the same, preserving everywhere the unbowed spirit of his soul; but neither was he provoked when his friends, who had come to comfort him, trampled upon him and added to his pains. Again, one who considers how a man might at the same time be gentle and high-spirited—so as to use his anger against sin, and his gentleness toward men—will find David noble in deeds of war, yet gentle and unmoved in requiting his enemies. Such too was Moses, rising up with great wrath against those who sinned against God, yet bearing with a gentle soul the slanders against himself. And everywhere, just as painters, when they paint images from images, look frequently at the model and strive to transfer its character to their own work of art, so too the man who is earnest to perfect himself in every part of virtue must look to the lives of the saints as to certain living and active statues, and make their goodness his own by imitation.

Prayers, again, succeeding the readings, take up the soul fresher and more vigorous, stirred by longing for God. And good prayer is that which produces in the soul a clear thought of God. And this is the indwelling of God: to have God established within oneself through memory. Thus we become a temple of God, when the continuity of memory is not broken by earthly cares, nor the mind disturbed by unexpected passions, but the lover of God, having fled all these, withdraws to God, driving out the passions that summon him to incontinence, and dwells among the pursuits that lead to virtue.

And first of all it is fitting to take care not to be unschooled in the use of speech, but to ask without contentiousness and to answer without ambition, not interrupting the one conversing when he says something useful, nor desiring to insert one's own argument for display, setting limits to speaking and to listening; to learn without shame and to teach without grudging; and if one has been taught by another, not to hide it, like worthless women who pass off illegitimate children as their own, but graciously to proclaim the father of the word. The middle pitch of voice is to be preferred, so that it neither escape the hearing by smallness nor be oppressive by the greatness of its strain. One should first examine within oneself what is to be said, and so make the word public. Be courteous in encounters, sweet in conversation, not hunting pleasantness through buffoonery, but having graciousness through kindly encouragement. Everywhere put away harshness, even when there is need to rebuke. For having first cast yourself down through humility, you will so be the more readily accepted by the one who needs the cure. Often, too, the prophet's manner of reproof is useful to us, who, when David had sinned, did not bring down the sentence of condemnation from himself, but, using the device of an assumed character, set the man himself as judge of his own sin, so that, having pronounced the verdict against himself, he could no longer blame the one who convicted him.

To the humble and lowly spirit there follows a grave eye bent toward the ground, a neglected appearance, unkempt hair, soiled clothing; so that what mourners do by design appears in us of its own accord. Let the tunic be drawn close to the body by a belt; yet let the girding be neither above the loins, for that is womanish, nor loose, so that the tunic flows about, for that is effeminate. And let the gait be neither sluggish, so as to accuse the soul of slackness, nor again vehement and hurried, so as to betray its impulses as unbalanced. The aim of clothing is one: to be a covering of the flesh sufficient against winter and summer. Let no brightness be sought in colour, nor fineness and softness in the making; for to scan the good colours in clothing is the same as the adornment of women, which they practise, dyeing their cheeks and their hair with a borrowed bloom. The tunic, moreover, ought to be of such thickness that the wearer needs no other to keep him warm. The sandal should be cheap as to its worth, yet fully serving its use.

And in a word, just as in clothing one ought to put first what is needful, so too in food bread will fill the need, and water will treat the thirst of the healthy man, and whatever side-dishes made from seeds are able to preserve the body's strength for its necessary uses. One should eat without displaying raging gluttony, but everywhere preserving steadiness, gentleness, and self-control regarding pleasures; nor even then keeping the mind idle in its thought of God, but making the very nature of the foods and the constitution of the body that receives them an occasion for glorifying God—how varied kinds of foods, suited to the particular nature of bodies, have been devised by Him who orders all things. Let prayers before food be made worthy of God's gifts, both those He gives now and those He has stored up for the future. Let prayers after food contain thanksgiving for what has been given and a request for what has been promised. Let one hour be appointed for food, the same recurring in its cycle, so that out of the twenty-four hours of the day and night this is scarcely the one expended on the body, while the rest the ascetic spends busy in the activity of the mind.

Let sleep be light and easily shaken off, naturally following upon a measured diet, and by design broken by cares for great things. For to be mastered by deep stupor, with the limbs relaxed so as to give leisure to irrational fancies, makes those who sleep so to be in a daily death. But what dawn is to others, midnight is to the ascetics of godliness, since the stillness of night especially grants the soul leisure, when neither eyes nor ears convey harmful sounds or sights to the heart, but the mind alone, by itself, is with God, correcting itself by the memory of its sins, setting itself limits for the avoidance of evil, and seeking from God His co-working toward the completion of what it pursues.
To Candidianus

When I took your letter into my hands, I had an experience worth telling. I was wary of it, as of something announcing public business, and during the time I was loosening the seal I looked at it with dread, as no Spartan under accusation ever looked at a Laconian dispatch-staff. But when I had loosed it and gone through it all point by point, I was moved to laughter—partly from pleasure at hearing nothing alarming, and partly because I was judging your case against that of Demosthenes. For he, since he furnished the means for only a few choristers and flute-players, no longer thought fit to be called Demosthenes, but a chorus-master; whereas you are the same man whether you furnish supplies or not—furnishing them, mind you, to more myriads of soldiers than the men to whom he provided provisions—and you write to us not from the height of your station, but in your accustomed manner. Nor do you relax at all in your zeal for letters, but, as Plato says, in the storm and tempest of affairs, standing apart as it were beneath some strong wall, you fill your soul with no disturbance; or rather, so far as in you lies, you do not let others be disturbed either.

Such are your affairs—great and admirable to those able to discern them, and again not admirable to one who judges by the whole purpose of your life. Hear now our own affairs as well, which are at once strange and yet such as regularly befall us.

A certain boorish man, one of those who dwell with us at Annisa, when a servant of mine had died, though he had said he had no contract with him, though he had not come to me, had laid no charge, had not asked to receive anything from me willingly, and had not threatened to use force if he did not get it, suddenly attacked my house with some others as senseless as himself, beat and bruised the women who were keeping it, broke down the doors, and carried off everything—some things taking for himself, and others setting out for plunder to whoever wished.

That we, then, may not be the last limit of weakness, and seem to everyone fit objects for attack, show now that zeal which you have displayed in all our affairs, and be entreated to bring it to bear in this matter too. For only thus would our freedom from trouble be preserved for us, if we were ranged alongside your energy. And it would be sufficient justice for us, if the man were arrested by the local magistrate and shut up in prison for a short time. For we are not indignant only over what we have suffered, but we also need security for the future.
To Olympius

What are you doing, my admirable friend, in driving our dear poverty, the nurse of philosophy, away from this retreat? For I think she would even bring a suit of ejectment against you, if she had any power of speech, on the ground that I had chosen to live with her—I who now praise Zeno, who, when he had lost everything in a shipwreck, uttered nothing ignoble, but said, "Well done, fortune, you are driving us into the threadbare cloak"; and who now praise Cleanthes, who drew water from the well for hire, by which he both kept himself alive and paid wages to his teachers. And Diogenes she never ceased to admire, who took pride in being content with only what nature provides, so that he threw away even his drinking-cup, when he had been taught by a child to drink by stooping with his hollowed hands. These and such things our housemate poverty might reproach you with, now driven out by your great gifts. And she might add a threat too: that, if I should catch you here again, I will show that your former state was Sicilian or Italian luxury—so exactly will I avenge myself with my own means.
So much, then, for that. But I was glad to hear that you have already begun your treatment, and I pray that you may profit by it. A service of the body free from pain would befit your holy soul.
To Nectarius, a letter of consolation

I had not yet passed the third or fourth day since I was struck by the report of this unbearable affliction, and I was still in doubt, both because the messenger of these grievous tidings was not even able to relate to me clearly what had happened, and because, in praying that it might not be true, I was loath to accept what was being noised abroad—when I received a letter from the bishop accurately confirming the unwished-for news. At this, how greatly I groaned and how many tears I shed, what need is there to say? For who is so stony of heart, or so wholly outside human nature, as to bear such a thing without feeling, or to have his soul seized by only moderate grief?

The heir of an illustrious house, the prop of a family, the hope of a fatherland, the offspring of godly parents, reared under countless prayers, in the very flower of his age, snatched away from the midst of his father's hands, is gone. What nature of adamant would these things not be enough to dissolve and bring to fellow-feeling? So it is no great matter if the calamity has touched us too to the depths, since from the first we have been wholly attached to you, making both your joys and your sorrows our own. And yet it seemed, at least up to the present time, that your griefs were few, and that in most things your affairs were carried along with the current; but suddenly, by the malice of a demon, all that prosperity of the house and that brightness of soul has vanished, and we have become a grim tale to the world. If, then, we should wish to lament and weep over what has befallen, the whole span of life will not suffice us; and all men groaning with us will not be able to match our mourning to the affliction; but even if the streams of the rivers should become tears, they will not suffice to fulfil the dirge over what has happened.

If, however, we are willing now to bring forth the gift of God which He has laid up in our hearts—I mean the temperate reasoning which knows how, even in prosperity, to set bounds to our souls, and in more sombre circumstances to bring us to remembrance of our human lot, and to suggest to us what we have seen and heard: that life is full of such afflictions, that the examples of human calamities are many, and above all, that it is a command of God that those who have believed in Christ should not grieve over those who have fallen asleep, because of the hope of the resurrection, and that for great endurance great crowns of glory are laid up with the Judge of the contest—if we permit reason to chant these things over us, perhaps we may find some moderate release from the evil. Therefore I exhort you, as a noble contestant, to stand firm against the magnitude of the blow, and not to fall beneath the weight of grief, nor to let your soul be swallowed up, convinced of this: that even though the reasons for the things ordered by God escape us, yet what is ordered by the Wise One who loves us is certainly to be accepted, even if it is painful. For He Himself knows how He apportions to each what is profitable, and why He sets unequal limits to our lives. For there is some cause, incomprehensible to men, for which some are taken from here sooner, while others are left to toil on longer in this painful life.

Therefore in all things we ought to revere His love for mankind and not be vexed, remembering that great and celebrated utterance which the great athlete Job sent forth, when he saw at a single table ten children crushed in a brief moment of time: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it seemed good to the Lord, so also has it come to pass." Let us make this wonder our own. Equal is the reward from the just Judge to those who display equal deeds of valour. We have not been robbed of the boy, but we have given him back to the One who lent him; nor has his life been destroyed, but it has been exchanged for the better; nor has earth hidden our beloved, but heaven has received him. Let us wait a little, and we shall be with him whom we long for. Nor is the time of separation long, since all in this life, as on a road, are pressing on toward the same lodging; in which one has already halted, another has just come, another is hastening on, but one end will receive them all. For even if he halted upon the road sooner, yet we shall all journey the same way, and the same resting-place awaits us all. Only let it be granted us, through virtue, to be made like to his purity, that by the guilelessness of our character we may attain the same rest as those who are infants in Christ.
To the wife of Nectarius, a letter of consolation

I was about to keep silent toward your gracious self, reasoning that, just as to an inflamed eye even the gentlest of remedies brings distress, so too to a soul afflicted by heavy grief, even though it bring much comfort, speech somehow seems troublesome when offered in the midst of anguish. But since it came to me that my words would be addressed to a Christian woman, long since trained in divine things and prepared for what is human, I did not think it right to omit what falls to me to do. I know what the inward feelings of mothers are; and when I consider in particular how kind and gentle you are toward all, I reckon how great, in all likelihood, is your pain over what has now happened. You have been bereaved of a child whom, while he lived, all mothers blessed, and prayed that their own might be such; and whom, when he died, they bewailed, as though each had buried her own in the earth. His death became a blow to two countries, both ours and that of the Cilicians. With him fell his great and illustrious family, shaken down as though a prop had been taken away from under it. O encounter with an evil demon, how great a calamity it had the strength to work! O earth, compelled to receive such an affliction! Perhaps even the sun shuddered, if it has any perception, at that grim sight. And what could one say so great as the helplessness of the soul suggests?

But our affairs are not unforeseen by Providence, since we have learned in the Gospel that not even a sparrow falls without the will of our Father. So if anything has come to pass, it has come to pass by the will of Him who created us. And who has resisted the will of God? Let us accept what has befallen; for by being impatient we neither set right what has happened, and we destroy ourselves besides. Let us not accuse the just judgment of God. We are too ignorant to test His unspeakable decrees. Now the Lord takes proof of your love toward Him. Now is the time present for you, through endurance, to receive the portion of the martyrs. The mother of the Maccabees saw the death of seven children and did not groan, nor did she shed an ignoble tear, but giving thanks to God because she saw them set free by fire and sword and the most cruel torments from the bonds of the flesh, she was judged of good repute before God and renowned among men. Great is the affliction, I too say; but great also are the rewards laid up from the Lord for those who endure.

When you became a mother and saw your child and gave thanks to God, you knew assuredly that, being mortal, you had given birth to one mortal. What, then, is strange, if the mortal has died? But it grieves us that it is untimely. It is uncertain whether it was not timely, since we do not know how to choose what is profitable for our souls, nor to set fixed terms to human life. Look around at the whole world in which you dwell, and consider that all things seen are mortal and all subject to corruption. Look up to heaven: this too will one day be dissolved. Look to the sun: not even this will endure. The stars all together, the creatures of land and water, the beauties about the earth, the earth itself—all are corruptible, all a little later will not be. Let the thought of these things be a consolation for what has happened. Do not measure the affliction by itself, for so it will appear unbearable to you; but comparing it with all human things, you will find from this its consolation. And above all I have this strong word to say: spare your husband. Be a consolation to each other. Do not make the calamity harder for him by consuming yourself in grief. On the whole, I do not think that words suffice for comfort, but I hold that there is need of prayer for the present circumstances. I pray, then, that the Lord Himself, touching your heart by His unspeakable power, may make light in your soul through good thoughts, so that you may have from within yourself the sources of consolation.
To Gregory, his friend

Even then I was not unaware, when I wrote to your wisdom, that every utterance about God is less than the thought of the speaker, and less than the desire of the seeker, since speech is by nature too weak to serve the things conceived in the mind. If, then, our thought is weak, and our tongue weaker than our thought, what could we expect from what was said, but to be charged with poverty of words? Yet not on this account was it possible to pass over in silence what was sought. For there is a danger of betrayal in not readily rendering answers about God to those who love the Lord. Those things, then—whether they seem to be sufficient, or whether they need some more exact addition—require their own occasion for correction.

But for the present we exhort you, as indeed we have already exhorted, to give yourself wholly to the advocacy of the truth, and to those impulses which arise in your mind from God toward the establishment of the good, being content with these and seeking nothing further from us—we who, being far less than is supposed, by our own weakness rather harm the argument than add any strength to the truth through our advocacy.
To the Caesareans, an apology for his withdrawal, and concerning the faith

I have often wondered what you have felt toward us, and whence comes so great an attachment to our littleness—small and slight and having perhaps nothing lovable about it—that you urge us with words, reminding us of friendship and fatherland, as though trying with a father's tenderness to turn back to yourselves certain exiles. As for my having become an exile, I confess it and do not deny it; but you will now learn the reason, since you long to hear it.

Above all, struck at that time by the unexpected, like those suddenly dismayed by abrupt noises, I did not keep hold of my reasonings, but fled far away into exile, and I lodged for a considerable time apart from you. Then, too, a certain longing crept over me for the divine doctrines and for the philosophy that concerns them. For how, I said, could I master the wickedness that dwells with me? Who would become my Laban, freeing me from Esau and leading me as a guide to the highest philosophy? But since, with God's help, I have attained my aim as far as I am able, having found a chosen vessel and a deep well—I mean the mouth of Christ, Gregory—grant us, I beg, grant us a little time. We ask this, not because we cherish a sojourn in the cities; for it has not escaped us that the evil one contrives his deceit for men through such things; but because we judge the company of the saints to be especially profitable. For in saying something about the divine doctrines and in hearing it more frequently, we acquire a settled habit of contemplation hard to lose. Such, then, is our case.

But you, my divine and most beloved of all heads, guard yourselves against the shepherds of the Philistines, lest any of them, unnoticed, stop up your wells and muddy the purity of the knowledge that concerns the faith. For this is always their care: not to teach the more guileless souls from the divine Scriptures, but to corrupt the truth by wisdom from outside. For the man who brings into our faith the ingenerate and the generate, who lays it down as doctrine that He who always is once was not, and that He who is by nature and always Father became a Father, and that the Holy Spirit is not eternal—is he not openly a Philistine, grudging the sheep of our patriarch, so that they may not drink from the pure water that leaps up unto eternal life, but may draw to themselves the oracle of the prophet: "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that can hold no water"—when one ought to confess God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, as the divine words and those who have understood them more loftily have taught?

To those who slander us with the charge of tritheism, let this be said: that we confess one God, not in number, but in nature. For everything that is called one in number is not really one, nor simple in nature; but God is confessed by all to be simple and uncompounded. Therefore God is not one in number. What I mean is this. We say the world is one in number, but not one in nature, nor indeed simple; for we divide it into the elements of which it is composed, into fire and water and air and earth. Again, man is named one in number; for we often speak of one man. But he is not simple, being composed of body and soul. Likewise too we will call an angel one in number, but not one in nature nor simple; for we conceive the substance of the angel as a hypostasis together with sanctification. If, then, everything that is one in number is not one in nature, and what is one in nature and simple is not one in number, while we say that God is one in nature, how do they bring number in upon us, when we altogether banish it from that blessed and intelligible nature? For number belongs to quantity, and quantity is yoked to bodily nature; for number belongs to bodily nature. And we have believed our Lord to be the Maker of bodies. Therefore every number signifies those things which have been allotted a material and circumscribed nature, while the monad and the unit are significant of the simple and incomprehensible substance. Whoever, then, confesses the Son of God or the Holy Spirit to be a number or a creature, unwittingly introduces a material and circumscribed nature. And by circumscribed I mean not only what is contained by place, but also what He who is about to bring it from non-being into being has comprehended in His foreknowledge, and what it is possible to comprehend by knowledge. Everything holy, then, which has a circumscribed nature and has its holiness as something acquired, is not incapable of receiving evil. But the Son and the Holy Spirit are a fountain of sanctification, by which the whole rational creation is sanctified in proportion to its virtue.

Yet we, according to the true account, say that the Son is neither like nor unlike the Father. For each of these is equally impossible. For likeness and unlikeness are spoken of according to qualities; and the divine is free of quality. But confessing identity of nature, we accept the consubstantial and flee the composite, since God and Father, who is God by His essence, has begotten the Son, who is God by His essence; for from this the consubstantial is shown. For He who is God by His essence is consubstantial with Him who is God by His essence.

But since man too is called god, as in "I said, you are gods," and the demon is called god, as in "The gods of the nations are demons"—yet the former are so named by grace, the latter falsely—God alone is God by His essence. And when I say "alone," I mean the holy and uncreated essence of God. For "alone" is said both of a particular man and of nature simply, in the universal sense: of a particular man, as, for example, of Paul, that he alone was caught up to the third heaven and heard unspeakable words that are not lawful for a man to utter; and of nature in the universal sense, as when David says, "Man, his days are as grass." For here he means not the particular man, but the universal nature; for every man is temporary and mortal. So too we understand those sayings spoken of nature: "Who alone has immortality," and "To the only wise God," and "No one is good except one, God" (for here "one" means the same as "alone"), and "Who alone stretched out the heaven," and again, "You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve," and "There is no God besides me." For "one" and "alone," said of God in Scripture, are not said in contradistinction to the Son or the Holy Spirit, but against those who are not gods but are falsely so named; as in "The Lord alone led them, and there was no foreign god with them," and "The sons of Israel removed the Baalim and the groves of Astaroth, and served the Lord alone," and again Paul: "As there are many gods and many lords, yet to us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things."

But here we inquire how, having said "one God," he was not content with the word (for we said that "alone" and "one," of God, signify the nature), but added "Father" and made mention of Christ. I suspect, then, that Paul, the chosen vessel, thought it not sufficient now to proclaim the Son God and the Holy Spirit God—which he showed by the phrase "one God"—unless he should also, by the addition of "Father," signify Him from whom are all things, and by the mention of "Lord" indicate the Word through whom are all things; and again, by the inclusion of "Jesus Christ," announce the incarnation and present the passion and make manifest the resurrection. For "Jesus Christ" brings such thoughts before us. Therefore before the passion the Lord forbids that He be proclaimed Jesus Christ, and charges the disciples to tell no one that He is Jesus the Christ. For it is His purpose, when He has fulfilled the dispensation, after the resurrection from the dead and the ascension into heaven, to permit them to proclaim Him as Jesus the Christ. Such too is the saying, "That they may know you the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent," and "Believe in God, and believe in me"; the Holy Spirit everywhere securing our thought, that we may not, by approaching the one, fall away from the other, and, attending to the theology, despise the dispensation, and so impiety arise in us through what is lacking.

But the words of the divine Scripture which the adversaries take and distort according to their own conscience, bringing them forward to us for the overthrow of the glory of the Only-Begotten, let us examine thus, unfolding their sense as far as we are able. And first let there be set before us, "I live because of the Father"; for this is one of the arrows shot at heaven by those who use it impiously. Here the saying does not, I think, name His pre-eternal life (for everything that lives because of another cannot be Life itself, just as what is warmed by another cannot be Heat itself; but Christ our God has said, "I am the Life"), but this life lived in the flesh and in this time, which He lived because of the Father. For by His will He sojourned in the life of men; and He did not say, "I lived because of the Father," but "I live because of the Father," clearly indicating the present time. And He can also call "life" that which Christ gives, having the Word of God in Himself. And that this is what is meant, we shall know from what follows. "And he who eats me," He says, "shall live because of me"; for we eat His flesh and drink His blood, becoming partakers, through the incarnation and the perceptible life, of the Word and of wisdom. For He named His whole mystical sojourn flesh and blood, and indicated the teaching composed of the practical, the natural, and the theological, by which the soul is nourished and prepared for the contemplation of beings for the time being. And this is perhaps what is indicated by the saying.

And again, "My Father is greater than I"; for the ungrateful creatures, the offspring of the evil one, use this saying too. But I have believed that from this very utterance it is shown that the Son is consubstantial with the Father. For I know that comparisons are properly made between things of the same nature. For we call one angel greater than another, and one man more just than another, and one bird swifter than another. If, then, comparisons are made between things of the same kind, and the Father is said by comparison to be greater than the Son, the Son is consubstantial with the Father. But there is also another thought laid up in the saying. For what wonder is it if He confessed the Father greater than Himself, being the Word and having become flesh, when He was seen to be less than angels in glory and than men in form? For "You have made him a little lower than the angels," He says; and again, "Him who was made a little lower than the angels"; and, "We saw him, and he had no form nor beauty, but his form was lacking beyond all men." All these things He endured because of His great love for mankind toward His own creation, that He might rescue the lost sheep and unite the one saved, and might bring back again, healthy, to his own fatherland the man who had gone down from Jerusalem to Jericho and on that account had fallen among robbers.

Or will the heretic reproach Him also with the manger, in which, being without speech, He was nourished by the Word? And will he bring forward His poverty, that the carpenter's son had no abundance even of a bed? On this account is the Son less than the Father, because for your sake He became dead, that He might free you from deadness and make you a partaker of heavenly life?—just as if one should also blame the physician, because, stooping over the sicknesses, he shares in the foul odour, that he may heal the afflicted.

For your sake too He is ignorant of the hour and the day of judgment; and yet nothing escapes the wisdom that truly is, for all things came into being through it, and no man is ever ignorant of what he has made. But He dispenses this because of your weakness, so that neither may those who have sinned, through the narrowness of the appointed time, fall into despondency, as though no time were left for repentance; nor again may those who war long against the opposing power desert their post because of the length of time. He dispenses for both, then, by His feigned ignorance: for the one cutting short the time because of the noble contest, and for the other reserving a season for repentance because of his sins. And yet, having in the Gospels numbered Himself among the ignorant because of the weakness of the many, as I said, in the Acts of the Apostles, conversing privately with them as with perfect ones, He says, with Himself excepted, "It is not for you to know times or seasons which the Father has set in His own authority."

And let these things be said in a coarser way, according to the first attempt. But now we must examine the sense of the saying more loftily, and knock at the door of knowledge, if somehow I might be able to rouse the householder, who gives spiritual loaves to those who ask Him, since they are friends and brothers whom we are eager to feast.

The holy disciples of our Saviour, having come beyond contemplation, as far as is possible for men, and having been purified by the Word, seek the end and long to know the ultimate blessedness, which our Lord declared that even His angels and He Himself are ignorant of; calling "day" the whole exact apprehension of the thoughts of God, and "hour" the contemplation of the unity and the monad, the knowledge of which He assigned to the Father alone. I suspect, then, that God is said to know that concerning Himself which is, and not to know that which is not. For God is said to know justice and wisdom, being Himself absolute justice and wisdom, but to be ignorant of injustice and wickedness; for God who created us is not injustice and wickedness. If, then, God is said to know that concerning Himself which is, and not to know that which is not (and our Lord, according to the conception of the incarnation and the coarser teaching, is not the ultimate object of desire), then our Saviour does not know the end and the ultimate blessedness. But neither do the angels know it, He says; that is, neither the contemplation in them nor the principles of their ministries are the ultimate object of desire. For the knowledge of these too is coarse in comparison with the face-to-face vision.

But the Father alone knows, He says, since He Himself is the end and the ultimate blessedness. For when we no longer recognize God in mirrors nor through other things, but approach Him as the one and only, then we shall know the ultimate end. For they say that all material knowledge is the kingdom of Christ, but the immaterial—and, as one might say, the contemplation of the Godhead itself—is the kingdom of God and the Father. And our Lord Himself too is the end and the ultimate blessedness, according to the conception of the Word. For what does He say in the Gospel? "And I will raise him up on the last day"; calling "resurrection" the passage from material knowledge to immaterial contemplation, and naming this knowledge "the last day," after which there is no other. For then our mind rises up and is roused to a blessed height, whenever it contemplates the unity and the monad of the Word.

But since our mind, coarsened, has been bound to the dust and is mingled with the clay and is unable to gaze upon contemplation bare, being led by the orderings akin to its own body, it perceives the activities of the Creator and recognizes Him for the time being from His effects, that thus, increased little by little, it may at length be strong enough to approach the very Godhead unveiled. According to this conception, I think, are said both "My Father is greater than I" and "It is not mine to give, but to those for whom it has been prepared by My Father." For this too is what is meant by Christ's delivering the kingdom to God and the Father, being a beginning and not an end, according to the coarser teaching, as I said, which is contemplated with reference to us and not with reference to the Son Himself. And that this is so, again, when the disciples in the Acts of the Apostles asked, "When will you restore the kingdom to Israel?", He says, "It is not yours to know times or seasons which the Father has set in His own authority"—that is, the knowledge of such a kingdom does not belong to those bound to flesh and blood.

For this contemplation the Father has laid up in His own authority; calling "authority" those over whom He has authority, and "His own" those who are not held by ignorance of the lower things. And do not understand "times" and "seasons" to mean perceptible ones, but certain intervals of knowledge produced by the intelligible sun. For that prayer of our Master must be brought to its end; for it is Jesus who prayed, "Grant to them that they also may be one in us, as I and you are one, Father." For God, being one, coming to be in each, unites them all; and number is destroyed by the sojourn of the monad.

Thus I have set upon the saying according to a second attempt. But if anyone should say something better, or piously correct our words, let him both say it and correct it, and the Lord will repay him on our behalf. For no envy lodges with us, since it was neither for the sake of contention nor of vainglory that we proceeded to this examination of the words, but for the benefit of the brethren, so that the earthen vessels which hold the treasure of God may not seem to be cheated by the stony-hearted and uncircumcised men, armed with foolish wisdom.

Again, through the wise Solomon in the Proverbs He is created: "The Lord," he says, "created me." And He is named the beginning of the evangelical ways that lead us to the kingdom of heaven—not a creature according to essence, but having become a way according to the dispensation. For "to have become" and "to have been created" signify the same thing. For as He became a way, and a door, and a shepherd, and an angel, and a sheep, and again a high priest and an apostle, the names being applied under different conceptions.

What, again, would the heretic say about the God who is unsubjected and who became sin for our sake? For it is written, "When all things shall be subjected to Him, then shall the Son Himself also be subjected to Him who subjected all things to Him." Do you not fear, man, that God is named unsubjected? For He makes your subjection His own, and in your striving against virtue He names Himself unsubjected. So too He once said that He Himself was the one persecuted; for "Saul," He says, "Saul, why do you persecute me?"—when he was running to Damascus, wishing to bind together the disciples of Christ. And again He names Himself naked, when one of the brethren is naked; for "I was naked," He says, "and you clothed me." And when another is in prison, He said that He Himself was the one imprisoned. For He Himself bore our weaknesses and carried our diseases. And one of the weaknesses is also insubordination, and this too He bore. Therefore the Lord makes our circumstances His own, taking up our sufferings out of His fellowship with us.

But the heretics take also "The Son can do nothing of Himself" for the ruin of those who hear them. To me, however, this saying too especially proclaims that the Son is of the same nature as the Father. For if each of the rational creatures can do something of itself, having free will, with its inclination toward the worse and toward the better, but the Son cannot do anything of Himself, the Son is not a creature. And if not a creature, He is consubstantial with the Father. And again, none of the creatures can do all that it wishes. But the Son, in heaven and on earth, did all that He wished. Therefore the Son is not a creature. And again, all creatures are either composed of opposites or capable of receiving opposites. But the Son is absolute justice and is immaterial. Therefore the Son is not a creature. And if not this, He is consubstantial with the Father.

And this examination of the cited sayings is sufficient for us, according to our ability. But now let us proceed in argument against those who set themselves against the Holy Spirit also, casting down every high thought of theirs that exalts itself against the knowledge of God. You say the Holy Spirit is a creature. But every creature is a servant of the Creator; for "all things," it says, "are your servants." And if it is a servant, it has its holiness as something acquired; and everything that has its holiness as something acquired is not incapable of receiving evil. But the Holy Spirit, being holy by His essence, has been named a fountain of sanctification. Therefore the Holy Spirit is not a creature. And if not a creature, He is consubstantial with God. But how can you call Him a servant, tell me, who through baptism frees you from servitude? For "the law," it says, "of the Spirit of life has freed me from the law of sin." But neither will you ever dare to call His essence changeable, looking to the nature of the opposing power, which has fallen like lightning from heaven and fell away from true life because it had its holiness as something acquired and change followed upon its evil purpose. Therefore, having fallen from the monad and cast away the angelic dignity, from his manner he was named the devil, his former and blessed state being quenched, and this opposing power kindled.

Then, if he calls the Holy Spirit a creature, he introduces a limited nature for Him. How, then, will "The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world" stand, and "Where shall I go from your Spirit?" But neither does he confess Him, as it seems, to be simple in nature. For he names Him one in number. But everything that is one in number is not simple, as I said. And if the Holy Spirit is not simple, He is composed of essence and sanctification; and such a thing is composite. And who is so foolish as to call the Holy Spirit composite, and not simple, and by the principle of simplicity consubstantial with the Father and the Son?

But if we must advance in the argument and behold the greater things, from this especially let us contemplate the divine power of the Holy Spirit. We have found three creations named in Scripture: one, the first, the bringing forth from non-being into being; a second, the change from the worse to the better; and a third, the raising of the dead. In these you will find the Holy Spirit working together with the Father and the Son. For there is the bringing into substance of the heavens. And what does David say? "By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of His mouth all their power." Again, man is created through baptism, for "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation." And what does the Saviour say to His disciples? "Go and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." You see here too the Holy Spirit present together with the Father and the Son. And what would you say also about the resurrection of the dead, when we shall fail and return to our dust? For "We are earth, and to the earth we shall depart," and "He will send forth the Holy Spirit, and He will create us, and He will renew the face of the earth." For what the holy Paul called resurrection, this David named renewal.

And let us hear again him who was caught up to the third heaven. What does he say? That "You are a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you." But every temple is a temple of God. And if we are a temple of the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit is God. And the temple of Solomon is also so called, but as of one who built it. And if in this way we are a temple of the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit is God, for "He who built all things is God." But if as of one worshipped and dwelling in us, let us confess that He is God. For "You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve." And if they object to the word "God," let them learn of what this name is significant. For God is named either from having placed all things or from beholding all things. If, then, "God" is said from having placed or from beholding all things, and the Spirit knows all the things of God, as the spirit in us knows our own things, then the Holy Spirit is God.

And again, if the sword of the Spirit is the word of God, the Holy Spirit is God; for the sword belongs to Him whose word it is also called. And if He is also named the right hand of the Father (for "The right hand of the Lord has wrought power," and "Your right hand, O Lord, has shattered the enemies"), and the Holy Spirit is the finger of God, according to the saying, "If I by the finger of God cast out demons"—which in another Gospel is written, "If I by the Spirit of God cast out demons"—then the Holy Spirit is of the same nature as the Father and the Son.

And about the adorable and holy Trinity let so much be said by us for the present; for it is not now possible to examine the argument concerning it more fully. But you, having received seeds from our lowliness, cultivate for yourselves a ripe ear of grain, since, as you know, we are required to render the interest on such things. And I trust in God that you will bear fruit thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold, because of the purity of your life. For "Blessed," it says, "are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." And do not think the kingdom of heaven to be anything else, brothers, than the true apprehension of beings, which the divine Scriptures also call blessedness. For "The kingdom of heaven is within you." And about the inner man nothing else is constituted but contemplation. The kingdom of heaven, then, would be contemplation. For of the things whose shadows we now behold, as in a mirror, later, freed from this earthly body and clothed with the incorruptible and immortal, we shall behold the archetypes. And we shall behold them, if at least we steer our own life toward what is right and make provision for the right faith, without which no one shall see the Lord. For "Into an ill-contriving soul," it says, "wisdom will not enter, nor dwell in a body subject to sin." And let no one object, saying that, ignorant of the things at our feet, you philosophize to us about the incorporeal and wholly immaterial essence. For I judge it absurd to let the senses be filled without hindrance with their own materials, while the mind alone is barred from its proper activity. For as sense reaches the perceptibles, so the mind reaches the intelligibles.

And at the same time this too must be said, that God who created us has made the natural faculties of judgment require no teaching. For no one teaches the sight to apprehend colours or shapes, nor the hearing sounds and voices, nor the smell fragrant and foul vapours, nor the taste juices and flavours, nor the touch soft and hard things, or hot and cold. Nor would anyone teach the mind to reach the intelligibles. And just as, if these senses suffer anything, they need only care, and easily fulfil their proper activity, so too the mind, bound to flesh and filled with the imaginings from it, needs faith and a right way of life, which make its feet like a deer's and set it upon the heights. This very thing the wise Solomon enjoins, and sometimes brings before us the unashamed worker, the ant, and through it sketches for us the practical way; and sometimes the wax-moulded instrument of the wise bee, and through it hints at natural contemplation, in which the account of the holy Trinity too is mingled, since from the beauty of creatures the Author of their being is contemplated by analogy.
But having given thanks to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, let us set an end to the letter, since every measure is best, as the proverb says.
To Maximus the philosopher

Words are truly the images of souls. We have come to know you, then, through your letter, as the saying goes, the lion from his claws; and we were glad to find you not idly disposed toward the first and greatest of goods, love toward God and toward one's neighbour. As a sign of the one we take your kindness toward us, and of the other, your zeal for knowledge. And that the whole consists in these two is plain to every disciple of Christ.

The writings of Dionysius which you seek came to us, indeed, and very many of them; but the books are not at hand, and for that reason we have not sent them. We are of this mind, however: we do not admire everything in the man; there are some things which we wholly reject. For of nearly this very impiety now so much noised abroad—I mean that of the "Unlike"—this man, so far as we know, is the first to have furnished the seeds to men. The cause, I think, was not wickedness of judgment, but his vehement wish to oppose Sabellius. I am accustomed, then, to liken him to a gardener straightening the distortion of a young plant, who then, by the excess of his counter-pull, misses the middle and draws the shoot to the opposite side. We have found something of the kind to have happened with this man too. For setting himself vehemently against the impiety of the Libyan, he was carried unawares, by his excessive zeal, into the opposite evil. For him it would have been enough to show that the Father and the Son are not the same in subject, and thus to have the victory over the blasphemer; but he, in order to prevail very clearly and abundantly, lays down not only a distinction of the hypostases, but also a difference of essence, a diminution of power, and a variation of glory. So it came about from this that he exchanged one evil for another and missed the rightness of doctrine. For this very reason he is of all kinds in his writings, now overthrowing the consubstantial, because of the man who had used it ill for the abolition of the hypostases, and now admitting it in the passages where he defends himself to his namesake. And besides this, concerning the Spirit too he let fall utterances least befitting the Spirit, banishing Him from the adored Godhead and numbering Him somewhere below with the created and ministering nature. Such, then, is the man.

But I, if I must speak my own view, accept the phrase "like in essence," if it has joined to it "without difference," as bringing us to the same as the consubstantial, according, of course, to the sound understanding of the consubstantial. This too the fathers at Nicaea understood, when, calling the Only-Begotten "Light from Light" and "true God from true God" and the like, they consequently added the consubstantial. For it is not possible to conceive any variation of light to light, nor of truth to truth, nor of the essence of the Only-Begotten to that of the Father. If, then, anyone takes it as I have said, I admit the phrase. But if anyone cuts off the "without difference" from "like"—as those at Constantinople have done—I suspect the word as belittling the glory of the Only-Begotten. For we are accustomed to conceive "likeness" often even in faint resemblances that fall far short of their archetypes. Since, then, I think the consubstantial is less liable to be misused, I too adopt it.

But why do you not visit us, my excellent friend, so that, being present with one another, we might discuss such matters together, and not entrust things of such moment to lifeless letters—especially when we have resolved not to make our views very public? So that you may not yourself say to us what Diogenes said to Alexander, that the distance from you to here is the same as from here to you. For we, by reason of our infirmity, are nearly always held, like plants, in the same place; and at the same time, having lived in obscurity, we count it among the first of goods. But you are strong, as they say, and at the same time, having made yourself a citizen of the world, you would do rightly to visit here too, as a part of your own country. For even if assemblies and cities befit you practical men, in which you display your deeds of virtue, yet for contemplation and the activity of the mind, by which we are joined to God, stillness is a good fellow-worker; and this we cultivate in abundance and without stint in our retreat, with the help, one may say, of God Himself who has granted it to us. But if you must by all means cling to the seats of power and despise us who lie on the ground, then at least write to us, and by this make us the gladder.
To a widow

There is a certain art of catching doves, of this kind. When those who busy themselves with such things have gained control of a single dove, and have made it tame and a sharer of their food, they then anoint its wings with perfume and let it mingle with those outside. The fragrance of that perfume makes that free flock a possession for the owner of the tame one; for the rest, drawn by the sweet scent, follow it and settle down with it.

But with what intent do I begin my letter from this? Because, having taken my son Dionysius, once called Diomedes, and anointed the wings of his soul with the divine perfume, I have sent him forth to your reverend self, so that you too may fly up together with him and reach the nest which the aforesaid has built among us. If, then, I should see these things in my lifetime, and your reverend self brought over to the lofty life, I shall need many persons worthy of God to fulfil for Him the honour that is owed.
Without address, on friendship

Having by the grace of God spent the holy day together with our children, and having truly kept a perfect feast to the Lord because of their surpassing love toward God, we have sent them forward in health to your nobility, praying to the God who loves mankind that to them too may be given a peaceful angel as helper and fellow-traveller, and that you may be reached by them in health and in every peaceful condition; so that, wherever you may be, serving the Lord and giving thanks to Him, you may gladden us, while we are in the world, as we hear of your affairs. And if the holy God should grant you to be freed sooner from these cares, we entreat you to prefer nothing to a stay among us. For I think you will not find any who so love you and lay claim to the friendship that is among you. So long, then, as the Holy One ordains this separation, deign on every occasion to console us with letters.
To Olympius

Formerly you wrote us little; now you write not even a little; and it seems that your brevity, advancing with time, is becoming complete silence. Return, then, to your custom, since we will no longer blame you for being laconic toward us in your letters; but even your short letters, being tokens of your great affection, we shall count as worth much. Only write to us.
To Olympius
Just as each of the other things in season comes at its proper season—in spring the flowers, in summer the ears of grain, in autumn the apple—so the fruit of winter is letters.
To Gregory, his friend

When my brother Gregory wrote to me that you had long wished to meet us, and added that this same thing had been resolved by you as well, I—partly because I am reluctant to believe, having often been deceived, and partly because I was distracted by occupations—was unable to wait. For I must now depart for Pontus, where perhaps at last, God willing, we shall put an end to our wandering. For at length, having given up the vain hopes I once had in you—or rather the dreams, if one must speak more truly, for I praise the man who said that hopes are the waking dreams of those who sleep—I went off to Pontus in search of a way of life. There indeed God has shown me a place exactly suited to my disposition, so that I see in reality such a thing as we often, in idleness and play, are accustomed to fashion in the mind.

For there is a high mountain covered with deep forest, watered toward the north by cold and clear streams. At its foot a level plain is spread out, continually made fertile by the moisture from the mountain. A forest of varied and all kinds of trees, growing of itself around it, becomes almost a fence to it, so that even the island of Calypso, which Homer plainly admired above all others for beauty, is small in comparison. For indeed it falls little short of being an island, since it is hedged about with defences on every side: deep ravines have broken away from it on two sides, and along its flank the river, flowing down from a cliff, is itself a wall, continuous and hard to cross; while on the other side the mountain, stretched out and joined to the ravines by crescent-shaped bends, walls off the approaches of the foot of the hill. There is one entrance to it, of which we are masters. And the dwelling itself a certain other ridge receives, holding up a lofty crest at its summit, so that the plain is spread out beneath the eyes from it, and from on high one may behold the river flowing around—affording, to my mind, no less delight than to those who look at the Strymon from Amphipolis. For the one, spreading into a lake with its more leisurely current, has almost been deprived even of being a river by its stillness; but the other, flowing the swiftest of any rivers I know, is for a little roughened by the neighbouring rock, from which it pours back and is wound into a deep eddy, affording a sight most pleasant to me and to every beholder, and a most ample resource to the people of the place, since it nourishes an untold multitude of fish in its eddies.

What need is there to tell of the exhalations from the earth, or the breezes from the river? The multitude of flowers, or of singing birds, another might admire; but I have no leisure to give my mind to these things. The greatest thing we can say of the place, however, is that, though suited by the favourableness of its situation to every kind of produce, it nourishes for me, the sweetest of all fruits, stillness; not only because it is free from the tumults of the town, but because it sends no traveller our way except those who mingle with us in hunting. For besides everything else it is also a nurse of game—not of bears or of wolves, your kind (God forbid), but it feeds herds of deer and wild goats and hares, and whatever is like these.

Do you not think, then, what danger I, the foolish one, was in, when I contended to exchange for such a place Tiberina, that pit of the inhabited world? You will pardon me, then, for now hastening toward it. For surely not even Alcmaeon, when he had found the Echinades, could endure his wandering any longer.
To Arcadius, count of the privy purse

The citizens of our metropolis have given a greater favour than they received, in furnishing me with the occasion for this letter to your honoured self. For the kindness on account of which they received the letter from us was theirs even before our letter, because of the habitual and natural gentleness that dwells in you toward all.

But we have counted it the greatest gain to have the occasion of addressing your inimitable nobility, praying to the holy God that, as you advance in your pleasing of Him and grow yet greater in the distinction that surrounds you, we ourselves may rejoice and share the gladness of those benefited by your governance; and that one day too those who deliver our letter to you may meet a gentle reception, and be sent away with all the rest, themselves also extolling your meekness, having learned forever that our embassy on their behalf to your unsurpassable nobility has not been useless to them.
Against Eunomius the heretic

The man who says that the discovery of beings is attainable has, of course, by some method and sequence, set his mind to range through the knowledge of beings; and, having trained himself by apprehension on the things that are easy to grasp and smaller, has thus advanced himself even to the apprehensive impression of what is beyond all conception.

Let him, then, who boasts that he has grasped the knowledge of beings explain what nature the smallest of the things that appear has, and let him tell what the nature of the ant is: whether its life is sustained by breath and respiration; whether its body is divided by bones; whether its frame is held together by sinews and ligaments; whether the position of the sinews is governed by an enveloping of muscles and glands; whether the marrow extends along the spinal vertebrae from the crown to the tail; whether, by the surrounding of the sinewy membrane, it gives the power of impulse to the moving limbs; whether there is in it a liver, and a gall-bladder upon the liver, and kidneys and heart and arteries and veins, membranes and diaphragms; whether it is smooth or covered with hair; whether it is single-hoofed, or has feet divided into many parts; how long a time it lives, and what is their manner of generation from one another; for how long the offspring is carried; and how it is that the ants are neither all on foot nor all winged, but some belong to those that go upon the ground, while others are borne through the air.

Let him, then, who vaunts the knowledge of beings first tell the nature of the ant; and then let him give the natural philosophy of the power that surpasses all mind. But if you have not yet grasped by knowledge the nature of the tiny ant, how do you boast that you can imagine the incomprehensible power of God?
To Origenes

Both heard, you gladden us, and read, through what you write, you afford us more vivid joys. And much thanks to the good God, who has allowed the truth to be in no way diminished by the betrayal of those who, supposedly, hold the upper hand, but has fulfilled the advocacy of the word of godliness through you. They, then, like hemlock or aconite, or any other man-slaying herb, having flowered for a little while, will quickly wither away; but to you the Lord will grant a reward, blooming and ever new, for the things spoken on behalf of His name.

In return for which may the Lord also grant you every prosperity of house, and pass on the blessing to your children's children. And your most noble children, the clear stamps of your goodness, I saw with pleasure and embraced, and I pray for them whatever their father himself would pray.
To Macarius and John

Neither do the toils of farming come strange to farmers, nor is the storm at sea unexpected to sailors, nor sweat surprising to those who labour for wages; nor, indeed, are the afflictions of the present world unforeseen by those who have chosen to live in godliness. But to each of those mentioned a toil of its own, familiar to those who pursue it, is yoked—not to be chosen for its own sake, but for the enjoyment of the goods that are expected. For hopes, which hold together and sustain the whole life of men, console the difficulty in each of these.

Of those, then, who labour for the fruits above the earth or those upon the earth, some have been wholly deceived in their hopes, having the enjoyment of what they expected only as far as imagination; while to those for whom it has befallen that the end turned out according to their wish, a second hope was again needed, the former having run past and quickly withered. But for those alone who have toiled for godliness, no falsehood has destroyed their hopes, no end has ruined their contests, since the kingdom of heaven, sure and lasting, succeeds them.

Let no false slander, then, disturb you, nor let the threat of those in power frighten you; let not the laughter and insult of acquaintances grieve you, nor the censure of those who pretend to care, who put forward, as the strongest bait for deceit, a pretence of advice—so long as the word of truth contends along with us. Let right reason fight against all these, calling to become its ally and helper the teacher of godliness, our Lord Jesus Christ, for whom even to suffer is sweet and to die is gain.
To Gregory, his friend

A letter came to me the other day from you, exactly yours, not so much by the character of the hand as by the peculiar quality of the letter. For the words were few, yet they presented much thought. To these we did not at once reply, because we ourselves were away from home, and the letter-carrier, having handed the letter to one of our friends, went off and departed. But now, through Peter, we address you, at once paying off the debt of greeting, and at the same time furnishing an occasion for a second letter. And surely there is no toil in a laconic letter, such as those are which come to us from you on every occasion.
To Leontius the sophist

Slow in coming are our letters to you, yet not slower than yours from there, and that when many people have come to us continually from your part of the world; if to all of these in turn you had entrusted letters, there would have been nothing to keep you from supposing that we were with you and, as it were, present and together enjoyed your company—so continuous was the throng of those reaching us.

But why do you not write? And yet there is no labour for a sophist except to write; or rather, even if your hand is at leisure, you will not even need to write, for another will serve you. There is need only of the tongue; and even if it does not converse with us, it will at any rate speak to someone of those present, and even if no one is present, it will discourse with itself; but be silent it will by no means, being sophistic and Attic, no more than the nightingales when spring rouses them to song.

For us, indeed, this constant press of business in which we now are might perhaps bring some excuse for our lack of letters; and the fact that we have, as it were, grown soiled by long disuse, sinking toward common speech, naturally makes us reluctant to address you sophists, who, unless you hear something worthy of your own wisdom, will be displeased and will not endure it. But for you, surely, the opposite is likely: to make your voice public on every occasion, being well able to speak, of all the Greeks I myself know. For I know, as I think, the most renowned among you. So there is no excuse for keeping silent. And so much for this.

I have sent also the work against Eunomius; whether one should call it play, or something a little more serious than play, I leave you yourself to judge. For your own purposes I think you no longer have need of it; but against those who turn the readers astray, I expect it will be to you no ignoble weapon—not so much trusting in the power of the composition, but knowing exactly that from few starting-points you are inventive toward many. And if anything in it appears to you weaker than the need requires, do not shrink from correcting it. For in this above all a friend differs from a flatterer: that the one converses to give pleasure, while the other does not abstain even from what is painful.
To Leontius the sophist

The worthy Julian seems to share something of the common state in his own affairs as well. For he too is dunned and severely charged, since everything now is full of dunnings and charges. Only that what is in arrears with him is not contributions, but letters. And yet whence he has fallen behind I do not know; for he always gave a letter and received one. Unless perhaps with you too that much-talked-of quadruple penalty is held in higher honour. For not even the Pythagoreans honoured the tetrad so much as those who now collect the public revenues honour the quadruple. And yet perhaps the opposite would be reasonable: that you, being a sophist and well supplied with so many words, should be the one liable to pay us the fourfold. And do not think that we write this out of vexation. For I rejoice even in your reproaches, since they say that to the good all things come with the addition of the good, so that even griefs and angers become them. At any rate one would more gladly see the man he loves angry, than another man fawning. So never cease bringing such charges. For these very charges will be letters, and to me no sound is more precious, nor brings greater pleasure.
On the perfection of the life of monks

Since many are the things made plain by the inspired Scripture which ought to be rightly accomplished by those who are eager to please God, I have been compelled, for the present, to set down in a brief reminder, concerning only those matters which were just now raised among you, what I have learned from the inspired Scripture itself; leaving the testimony for each point, which is easy to take, for those occupied in reading to recognize, who will be able to remind others also.

That the Christian ought to think thoughts worthy of the heavenly calling, and to conduct himself worthily of the Gospel of Christ. That the Christian ought not to be lifted up, nor drawn away by anything from the remembrance of God and of His wishes and judgments. That the Christian, having become in all things superior to the justifications of the law, ought neither to swear nor to lie. That he ought not to blaspheme; that he ought not to insult. That he ought not to fight; that he ought not to avenge himself; that he ought not to render evil for evil; that he ought not to be angry. That he ought to be long-suffering, whatever he suffers, and to reprove the wrongdoer at the right time, not in the passion of his own vengeance, but in the desire for his brother's correction, according to the commandment of the Lord. That he ought not to say anything against an absent brother with the aim of slandering him, which is detraction, even if what is said be true. That he ought to turn away from one who slanders a brother.

That he ought not to utter witticisms. That he ought not to laugh, nor to put up with those who make others laugh. That he ought not to talk idly, saying anything that is neither for the benefit of the hearers nor for the necessary use granted us by God; so that those who work should be eager, as far as possible, to work in stillness, and that those entrusted, after testing, with the dispensing of the word should themselves direct good words toward the workers, for the building up of the faith, that the Holy Spirit of God be not grieved. That none of those who come in by authority ought to approach or speak to any of the brothers, before those appointed to the care of good order in all things have judged how it pleases God for the common good. That he ought not to be enslaved to wine, nor to be passionate about meat, and in general not to be a lover of pleasure regarding any food or drink; for he who contends exercises self-control in all things. That of the things given to each for use, he ought to hold or hoard nothing as his own; yet in his care he should attend to all things as the Master's, overlooking nothing of what is cast aside or neglected, should it so happen. That no one ought to be his own master, but, as one handed over by God into servitude to the brothers of like soul, he should so both think and do all things, each in his own order.
