That he ought not to murmur, neither in the scarcity of things needful nor in the toil of labours, since those appointed have the authority of judgment concerning each. That there ought to be no outcry, nor any other gesture or motion by which anger is shown, or distraction from the full assurance of the presence of God. That he ought to measure his voice to the need. That he ought not to answer anyone boldly or contemptuously, or to do anything so, but in all things to show gentleness and respect toward all. That he ought not to wink with the eye in guile, or to use any other gesture or motion of a limb which grieves a brother or shows contempt.

That he ought not to adorn himself in garments or sandals, which is vanity. That he ought to use cheap things for the body's need. That he ought to spend nothing beyond the need and for lavishness, which is misuse. That he ought not to seek honour, or to lay claim to the first places. That each ought to prefer all others to himself. That he ought not to be insubordinate. That he who is able to work ought not to eat idle, but even one occupied with some of the things accomplished for the glory of Christ should force himself to the zeal of the work within his power. That each ought, by the approval of those set over him, with reason and full assurance, so to do all things, even down to eating and drinking, as done for the glory of God. That he ought not to pass from one work to another without the approval of those appointed to direct such things, except where some unavoidable necessity should suddenly call him to the aid of one who has failed. That each ought to remain in that to which he was appointed, and not, overstepping his own measure, encroach upon things not appointed to him, unless those entrusted with these matters should judge that someone needs help. That no one ought to be found going from one workshop to another. That he ought not to do anything out of contentiousness or strife with anyone.

That he ought not to envy another's good repute, nor rejoice over anyone's shortcomings. That he ought, in the love of Christ, to grieve and be crushed over a brother's shortcomings, and to rejoice over his good deeds. That he ought not to be indifferent toward those who sin, or to keep silent over them. That he who reproves ought to reprove with all tenderness, in the fear of God and with the aim of turning back the sinner. That he who is reproved or rebuked ought to receive it readily, recognizing his own benefit in the correction. That, when one is accused by another, he ought not, in the presence of that man or of any others, to contradict the accuser; but if ever the accusation should appear unreasonable to someone, let him raise the matter privately with the accuser, and either give satisfaction or be satisfied.

That each ought, as far as he is able, to attend to the one who has anything against him. That he ought not to bear a grudge against one who has sinned and repented, but to forgive him from the heart. That he who says he repents of a sin ought not only to be pricked in conscience for what he sinned, but also to produce fruits worthy of repentance. That he who has been chastised for his first sins and been deemed worthy of forgiveness, if he sins again, prepares for himself a worse judgment of wrath than the former. That he who, after the first and second admonition, persists in his fault ought to be made known to the one set over him, in case, being rebuked by more, he may be put to shame. And if not even thus he is corrected, he is to be cut off henceforth like a scandal, and to be regarded as a heathen and a tax-collector, for the security of those who carry on the zeal of obedience, according to what is said, "When the impious fall, the righteous become fearful." And one ought also to mourn over him, as over a limb cut off from the body.

That the sun ought not to set upon a brother's provocation, lest the night come between the two and leave behind, on the day of judgment, an inexcusable charge. That he ought not to await an occasion for his own correction, since he has no security concerning the morrow, for many, having planned many things, did not reach the morrow. That he ought not to be deceived by the filling of the belly, through which come nocturnal fancies. That he ought not to be distracted into immoderate labour and overstep the bounds of self-sufficiency, according to the apostle who said, "Having food and covering, with these we shall be content"; since superfluity beyond the need shows an image of greed, and greed bears the verdict of idolatry. That he ought not to be a lover of money, nor to store up for useless ends what he ought not. That he who draws near to God ought to embrace possessionlessness in all things, and to be nailed to the fear of God, according to him who said, "Nail down my flesh with fear of you; for I have feared because of your judgments."

And may the Lord grant that you, having received with all full assurance what has been said, may show forth, for the glory of God, fruits worthy of the Spirit, by the good pleasure of God and the co-working of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
A letter of commendation to a monk

The bearer, as he says, having condemned the vanity of this life and learned that the delights of this present life have their downfall here, providing only fuel for the eternal fire and having a swift passage, has come to me, wishing to depart from this wretched and much-groaning life, to leave behind the pleasures of the flesh, and henceforth to set out upon the road that leads to the mansions of the Lord. Since, then, it is necessary—if he is indeed by nature set in desire for the truly blessed manner of life, and has within his own soul the good and praiseworthy love, having loved the Lord our God with all his heart, with all his strength, and with all his mind—that there be shown to him by your godliness the things hard and difficult to meet in the narrow and afflicted way, and that he be established in the hope of the goods not now seen for the present, but laid up in the promises for those worthy of the Lord.

Therefore I write and exhort your incomparable perfection in Christ to give him his form, if it be possible, and to accomplish even without me both his renunciation in a manner pleasing to God, and his grounding according to what has seemed good to the holy fathers and has been set down by them in writing; and that there be set before him already all that seems good to ascetic exactness, and that thus he be brought to the life, having of his own free choice taken up the contests on behalf of godliness, and submitted himself to the kindly yoke of the Lord, and lived in imitation of Him who for our sake became poor and bore flesh, and having run, according to the goal, toward the prize of the upward calling, may obtain acceptance from the Lord. For when he was eager here to receive the crown of the love that is according to God, I deferred it, wishing, together with your godliness, to anoint him for such contests, and to set over him as trainer one of you whom he may himself ask for—one who trains him well and makes him a proven wrestler through diligent and blessed care, wounding and overthrowing the world-ruler of the darkness of this age and the spiritual hosts of wickedness, against which, according to the blessed apostle, is our struggle. What, then, I wished to do together with you, let your love in Christ do even without me.
To Athanasius, father of Athanasius the bishop of Ancyra

That to make one's life superior to a man's slanders is among the hardest of things—not to say among the impossible—I myself am persuaded, and I think your goodness does not doubt it. Yet to give no handle from oneself, either to those who closely watch our affairs or to those who lie in wait, out of malice, for our slips—this is both possible and proper to those who lead their own life prudently and according to the aim of godliness. But do not think us so easy or so easily led as to admit, without examination, the disparagements of any chance persons. For we remember the spiritual injunction that bids us not receive an empty report.

But since you yourselves say—you who have studied the art of words—that things visible are signs of things unseen, this we ask (and do not take it amiss if anything be said by us in the form of teaching; for God chose the weak things of the world and the things despised, and through them often accomplishes the salvation of those who are saved): what I mean and enjoin is this—that every word and every fitting action should be carried out with circumspection; and, according to the apostolic injunction, that no offence be given in anything. For I hold it fitting that the life of a man who has sweated much over the learning of words, who has directed the governments of nations and cities, and who has zeal for the great virtue of his ancestors, should be set forth as a model of virtue.

As for your disposition toward your children, you ought not now to show it in word, who have long since shown it from the time you became a father—not only using the natural affection which even the irrational creatures display toward their offspring, as you yourself said and as experience shows, but also heightening your love, plainly from deliberate choice, in proportion as you see them to be such as are worthy of a father's prayers. So that we have no need to be persuaded about these things, for the testimony from the deeds themselves is sufficient.

This, however, it is not unseasonable to add for the sake of the truth: that it is not the brother Timothy, the chorepiscopus, who reported to us the things that were noised abroad. For neither in conversation nor by letter does he appear to have uttered anything, small or great, touching slander concerning you. So that we do not deny having heard something, but it is not Timothy who contrives the slanders against you. And hearing it, we shall at all events, if nothing else, do at least what Alexander did, and keep one of our ears uncorrupted in reserve for the one slandered.
To Athanasius, bishop of Ancyra

Some of those who have come to us from Ancyra have reported to me—and these are many, not easy even to number, yet all speaking in agreement—that you, the dear head (how could I put it kindly?), do not remember us as pleasantly as may be, nor in your own manner. But nothing human astonishes me, be assured, nor is the change of any of all men unexpected to me, since I learned long ago the weakness of our nature and its readiness to be overturned toward the contrary. Hence neither, if anything of ours has changed, and instead of the former honour there now come reproaches and insults upon us, do I make much of this. But that did appear to me truly strange and beyond nature: that you should be one so disposed toward us as to be angry with us and to be harsh, and even now to threaten somewhat, as the report of those who heard goes.

At the threats, indeed, I laughed outright (for the truth shall be told). Surely I would be wholly a child, to fear such bugbears. But this seemed to me both fearful and worthy of much concern: that your exactness, which we have believed to be preserved among the few as a prop of rightness and a seed of the ancient and true love, for the comfort of the churches, should so far share in the present state of things as to make the blasphemies of chance persons of more authority than our long experience, and to be led, without proofs, to the suspicion of absurd things. And yet why do I say "suspicion"? For one who has been indignant and has uttered threats, as they say, seems to have shown the anger not of one who suspects, but of one already clearly and irrefutably persuaded.

But, as I said, we refer the cause to this present time; since how great a labour was it, my admirable friend, in a short letter to discuss, as it were, alone with one alone, the matters you wished?—or, if you did not trust such things to writing, to summon me to yourself? But if by all means it had to be spoken, and the ungovernableness of your anger gave no time for delay, yet you might surely have used as the minister of your words to us some one of your intimates who is by nature able to keep secrets. But as it is, whose ears have not been filled, of those who visit you on any sort of business, with the report that we write and compose certain ruinous things? For this is the word they say you used, those who recount your words verbatim. And though I have led my own mind over many possibilities, it does not in the least release me from my perplexity.

So that something of this kind too came to me: whether one of the heretics, having maliciously inscribed my name upon his own writings, grieved your rightness and led you to let fall that utterance. For surely it is not for the things written by us against those who dared to call the Son unlike in essence, and God to God and Father, or against those who blasphemed that the Holy Spirit is a creature and a thing made, that you would have endured to bring this reproach upon us—you who carried through those great and far-famed contests on behalf of orthodoxy. You yourself would resolve our perplexity, if you would openly declare the things that moved you to grief against us.
To Caesarius, brother of Gregory.

Thanks be to God, who has displayed his own wonders in you also, and has rescued you out of so great a death, restoring you both to your country and to us, your kinsmen. It remains, then, for us not to be found ungrateful, nor unworthy of so great a benefit, but, according to our ability, to proclaim the marvels of God, and to celebrate in song that love for humanity of which we have had experience in deed, and to render thanks not in word alone, but to become also in deed such men as we are now persuaded we ought to be, judging from the wonders worked in your case.

And we exhort you to serve God yet more fully, ever increasing your reverence by fresh additions and advancing toward perfection, so that we may be shown to be wise stewards of our life, for which the goodness of God has kept us in reserve. For if it is a command laid upon all of us to present ourselves to God as men alive from the dead, how much more does this hold for those who have been lifted up from the very gates of death? And this, I am persuaded, would best be accomplished if we were willing always to keep the same mind that we had at the moment of our danger. For surely there came home to us then the emptiness of life, and how nothing human is trustworthy or secure, since all things are so easily subject to reversal. And surely there arose in us, as was natural, some repentance for what had gone before, and a promise concerning what should follow, that, if we were preserved, we would serve God and attend to ourselves with all exactness. For if the peril of death pressing upon us gave us any thought at all, I suppose that you reasoned then on these very things, or very near to them.

And so we have come to stand answerable for the payment of a necessary debt. With these things in mind — at once overjoyed at the gift of God, and at once anxious about the things to come — I have taken courage to remind your perfection. And it is for you to receive our words kindly and gently, as was your custom also in our conversations face to face.
To Eusebius, bishop of Samosata.

When, by the grace of God and the help of your prayers, I seemed to be recovering a little from my illness and to be gathering up my strength again, then the winter set in, shutting me up at home and forcing me to keep within the district. For though it came on much milder than usual, it was nevertheless enough to hinder me — not only from travelling through it, but even from being able to put out a little way beyond my room.

Yet this too is no small thing for me, to be counted worthy to converse by letter with your reverence, and already to find rest beforehand in the hope of your replies. And if the season would allow it, and some span of life were still left to us, and the famine did not make the road impassable for us, then quickly, through your prayers, would we attain our desire; and overtaking you at your hearth, we would, at full leisure, take our fill of the great treasures of the wisdom that is in you.
To the church of Neocaesarea, in consolation.

What had befallen demanded our own presence, both that we might join with you, his nearest kin, in rendering the honour due to the blessed man, and that, from the very sight of those in mourning, we might share in the dejection occasioned by the loss, and that we might take part with you in your necessary deliberations. But since many things hindered our bodily presence, it remained for us to share with you, by letter, in what has come to pass.

Now the wonders of the man — on whose account above all we reckon our loss to be past bearing — no measure of a letter could contain; and in any case it is untimely to bring forward a discourse upon the multitude of his noble deeds when our soul has so collapsed beneath grief. For which of his deeds is of such a kind that it would be fitting either to let it fall from our memory or to pass it over in silence? To tell them all at once, in a single stroke, is impossible; and to tell them in part, I fear, would carry a betrayal of the truth. There has departed from us a man who, most conspicuously of all in his own time, surpassed all human goods together — a support of his country, an ornament of the churches, a pillar and ground of the truth, a stay of faith in Christ, a security to his own, most hard to fight against for his adversaries, a guardian of the laws of the fathers, an enemy of innovation; showing in himself the ancient form of the Church, and shaping the appearance of the church under him after the model of the ancient order, as from some sacred and venerable image, so that those who lived with him seemed to have lived with the men who shone forth like luminaries two hundred years ago and more.

Thus the man brought forward nothing of his own, nothing that was the discovery of a more recent mind, but, according to the blessing of Moses, he knew how to bring forth from the inner shrine of his heart, out of good treasures, old things and old, and old things from before the face of the new. For this reason also he was deemed worthy of precedence in the assemblies of his peers, not according to his age, but he stood above them all by the antiquity of his wisdom, reaping the first place by common consent. How great is the gain of such a training, no one would inquire who looks to you. For you alone, of those we know — or at most among very few — have, through his steering, led a life unshaken in so great a storm and tempest of affairs. For the squall of heretical spirits never touched you, that brings drownings and shipwrecks upon souls easily overturned. And may it never touch you, O Master of all things, who to your servant Gregory, who from the beginning laid the foundation of the Church, gave the grace of an untroubled calm reaching over the longest time.

Do not you betray that grace in the present moment; nor, by immoderate lamentation and by giving yourselves over to grief, surrender the seasons of what is necessary to those who lie in wait. But if you must by all means lament — though indeed I say you must not, that we may not in this be made like those who have no hope — yet, if it seems good to you, like some mourning chorus setting your leader at your head, weep over what has befallen more tunefully, in concert with him.

And yet, even if the man had not been driven to extreme old age, still, for the length of his oversight over you, he was not wanting in years of life. And of his body he partook only so far as to show through it the endurance of his soul amid his sufferings. But perhaps one of you might suppose that time too is an increase of fellow-feeling and an addition of affection, not an occasion of satiety to those who have had the experience, so that, the longer the time in which you have known his benefaction, the more keenly you feel his loss. Yet to the devout even the shadow of a righteous body is worth the whole. And may there be many of you of this mind. For neither do I myself say that one ought to be indifferent toward the man, but I counsel you to bear the grief in human measure; since whatever can be said by those who bewail the loss does not escape even me.

The tongue is silent that flooded the ears like rivers; and the depth of his heart, for now grasped by no one, has flown away, departing, weaker than dreams so far as men are concerned. Who was keener than he to foresee the future? Who, in so steady and firm a temper of soul, was able to come upon affairs quicker than lightning? O city, already overtaken by many sufferings, yet by none so wounded in the very vitals of your life! Now has the fairest ornament withered away from you; the church is shut up, the festivals are gloomy, the sacred council longs for its chief; the mystical words await their expounder, the children their father, the elders their contemporary, the magistrates their leader, the people their patron, those in need of sustenance their nourisher; all calling upon him by the names dearest to them, each over his own grief raises a lament of his own and proper to himself.

But where is my discourse carried away by the pleasure of weeping? Shall we not sober ourselves? Shall we not become our own again? Shall we not look to the common Master, who, having entrusted each of the saints to serve his own generation, has called them back again to himself at the fitting times? Now is the time to remember his words, who, in addressing you in assembly, always charged you, saying, Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers. Many are the dogs. Why do I say dogs? Rather they are grievous wolves, hiding their treachery under the appearance of sheep, who everywhere throughout the world tear apart the flock of Christ. Against these you must be on guard, under the oversight of some watchful shepherd. Him it is yours to ask, keeping your souls pure of all contentiousness and love of pre-eminence, and the Lord's to appoint — who, from the great patron of your church, Gregory, down to this blessed man, by adding ever one upon another and fitting them together, as from some joining of precious stones, has bestowed upon your church a beauty wonderful to behold. So that one must not despair of those to come. For the Lord knows those who are his, and would bring into your midst those whom we, perhaps, do not expect.

Long now have I wished to make an end of speaking, but the pain of my heart does not permit it. Yet I charge you, by the fathers, by the right faith, by this blessed man, to rouse up your soul, each one judging the common concern to be his own, and reckoning that he himself will be the first to reap the outcome, whichever way affairs turn; and not, as happens with the many, to thrust off the care of common things upon his neighbour, and then, with each one slighting affairs in his own thought, that all should, unawares, draw down upon themselves a private evil through their negligence.

These things, whether as the sympathy of neighbours, or as the fellowship of those who share the same faith, or — what is truer — of those who obey the law of love and shun the danger that comes of keeping silent, receive with all goodwill, being persuaded that you are our boast, as we are yours, in the day of the Lord; and that, by the shepherd who shall be given to you, we shall either be the more united in the bond of love, or else come to complete separation — which may it not be, nor shall it be, by the grace of God, nor would I myself now utter anything of ill omen. But this we wish you to know, that even though we did not have the blessed man as one running together with us toward the peace of the churches — owing to certain prejudices, as he himself assured us — yet, in our agreement of faith with him and in his always calling us a partner in the struggles against the heretics, we never, with God as witness and with the men who have had experience of us, at any time fell short.
To the church of Ancyra, in consolation.

The shock of the most grievous tidings of the evil that has befallen imposed upon us a long silence. But now that we have somewhat recovered from the speechlessness which we suffered — like men struck dumb in their hearing by a great thunderclap — we have of necessity groaned over what has happened, and, lamenting all the while, have sent forth this letter to you; not for the sake of consolation (for what word could be found to heal so great a calamity?), but to signify to you by this voice, as far as we are able, the pain of our heart. Now I had need of the laments of Jeremiah, or of any other of the blessed men who, with feeling, bewailed the magnitude of a calamity.

A man has fallen who was truly a pillar and ground of the Church; or rather, he himself, lifted up to the blessed life, has departed from us; but the danger is not small that many, when this support has been taken from under them, may fall together with it, and the unsoundness of some be laid bare. There is closed a mouth of righteous boldness, teeming with words of grace for the building up of the brotherhood. Gone are the counsels of a mind that was truly moved in God. Oh, how many times — for I will accuse myself — it came over me to be vexed at the man, that, having become wholly given to the desire to depart and to be with Christ, he did not, for our sake, prefer to remain in the flesh. Upon whom, now, are we to lay off the cares of the churches? Whom shall we take as a partner in our griefs? Whom as a sharer of our gladness? Oh, the dreadful and gloomy desolation indeed! How exactly have we been made like a pelican of the wilderness!

But surely the members of the Church that were joined together — as it were by a single soul, his oversight, fitted into one fellow-feeling and exact communion — are kept firmly, through the bond of peace, in their spiritual jointure, and will be kept so forever; God granting that the works of that blessed soul, all that he contended for on behalf of the churches of God, abide steadfast and unmoved. Yet the struggle is not small, lest again certain rivalries and dissensions, kindled over the choice of the one who is to preside, should overturn all the labour together through some chance quarrel.
To Eusebius, bishop of Samosata.

If I were to write out one after another all the reasons by which I have been held back up to the present, eager though I am to come to your reverence, I should fill out the length of an endless history. The successive illnesses, the harshness of the winter, the press of affairs — these I forbear to mention, since they are known and have already been declared to your perfection. But now I have been deprived even of my mother, the one consolation I had in life — and this too taken from me because of my sins. And do not laugh at me as though, at this age, I were bewailing an orphan's lot; but pardon me if I cannot endure with composure the parting from a soul whose equal I see in none of those left to me. So again my ailments have returned to me, and again I lie upon my bed, tossing upon strength altogether small, and all but expecting, with every hour, the necessary end of life.

And the churches are in nearly the same condition as my body — no good hope showing itself anywhere, while affairs ever slide away toward the worse. Yet for now Neocaesarea and Ancyra have seemed to have successors to those who have departed, and up to this moment they are at rest. But neither have those who plot against us been permitted, up to the present, to do anything worthy of their anger and bitterness; and the cause of this we plainly ascribe to your embassies on behalf of the churches. Therefore do not grow weary in praying for the churches and in entreating God. Give my warmest greetings to those who have been counted worthy to minister to your holiness.
To Eusebius, bishop of Samosata.

The famine has not yet released us, and so a stay in the city is necessary for us, whether for the sake of administration or out of sympathy with the afflicted. For this reason I was unable even now to share the road with our most reverend brother Hypatius — whom I call brother not merely for the sake of a courteous title, but because of the kinship that belongs to us by nature; for we are of the same blood.

What manner of sickness he labours under has not escaped even your honour. And it grieves us that every hope of relief has been cut off for him, since those who possess the gifts of healing have not been permitted to do for him any of the things that are customary. For this reason he again calls upon the help of your prayers. And do you be entreated to give him your accustomed support, both for the sake of your own compassion toward the sick and for our sake, who plead on his behalf; and, if it be possible, to summon to yourself the most devout of the brethren, so that the treatment may be applied to him under your own eyes. But if this be impossible, then deign to send him on his way with a letter and to commend him to those before him.
To Sophronius, the magister.

Our most God-beloved brother Gregory the bishop is also having his share of these times; for he too, along with all the rest, is in distress, struck by insult upon insult as by so many unexpected blows. For men who do not fear God — driven on, perhaps, by the very magnitude of the troubles — assail him with the charge that he received money from Caesarius.

And it is not the weight of the loss that troubles him, for long ago he learned to despise money; but that, having received only the merest trifle of Caesarius's estate — because his property fell into the hands of servants and of men no better in character than servants, who with great licence divided among themselves the most valuable things and kept back for these others scarcely anything at all — the little they kept, supposing it to be liable to no claim, they at once spent upon the needy, both of their own choice and at the bidding of the departed. For he is said to have said this as he was dying, that I wish all that is mine to become the property of the poor. So, as ministers of Caesarius's command, they at once administered it profitably. And now the upshot is the poverty of a Christian and the meddlesome zeal of one of the men of the market-place. For this reason it has occurred to me to make it known to your wholly praiseworthy nobility, so that you may at once honour the man, whom you have known of old, and glorify the Lord, who takes upon himself what is done to his servants, and honour us, who are your own particular friends; and that you may speak to the Count of the Treasury about him as is fitting, and devise a way, by your great sagacity, for him to be rid of these insolent and intolerable annoyances.

For surely no one is so ignorant of the man as to suppose anything unbecoming of him — that he is feigning all this out of attachment to money. For close at hand is the proof of his liberality: he gladly gives up to the treasury the remnants of his estate, so that his property may be received, while the advocate of the treasury answers those who fasten upon him and demand the receipts, on account of our own unfitness for such matters. For your perfection may learn that, as long as it was possible, no one went away having failed of what he wished, but each obtained without trouble what he sought, so that many even regretted that they had not asked for more from the start. And this above all has made the assailants many; for, looking to the example of those who went before, one after another succeeds in bringing false charges.

Against all this, then, we entreat your dignity to stand firm, and, as it were, to check some flood and cut short the continuity of these evils. And you know how to aid the matter, so that you need not wait to be taught the manner by us, who, through our inexperience of the affairs of life, are ignorant of this very thing — how relief might come to us. Be yourself, then, both counsellor and protector, finding out the form of help through your own great prudence.
To Aburgius.

And who knows how to honour an old friendship, to reverence virtue, and to feel grief along with those who suffer, as you yourself do? Since, then, troubles have overtaken our most God-beloved brother Gregory the bishop — troubles not otherwise to be borne, and most of all contrary to his character — it has seemed to us best to take refuge in your protection, and to try to find from you some release from his misfortunes. For it is an intolerable misfortune that a man neither fitted for it nor willing should be compelled to plead lawsuits, that a poor man should be dunned for money, and that one who long ago resolved to pass his life in quiet should be dragged into the public eye and made the object of demagoguery. Whether, then, you judge it useful to speak with the Count of the Treasury, or with certain others, will be for your sagacity to decide.
To Eusebius, bishop of Samosata.

How could we keep silent in the present circumstances? Or, if we cannot endure to do so, how could we find any adequate word for what is happening, so that our voice should not be like a mere groan, but like a lament that sufficiently signifies the weight of the evil? Tarsus too is lost to us. And this is not the only dreadful thing, intolerable as it is; for there is something harder still than this — that so great a city, so favourably situated as to join together by itself the Isaurians and Cilicians, the Cappadocians and the Syrians, should become an incidental casualty of the madness of one or two men, while you delay and deliberate and look to one another. The best course, then — after the device of the physicians (and surely I have a great abundance of such examples, owing to the sickness that dwells with me), who, when the magnitude of the pain grows excessive, contrive for the patient an insensibility to his sufferings — is for our own souls, that they may not be held fast by unbearable pains, to pray together for an insensibility to these evils. Yet, wretchedly off as we are, we have one consolation: to look to your gentleness, and from the thought and remembrance of you to soothe the grieving part of our soul. For just as it brings the eyes some relief, when they have gazed intently upon bright things, to turn back to dark and verdant colours, so to our souls the memory of your gentleness and good measure is, as it were, a gentle touch that takes away the pain; and most of all when we reflect that you have done everything that lay in your power. By this you have sufficiently shown to us men also — if we judge matters fairly — that nothing has perished through any fault of yours, and you have won for yourself with God a great reward for your zeal in good things. And may the Lord grant you to us and to his own churches, for the benefit of life and the correction of our souls, and may he count us worthy once again of your profitable company.
Without address, on behalf of Leontius.

I have written to you about many matters as being of concern to me, and I shall write to you about still more. For it is impossible that those in need should fail, nor is it possible for us to refuse them the favour. Yet there is no one nearer to me, nor more able to give me rest by any kindness shown to him, than our most reverend brother Leontius. Deal with his household, then, as you would if you found me myself — not in this poverty in which I now am, with God's help, but having come into some prosperity and possessed of fields. For it is clear that you would not have made me a poor man, but would have preserved what I had, or even increased my means. This, then, we entreat you to do in the case of the man's household of which I have spoken. And your reward for all this is the usual one from me: a prayer to the holy God for the labours you undertake, since you are honourable and good, and forestall the requests of those in need.
Without address, concerning assistance.

The presbyter of this place has long, I think, been known to your nobility as one brought up together with me. What else, then, need I say to shame your kindness into looking upon him as your own and helping him in his affairs? For if you love me — as indeed you do — it is plain that you are also disposed to give rest, with all your power, to those whom I hold in my own stead. What, then, is it that I ask? That the old assessment be preserved for him. For he labours not a little in ministering to my livelihood, since I, as you yourself know, possess nothing of my own, but make do with what belongs to my friends and kinsmen. As you would regard my house, then — or rather your own — so regard the house of this brother; and in return for your kindness to him, God will grant to you, and to your house, and to all your family, his accustomed help. And know that it is a matter of great care to me that the man should suffer no injury from the reassessment.
Without address, on behalf of a foster-brother.

I look now with some misgiving on the multitude of my letters. Under compulsion, and unable to bear the burdensomeness of those who press their demands upon me, I am forced to speak out; yet I write nonetheless, having no other way to find relief than to give them the letters they ask of us at every turn. I am afraid, then, that, since many bring forward letters, this brother too may be reckoned as one of the many. For I confess that I have many friends and kinsmen in my native country, and that I myself have been placed in the rank of a father, on account of this office to which the Lord has appointed us. But this one I have as a foster-brother, a son of the woman who nursed me, and I pray that the house in which I was reared may remain in its same condition, so that the sojourn of your orderly self, which benefits all, may not become to the man any occasion for grief. But since even now I am still maintained from that same house, having nothing of my own and content with what belongs to those dear to me, I beg you so to spare the household in which I was reared as to preserve for me the provision of my sustenance. And may God in return count you worthy of eternal rest.

This, however, as the truest thing of all, I wish your orderly self to know: that most of his slaves came to him from us, as the wage of our upkeep, our parents having provided them. And the wage is not an outright gift, but a use for the term of life. So that, if any burden arises concerning them, he is free to send them back to us, and we shall, by another road, again become liable to the taxes and the collectors.
To his brother Gregory, on the difference between essence and hypostasis.

Since many, in dealing with the mystical doctrines, do not distinguish what is common to the essence from the account of the hypostases, and so fall into the same confusion of thought, and suppose that it makes no difference whether one speaks of "essence" or "hypostasis" — whence it has seemed good to some of those who accept such things without examination to say that, as there is one essence, so there is also one hypostasis; and conversely, those who admit three hypostases suppose that they must, on the strength of this admission, lay down a division of essences in the same number — for this reason, that you too may not suffer the like, I have made for you a brief memorandum on the subject. The sense of what is being said is, to set it forth in few words, as follows.

Of all names, some, being applied to many things differing in number, have a more general signification, as for instance "man." For he who utters this word, indicating by the name the common nature, does not circumscribe by the utterance any particular man who is known individually by the name. For Peter is no more a man than is Andrew, or John, or James. The commonness, then, of what is signified, extending alike to all who are ranged under the same name, has need of a further distinction, by which we shall recognize not man in general, but Peter or John.

Other names have a more particular indication, by which it is not the commonness of the nature that is contemplated in what is signified, but the circumscription of some particular thing, having no fellowship, in respect of its individuality, with what is of the same kind — as for instance "Paul" or "Timothy." For such an utterance is no longer borne toward the common element of the nature, but, separating it off from the comprehensive signification, presents through the names the impression of certain circumscribed things. When, therefore, there are two or more men of the same kind together — say Paul and Silvanus and Timothy — and an account of the essence of the men is sought, no one will give one account of the essence in the case of Paul, another in the case of Silvanus, and another in the case of Timothy; but the very terms by which the essence of Paul is shown will fit the others also; and those who are described by the same account of essence are of one essence with one another. But when, having learned the common element, one turns his contemplation toward the particulars by which one is distinguished from the other, then the account that makes each one known will no longer agree in all respects with the account of the other, even though in some points it be found to hold the common element.

This, then, is what we say: that what is spoken of individually is indicated by the term "hypostasis." For he who says "man" has, by the indefiniteness of the signification, produced in the hearer a certain scattered notion, so that the nature is indicated by the name, but the subsisting thing, individually indicated by the name, is not signified. But he who says "Paul" has shown the nature subsisting in the thing indicated by the name.

This, then, is the hypostasis: not the indefinite notion of the essence, which finds no fixity from the commonness of what is signified, but that which presents and circumscribes, in a particular thing, the common and uncircumscribed element through the properties that appear in it; as the Scripture also is wont to do such a thing, in many other places, and in the history of Job. For when it was about to recount his affairs, having first mentioned the common element and said "a man," it at once marks him off by his individuality with the addition of "a certain." But the description of the essence, as bringing no gain toward the present aim of the discourse, it passed over in silence; and it characterizes the particular man by his own distinguishing marks, naming his place and the marks of his character, and whatever of external things, brought in along with these, served to separate and set him apart from the common signification — so that through all these the description of the man recorded should become vivid: from his name, from his place, from the properties of his soul, from the external things observed about him. For had it given the account of the essence, there would have been no mention of any of these things in the interpretation of the nature; for the account would have been the same as in the case of Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite, and each of the men mentioned there.

The account of the difference, then, between essence and hypostasis which you have learned in matters concerning ourselves, transferring it also to the divine doctrines, you will not go astray. Whatever your notion supposes the being of the Father to be — for there is no defined concept upon which to fix the soul, because of our conviction that it is above all concept — this you will conceive also of the Son, and this likewise of the Holy Spirit. For the account of the uncreated and the incomprehensible is one and the same in the case of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. For the one is not more incomprehensible and uncreated, the other less. And since it is necessary, through the individual marks, to hold the distinction within the Trinity unconfused, what is contemplated in common — I mean, for instance, the uncreated, or what is above all comprehension, or anything of the kind — we shall not bring in to determine the individuality, but we shall seek only those things by which the notion of each is set apart clearly and unmixed from what is contemplated together with it.

It seems to me good, then, to trace out the matter thus. Whatever good reaches us from the divine power, we say is the working of the grace that works all things in all; as the Apostle says, that "all these things works one and the same Spirit, dividing to each individually as he wills." But when we inquire whether the supply of good things, taking its origin from the Holy Spirit alone, thus comes to those who are worthy, we are again guided by the Scripture to believe that the Author and Cause of the supply of the good things wrought in us through the Spirit is the Only-begotten God. For we have been taught by holy Scripture that all things came into being through him, and have their consistence in him. When, therefore, we are lifted up also to that conception, again, led up by the divinely inspired guidance, we are taught that through that power all things are brought from non-being into being — yet not from that power without a beginning either; but there is a certain power subsisting unbegotten and without beginning, which is the cause of the cause of all things that are. For from the Father is the Son, through whom are all things, with whom the Holy Spirit is always inseparably conceived. For it is not possible to come into a thought of the Son without being first illumined by the Spirit. Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit, from whom all the supply of good things to the creation flows as from a fountain, is dependent upon the Son, with whom it is apprehended without interval, and has its being attached to the cause of the Father, from whom also it proceeds — this it has as the distinguishing mark of its individuality in respect of hypostasis: to be made known after the Son and together with him, and to subsist from the Father.

But the Son, who makes known through himself and with himself the Spirit that proceeds from the Father, alone shining forth as Only-begotten from the unbegotten Light, has, in the individuality of his distinguishing marks, no fellowship either with the Father or with the Holy Spirit, but is made known alone by the marks that have been named. And the God who is over all has, as the special distinguishing mark of his own hypostasis, this alone: to be Father, and to subsist from no cause; and through this mark again he too is recognized in his individuality. For this reason we say that the marks contemplated in the Trinity, by which the individuality of the persons handed down in the faith is presented, are, within the commonness of the essence, incompatible and uncommunicable — each one being apprehended distinctly by his own marks — so that through the said marks the separateness of the hypostases is discovered. But in respect of the infinite, the incomprehensible, the being uncreated, the being circumscribed by no place, and all things of this kind, there is no variation in the life-giving nature — I mean in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit — but there is contemplated in them a certain continuous and unbroken fellowship. And by whatever notions one may comprehend the majesty of any one of those believed in the Holy Trinity, by those same notions he will proceed, without variation, beholding the glory in Father and Son and Holy Spirit, the mind treading no void interval between Father and Son and Holy Spirit. For there is nothing inserted between them, neither any other subsisting thing besides the divine nature, such as to be able to divide it from itself by the intrusion of something foreign, nor the emptiness of any subsistenceless interval that should make the harmony of the divine essence with itself stand gaping, dividing the continuity by the insertion of the void. But he who has conceived the Father has conceived him by himself, and has at the same time admitted the Son into his thought; and he who has grasped the Son has not severed the Spirit from the Son, but has impressed within himself a faith of the three, mingled together — consequently, in respect of order, but conjointly, in respect of nature. And he who has spoken of the Spirit alone has comprehended, in this confession, also him whose the Spirit is. And since the Spirit is Christ's and from God, as Paul says, just as he who takes hold of one end of a chain draws with it the other end also, so he who has drawn the Spirit, as the prophet says, has through it drawn along the Son and the Father together. And if one truly grasps the Son, he will hold him on either side, on the one drawing along his own Father, on the other his own Spirit. For neither can he who is ever in the Father be cut off from the Father, nor will he who works all things in his own Spirit ever be separated from his own Spirit. Likewise too he who has received the Father has received with him, in power, the Son and the Spirit. For it is not possible to conceive a severance or division in any way at all, so that either the Son should be conceived apart from the Father, or the Spirit be disjoined from the Son; but there is apprehended among them a certain ineffable and inconceivable fellowship and at the same time distinction, neither the difference of the hypostases tearing apart the continuity of the nature, nor the commonness in respect of the essence dissolving the individuality of the distinguishing marks. And do not marvel if we say that the same thing is both conjoined and distinguished, and conceive — as it were in a riddle — a new and paradoxical conjoined distinction and distinguished conjunction. For if one would not hear the statement contentiously and with a view to cavil, even among sensible things it is possible to find such a thing.

And receive my account as an illustration and shadow of the truth, not as the very truth of the things themselves; for it is not possible that what is contemplated in illustrations should fit in every respect the things for which the use of the illustrations is taken up. Whence, then, do we say that the distinguished and at the same time conjoined is to be reasoned out from the things that appear before us to the senses? You have at some time, in the spring, beheld the brightness of the bow in the cloud — I mean that bow which common speech is wont to call the rainbow; which those skilled in such matters say is formed when a certain moisture is mingled with the air, the force of the winds pressing the moist and dense element in the vapours, when it has now become cloud-like, into rain. And they say it is formed thus: when the ray of the sun, running aslant beneath the dense and overshadowing mass of cloud, then fixes its own circle straight upon some cloud, there comes about, as it were, a bending and return of the light upon itself, the radiance being dissolved backward from the moist and glistening surface. For since it is the nature of fiery flashings, if they fall upon any smooth surface, to be bent back again upon themselves, and since the shape of the sun is circular, the circle made by the ray in the moist and smooth air must of necessity, in accordance with the shape of the sun's circle, be traced upon the air lying near the cloud by the glistening radiance. This radiance, then, is both continuous with itself and divided. For, being of many colours and many forms, it is imperceptibly blended with itself in the varied hues of its dye, secretly stealing from our eyes the meeting of the differing colours with one another; so that there is no recognizing the place in between that mingles through itself and separates the difference of the hues — the blue from the flame-coloured, or the flame-coloured from the purple, or that from the amber. For the radiances of all of them, seen at the same time, are far-shining, and, stealing away the signs of their conjunction with one another, escape detection, so that it is impossible to find out how far the fiery or the emerald part of the brightness extends, and from what point it begins to be no longer such as it is seen to be in the far-shining whole.

Just as, therefore, in the illustration we clearly distinguish the differences of the colours, and yet it is not possible for the sense to grasp the interval of one from the other, so reckon it possible to reason also concerning the divine doctrines: that the individualities of the hypostases, like some flower of those appearing in the rainbow, flash upon each of those believed in the Holy Trinity; but that, in respect of the individuality of the nature, no difference of one from the other is conceived, and that within the commonness of the essence the distinguishing individualities shine upon each. For there too, in the illustration, the essence that flashed forth that many-coloured radiance was one — that which was reflected through the sun's ray — while the flower of what appeared was of many forms; the discourse teaching us, even through the creation, not to be dismayed at the statements concerning the doctrine when, falling into what is hard to contemplate, we grow dizzy at the assent to what is said. For just as in the case of the things that appear to the eyes the experience proved stronger than the reasoning about the cause, so also, in the case of the doctrines that have risen above us, faith is stronger than the apprehension that comes through reasonings, teaching both what is separate in hypostasis and what is conjoined in the essence. Since, then, the discourse has contemplated something common in the Holy Trinity and something individual, the account of the commonness is referred to the essence, while the hypostasis is the sign of what is individual in each.

But perhaps someone may suppose that the account given of hypostasis does not agree with the sense of the Apostle's writing, where he says concerning the Lord that he is "the radiance of his glory and the express image of his hypostasis." For if we have given out that the hypostasis is the concurrence of the properties about each, and it is agreed that, as in the case of the Father, there is something individually contemplated, by which alone he is recognized, and in the same manner the like is believed concerning the Only-begotten — how is it that here the Scripture testifies the name of "hypostasis" of the Father alone, and calls the Son the form of the hypostasis, characterized not by his own marks but by those of the Father? For if the hypostasis is the sign of what is individual in the existence of each, and it is agreed that what is proper to the Father is to be unbegotten, while the Son has been formed by the properties of the Father, then it no longer remains for the Father to be called, in a special sense and of him alone, "unbegotten," if indeed the existence of the Only-begotten is characterized by what is individual to the Father.

But we say this: that the Apostle's discourse fulfils here another aim, with a view to which he used these expressions, calling him "radiance of the glory" and "express image of the hypostasis." He who has accurately understood this will find nothing at variance with what we have said, but the discourse carried through upon a certain individual notion. For the apostolic discourse is not concerned with how the hypostases may be distinguished from one another through the marks that appear, but with how the genuine, the undivided, and the conjoined character of the Son's relation to the Father may be conceived. For he did not say, "Who being the glory of the Father" — although the truth is indeed so — but, passing this over as agreed, and teaching us not to conceive one kind of glory in the case of the Father and another in the case of the Son, he defines the glory of the Only-begotten to be the radiance of the very glory of the Father, establishing the Son to be conceived together with the Father without interval, from the illustration drawn from light. For as the radiance is from the flame, and yet the radiance is not later than the flame, but at the very moment the flame blazes up the light flashes forth along with it, so he wishes the Son also to be conceived as from the Father, yet not the Only-begotten to be marked off from the existence of the Father by any extension of interval, but ever to apprehend, together with the cause, that which is from it.

In the same manner, then, as if interpreting the meaning already given, he says also "express image of the hypostasis," guiding us by bodily illustrations toward the understanding of things invisible. For as the body is altogether in a shape, yet the account of the shape is one thing and the account of the body another, and one giving the definition of each of these would not bring it into agreement with the account of the other — and yet, even though in discourse you distinguish the shape from the body, the nature does not admit the distinction, but the one is conceived conjointly with the other — so the Apostle thinks it necessary, even though the account of the faith teaches the difference of the hypostases to be unconfused and divided, yet also to present the closeness and, as it were, the connaturality of the Only-begotten to the Father through the words used; not as though the Only-begotten were not in hypostasis, but as not admitting any mean term in his union with the Father; so that he who has gazed with the eyes of the soul upon the express image of the Only-begotten should come also into a thought of the Father's hypostasis, the individuality contemplated in them not being exchanged or mingled together, so as to ascribe begetting to the Father or unbegottenness to the Son, but as though it were not possible, separating the one from the other, to apprehend by itself alone what remains. For it is not possible, when one has named "Son," not to come also into a thought of the Father, this appellation indicating the Father along with him by relation.

Since, therefore, "he who has seen the Son sees the Father," as the Lord says in the Gospels, for this reason he says that the Only-begotten is the express image of the Father's hypostasis. And that the meaning may be still better recognized, we shall take in also other expressions of the Apostle, in which he calls him "image of the invisible God," and again "image of his goodness" — not in that the image differs from the archetype in respect of invisibility and goodness, but that it may be shown to be the same as the prototype, even though it be other. For the account of an image could not be preserved unless it had the clearness and unchangeable likeness throughout. Therefore he who has understood the beauty of the image comes into a thought of the archetype. And he who has taken into his mind, as it were, the form of the Son has impressed upon himself the express image of the Father's hypostasis, beholding through this the Father — not beholding the unbegottenness of the Father in the image (for then it would have been throughout the same and not other), but discerning the unbegotten beauty in the begotten. For just as he who has understood, in a clean mirror, the impression of the form that has come to be in it has had a clear knowledge of the face that was imaged, so he who has recognized the Son has received in his heart, through the knowledge of the Son, the express image of the Father's hypostasis. For all things that are the Father's are seen in the Son, and all things that are the Son's are the Father's, since the whole Son also abides in the Father and again has the whole Father in himself. So that the hypostasis of the Son becomes, as it were, the form and face of the knowledge of the Father; and the hypostasis of the Father is recognized in the form of the Son, the individuality contemplated in them remaining for the clear distinction of the hypostases.
Julian to Basil.

The proverb says, "It is no war you announce"; and I would add, from the comedy, "O you who have announced a golden message of words." Come, then, show it in deed, and hasten to us; for you will come as friend to friend.

The common and continual occupation with affairs seems, indeed, somewhat burdensome to those who make it a secondary matter; but those who share in the responsibility are, as I persuade myself, fair-minded and intelligent, and altogether equal to everything. So I give myself relief, so that it is possible for me, while neglecting nothing, also to be at rest; for we are together with one another not merely with that courtly dissembling — of which I suppose you have had experience up to now, by which, while praising, men hate with a hatred as great as they bear not even to their bitterest enemies — but, with the freedom that befits us, both convicting one another when need be and rebuking, we love one another no less than the closest of comrades. Hence it is possible for us — and may envy be far off — both to be diligent at our ease and, while diligent, not to be wearied, and to sleep without fear, since even when awake I have kept watch not for myself more than for all the rest, as is fitting.

These things, perhaps, I have prated and chattered to you, having suffered a fit of folly — for I have praised myself, like Astydamas — but I have written them in order to persuade you that your presence, as that of a man of sense, will rather be of profit to us than take anything from the season. Hasten, then, as I said, using the public post. And when you have stayed with us as long as is pleasing to you, you shall go on, sent by us, with whatever escort you wish, as is fitting.
Julian to Basil.

Displaying, up to the present, the gentleness and love of mankind that is inborn in me from childhood, I have brought into subjection all who dwell beneath the sun. For lo, every race of barbarians, as far as the bounds of Ocean, has come bringing me gifts at my feet. Likewise also the Sagadares, reared beside the Danube, of strange and many-coloured aspect, like beetles, in whom there is no sight resembling that of human beings, but a savage form — these, in the present circumstances, grovel in my tracks, promising to do for me those things that befit my sovereignty. Nor is it in this alone that I am drawn on, but I must with great speed overtake the land of the Persians and put to flight that Sapor, who has become the descendant of Darius, until he becomes tributary and subject to me; and at the same time lay waste the country round about of the Indians and of the Saracens, until all these too come, in a second rank, to be tributary and subject to me.

But you yourself have thought beyond their power, saying that you are clothed in piety, while putting forward shamelessness; and everywhere proclaiming that I have become unworthy of the empire of the Romans. Do you not yourself know that I have become the descendant of Constantius the mighty? And though these things are thus known to us on your account, we have not departed from our former disposition, in which, while still young in age, both I and you partook. But with a serene mind I decree that ten hundred pounds of gold be sent to me by you on my passage by Caesarea, while I am still upon the highway, coming with great speed to the Persian war; for I am ready, if you do not do this, to demolish every place in Caesarea, and to overthrow the fair works long ago raised up in it, and to set up in their place temples and images, so that I may persuade all to yield to the emperor of the Romans, and not to lift themselves up. The gold named, then, weighing and measuring it out by number, scale, balance, and weight, send to me securely by one of your household who is faithful to you, sealing it with your own ring, so that I, having recognized — even if late, beyond the season — the inexorable thing, may become serene toward you concerning your offences. And what I have read, I have known and condemned.
Basil to Julian, in reply.

Small are the brave deeds of your present fortune, and paltry the prowess of that valour which you yourself have displayed against us — yet not against us, but against yourself. As for me, I am held fast by trembling whenever I take it into my mind that you have been clothed in the purple, and that your dishonoured head has been adorned with a crown, which, apart from piety, renders your sovereignty not honoured but dishonoured. But you yourself, having returned and become exceedingly great — as wretched and beauty-hating demons have dragged you to this — have begun not only to think beyond all human nature, but even to lift yourself up against God, and to insult the Church, the mother and nurse of all, employing a message to me, the most worthless of men, that a thousand pounds of gold be sent to you by me.

And the weight of the gold did not astound my mind, great though it is, but it made me weep bitterly over so swift a ruin of yours. For I have considered within myself that both I myself and your nobility learned together the sacred and best of letters. Each of us went through the holy and divinely inspired Scriptures, and nothing then escaped you; but in the present you have become bereft of order, encamped about by such a temper of mind. You knew us before yesterday, most serene one, that we do not order our lives by greed for money; and now, in the present circumstances, you have demanded that ten hundred pounds of gold be sent to you by us. Be willing, then, to spare us, most serene one — us who possess only so much that, if we should wish to eat today, it will not suffice us. For with us, as is fitting, the art of cooks lies idle, and their knife holds no converse with blood. The greatest of the foods among us, in which our abundance lies, are leaves of herbs with the coarsest bread and sour wine; so that our senses, not being astounded by gluttony, may not order their life in folly.

Lausus too, your distinguished tribune, who is genuine to you in your earnest concerns, reported this to me also: that a certain woman made an appearance before your serenity over the ruin of her child, who had been killed by poisoning, and that it has been judged by you that sorcerers should nowhere exist, but that, where they do exist, they should be put to death — or that those alone should be preserved whose contest is with the beasts. And this, rightly judged by you, has seemed strange to me. For it is full of all laughter, how you undertake to heal the great pains of wounds with little remedies. For, having insulted God, you make in vain provision for widows and orphans. For the one course is mad and perilous, the other belongs to a compassionate and sympathetic man.

It is burdensome for us, who are private men, to speak to an emperor, but more burdensome still will it seem to you to speak to God. For no mediator between God and men will appear. What you have read, however, you have not understood; for had you understood, you would not have condemned . . .
To Chilon, his disciple.

I shall become to you, true brother, the author of a saving work, if you would gladly take counsel from us as to what should be done — most of all concerning those matters about which you yourself entreated us to counsel you. For to begin upon the solitary life has perhaps been ventured by many, but to bring it to a worthy completion has, it may be, been achieved with toil by few. And surely the end lies not in the purpose alone, but in the end is the gain of all the toils. There is, then, no profit for those who do not press on toward the end of the aim, but set up the monastic life only as far as its beginning; nay rather, they leave their own purpose a laughing-stock, charged with unmanliness and lack of resolve by those outside. For the Lord also says concerning such men: "Who, wishing to build a house, does not first sit down and reckon the cost, whether he has what is needed for its completion, lest, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, those who pass by begin to mock him, saying, This man laid a foundation and was not able to finish?" Let the beginning, then, have its advance eagerly toward the achievement. For the most noble athlete Paul also, wishing us not to rest content in the good things lived through in the past, but to advance forward day by day, says: "Forgetting the things behind, and stretching out toward the things before, I press on toward the goal, to the prize of the upward calling." For such is the whole life of men: not content with what is past, but nourished not so much by what is past as by what is to come. For what does yesterday's fullness of the belly profit a man, when today the inborn hunger does not find its proper solace of food? So neither is there any gain to the soul from yesterday's achievement, when today's right action is left undone. For "such as I find you," he says, "such will I judge you."

Therefore vain is the toil of the righteous, and blameless the way of the sinner, when a change has supervened — the one being turned from the better to the worse, the other from the worse to the better. These things one may hear Ezekiel also laying down, as in the person of the Lord. "For if," he says, "the righteous man turns aside and transgresses, I will by no means remember the righteous deeds which he did before, but in his sin he shall die." And the same he says also concerning the sinner: "If, turning back, he does righteousness, he shall live by it." For where are the many labours of Moses the servant, when the contradiction of a single moment cancelled his entrance into the land of promise? And where is the company of Gehazi with Elisha, when for love of money he drew leprosy upon himself? And what profit was there for Solomon in the multitude of his wisdom, and his former such mind toward God, when later, from his madness for women, he fell away into idolatry? But neither did his elation leave the blessed David blameless, on account of his transgression concerning Uriah. And the falling away of Judas from the better to the worse was enough, for the security of one who lives the life that is according to God; who, having for so long a time been a disciple of Christ, afterwards, having sold out his teacher for a paltry gain, wrought a noose for himself. Let this, then, be known to you, brother, that not he who begins well, this man is perfect, but he who lays it down well, this man is approved with God.

Give no sleep, then, to your eyes, brother, nor slumber to your eyelids, that you may be saved like a gazelle from the snares, and like a bird from the trap. For see that you are passing through the midst of snares, and walking upon a high wall, from which the fall is not without danger to him who falls. Do not, then, at once stretch yourself out to the height of asceticism; and above all do not be confident in yourself, lest from inexperience you fall from the height of asceticism. For better is the advance little by little. Steal away, then, gradually the pleasures of life, doing away with yourself every habit, lest, by provoking all the pleasures at once together, you bring upon yourself a crowd of temptations. And whenever you have prevailed by main force over one passion of pleasure, set yourself in array against the other pleasure, and thus you will in good time prevail over all the pleasures. For the name of pleasure is one, but the things are diverse. Therefore, brother, be first of all patient under every temptation. And by what kind of temptations is the believer tested? By worldly losses, accusations, false charges, disobediences, slanders, persecutions. In these and the like the believer is tested.

Then be also quiet — not headstrong in speech, not contentious, not quarrelsome, not vainglorious, not given to interpreting, but loving the faith; not much in talk, but be always ready, not for teaching, but for learning. Do not busy yourself with worldly lives, from which no profit comes to you. For it says: "That my mouth may not speak the works of men." For he who gladly speaks the things of sinners readily wakens up the pleasures against himself. Rather busy yourself with the life of the righteous; for thus you will find profit for yourself. Do not be fond of display, going about the villages or the houses, but flee these as snares of souls. And if anyone, through much devotion, invites you into his own house for many reasons, let such a man learn to follow the faith of the centurion, who, when Jesus was hastening to him for the sake of a healing, declined, saying: "Lord, I am not worthy that you should come under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant shall be healed." And when Jesus said to him, "Go, as you have believed, so be it done to you," the servant was healed from that hour. Let this, then, be known to you, brother, that it was not the presence of Christ but the faith of him who asked that set the sick man free. So now too, while you pray in whatever place you may be, and the sick man believes that by your prayers he will be helped, all will turn out for him according to his heart's desire.

Do not love your own kin more than the Lord. For "he who loves," he says, "father or mother or brothers above me, is not worthy of me." And what does the Lord's commandment will? "If anyone," he says, "does not take up his cross and follow me, he cannot be my disciple." If you died together with Christ to your kinsmen according to the flesh, why do you wish again to dwell among them? And if what you tore down for Christ's sake you build up again for the sake of your kinsmen, you set yourself up as a transgressor. Do not, then, on account of a debt owed to your kinsmen, withdraw from your place; for in withdrawing from your place, perhaps you will withdraw also from your way of life. Do not be one who delights in crowds; not fond of your district, not fond of your city; but fond of the wilderness, abiding ever upon yourself without distraction, accounting prayer and psalmody your work.

Do not slight the readings either, especially of the New Testament, because from the Old Testament harm often comes — not that what was written is harmful, but that the mind of those harmed is weak. For all bread is nourishing, yet harmful to the sick; so then all Scripture is inspired of God and profitable, and there is nothing common through it, except that to him who reckons it to be common, to that man it is common. "Prove all things; hold fast what is good; abstain from every form of evil." For "all things are lawful, but not all things are profitable." Be, then, in all things, toward those who meet with you, inoffensive, cheerful, loving the brethren, pleasant, lowly in mind, not falling away from the aim of hospitality through costliness of foods, but content with what is at hand; take nothing from anyone beyond the daily need of the solitary life. And above all flee gold as a plotter against the soul, and the father of sin, and a servant of the devil. Do not, on the pretext of ministering to the poor, set yourself up as liable to the charge of love of money. And if anyone brings you money for the sake of the poor, and you know that there are certain ones in want, counsel that very man to whom the money belongs to carry it off himself to the needy brethren, lest the receiving of money should defile your conscience.

Flee pleasures; pursue self-control; and train the body with toils, and accustom the soul to temptations. Reckoning the dissolution of body and soul to be the deliverance from every evil, await the enjoyment of the eternal good things, of which all the saints have become partakers. And do you, weighing it out without ceasing, set the pious reasoning over against the diabolical thought, as upon a balance, yielding to this by the inclination of the scale. And most of all when the wicked thought rises up and says: "What profit is there to you in the stay in this place? What gain to you in the withdrawal from the company of men? Or do you not know that the bishops appointed by God over the churches of God live in their accustomed manner together with men, and continually celebrate the spiritual assemblies, in which above all there comes profit to those present? For there are revelations of proverbial riddles, solutions of apostolic teachings, exposition of evangelical thoughts, the hearing of theology, the meetings of spiritual brethren who furnish to those who meet them great benefit from the sight of their face. But you, having set yourself apart from so many good things, sit here, made savage perhaps with the wild beasts. For you see here great stillness, no little inhumanity, lack of teaching, estrangement from the brethren, and the spirit having much idleness concerning the commandment of God."

When, therefore, the wicked thought rises up with such and so many specious pretexts and wishes to break you down, set against it, through the pious reasoning, the experience of the matter, saying: "Since you say to me that the things in the world are good, for this reason I have removed hither, having judged myself unworthy of the world's good things. For the evils are mingled with the world's good things, and the evils far prevail. For when I was once present at the spiritual assemblies, I scarcely ever met with one brother who, to all seeming, feared the Lord, but was held fast by the devil; and I heard from him clever words and fables fashioned for the deceiving of those who met him. And after him I met with many thieves, robbers, tyrants. I saw the unseemly aspect of drunkards, the blood of those who were oppressed. And I saw also the beauty of women, tormenting my chastity; and the deed of fornication I escaped, but my virginity I defiled in the thought of my heart. And I have heard many words profitable to the soul, yet in none of the teachers did I find virtue worthy of the words. And after this, again, I heard countless tragedies, clothed in enervated strains. Again I heard the sweetly sounding lyre, the clapping of the dancers, the voice of the jesters, much folly and ribaldry, the shout of an unspeakable crowd. I saw the tears of the plundered, the pains of those led off by tyranny, the wailing of the tortured. And I saw, and behold, it was no spiritual assembly, but a sea churned and troubled by the wind, eager to cover all together with its waves."

Tell me, O evil thought, and demon of temporary pleasure-loving and vainglory: what profit is there to me in the beholding and hearing of these things, when I am able to help none of those wronged, and am permitted neither to defend the powerless nor to set right those who go astray, and am likely, perhaps, to bring even myself to ruin besides? For just as a little clean water is made to vanish by a great storm of wind and dust, so the things we think we do well in life are covered over by the multitude of evils. For the tragedies, like stakes, are driven into the hearts of those who pass their life in good cheer and joy, that they may darken the purity of psalmody. And the wailings and the lamentation of men wronged by their own kind are brought on, that the endurance of the poor may be displayed. What profit, then, is there to me, except plainly the harm of the soul?

For this reason, therefore, I remove to the mountains like a sparrow; for like a sparrow I was delivered from the snare of the hunters. For I pass my life in this wilderness, O evil thought, in which the Lord himself dwelt.
