Here is the oak of Mamre; here is the heaven-bearing ladder, and the encampments of the angels that appeared to Jacob; here is the wilderness in which the people, sanctified, received the law, and thus, entering into the land of promise, saw God. Here is Mount Carmel, in which Elijah, encamping, was well-pleasing to God. Here is the plain in which Ezra, having withdrawn, poured forth all the God-inspired books at God's command. Here is the wilderness in which the blessed John, eating locusts, preached repentance to men. Here is the Mount of Olives, to which Christ went up and prayed, teaching us to pray. Here is Christ, the friend of the wilderness; for he says: "Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Here is the narrow and afflicted way that leads to life. Here are the teachers and prophets who wandered in deserts and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth. Here are apostles and evangelists, and the desert-dwelling life of the monks.

These things, then, I have willingly taken upon myself, that I may receive what has been promised to the martyrs of Christ and to all the other saints; that I may say without falsehood: "Because of the words of your lips I have kept hard ways." For I have learned that God-loving Abraham obeyed the voice of God and removed into the wilderness; that Isaac was oppressed, and Jacob the patriarch was a sojourner; that chaste Joseph was sold; that the three children, discoverers of self-control, fought the fire; that Daniel was twice cast into the den of lions; that Jeremiah, who spoke boldly, was condemned to a pit of mire; that Isaiah, the beholder of hidden things, was sawn asunder; that Israel was led captive; that John, the reprover of adultery, was beheaded; that the martyrs of Christ were slain. And why do I make a long discourse? Seeing that the Saviour himself was crucified for us, that by his own death he might give us life, and might anoint and draw us all to endurance. To him I press on, and to the Father, and the Holy Spirit. I strive to be found genuine, having judged myself unworthy of the world's good things — yet I am not for the world's sake, but the world is for mine.

Reckoning these things, then, within yourself, and accomplishing them earnestly according to what has been said to you, strive for the truth unto death. For Christ also became obedient unto death. But the Apostle too says: "See that there be not at any time in any of you an evil heart, to depart from the living God; but exhort one another, and build up one another, while it is called Today." For "Today" signifies the whole time of our life. Living, then, in this manner, brother, you will both save yourself, and gladden us, and glorify God unto the ages of ages. Amen.
An admonition to the young.

Learn, you who live the solitary life and are a faithful man and a worker of piety, and be taught the evangelical way of life: the subjection of the body, a lowly mind, purity of thought, the doing away with anger. When pressed into service, add more for the Lord's sake; when robbed, do not go to law; when hated, love; when persecuted, endure; when slandered, encourage. Be made dead to sin, be crucified to God; transfer your whole care upon the Lord, that you may be found where are the tens of thousands of angels, the assemblies of the firstborn, the thrones of the apostles, the seats of honour of the prophets, the sceptres of the patriarchs, the crowns of the martyrs, the praises of the righteous. Long to be numbered with those righteous ones, in Christ Jesus our Lord. To him be the glory unto the ages. Amen.
To a monk who had fallen away.

We do not bid you "rejoice," because there is no rejoicing for the impious. For unbelief still holds me, and it does not come into my heart that you have done so great an outrage and so vast a deed, if indeed, to all appearance, it now stands thus with everyone. For I marvel how so great wisdom was swallowed up, how so great exactness was dissolved, whence so great a blindness was poured around you, how, having thought out nothing at all, you wrought such and so great a ruin of souls. For if this is true, you have handed over your own soul also to the abyss, and you have slackened the strength of all who hear of this impiety. You have set aside the faith, you have missed the good contest. Therefore I grieve over you. For what priest, hearing it, will not lament? What churchman is not stricken? What layman is not gloomy? What ascetic does not mourn? Perhaps even the sun darkened at your fall, and the powers of the heavens were shaken at your ruin. Even the senseless stones wept at your madness, and even the enemies wept at the excess of your lawlessness.

Oh, the great hardness! Oh, the dreadful brutality! You did not fear God, you did not reverence men, you were not abashed before friends; but all together you wrecked, all together you were despoiled. Therefore again I grieve over you, wretched one. You who proclaimed to all the strength of the kingdom have fallen from the kingdom. You who instilled in all the fear of teaching had no fear of God before your eyes. You who preached holiness are found accursed. You who took pride in possessing nothing are found pilfering money. You who, by your instruction, set forth the chastisement of God have yourself procured chastisement beforehand for yourself. How shall I lament you? How shall I grieve over you? How has the morning star, that rose at dawn, fallen and been shattered upon the earth? The two ears of everyone who hears will ring. How has the Nazarite, who shone above gold, become darker than soot? How has the precious son of Zion become a useless vessel? He whose memory of the divine Scriptures was spoken of by all, today has his memorial perished with a crash. The keen-witted has swiftly perished. The man of much understanding has wrought an intricate sin. For those who were profited by your teaching have been harmed by your ruin. Those who lent their ears to your discourse have stopped their ears at your ruin. And I, lamenting and gloomy, and undone on every side, and eating ashes as bread, and having cast sackcloth upon my wound, recite to you such eulogies; or rather, composing funeral discourses, I continue uncomforted and without remedy; for comfort is hidden from my eyes, and there is no salve to lay on, neither oil nor bandages; for my wound is grievous. Whence shall I be healed?

If, then, any hope of salvation still remains to you, if any slight memory of God, if any longing for the good things to come, if any fear of the chastisements stored up for the impenitent, sober yourself quickly, lift up your eyes to heaven, come to your senses, cease from your wickedness, shake off the drunkenness poured around you, rise up against him who cast you down. Be strong to rise up from the earth. Remember the good shepherd, that, pursuing, he will rescue you. Even if it be but two legs, or the lobe of an ear, leap away from him who wounded you. Remember the compassions of God, that he heals with oil and wine. Do not despair of salvation. Take up the memory of the things written, that he who falls rises again, and he who turns away returns; the stricken is healed, the prey of the beast escapes, he who confesses is not cast out. For the Lord does not will the death of the sinner, so much as that he should turn and live. Do not, as though fallen into a depth of evils, despise it.

It is a time of forbearance, a time of long-suffering, a time of healing, a time of correction. Have you slipped? Rouse yourself. Have you sinned? Be still. Do not stand in the way of sinners, but leap away. For when, having turned back, you groan, then you will be saved. For out of toils comes health, and out of sweats comes salvation. See, then, that you do not, in wishing to keep certain compacts with men, transgress your compacts with God, which you confessed before many witnesses. Do not, then, on account of any human reasonings, shrink from coming to me. For I will take up my dead and lament him, I will heal, I will weep bitterly over the affliction of the daughter of my people. All receive you, all will toil with you. Do not give up; remember the days of old. There is salvation, there is correction. Take courage, do not despair. There is no law condemning you to death without mercies, but grace that defers the chastisement, awaiting the correction. The doors are not yet shut; the bridegroom hears; sin does not have dominion. Wrestle again; do not be slack; and have pity on yourself, and on us all, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be the glory and the might, now and ever, unto the ages of ages. Amen.
To a monk who had fallen away.

A twofold fear has darted into the recesses of my mind out of your case. For either some unfeeling manner, taking the lead, casts me into the charge of misanthropy, or again, if I am willing to feel with you and to grow soft toward the passions, it shifts me wrongly. Wherefore, as I am about to trace out this letter of mine, I have nerved my hand, which had grown numb at the thought; but my face, perplexed from dejection over you, I had not strength to change, so great a shame being poured over me on your account, that the very closing of my mouth fails at once, my lips turning aside to weeping. Alas, what shall I write, or what shall I think, caught at the crossroads?

If I come to the memory of your former vain conduct, when wealth and the low-creeping bit of glory flowed about you, I shudder; when there followed you a crowd of flatterers and the temporary enjoyment of luxury, with manifest danger and unjust gains; and when on the one hand the fears of the magistrates fanned away your thought of salvation, and on the other the tumults of the public revenues shook your hearth, and the press of evils dashed your mind away from him who was able to help you; when little by little you began to look about for the Saviour, who brought your fears for your benefit and rescued and sheltered you, while you played against him in your times of security; when you trained yourself for a change to a holy manner of life, casting off as refuse your perilous abundance, and renouncing the service of a household and the company of a wife. And, wholly lifted up, like a stranger and a wanderer, exchanging fields and cities, you ran down to Jerusalem, where I too, dwelling with you, counted you blessed for your athletic toils, when, continuing fasting through the weekly cycles, you pursued the love of wisdom toward God; at the same time fleeing, by the discipline of change, the company of men, and, having fitted to yourself quiet and the solitary way, you turned aside from the tumults of the city. Piercing your body with rough sackcloth, and girding your loins with a hard belt, you patiently crushed your bones. Hollowing out your flanks with privations as far as the parts of the back, you renounced even the use of soft swaddling-bands, and, drawing in your sides from within, like a cupping-glass, you forced them to cleave to the regions of the kidneys; and, having emptied all the fat of the flesh, you nobly dried up the channels of the lower belly, and, having contracted the belly itself with fastings, you shadowed the parts of the ribs, like the jutting of a roof, over the members of the navel; and, with the whole instrument of the body drawn in, in the hours of the night confessing to God, you smoothed your beard, drenched, with the channels of your tears. And what need is there for me to recount each thing? Remember how many mouths of the saints you kissed in greeting, how many sacred bodies you embraced, how many cherished your hands as undefiled, how many servants of God, like worshippers, ran beneath your knees, clinging to them.

And what is the end of these things? The slander of an adulterous report, flying swifter than an arrow, wounds our ears, piercing our inward parts with a sharper sting. What so artful versatility of the deceiver led you round into so deadly a tripping-up? What manifold nets of the devil, having girt you about, have proved the workings of virtue motionless? Where, for me, are the tales of your toils? They are gone. For is it right to disbelieve? And how shall we not, from the things that are evident, accept also for belief what was hitherto unseen? — if you shut up with dreadful oaths the souls that had fled for refuge to God; whereas, by careful watching, the surplus beyond the Yes and the No is assigned to the devil.

At one and the same time, then, you have become surety for a deadly perjury, and, having debased the stamp of asceticism, you have sent up the shame as far as the apostles and the Lord himself. You have shamed the boast of chastity, you have blamed the profession of self-control; we have become a tragedy for captives, our affairs are made a drama for Jews and Greeks. You have cut asunder the resolve of monks; the more exact you have led into fear and cowardice, still marvelling at the power of the devil; the indifferent you have turned over to a zeal for licentiousness; you have loosed, so far as in you lay, the boast of Christ, who says, "Take courage, I have overcome the world and the ruler of it"; you have mixed for your country a bowl of evil report. Truly you have brought to deed the saying of the Proverb: "As a deer shot through to the liver."

But what now? The tower of strength has not fallen, brother; the remedies of conversion have not been blamed; the city of refuge has not been shut off. Do not remain behind in the depth of evils. Do not give yourself over to the manslayer. The Lord knows how to set upright those who have been cast down. Flee — not far off, but run back to us. Take up again your youthful toils, dissolving by a second course of right deeds the ground-creeping and filthy pleasure. Look up to the day of the end, which has so drawn near to our life; and learn how the children of Jews and Greeks are now being driven together toward the worship of God; and do not, once and for all, deny the Saviour of the world, lest that most terrible sentence overtake you: "I do not know you, who you are."
To a virgin who had fallen away.

Now is the time to cry aloud that prophetic word, and to say: "Who will give water to my head, and to my eyes a fountain of tears, and I will weep for the wounded of the daughter of my people?" For even if a deep silence holds these, and they lie, once for all stupefied by the terrible thing, deprived even of the sensation of their suffering by the mortal blow, yet we must not pass by so great a fall without tears. For if Jeremiah judged those wounded in body in war to be worthy of countless laments, what could one say in the face of so great a calamity of souls? "Your wounded," he says, "are not the wounded of the sword, and your dead are not the dead of war." But it is the sting of death indeed, the grievous sin, that I bewail, and the fiery darts of the evil one, which barbarously consumed souls together with bodies.

Surely the laws of God would groan greatly, looking upon so great a pollution upon the earth — those laws which ever forbid and cry aloud, of old: "You shall not covet your neighbour's wife," and through the holy Gospels: "Everyone who looks upon a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart." But now they look upon her, the bride of the Master, whose head is Christ, committing adultery without fear. And the very spirits of the saints would groan: Phinehas the zealous, that it is not now permitted to him, taking the spear in his hands, to avenge bodily the abomination; and John the Baptist, that he cannot, leaving the regions above, as he then left the wilderness, run to the reproof of the lawlessness, and, if he must suffer anything, lay down his head rather than his boldness of speech. Or rather, perhaps, if indeed for us also, after the manner of blessed Abel, he too, though dead, still speaks, even now John cries out and calls aloud, more than then concerning Herodias: "It is not lawful for you to have her." For even if the body of John, by the necessity of nature, received the divine limit, and his tongue is silent, yet "the word of God is not bound." For he who, because the marriage of a fellow servant was set at nought, carried his boldness of speech as far as death — what would he suffer, looking upon so great an outrage done to the holy bridal-chamber of the Lord?

But you, having cast off the yoke of that divine union, and having run away from the undefiled bridal-chamber of the true King, and having fallen shamefully into this dishonoured and impious corruption, since you have no way to escape this bitter accusation, and there is for you no manner nor device to cover over this terrible thing, you advance to meet your daring. And since, being impious, you have fallen into a depth of evils and now despise it, you deny the very compacts made with the true Bridegroom, crying out that you are not a virgin, and that you never made the promise — you who received many tokens of virginity, and displayed many.

Remember the good confession which you confessed before God and angels and men. Remember the venerable company, and the sacred choir of virgins, and the congregation of the Lord, and the Church of the holy ones; and your grandmother, grown old in Christ, yet still young and at the height of virtue; and your mother in the Lord, contending against her, and striving with strange and unwonted toils to break down the habits of common life; and your sister likewise, partly imitating those, partly ambitious even to surpass them, and outstripping by her virginal advantages the achievements of her forebears, and calling you, her sister, as she thought, to the contest of equals, both by word and by life, with all diligence. Remember these things, and the angelic dance about God in their company, and the spiritual life in the flesh, and the heavenly citizenship upon earth; remember the days without disturbance, and the nights full of light, and the spiritual songs, and the melodious psalmody, and the holy prayers, and the pure and undefiled bed, and the virginal procession, and the temperate table, and those who prayed earnestly that your virginity might be kept for you uncorrupted.

Where is that venerable habit, where the orderly bearing, and the plain dress befitting a virgin, and the blush, beautiful, that came of modesty, and the pallor, comely, that blossomed from self-control and watching, shining forth more gracefully than any fair colour? How often in prayers, for the sake of keeping your virginity unspotted, did you perhaps pour out tears? How many letters did you trace to the saints, by which you besought them to pray for you — not that you might obtain a human marriage, much less this dishonoured corruption, but that you might not fall away from the Lord Jesus? How many gifts of the Bridegroom did you receive? And what need is there to speak of the honours paid you for his sake by those who were his — the living together with virgins, the processions with them, the receptions by virgins, the eulogies upon virginity, the virginal blessings, the letters addressed to you as to a virgin? But now, having received a little breath of the airy spirit that now works in the sons of disobedience, you have denied all those things, and have bartered that precious and much-fought-for possession for a brief pleasure, which for a season anoints your throat, but afterwards you will find bitterer than gall.

At these things, who would not, grieving, say: "How has the faithful city, Zion, become a harlot?" And how would not the Lord himself declare to one of those who now walk in the spirit of Jeremiah: "Have you seen what the virgin of Israel has done to me? I betrothed her to myself in faith and incorruption, in righteousness, and in judgement, and in mercy and compassions, as I promised her also through Hosea the prophet. But she has loved strangers, and while I, her husband, am living, she is named an adulteress, and is not afraid to become another man's." And what, then, would the bridesman, the divine and blessed Paul — both that ancient one, and this new one under whose mediation and teaching you, having left your father's house, were joined to the Lord — what would each say, sorrowing deeply over so great an evil? "For the fear which I feared has come upon me, and that which I dreaded has met me. For I espoused you to one husband, to present you a pure virgin to Christ, and I feared ever lest somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve in his craftiness, so your thoughts should at some time be corrupted." For this very reason I tried ever, with countless charms, to allay the tumult of the passions, and with countless guards to keep safe the bride of the Lord, and I always set forth the life of the unmarried woman — that the unmarried woman alone cares for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit. And I expounded the dignity of virginity, and, calling you a temple of God, I gave, as it were, a wing to your eagerness, lifting you up toward Jesus, and by the fear of the terrible thing I helped you not to fall, saying: "If anyone corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt him." And indeed I added also the security that comes from my prayers, that somehow your whole body and soul and spirit might be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. But in vain have I laboured all these things upon you, and the end of those sweet toils has come out bitter for me; and I must groan again over her over whom I ought to have rejoiced. For behold, you have been deceived by the serpent more bitterly than Eve. For not your thoughts only have been corrupted, but together with those, your very body also; and that dreadful thing, which I shrink even to utter, and cannot keep silent (for it is like a fire burning and blazing in my bones, and I am undone on every side, and cannot bear it): you have taken the members of Christ and made them members of a harlot.

This alone, among all evils, is incomparable; this is a new daring in the world. "For pass over," he says, "to the isles of Chittim, and see; and send to Kedar, and consider exceedingly, whether such things have been done, whether the nations will change their gods, who yet are not gods. But the virgin has changed her glory, and her glory is in her shame. The heaven was astonished at this, and the earth shuddered exceedingly the more." The Lord says even now that the virgin has done two evil things: she has forsaken me, the true, the holy Bridegroom of holy souls, and has run away to an impious and lawless corrupter of soul and body together. She has departed from God her saviour, and has presented her members as slaves to uncleanness and lawlessness. She has forgotten me, and has gone after her lover, by whom she shall not be profited.

It were better for him if a millstone for an ass were hung about his neck, and he were cast into the sea, than that anyone should cause a virgin of the Lord to stumble. Has a self-willed slave gone so far in madness as to fling himself upon his master's bed? Or what robber has been led on to so great a madness as to lay hold of the very offerings of God — not lifeless vessels, but living bodies, having a soul dwelling within, made after the image of God? Who from of old has been heard of, who has dared, in the midst of a city and at full noonday, to inscribe upon a royal image the forms of unclean swine? He who has set at nought a human marriage dies, without mercies, at the word of two or three witnesses; of how much worse punishment, do you think, will he be deemed worthy who has trampled upon the Son of God, and corrupted the bride betrothed to him, and outraged the spirit of virginity? But "she was willing," he says, "and I did not force her against her will." Why, even that wanton mistress, the Egyptian woman, was mad with passion for the fair Joseph, but the madness of the licentious woman did not overcome the virtue of the chaste man, nor, though she forced him with her hands toward the transgression, was he forced. "But this was determined by her," he says, "and she was no longer a virgin; and if I had not been willing, she would have been corrupted by another." For "the Son of Man," he says, "had to be betrayed, but woe to him by whom he was betrayed"; and "the offences must come, but woe to him through whom they come."

At these things, "Does not he who falls rise again? Or does not he who turns away return?" Why has the virgin turned away with a shameless turning, even though she heard Christ the Bridegroom saying through Jeremiah: "And I said, after she had committed all these fornications, Return to me; and she did not return." "Is there no balm in Gilead? Or is there no physician there? Why has there not arisen healing for the daughter of my people?" Surely you would find in the divine Scripture many remedies against the evil, many medicines from ruin unto salvation: the mysteries concerning death and resurrection, the words concerning the dreadful judgement and eternal chastisement, the doctrines concerning repentance and the forgiveness of sins, those countless examples of conversion — the drachma, the sheep, the son who devoured his living with the harlots, the lost and found, the dead and come to life again. Let us use these as remedies against the evil; through these let us heal our own soul.

Take into your mind the last day (for surely you will not live the age alone), and the distress, and the choking, and the hour of death, and the pressing sentence of God, and the angels hastening on, and the soul in these things terribly disturbed and bitterly scourged by a sinful conscience, and turning back pitiably toward the things here, and the inexorable necessity of that long departure. Trace out for me in your mind the final overthrow of our common life, when the Son of God shall come in his glory with his angels. For he will come and will not keep silence, when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and to render to each according to his deed; when that trumpet, sounding something great and dreadful, shall waken those who have slept from of old, and they who have done good things shall come forth to the resurrection of life, but they who have done evil things to the resurrection of judgement. Remember the vision of God granted to Daniel, how he brings the judgement before our eyes. "I beheld," he says, "until thrones were set, and the Ancient of Days sat, and his garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head as pure wool; his wheels were burning fire. A river of fire drew on before him; a thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. The judgement sat, and the books were opened" — the good, the evil, the manifest, the hidden, the deeds, the words, the thoughts, all of them at once, clearly revealing them to the hearing of all, both angels and men. In the face of these things, what manner of men must those be who have lived ill? Where, then, will that soul sink down, which, in the sight of so many beholders, is suddenly seen full of shame? With what body will it endure those endless and unbearable scourges, where there is unquenchable fire, and a worm chastising immortally, and a dark and dreadful depth of Hades, and bitter wailings, and a fearful shrieking, and weeping and gnashing of teeth, and the terrors have no end? From these there is no deliverance after death, nor any device, nor contrivance, of slipping through the bitter places of chastisement.

These things it is possible to flee now. While it is possible, let us raise ourselves from our fall, and let us not despair of ourselves, if we depart from the evils. Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners. Come, let us worship and fall down before him, and weep before him. The Word, calling us to repentance, cries out and calls aloud: "Come to me all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." There is, then, a way of salvation, if we are willing. Death, having prevailed, swallowed us up; but know well that again God has taken away every tear from every face of those who repent. "The Lord is faithful in all his words." He does not lie who said: "Though your sins be as crimson, I will make them white as snow; and though they be as scarlet, I will make them white as wool." The great physician of souls is ready to heal your suffering — he who is ready to set free not you alone, but all who have been enslaved to sin. His are the words; that sweet and saving mouth spoke them: "They who are strong have no need of a physician, but they who are ill. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." What pretext, then, have you, or any other, while he cries these things aloud? The Lord wishes to cleanse you from the pain of your wound, and to show you light out of darkness. The good shepherd seeks you, who left the sheep that had not gone astray. If you give yourself up, he, the lover of mankind, will not shrink, nor will he count you unworthy to bear you upon his own shoulders, rejoicing that he has found his lost sheep.

The Father stands and awaits your return from your wandering. Only depart from your sin, and, while you are still far off, he will run and fall upon your neck, and with friendly embraces will enfold you, now already cleansed by repentance. And he will clothe with a robe, the first robe, the soul that has put off the old man with his deeds; and he will put a ring upon hands washed clean of the blood of death, and will put shoes upon feet that have turned from the evil way to the course of the gospel of peace. And he will proclaim a day of gladness and joy to his own, both angels and men. And in every way he will keep festival over your salvation. "For verily I say to you," he says, "that there is joy in heaven before God over one sinner that repents." And even if one of those who think they stand should accuse you, that you were received quickly, the good Father himself will plead on your behalf, saying: "It was meet to make merry and be glad, for this my daughter was dead and is alive again, and was lost and is found."
To Gregory, his comrade.

Who will give me wings like a dove, or how may my old age be renewed, so that I might be able to cross over to your love, and both find rest for the longing that I have toward you, and recount the griefs of my soul, and through you find some consolation of my afflictions? For upon the falling asleep of the blessed Eusebius the bishop, no small fear has taken hold of us, lest those who long lay in wait against the church of our metropolis, and who wish to fill it with the tares of the heretics, having now seized their opportunity, should root up, by their own wicked teachings, the piety sown with much labour in the souls of men, and cut asunder its unity — which indeed they have done in the case of many churches. And since letters have come to us also from the clergy, entreating that they be not overlooked at such a time, looking around me in a circle I remembered your love, and your right faith, and the zeal you ever have on behalf of the churches of God.

And for this reason I have sent the beloved Eustathius, the fellow deacon, to entreat your venerable dignity and to prevail upon you to add to all your labours on behalf of the churches the present one also, and both to give rest to my old age by your company, and to set the renowned piety right for the orthodox church, giving to it, together with us (if indeed we should be counted worthy to share with you in the good work), a shepherd according to the will of the Lord, able to guide his people aright. For we have before our eyes a man whom you yourselves are not unaware of; whom, if we should be counted worthy to obtain, I know that we shall acquire great boldness toward God, and shall lay up a very great benefit for the people who have called upon us. But I entreat you again and many times, laying aside all hesitation, to come and to forestall the difficulties that arise from the winter.
To Eusebius, bishop of Samosata.

It was scarcely possible for us to find a deacon to carry letters to your reverence, since those among us have so cowered before the winter that they cannot endure to put out even the smallest distance from their rooms. For we have been snowed under by so great a quantity of snow that, buried in our very houses, we have lurked in our hiding-places for two months already. You will, then, surely pardon us — knowing both the timidity of Cappadocian ways and the sluggishness of our bodies — if we did not write sooner, nor bring to the knowledge of your honour the things from Antioch; which, in any case, it is stale and cold to make known to you, who learned them long ago, as is likely. Yet, reckoning it no trouble to signify even what is already known, we have sent the letters carried by the reader. And so much for these things.

As for Constantinople, it has had Demophilus now a long time, as these men themselves will report, and as has surely been proclaimed beforehand to your holiness. And a certain fiction of orthodoxy and devotion about him is bruited abroad in agreement by all who arrive, so that even the divided parts of the city have come together into one, and some of the neighbouring bishops have accepted the union. But our own people have appeared no better than our hopes; for, coming upon us at once, on the very heels of your departure, they said many grievous things and did many, and at last withdrew, confirming the schism for us. Whether, then, anything better will come about, and whether they will cease from their malice, is unclear to all save God alone. Such, then, is the present state of things.

The rest of the church stands firm by the grace of God, and prays, together with the spring, to see you again in our country, and to be renewed through your good teaching. And as for me, my body is no better than usual.
To Arcadius, bishop.

I gave thanks to the holy God upon meeting with the letters of your devotion, and I pray both that I myself may be worthy of the hope you have concerning us, and that you may receive a perfect reward for the honour you pay us, with which, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, you honour us. And we rejoiced exceedingly that, having taken up also a care befitting a Christian, you raised a house to the glory of the name of Christ, and loved indeed, according to what is written, "the beauty of the house of the Lord," preparing for yourselves the heavenly abode that is made ready, in rest, for those who love the name of Christ. And if we are able to look out for relics of martyrs, we pray that we ourselves also may contribute to your zeal. For if "the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance," we shall, plainly, be partakers of the good remembrance that shall be given to you by the holy one.
To Innocent, bishop.

And to whom else did it belong both to instil courage in the fearful and to waken those who sleep, than to your reverence — the reverence of our Master — who have made known your perfection in all things, in this also: that you deigned to condescend even to us, the lowly, as a true disciple of him who said, "I am there in the midst of you, not as one who reclines at table, but as one who serves"? For you yourself deigned to minister to us your spiritual gladness, and by your honoured letters to take up our souls, and, as it were, to embrace the infancy of children with your own greatness.

Pray, then — we beseech your good soul — that we may be worthy both to receive the benefits that come from your greatness, and to obtain a mouth and wisdom to dare to answer you, who are led by the Holy Spirit; of whom, hearing that you are a friend and a true glorifier, we acknowledge great thankfulness for your firm and unswerving love toward God; praying that our portion may be found among the true worshippers, among whom we are persuaded that your perfection also is. And of the great and true Bishop, who has filled the whole world with his own wonder, of the Lord, we make our entreaty.
To Bosporius, bishop.

How deeply, do you suppose, my soul was pained when I heard of that slander which certain men poured out against me — men who do not fear the Judge who will destroy all that speak falsehood — so that for nearly the whole night, brooding over the words of your charity, I lay sleepless; with such force did grief lay hold of the very middle of my heart. For truly, as Solomon says, slander brings a man low; and no one is so insensible as not to suffer in soul and be bowed to the ground when he falls in the way of mouths ready for falsehood. Yet we must bear all things, endure all things, committing the vindication of ourselves to the Lord, who will not overlook us; for he that slanders the poor provokes his Maker. Those, however, who have composed this strange drama of blasphemy against us seem to disbelieve the Lord altogether, who has declared that we shall give account even for an idle word in the day of judgment.

But tell me, did I pronounce anathema against the most blessed Dianius? For this is what they have proclaimed against me. Where, or when? In whose presence? On what pretext? In bare words or in writing? Following others, or myself taking the lead and being the author of the deed? Oh, the shamelessness of those who utter anything so lightly! Oh, the contempt for the judgments of God! Unless indeed they will add to their fiction this further piece of stage-drama as well: that I had at some time gone out of my mind, so as to be ignorant myself of my own words. For while I was in my own right reason, I am conscious of having done no such thing, nor of having taken the initiative for it. Rather I am conscious of this: that from my earliest years I was reared in affection for him, and looked up to the man — venerable to behold, magnificent, and with all the dignity of a priest in his very appearance. And when in time I came also to the use of reason, then I came to know him also by the good qualities of his soul, and rejoiced in his company, learning the simplicity, nobility, and generosity of his ways, and all else that was characteristic of the man: the gentleness of his soul, that combination of greatness and mildness, his graciousness, his freedom from anger, his cheerfulness and accessibility tempered with dignity. So that I counted him among the most distinguished men in virtue.

Yet toward the end of his life — for I will not hide the truth — I grieved over him with a grief beyond bearing, together with many in our country who fear the Lord, on account of his signing the creed brought from Constantinople by the party of George. Then, such was that man in mildness of disposition and forbearance — bearing with all in fatherly tenderness so as to satisfy them — that, having already fallen into the sickness from which he departed this life, he summoned me and said: with the Lord as his witness, that he had set his hand to the document from Constantinople in simplicity of heart, but had in no way chosen to set aside the faith put forth at Nicaea by the holy fathers, nor did he hold otherwise in his heart than as he had received it from the beginning; nay, he prayed that he might not be separated from the portion of those blessed three hundred and eighteen bishops who proclaimed the doctrine of true religion to the world. So that I, on receiving this assurance, dissolving every doubt of my heart — as you yourself know — came forward to communion with him, and ceased from my grief.

Such, then, was our relation to the man. But if anyone says that he knows me to have uttered some unlawful blasphemy against him, let him not whisper it in a corner in slavish fashion, but let him stand forth into the open and refute me with frankness.
To the canonical sisters.

As greatly as a grievous report, ringing in our ears, formerly distressed us, so greatly did our most God-loving brother, Bishop Bosporius, gladden us by relating better things concerning your reverence. For he said that, by the grace of God, all those things noised abroad were fabrications of men who do not accurately know the truth of your position. He added, moreover, that he had found among you unholy slanders against us as well — such as those would utter who do not expect to give account even for an idle word to the Judge in the day of his just recompense. So that I gave thanks to the Lord, both being myself healed of the injury concerning you, which, as it seems, I had received through the slander of men, and hearing that you had laid aside the false suppositions concerning us which you had taken up.

In setting before you his own position, our brother at the same time demonstrated ours entirely. For the conviction of faith is one and the same in both of us, since we are heirs of the same fathers who once at Nicaea proclaimed the great message of true religion. In that creed everything else is altogether beyond slander; but the term "of one substance," wrongly understood by some, there are those who have not yet accepted. These one might justly blame, and yet again deem worthy of pardon. For not to follow the fathers, and to set one's own opinion above their authoritative word, is worthy of accusation as being full of arrogance; but again, to hold the term suspect when others have slandered it — this somewhat acquits them of the charge in a measure. And indeed, those who assembled against Paul of Samosata found fault with the expression as not well-marked. For they said that the term "of one substance" presented the notion of a substance and of the things derived from it, so that the substance, being divided, lent the name "of one substance" to the parts into which it was divided. Now in the case of bronze and the coins made from it this notion has some reasonable application; but in the case of God the Father and God the Son no prior or superior substance is contemplated above the two; for to conceive or utter this is beyond all impiety. What could be prior to the Unbegotten? And by this blasphemy faith in the Father and the Son is also destroyed; for things that derive their existence from one source are brothers to one another.

And since at that time there were still those who said that the Son had been brought into being from nothing, in order to cut off this impiety also they affixed the term "of one substance." For the union of the Son with the Father is timeless and without interval. The preceding words also show that this was the mind of those men. For having said "Light from Light," and that the Son was begotten from the substance of the Father and not made, they appended to these the term "of one substance," showing that whatever account of light one renders in the case of the Father, this will also fit in the case of the Son. For true light compared with true light, according to the very notion of light, will admit of no variation. Since, then, the Father is light without beginning, and the Son is begotten light, and each is light and light, they rightly said "of one substance," in order to present the equal honour of their nature. For things that are brothers to one another are not called "of one substance," as some have supposed; but when both the cause and that which has its existence from the cause are of the same nature, they are called "of one substance."

This term also corrects the evil of Sabellius; for it destroys the identity of person and introduces the perfect notion of distinct persons. For a thing is not "of one substance" with itself, but one thing with another; so that the term is well and reverently put, both defining the distinctness of the persons and presenting the unvarying sameness of the nature.

And when we are taught that the Son is from the substance of the Father, and begotten but not made, let us not sink into bodily notions of passions. For the substance was not divided from the Father into the Son, nor did it beget by flowing forth, nor by putting forth, as plants put forth their fruits; but the manner of the divine begetting is unspeakable and inconceivable to human reasonings. For it is the mark of a truly low and fleshly mind to liken the eternal to the corruptible and the temporary, and to think that, as in bodily things, so God too begets in like manner. Whereas one ought to derive from the contraries the grounds for true religion: that, since mortal things are thus, the immortal is not thus. We must therefore neither deny the divine begetting, nor defile our minds with bodily notions.

The Holy Spirit is numbered together with the Father and the Son, because he too is above creation; and he is ranked as we have been taught in the Gospel by the Lord, who said: "Go, baptize into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." But he who sets the Spirit before the Son, or calls him older than the Father, opposes the ordinance of God, and is a stranger to the sound faith, not keeping the manner of glorifying that he received, but devising for himself a novelty of speech to please men. For if the Spirit is above God, he is not from God. For it is written: "The Spirit is from God." And if he is from God, how is he older than that from which he is? And what madness is it, when the Unbegotten is one, to call anything else higher than the Unbegotten? But neither is he prior to the Only-begotten; for there is nothing between the Son and the Father. And if he is not from God, but is through Christ, then he does not exist at all. So that the innovation concerning the order involves the setting aside of his very existence, and is a denial of the whole faith. It is therefore equally impious both to bring him down to creation and to set him above either the Son or the Father, whether in time or in rank.

These, then, are the things that I heard your reverence inquires about. But if the Lord grant that we come together with one another, perhaps we may say something further about these matters as well, and we ourselves may find from you some assurance about the things we inquire into.
To the chorepiscopi.

The strangeness of the matter about which I write — the very fact that it was so much as suspected and spoken of — filled my soul with pain; and for a while it seemed to me past belief. Let the letter concerning it, therefore, be received by the man who is conscious of guilt as a remedy, by the man who is not conscious of it as a safeguard, and by the man who is indifferent — which I pray may not be found in your case — as a solemn warning.

What is it that I am speaking of? They say that some of you take money from those being ordained, and screen it under the name of piety. This is the worse fault. For if a man does evil under the guise of good, he deserves a double punishment: both because he does the thing that is not good, and because, to accomplish his sin, he has used, as one might say, good as his accomplice. If these things are so, let them be done no more in the future, but let them be corrected; since one must say to him who receives the money what was said by the apostles to the man who wished to give money, that he might purchase a share of the Holy Spirit: "Your money perish with you." For lighter is the guilt of him who through ignorance wishes to buy than of him who sells the gift of God. For a sale was made; and what you received freely, if you sell it, you shall be stripped of the grace, as one sold to Satan. For you bring trafficking into spiritual things, and into the Church where we have been entrusted with the body and blood of Christ. These things ought not so to be done. As for the trick they use, I will tell it: they think they do not sin because they do not take beforehand, but take after the ordination. But to take is to take, whenever it may be.

I exhort you, therefore: lay aside this revenue, or rather this approach that leads to hell; and do not, by defiling your hands with such takings, make yourselves unworthy to perform the holy mysteries. Pardon me — first as having disbelieved, and then, now that I am convinced, as threatening. If anyone after this letter of mine should do any such thing, he shall withdraw from the altars here, and shall seek out some place where, buying the gift of God, he can sell it again. For we and the Churches of God do not have such a custom.

I will add one thing and have done. These things happen through love of money; and love of money is both the root of all evils and is named idolatry. Do not, then, honour idols before Christ for a little silver; nor again imitate Judas, betraying for gain a second time him who was once crucified for us. For both the fields and the hands of those who receive the fruits of these things shall be called Akeldama.
To the chorepiscopi.

It greatly grieves me that the canons of the fathers have now failed, and that all strictness has been driven out of the Churches; and I fear that, as this indifference advances little by little along its way, the affairs of the Church may come into utter confusion. The custom long established in the Churches of God used to receive those who minister to the Church only after testing them with all strictness; and their whole manner of life was scrutinized — whether they were not abusive, not drunkards, not quick to quarrel, whether they disciplined their youth, so that they might be able to attain that holiness without which no one shall see the Lord. And the presbyters and deacons who lived with them used to examine this, and refer it to the chorepiscopi, who, receiving the votes of those who truly bore witness, and reminding the bishop, would thus enroll the minister in the order of the clergy.

But now, first, having thrust me aside, and not even deigning to refer the matter to me, you have taken the whole authority into your own hands. Then, growing careless of the matter, you have permitted presbyters and deacons to introduce into the Church whomever they wish, out of unexamined lives, by personal favour — whether from kinship or from some other friendship — the unworthy. So that many ministers are numbered in each village, but not one worthy of the ministry of the altar, as you yourselves bear witness, being at a loss for men in the elections.

Since, then, I see the matter now advancing to an incurable state — especially now that the greater number, through fear of conscription, are foisting themselves into the ministry — I have necessarily come to the point of renewing the canons of the fathers. And I charge you to send me the register of those who minister in each village, and by whom each was introduced, and what manner of life he leads. You yourselves are to keep the register beside you, so that your records may be compared with the documents laid up with us, and so that it may not be possible for anyone to enroll himself whenever he wishes. So then, after the first registration, if any were introduced by presbyters, let them be cast back among the laity. And let a fresh examination of them be made by you; and if they are worthy, let them be received by your vote. Cleanse the Church by driving out from it the unworthy. And for the future, examine the worthy and receive them, but do not number them before referring to us; or else know that he who is received into the ministry without our judgment shall be a layman.
To Paregorius, presbyter.

I have read your letter with all patience, and I marvel how, when you could have made your defence to us briefly and easily by your deeds, you choose instead to persist in the things charged against you, and attempt to treat what is incurable with long arguments. We are neither the first nor the only ones, Paregorius, to lay down the law that women should not live together with men. Read the canon put forth by our holy fathers in the synod of Nicaea, which plainly forbade the keeping of women brought in to live with the clergy. Celibacy has its dignity precisely in this — in being separated from cohabitation with a woman. So that if a man, while professing celibacy in name, does in deed the things of those who live with women, he plainly pursues the dignity of virginity in title, but does not withdraw from the unseemly thing that gives pleasure.

So much the more readily, then, ought you to have yielded to our request, inasmuch as you say you are free from every bodily passion. For I am neither persuaded that a man of seventy lives with a woman with passion, nor have we ordained what we ordained as though some unseemly act had occurred; but because we were taught by the apostle not to put a stumbling-block or an offence in a brother's way. And we know that what is done innocently by some becomes for others an occasion of sin. For this reason we have enjoined, following the ordinance of the holy fathers, that you separate from the woman.

Why, then, do you accuse the chorepiscopus and recall an old enmity? Why do you find fault with the chorepiscopi as having ears too ready to admit slanders, instead of with yourself for not enduring to withdraw from your habitual association with the woman? Cast her, then, out of your house, and place her in a convent. Let her be with virgins, and you be ministered to by men, so that the name of God may not be blasphemed because of you. But as long as you do these things, the ten thousand sentences which you write in your letters will profit you nothing, but you will die in idleness, and will give account to the Lord for your idleness. And if you dare, without correcting yourself, to cling to the priesthood, you shall be anathema to all the people, and those who receive you shall be excommunicated throughout every Church.
To Pergamius.

I am by nature prone to forgetfulness, and there has come upon me besides a multitude of occupations, intensifying the natural weakness. So that even if I do not remember receiving a letter from your nobility, I am persuaded that you wrote to us; for you would by no means say what was false. As for my not having answered, I am not the cause, but rather you, who did not demand a reply. But now this letter comes to you, both making good my defence for what has passed and giving the beginning of a second exchange of greetings. So that, when you write to us, do not think of yourself as beginning a second round of correspondence, but as paying off your debt upon the present occasion. For even if our letter is a repayment of one who took the lead, yet by exceeding more than double in measure it will discharge both obligations at once. You see what sophistries necessity compels us to?

But cease, my excellent friend, from bringing in great charges within little words — charges, indeed, that admit of no exceeding in wickedness. For forgetfulness of friends, and the contempt that comes from power, together contain all that is dreadful. For if we do not love according to the Lord's commandment, then we do not even bear the stamp set upon us; and if we have been puffed up with empty pride and arrogance, we fall into the inescapable judgment of the devil. So that, if you held such an opinion of us and used these words, pray that we may flee the wickedness which you have discovered in our character; but if it was through some unexamined habit that your tongue came to these words, we will console ourselves and beg your kindness to add to them the testimonies that come from deeds. For know this well: that the present anxiety has become for us an occasion of humility, so that we shall forget you only when we are ignorant even of ourselves. Do not, then, ever make your occupations a sign of character and ill-nature.
To Meletius, bishop of Antioch.

If somehow the greatness of the joy which you produce in us, as often as you write, were made plain to your godliness, I know that you would never let a chance of writing pass by; nay, you would even contrive on every occasion to make your letters to us many, knowing the reward laid up by our loving Master for the refreshment of the afflicted. For all things here are filled with pain, and our only escape from troubles is the thought of your holiness — a thought made more vivid to us by converse through your letters, which are filled with all wisdom and grace. So that when we take your letter in hand, we first observe its length, and love it the more, the more it abounds in fullness. Then, as we go through it, we rejoice at every part of the discourse we come to, but as we draw near the end of the letter we are troubled. So entirely is everything you say in your letters good. For out of a good heart comes that which abounds, and it is good.

And if we were counted worthy through your prayers, while we are yet on earth, of meeting you face to face, and of receiving from the living voice itself profitable teachings, or provisions both for the present age and the age to come, we should judge this the greatest of goods, and set it for ourselves as a foretaste of God's favour. And we were already in the grip of this impulse, had not our most genuine and altogether brother-loving brethren restrained us; and that I might not publish my purpose by letter, I have explained the matter in detail to our brother Theophrastus, to report each particular to your perfection.
To his brother Gregory.

How could I do battle with you by letter? How could I rebuke you worthily for your kindness in all things? Tell me, who is caught a third time in the same nets? Who falls a third time into the same snare? Not even one of the brute beasts would easily suffer this. You fabricated a letter for me and brought it as though from the most reverend bishop and our common uncle, deceiving me — I know not why. I received it as brought by you from the bishop. For why should I not have? Out of excessive joy I showed it to many of my friends; I gave thanks to God. The fabrication was exposed, the bishop himself with his own voice disowning it. We were put to shame over it; we prayed that the earth might open beneath us, having been clothed in the reproach of trickery and falsehood and deceit. A second time again they delivered me a letter, as sent from the bishop himself by the hand of your servant Asterius. Neither did the bishop truly send that one, as our most reverend brother Anthimus reported to us. A third time again Adamantius came to us bringing one. How was I to receive the things sent through you and your people? I could have prayed to have a heart of stone, so as neither to remember the past nor to feel the present — to bear every blow with my head bowed to the earth, like the cattle. But what am I to do against my own reason, which after one and a second trial can no longer admit anything without examination?

I have written these things in reproach of your simplicity, which, though in no way fitting for Christians otherwise, I see to be unsuited to the present time as well; so that at least for the future you may both guard yourself and spare me. For — since I must speak to you with frankness — you are an untrustworthy agent in such matters. Yet whoever those may be who have written, we have answered them as is fitting. Whether, then, you yourself were laying a trial for me, or whether you truly received the letter from the bishops and sent it, you have the replies. But it would have been more fitting for you to have other concerns at the present time, being a brother and not yet having forgotten nature, and not regarding us in the place of an enemy, since we have come into a manner of life that wears down our body and afflicts even our soul by surpassing our strength. But nevertheless, since you are so set on war, for this very reason you must now be present and share in our affairs. "For brothers," it is said, "should be useful in times of need."

But if the most reverend bishops truly accept a meeting with us, let them make known to us a fixed place and time, and send for us by their own men. For just as I do not refuse to go myself to meet my uncle, so, if the summons is not made with the fitting form, I will not endure it.
To his uncle Gregory.

I have kept silent. But shall I keep silent forever, and endure any longer to ratify against myself the most grievous loss of silence — neither writing myself nor hearing one address me? For I, who have persevered until now in this gloomy resolve, think it fitting that I too should say the words of the prophet: "I endured like a woman in travail" — ever longing either for a meeting or for words, and ever failing of it through my own sins. For indeed I can conceive of no other cause for what is happening, except this conviction: that I am paying the penalty for old sins, in this separation from your charity — if indeed it is right to use the word "separation" of you, even toward any chance acquaintance, much less toward us, to whom from the beginning you have stood in a father's place.

But my sin now, like some deep cloud overshadowing me, has brought on forgetfulness of all those things. For whenever I look — beyond the fact that what is happening brings me grief — and see nothing else achieved by it, how should I not reasonably attribute the present to my own faults? But whether sins are the cause of what has befallen, let this be the end of my hardships; or whether something was being arranged by Providence, then surely the purpose has been fully accomplished. For the time of the loss has been no small one. Therefore, no longer able to bear it, I have been the first to break silence, exhorting you to remember both us and yourself — you who, beyond what was likely from kinship, showed care for us throughout your whole life — and to love the city now for our sake, and not to estrange yourself from the city on our account.

If, then, there is any consolation in Christ, any fellowship of the Spirit, any tender mercies and compassions, fulfil our prayer: here put a stop to what is gloomy, give some beginning of brighter things for the time to come, yourself leading the others toward what is best, and not following another into what ought not to be. For no bodily feature was ever thought so much a man's own as the peaceful and gentle quality of your soul. It would befit such a man to draw the others toward himself, and to make all who come near you, as if filled with the fragrance of some sweet ointment, partake of the kindness of your character. For even if there is something resisting now, yet a little later it too will recognize the good of peace. But as long as slanders find room by reason of the separation, the suspicions must ever grow worse. Now it is not fitting even for those others to neglect us, but most of all for your honour. For if we are doing any wrong, we shall become better by being admonished — and this is impossible without a meeting; but if we are doing no wrong, for what cause are we hated? These, then, are the arguments I put forward in my own defence.

But what the Churches might say on their own behalf — reaping no good from our separation — it is better to pass over in silence. For I have used these words not in order to give pain, but in order to put a stop to what is painful. Nothing whatever has escaped your understanding; rather you yourself would discover by your mind, and tell others, things much greater and more perfect than we conceive — you who even before us saw the injuries of the Churches, and are grieved more than we, having been taught long ago by the Lord to despise none of the least. But now the injury is not confined to one or two, but whole cities and peoples share in our misfortunes. And what need is there even to speak of the report that there will be about us beyond our borders, what kind it will be? It would befit your magnanimity, then, to leave contentiousness to others — or rather to root it even out of their souls, if that be possible — and yourself to conquer what is painful by patience. For to retaliate belongs to anyone who is angry, but to be higher than anger itself, this belongs to you alone, and to anyone whose virtue is near yours. But this I will not say: that he who is harsh with us lets loose his anger upon those who have done no wrong.

Whether, then, by your presence, or by letter, or by a summons to yourself, or in whatever way you please, comfort our soul. For it is our prayer that your godliness should appear in the Church, and that you should heal both us together and the people, by your very sight and by the words of your grace. If, then, this be possible, it is best of all; but if something else should seem good, that too we will accept. Only be entreated to make known to us firmly what commends itself to your wisdom.
To his uncle Gregory.

Even before, I was glad to see my brother. For why should I not have been, since he is my own brother, and such a one? And now too I received him with the same disposition when he came, turning aside nothing of my own affection. For God forbid that I should ever suffer anything that would make me forget nature and be set at war with my own kin. But I counted the presence of the man a consolation both for the infirmities of the body and for the other pains of the soul; and I was overjoyed at the letters brought by him from your honour — letters which I had long desired to come, for no other reason than that we too might not add some gloomy tale to life, as though there were some separation among those most closely related to one another, providing pleasure to enemies, but misfortune to friends, and displeasing to God, who set perfect love as the mark of his own disciples. Therefore I too answer, necessarily exhorting you to pray for us, and in other respects to care for us as your own.

But since we ourselves, through want of understanding, are not able to comprehend the meaning of what is happening, we have judged it best to consider that account true which you yourself shall deign to set forth to us. And it is necessary that the remaining matters also be determined by your great wisdom: our meeting with one another, and the fitting time, and a suitable place. If, then, your dignity altogether deigns to come down to our lowliness, and to share some discourse with us — whether you wish the meeting to be with others or by yourself — we will obey, having once for all counselled ourselves to this: to serve you in love, and to do in every way the things enjoined upon us by your reverence for the glory of God. The most reverend brother we have in no way compelled to tell us anything by word of mouth, because his account was not previously borne witness to by his deeds.
To Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

I have read the letter of your holiness, in which you lament the governor of Libya, that man of ill-omened name. And we have bewailed our own country, that it is the mother and nurse of such evils; and we have bewailed also our neighbour Libya, reaping the harvest of our evils, and delivered over to the brutish character of a man who lives at once in cruelty and licentiousness. This, then, was the wisdom of the Preacher: "Woe to you, city, whose king is young" — and here there is something still more grievous — "and whose rulers eat not by night, but in the middle of the day are licentious," more irrational than the beasts, raging after the marriages of others. For that man the scourges await, from the just Judge, to be measured back to him in equal measure — the very scourges that he himself first laid upon God's saints.

He has been made known also to our Church by the letter of your godliness, and all will count him a thing accursed, sharing with him neither fire, nor water, nor shelter — if indeed any good comes to those so possessed by such evil from a common and unanimous condemnation. Sufficient for him is this pillar of record, even the very letters being read everywhere. For we shall not cease to display them to all his kindred and friends and strangers; and assuredly, even if the penalties do not lay hold of him at once, as in the case of Pharaoh, yet at some later time they will bring him a heavy and painful retribution.
To the Church of Parnassus, a letter of consolation.

Following an ancient custom that has prevailed from a long succession, and showing forth to you the fruit of the Spirit, the love that is according to God, we visit your reverence by letter, sharing with you both the grief over what has befallen and the anxiety over the matters in hand. Concerning your griefs, then, we say only this much: that it is time for us to look to the precepts of the Apostle, and not to grieve "as do the rest, who have no hope"; yet neither to be unfeeling toward what has happened, but to feel the loss, while not sinking down under grief — counting the shepherd blessed in his end, as one who closed his life in a ripe old age and rests in the highest honours from the Lord.

Concerning the rest, we have this to exhort: that it is fitting, laying aside all dejection, to come to yourselves, and to rouse yourselves to the necessary provision for the Church, so that the holy God may take care of his own flock, and may grant you a shepherd according to his will, who will shepherd you with knowledge.
To the governor of Neocaesarea.

"The wise man, though he dwell far off in the land, though I never look upon him with my eyes, I judge a friend": this is a saying of Euripides the tragedian. So that, if — though a meeting face to face has not yet granted us the knowledge of your greatness of soul — we say that we are your friends and intimates, do not judge the word to be flattery. For we have report as the patron of our friendship, proclaiming your qualities with a loud voice to all men. Yet from the time when we met the most reverend Elpidius, we came to know you so well, and were so utterly captivated by you, as though we had spent much time together and had knowledge of the good qualities in you through long trial. For the man did not cease recounting to us each of the things concerning you: the magnificence of your soul, the loftiness of your mind, the gentleness of your ways, your experience in affairs, your judicious understanding, the dignity of your life tempered with cheerfulness, the power of your speech, and all else that he himself enumerated through much converse with us, but which it was not possible for us to write, lest we draw out the letter beyond measure. How, then, should I not love such a man? How could I master myself so as not to make plain, even with a loud cry, the feeling of my soul?

Receive, then, this address, O admirable man, offered to you out of true and guileless friendship; for our ways are far from slavish flattery. And hold us numbered in the list of your own friends, showing yourself by frequent letters and consoling us for your absence.
To Hesychius.

There were many things from the first that bound me to your honour: the common love for letters, often spoken of by those who have made trial of you, and our long-standing friendship with that admirable man Terentius. But when that man who is best in all things, and who fulfils for us every name of close kinship, the most reverend brother Elpidius, came to speak with us, and recounted each of the good qualities in you — and he is most able, if anyone is, both to understand a man's virtue and to set it forth in words — he so kindled in us the longing for you, that we pray you may one day come to our old hearth, so that not by hearsay only but by experience we may enjoy the good qualities in you.
To Atarbius.

And what end will there be to silence, if I, claiming the privileges due to age, should wait for the beginning of the address to come from you, while your charity should wish to persist still longer in the harmful resolve of keeping quiet? Yet nevertheless I, having reckoned that defeat in matters of friendship has the force of victory, confess that I yield to you the ambition of seeming to have prevailed over my own resolve. I myself have come first to writing, knowing that love bears all things, endures all things, nowhere seeks its own — and for this reason never falls. For he who in love submits to his neighbour is not abased. So then, that you too, at least for the time to come, showing forth the first and greatest fruit of the Spirit, love, may cast off the gloom of the angry, which you hint at toward us by your silence, and may take up joy in your heart, peace toward the brethren who are of one mind with you, zeal and care for the continuance of the Churches of the Lord. For know this: that if we do not take up an equal struggle on behalf of the Churches to that which those opposed to sound teaching maintain for their overthrow and utter destruction, there is nothing to prevent the truth from being swept away by the enemies and gone, and ourselves too from sharing in the judgment, unless with all zeal and eagerness, in concord with one another and in agreement according to God, we show all possible care for the union of the Churches.

I exhort you, then: cast out from your soul the thought that you need no other for communion. For it is not the part of one who walks in love, nor of one who fulfils the commandment of Christ, to cut himself off from union with the brethren. And at the same time I wish your good purpose to consider this also: that the evil of war, going round in a circle, may one day enter even to us; and if, along with the others, we too share in the injury, we shall not find any to grieve with us, because in the time of our prosperity we did not first lay down for the wronged the contribution of fellow-feeling.
To Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

I think that no one is so greatly grieved by the present condition of the Churches — or rather, to speak more truly, their confusion — as your honour: comparing the present with the ancient state, and considering by how much these things differ from those, and that, if affairs slip down toward the worse with the same momentum, there will be nothing to prevent the Churches from being utterly transformed within a short time into some other shape. These things I have often pondered with myself, that if the perversion of the Churches appears so pitiable to us, what kind of soul is it likely that one has over these matters who has had experience of the ancient stability and concord in the faith of the Churches of the Lord? But just as the greater part of the grief surrounds your perfection, so we think it fitting that the greater part of the care for the Churches should also belong to your wisdom. I myself have long known, according to the moderate grasp of affairs that is in me, having recognized one road of help for the Churches in our region: the agreement of the Western bishops. For if they were willing to display, on behalf of the diocese of our parts, the same zeal which they took up on behalf of one or two in the West who were detected in false doctrine, perhaps some benefit might come to the common cause, the rulers being abashed at the trustworthiness of the multitude, and the peoples everywhere following them without dispute.

Who, then, is more able than your understanding to accomplish these things? Who keener to discern what is needful? Who more practical in effecting what is useful? Who more sympathetic toward the affliction of the brethren? Who in all the West is more reverenced than your most venerable grey hairs? Leave behind some memorial to life worthy of your manner of conduct, most honoured father. Crown those countless contests on behalf of true religion with this one work. Send forth from the holy Church under you men powerful in sound teaching to the bishops in the West; relate to them the misfortunes that have overtaken us; suggest a manner of relief; become a Samuel to the Churches; suffer along with the peoples who are at war; offer up prayers for peace; ask grace from the Lord, to leave behind some memorial of peace to the Churches. I know that letters are weak as a means of counsel for so great a matter. But neither do you yourself need exhortation from others — no more than the noblest of athletes need the encouraging shouts of children — nor do we teach one who is ignorant, but we intensify the impulse of one who is already zealous.

For the rest of the East, then, perhaps you need also the cooperation of more men, and it is necessary to wait for those from the West. But the good order of the Church in Antioch plainly depends on your godliness — so as to manage some, to quiet others, and to give back its strength to the Church through agreement. For you yourself know more exactly than anyone that, according to the wisest of physicians, you ought to begin your treatment from the most vital parts. And what could be more vital to the Churches throughout the world than Antioch? If it should happen that this city returned to concord, nothing would prevent it, like a strong head, from supplying health to the whole body. And truly the ailments of that city need your wisdom and gospel sympathy; for it has not only been cut apart by the heretics, but is also torn asunder by those who claim to think the same things as one another. To unite these and to bring them together into the harmony of one body belongs to him alone who by his unspeakable power grants even to dry bones their return again to sinews and flesh. And in all things the Lord works great things through those worthy of him. Here too, then, we hope that the ministry of such great matters befits your greatness of soul: to calm the tumult of the people, to put an end to the partial leaderships, to subject all to one another in love, and to restore to the Church its ancient strength.
To Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

To me it seemed sufficient, in my former letter, to indicate this much to your honour: that all that is sound in the faith among the people of the holy Church of Antioch must be brought into one agreement and union — meaning thereby to make clear that the parts now divided into many should be joined to the most God-loving bishop Meletius. But since this same beloved fellow-deacon of ours, Dorotheus, has sought a clearer expression on these matters, we necessarily note that it is the prayer of all the East, and is desired by us who are bound to him in every way, to see him guiding the Church of the Lord — being blameless in faith, admitting no comparison with the others in his life, and presiding, so to speak, over the body of the whole Church, while the rest are like the cut-off portions of parts.

So that from every side it is both necessary and profitable that the others be joined to this man, as the lesser rivers to the great; and that some arrangement be made concerning the others, fitting for them too, bringing peace to the people, and suited to your understanding and renowned skill and zeal. And surely it has not escaped your surpassing wisdom that these same things have already seemed good to those of like mind with you in the West, as the letters brought to us by the blessed Silvanus show.
To Meletius, bishop of Antioch.

For a while we wished to keep with ourselves the most reverend brother Dorotheus, the deacon, so that, sending him off at the conclusion of affairs, we might make known to your honour through him each of the things accomplished. But since, putting it off from day to day, we were drawn out to a great length of time, and at the same time, as happens in a difficult situation, some deliberation fell upon us concerning what should be done, we sent the aforesaid man to reach your holiness, both to report each matter himself and to show our memorandum, so that, if the things we have conceived should appear to be of use, they might be set to work with zeal by your perfection.
