To speak briefly, the resolve has prevailed that this same brother of ours, Dorotheus, should cross over to Rome, to rouse some of those from Italy to a visitation of us, going by sea so as to escape those who would hinder them. For I have seen that those in power beside the rulers neither wish nor are able to remind them concerning the men who have been cast out, but count it gain to see nothing worse happening in the Churches. If, then, the plan should commend itself as useful to your wisdom also, you will deign both to draft letters and to dictate memoranda concerning the matters about which he must speak, and to whom. And so that the letters may carry some trustworthiness, you will assuredly take along with you those of one mind, even if they are not present. Matters here are still uncertain, Euippius having arrived but as yet revealed nothing. They threaten, however, a gathering of those of like mind with them, both from Armenia of the Tetrapolis and from Cilicia.
To Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

The opinion which we have long held concerning your honour, the passing of time always confirms; nay, it even increases it by the additions of the particulars that occur from time to time. For while it suffices for most of the others that each should look to his own affairs, this is not enough for you, but your care for all the Churches is as great as the care that lies upon you for the one entrusted to you personally by our common Master. For you let no time pass without conversing, admonishing, writing, and sending out men on every occasion to suggest what is best. And now too we have received with great joy the most reverend brother Peter, sent forth from the sacred body of the clergy under you, and we have approved the good purpose of his journey, which he shows forth according to the instructions of your honour, drawing in those who resist and joining together what has been torn apart. Whence we too, wishing to contribute something to the zeal for this matter, thought we should give a most fitting beginning to affairs if, as to the summit of all, we should run up to your perfection, and use you both as counsellor and as guide of our actions. Therefore we have also sent up to your godliness the brother Dorotheus, deacon of the Church under the most honoured bishop Meletius, a man possessed of good zeal for the rightness of the faith, and himself desiring to see the peace of the Churches, so that, following your suggestions — which you are able to make safer both by your age and by your experience of affairs, and by having beyond others the counsel that comes from the Spirit — he may thus set his hand to the things being undertaken.

Him you will of course receive, and will look upon with peaceful eyes, supporting him by the help of your prayers, and furnishing him with letters, or rather even yoking to him some of the zealous men there, and so guide him to the matters before us. It has seemed fitting to us also to write to the bishop of Rome, that he should examine the affairs here and give his opinion; so that, since it is difficult for some to be sent from there by a common and synodical decree, he himself should take authority in the matter, choosing out men able both to bear the toils of the journey and, by gentleness and firmness of character, to admonish the perverse among us — men who use speech suitably and prudently, and have with them all the proceedings after Ariminum, for the annulling of what was done there under compulsion; and this, with no one knowing, that they should arrive among us here silently by sea, so as to forestall the notice of the enemies of peace.

This too is sought by some of those here, necessarily, as it appears even to us ourselves: that they should banish the heresy of Marcellus as grievous and harmful and alien to the sound faith. For up to now, in all the letters they write, they do not cease anathematizing on every side and banishing from the Churches that ill-named Arius; but against Marcellus, who showed forth an impiety diametrically opposed to his, and was impious against the very existence of the Only-begotten's Godhead, and wrongly understood the title of the Word, they appear to bring no censure at all. He grants that the Only-begotten is called Word, having come forth according to need and on occasion, but again having returned to him from whom he came forth — neither existing before the going forth, nor subsisting after the return. And the proof of this is found in the books of that unjust composition laid up with us. Yet nevertheless they have nowhere appeared to censure him, and that too while bearing the charge of having received him from the first, in ignorance of the truth, into ecclesiastical communion. The present circumstances, then, fittingly require that he be mentioned, so that those who want a pretext may have no pretext, and so that, by joining the sound to your holiness, they may make plain to all those who waver toward the true faith; so that for the future we may know those of one mind with us, and not, as in a night-battle, have no distinction between friends and enemies. We only beg that the aforesaid deacon be sent out immediately on the first sailing, so that at least in the coming year something may be done of the things for which we pray.

That other matter you will of course understand and attend to even before our words: that those who arrive, if God will, should not leave the schisms in the Churches, but should by every means drive together into union those who think the same things, even if they find some holding occasions of private differences with one another — so that the orthodox people may not be cut into many parts by joining in the secession of their leaders. For we must be zealous to count all things second to peace, and above all to take care of the Church in Antioch, so that the right party in it should not be weakened by being split over persons. Or rather, you yourself will attend to all these things later, when, as we pray, with God working with you, you take all men as entrusting to you the settlement of the Churches.
Without inscription, concerning a synod.

To renew the bonds of ancient love, and to bring back again to its prime the peace of the fathers — that heavenly and saving gift of Christ, withered by time — is necessary for us and profitable, and I well know that it will appear delightful also to your Christ-loving disposition. For what could be more gracious than to behold those divided by so great a number of places bound, through the union of love, into one harmony of members in the body of Christ? Almost the whole East, most honoured father — by the East I mean the regions from Illyricum as far as Egypt — is shaken by a great storm and surge, since the heresy long ago sown by the enemy of the truth, Arius, but now sprung up to shamelessness and yielding, like some bitter root, its deadly fruit, now prevails. This is because the leaders of right doctrine in each diocese have fallen from the Churches through slander and ill-treatment, and the strength of affairs has been delivered over to those who take captive the souls of the more simple. We expected one deliverance from these things: the visitation of your compassion. And the marvel of your love in time past has ever cheered our souls, and for a little while we were strengthened in spirit by a brighter report, as though some visitation from you would come to us. But when we failed of this hope, no longer able to bear it, we have come to entreat you by our letter to rouse yourselves to our aid, and to send some of those of one mind with you — either to reconcile those at variance, or to bring back the Churches of God to friendship, or at least to make the authors of the disorder more plain to you; so that for the future it may be clear to you also with whom it is fitting to have communion.

We seek nothing new at all, but what was customary to the rest of the blessed and God-loving men of old, and especially to you. For we know, by the succession of memory — being taught both by our fathers who were asked, and from letters preserved among us even now — that that most blessed bishop Dionysius, who shone among you for rightness of faith and for the rest of his virtue, visited our Church of Caesarea by letters, and exhorted our fathers by letters, and sent ransom for the brotherhood who were being redeemed from captivity. But now our affairs are in a more grievous and gloomy state, and need greater care. For we lament not the overthrow of earthly buildings, but the capture of Churches; nor a bodily slavery, but a captivity of souls, worked each day by the champions of the heresy. So that, unless you rouse yourselves at once to our aid, a little later you will not even find those to whom you may stretch out your hand, when all have come under the dominion of the heresy.
Basil to Gregory.

I received the letter of your reverence by the most reverend brother Hellenius; and what you hinted to us, he himself related plainly. And when you have heard how we were disposed, you will surely have no doubt. But nevertheless, since we have resolved to make our love for you higher than all grief, we received even these things as was fitting, and we pray the holy God that the remaining days or hours may be so preserved in our disposition toward you, as also in the time past, in which we are conscious of having failed ourselves in nothing, whether small or great.

But if a certain person, lately ambitious to peer into the life of Christians, and then thinking it brings him some dignity to rub shoulders with us, both fabricates what he never heard and expounds what he never understood, there is nothing to wonder at. But this is the wondrous and astonishing thing: that he has as hearers of these things the most genuine to me of the brethren among you — and not hearers only, but disciples, as it seems. Even if it were otherwise astonishing that such a man should be the teacher and I the one torn to pieces, yet the overturning of the times has trained us not to be vexed at anything. For long ago things more dishonouring than these became familiar to us, on account of our sins. I, then, if I have not yet given his brethren proof of my doctrine concerning God, have nothing to answer even now; for those whom the long time did not persuade, how shall a brief letter convince? But if those proofs are sufficient, let the words of the slanderers be reckoned as nonsense. Except for this: that if we permit unbridled mouths and untaught hearts to speak of whatever they wish, and have our ears ready to receive it, not only shall we accept what belongs to others, but others too will accept what is ours.

The cause of these things is that which I long ago exhorted should not be — and now, despairing, I keep silent about it — namely, that we do not meet one another. For if, according to the ancient compacts, and according to the care now owed by us to the Churches, we passed the greater part of the year with one another, we should not have given an opening to the slanderers. But you, if you please, let these men go, and be entreated yourself to labour together with us in the contest before us, and to meet, along with us, him who wages war against us. For if you only appear, you will check his impulse, and break up those banded together for the overthrow of our country's affairs, making it known to them that you yourself, by the grace of God, take the lead of our assembly, and you will stop every unjust mouth of those who speak iniquity against God. If this happens, the very facts will show who follows you in good things, and who turns aside and through cowardice betrays the word of truth. But if the affairs of the Church are being betrayed, I have little concern to persuade by words those who value me at so much as men, not yet taught to measure themselves, may esteem me. For before long, by the grace of God, the demonstration through deeds will refute the slanders; since we expect, for the sake of the word of truth, perhaps to suffer something even greater — but if not, certainly to be driven out of the Churches and our country. And if none of the things expected should happen, the tribunal of Christ is not far off. So that, if you seek a meeting for the sake of the Churches, I am ready to hasten wherever you may summon me; but if it is that I should refute the slanders, I have no leisure now to answer concerning these things.
To Hesychius.

I know both your love for us and your zeal for what is good. Therefore, needing to prevail upon the most beloved son Callisthenes, I thought that, if I took you as a partner in the matter, I should more easily accomplish what I am eager for. The man has been aggrieved against the most learned Eustochius, and aggrieved with a just grievance. He charges his servants with insolence and madness against him. Him we ask to be persuaded — content with the fear with which he frightened both the insolent men themselves and their masters — to put an end to the quarrel by granting the favour. For thus both things will be his: dignity in the eyes of men, and good repute in the eyes of God, if he is willing to mix forbearance with the fear. Do you yourself, then, if there is any prior friendship and intimacy of yours toward the man, ask this favour from him; and whomever you know in the city to be able to prevail upon him, take as partners in the matter, telling them that what is done will be most gratifying to me.
And send back the fellow-deacon, having accomplished the things for which he was sent. For I am ashamed, when men have taken refuge with me, not to be able to be of any use to them.
To Callisthenes.

I gave thanks to God on reading the letter of your nobility: first, because an address came to me from a man who chooses to honour us — for we count the converse of the best men worth much; and second, as a cause for gladness, that I meet with good remembrance. And the token of remembrance is a letter, which, when I had received it and learned the meaning in it, I marvelled how truly, according to the opinion of all, you rendered me a father's reverence. For that, though inflamed and angered and having set out for vengeance on those who had grieved you, you yet relaxed much of your vehemence, and made us masters of the matter, gave us cause to rejoice as over a spiritual child. In return for these things, then, what else remains but to pray good things for you? That you may be most pleasant to friends, terrible to enemies, and to all alike worthy of reverence; so that those who have failed in any of their duties, perceiving the gentleness in you, may reproach themselves for having sinned against one so good.

Since, then, you have ordered the servants to be led to the place where they displayed their disorderly conduct, I ask to learn the purpose for which your kindness seeks this. For if you yourself will be present, and yourself exact the penalty for what was dared, the slaves will be present. For what else need happen, if this has been decided by you? But we shall not know what favour we shall have received, if we do not avail to rescue the slaves from punishment. But if your business on the highway detains you, who is there to receive the men there? Who is to punish them in your stead? Yet if it seems good to you that they come into your sight, and this has been fully decided, command their appearance to be at Sasima, and there show the gentleness and magnanimity of your character. For having taken in hand those who provoked you, and having in this shown the negligible esteem of your dignity, let them go unharmed, as we asked in our former letter — giving us the favour, and awaiting from God the recompense for what you do.

And I say these things, not as though the matter ought so to be concluded, but yielding to your impulse, and fearing lest something undigested of your anger remain; and just as, in the case of inflamed eyes, even the gentlest of remedies seems painful, so now too our word may exasperate you rather than calm you. For the most seemly thing — able to bring you the greatest honour, and sufficient for me as a matter of dignity before my own friends and contemporaries — would be that the vindication be entrusted to us. But surely, even if it has been sworn by you to give them up for punishment according to the laws, neither is our reproof less effective for vindication, nor is the divine law less honourable than the statutes current in life.

But it was possible that they, being here turned to our laws — in which you yourself too have the hope of salvation — should both free you from the necessity of your oath, and themselves fulfil a penalty proportionate to the offences.

But again I make the letter long. For out of my great eagerness to be persuasive to you, I cannot bear to pass over in silence any of the things that come to mind, fearing lest on this account my request become ineffectual, my instruction having been made deficient. But, O most honoured and genuine nursling of the Church, confirm for me too the hopes which I now have in you, and the testimonies of all, in harmony, concerning your good temper and gentleness; and write to the soldier to depart from us quickly, who has now left nothing undone of grievance and insolence, choosing rather not to grieve you than to have all of us as his own and as friends.
To Martinianus.

At how great a price do you think I would value our coming together one day, and being longer in your company, so as to enjoy all the good qualities in you? For if it is a great proof of culture "to have seen the cities of many men and to have known their mind," I think your conversation grants this in a short time. For what difference is there between seeing many men one by one, or one who has taken up in himself the experience of them all? Rather, I would say that there is even a very great difference, in that it procures a knowledge of good things without toil, and gathers the history of virtue pure from any admixture of the worse. For whether it be an excellent deed, or a saying worthy of remembrance, or the polities of men surpassing others, all is laid up in the storehouse of your soul. So that not for a year only, as Alcinous listened to Odysseus, but for all my life I would pray to listen to you, and on this account at least this life would seem long to me, even though I am ill-disposed toward it. Why, then, do I write now, when I ought to be present? Because my suffering country urges me to herself. For what she has suffered, you are not ignorant, my excellent friend: that, in the manner of Pentheus, certain real Maenads, demons, have torn her apart. For they divide her, and divide her again — like the bad physicians, making the wounds more grievous by their own inexperience. Since, then, she is worn out with being cut up, it remains to tend her, as one who is sick. The citizens, therefore, have written urging us; and it is necessary to go to meet them, not as men who will be of any use to affairs, but as those who avoid the blame that comes from absence. For you know how ready to hope are those in distress, and how ready, too, to find fault, ever turning their accusations upon what has been neglected.

And yet for this very reason I had need to come together with you and to obtain your opinion; or rather, to entreat you to devise something vigorous and befitting your spirit, and not to overlook our country brought to her knees, but to reach the camp and say, with that frankness which is yours, that they should not think they have gained two provinces instead of one. For they did not bring in the second from some other inhabited world, but have done something very like what one would do who, possessing a horse or an ox, should then cut it in two and think he had two instead of one; for he has not made two, and has destroyed the one. Say also to those in power that they do not increase the kingdom in this way, for power lies not in number but in actual resources. Since now we suppose that some, perhaps through ignorance of the truth, others through not wishing to grieve by their words, and others because they do not care, overlook what is being done. If, then, it were possible for him to come to the emperor, this would be best for affairs, and befitting your noble purpose in life. But if it is otherwise burdensome, both because of the season of the year and because of your age, which, as you yourself said, has reluctance bred in it, yet at least to write costs no toil. So that, granting to your country the help that comes from letters, first you will be conscious to yourself of having left undone nothing of what lay in your power, and then too you will give sufficient consolation to the suffering, by the very appearance of sharing their pain. But would that it were possible for you, standing over the affairs, to take in with your eyes the gloomy sights themselves. For thus perhaps, moved by the very vividness of what is seen, you would have uttered some voice befitting both your great mind and the dejection of the city. But as for us who relate these things, do not disbelieve us. Or is it that we truly needed a Simonides, or some such lyric poet, skilled to lament over sufferings vividly? And yet why do I speak of Simonides? I ought rather to say Aeschylus, or whoever else, like him, vividly setting forth the magnitude of a calamity, lamented it with a loud voice.

For those assemblies and discourses, the meetings of distinguished men in the market-place, and all that formerly made our city renowned, have failed us; so that one of those concerned with learning and letters would now be less likely to set foot in the market-place than formerly at Athens those condemned to disgrace, or those whose hands were not clean. In their place has been brought in the boorishness of certain Scythians or Massagetae; and there is one voice, of those demanding payment and those demanded of and those torn with scourges. The porticoes on either side, echoing dismally, seem to give forth a voice of their own, lamenting over what is happening. The gymnasia are closed, and the nights are without light, and the struggle for mere life does not let us reckon anything. For the danger is no slight one: that, when the men in power have been withdrawn, all things may be brought down together, like props that have fallen. And what account could reach our evils? Some have gone off in flight, a part of our council, and not the meanest, having preferred perpetual exile to Podandus. And when I say Podandus, think that I mean the Spartan Ceadas, or, if anywhere in the world you have seen a natural pit — such as some have spontaneously taken to calling Charonian, breathing out an air that breeds disease — count the evil of Podandus to be like some such thing. Of the three parts, then, some flee, having removed themselves with their very wives and hearths; others are led off like captives, the most and the best of those in the city, a pitiable sight to friends, but fulfilling a prayer for enemies — if indeed there has been anyone at all who has so cursed us. A third part, somewhere, is left; and these, both not bearing the loss of their familiar friends, and at the same time being proved too feeble for the need, have given up on life itself.

These things we exhort you to make plain to all by your own voice and your own just frankness, which you have from your life, declaring clearly beforehand that, unless they quickly change their counsel, they will not even have any toward whom to display their humanity. For either you will be of some use to the common cause, or you will at least have done what Solon did, who, when he could not defend the citizens who were left behind, the acropolis being already held, put on his arms and sat before his doors, plain by his very posture as not consenting to what was happening. But this I know exactly: that even if someone now should not accept your opinion, a little later it will add to you the greatest reputation both for goodwill and for understanding, when he sees affairs turn out according to your prediction.
To Aburgius.

Many as are the things that have made your character surpass that of others, nothing is so peculiarly your own as your zeal for your country, since you render to her the just recompense — to her from whom you set out and became so great that your distinction is known throughout the whole inhabited world. This country, then, which bore and nourished you, has come round to the incredibility of the old tales; and one who came upon our city, even among those most familiar with it, would not recognize her, so utterly has she been changed all at once into complete desolation, many of those engaged in public affairs having been taken from her even before, and now nearly all having been removed to Podandus. Mutilated of these, those who are left have themselves also fallen into utter despair, and have engendered in all so great a weight of dejection that the city is now scant even of inhabitants, and the place here has become a dreadful desolation — a pitiable sight to friends, but bringing much joy and gladness to those who long ago lay in wait for our downfall. Whose part, then, is it to stretch out a hand to us? Or whose to shed a sympathetic tear over us, but your gentleness, who would sympathize even with a strange city suffering such things, much more with the one that brought you into life? If, then, there is any power in you, show it to us now, in the present need. And surely you have great weight with God, who has on no occasion forsaken you, and has given you many proofs of his favour toward you; only if you are willing fully to rouse yourself to the care of us, and to use the power that is yours for the help of your fellow citizens.
To Sophronius the Master.

The greatness of the calamities that have overtaken my native country compelled me, when I reached the camp, to lay before your nobility of soul, and before all the rest of you who hold the highest power over affairs, the despondency that grips our city. But since bodily illness and the care of the churches detain me, I have hastened, for the time being, to pour out my grief in writing to your magnanimity, knowing well that no ship swallowed up by violent winds in the open sea ever vanished so suddenly, no city ground to nothing by earthquakes or flooded over by waters ever passed into so instantaneous a ruin, as ours has been engulfed by this strange new ordering of affairs and reduced to utter destruction. Our condition has become a byword. For our civic body is gone; and the whole order of the city, abandoning, in its dejection toward the rulers, its dwelling in the town, now wanders through the countryside. Even the provision of necessities has at last failed, and altogether a most untimely spectacle has come about: a city that once gloried in its men of learning and in everything else by which prosperous cities live free from want.

We have judged that one consolation, as far as is possible amid such evils, remains to us: to groan over our sufferings to your gentleness, and to entreat you, if there be any power to do so, to stretch out a hand to our city, which has been brought to its knees. As for the means by which you might come to the aid of our affairs at the right moment, I myself am not able to suggest it; but for you, by your sagacity, it will be altogether easy to find it, and, by the power given you from God, no hard matter to make use of what you have found.
Without address, concerning Therasius.

This one benefit, among others, we have enjoyed from the good government of the great Therasius: the frequent visits of your eloquence to us. And in this very same thing we have suffered loss, now that we are deprived of the governor. But since whatever has once been granted to us by God remains secure and dwells in one another's souls through memory, even if we are separated in body, let us at least write to one another continually and speak of what is necessary, and most of all now, when the winter has concluded this brief truce.

We hope that you will not desert that most admirable man Therasius, having judged it fitting to share in such cares with him; or rather, that you will gladly welcome a pretext, even an unnecessary one, that affords you the chance both to see your friends and to be seen by them. Though I have much to say, and about many matters, I have put it off until our meeting, since I do not think it safe to entrust such things to letters.
Without address, on behalf of Elpidius.

Your good zeal on behalf of our most reverend companion Elpidius has not escaped us — how, with your customary discernment, you gave the governor an occasion for kindness. We now beg you, by this letter, to bring that favour to completion, and to remind the governor to settle the man in our native country by his own order, with nearly the whole charge of public affairs hanging upon him. Thus you will have many specious pretexts to put before the governor, on the strength of which he will of necessity command the man to remain in our country. As for how things stand here, and how valuable the man is to our affairs, you will by no means need to be told by us, since you yourself, by your own discernment, know it exactly.
To Eustathius, bishop of Sebasteia.

Even before receiving your letter, I knew the labour you undergo on behalf of every soul, and especially on behalf of our lowliness, since I have been set forward in this contest. And when I received the letter from the most reverend Eleusinius, and beheld his very presence, I gave glory to the Divine for granting us such a champion and comrade-in-arms, through spiritual aid, in the struggles for true religion. Let your unsurpassable godliness know that up to now certain assaults have been made against us by the great rulers — and violent ones — the prefect and the official of the bedchamber having spoken with personal feeling on behalf of the opposing party; but that so far, by the mercy of God, we have endured every assault unshaken, He having granted us the cooperation of the Spirit and through Him strengthened our weakness.
To Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

The further the maladies of the churches advance toward the worse, the more all of us turn to your perfection, persuaded that there remains to us one consolation amid our troubles: your patronage. By the power of your prayers, and by your knowledge of how to counsel what is best in our affairs, you are believed — by all alike who know your perfection even a little, whether by report or by experience — to be the one who will bring us safe through this fearful storm. Do not, then, slacken in praying for our souls and in rousing us by your letters; for if you knew how great their benefit is, you would never let pass an opportunity of writing to us. And if we should be counted worthy, through the cooperation of your prayers, to see you and to enjoy the good things in you, and to add to the history of our life the meeting with your truly great and apostolic soul, we should reckon that for all we have suffered in our whole life we had received, from the loving-kindness of God, a consolation to counterbalance it.
To Bishop Innocent.

As glad as I was to receive the letter of your love, so much was I grieved that you have laid upon us a burden of anxiety that is beyond our strength. For how could we, across so great a distance, take in hand so great an administration? While the Church still has you, it rests upon you as upon its own supports; but if the Lord should ordain something concerning your life, whom can I send from here, of rank equal to yours, for the care of the brethren? What you sought in your letter you sought well and prudently, wishing to see, while still alive, the man who is to govern after you the chosen flock of the Lord — a thing that the blessed Moses also both desired and saw. Since, then, the place is great and renowned, and your own work is named among many, and the times are hard, requiring a great helmsman because of the continual squalls and the surging waves that rise up against the Church, I did not think it safe for my own soul to deal with the matter carelessly, remembering above all what you wrote — that you mean to stand against me before the Lord and to call me to judgment for the neglect of the churches.

That I may not, then, come into judgment with you, but rather find you a sharer in my defence before Christ, I looked round about in the council of the presbyterate in the city, and chose out the most honoured vessel, the grandson of the blessed Hermogenes, who wrote the great and unbreakable creed at the great synod: a presbyter of the church now these many years, steadfast in character, experienced in the canons, exact in the faith, living to this day in self-control and ascetic discipline — even though the strictness of his hard life has by now worn away his flesh; poor, with no means of livelihood in this world, so that he does not even have a sufficiency of bread, but weaves out his life by the labour of his hands together with the brethren who dwell with him. It is my wish to send you this man.

If, then, you yourself have need of such a man — and not merely of some younger man fit only to be sent about and to carry out the needs of daily life — be so good as to write to me quickly, at the first opportunity, that I may send you this man, who is chosen of God and fit for the task, reverend to those who meet him, and one who instructs his opponents with gentleness. I could indeed have sent him at once; but since you had already, in advance, asked for a man — in other respects good and dear to us, but falling far short of the man I have described — I wished to make my own mind plain to you, so that, if you have need of such a man, you may either send one of the brethren to escort him during the fasts, or write to us, if you have no one able to bear the toil of the journey as far as us.
To Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

When we look at the state of things and observe the difficulties by which every good activity is hindered and held back as if by some chain, we come to utter despair of ourselves. But when, on the other hand, we look to your venerable dignity and reflect that the Lord has reserved you as a physician of the maladies in the churches, we take up our reasonings again, and rise up from the fall of despair to the hope of better things. The whole Church is dissolved, as not even your wisdom is unaware. And you surely see what is happening everywhere, as if from some high watchtower of mental contemplation: how, just as on the open sea, when many are sailing together, by the force of the swell all are dashed against one another, and shipwreck follows — partly from the outward cause that violently stirs the sea, partly from the confusion of those aboard, who oppose and thrust at one another. Let it suffice to leave the matter at the image, since neither does your wisdom permit anything more, nor does the present condition allow us freedom of speech. And for these things who is a sufficient helmsman? Who is trustworthy enough to rouse the Lord to rebuke the wind and the sea? Who but the man who from boyhood has wrestled in the contests for true religion?

Since, then, all among us that is sound in the faith has now set itself in earnest toward fellowship and union with those of like belief, we have come with confidence to the entreaty of your long-suffering: to write one letter to us all, containing an exhortation of what must be done. For so they wish the beginning of these communications of fellowship to come to them from you. But since perhaps they appear suspect to you, through the memory of what is past, do this, most God-loving father: send to me the letters to the bishops, either by one of the faithful from there, or also by the brother Dorotheus, our fellow deacon; and having received them, I will not deliver them earlier — not until I have received the replies from them. But if not, I shall have sinned against you all the days of my life. And surely this is no more to be feared than what he said of old to the father, or what I now say to you, my spiritual father. But if this is in every way forbidden by you, at least free us from the blame attaching to the embassy, since it is without guile and without contrivance, out of a longing for peace and for our union with one another among those of one mind in the things pertaining to the Lord, that we have come to this mediation and intercession.
To a Tax Assessor.

My familiarity with your nobility, and our meeting face to face, has been very brief; but the knowledge gained from hearsay, through which we are joined to many of the eminent, is neither slight nor to be despised. And whether you, too, have some account of us from report, you would yourself know better. What we have of you, in any case, is such as I have said. Since God has called you to a task that offers occasion for kindness — through which it is possible to set right our native country, which has been utterly levelled to the ground — I think it fitting for me to remind your goodness of this, so that, in hope of the recompense from God, you may be willing to show yourself such a man as both to be counted worthy of undying remembrance and to become an heir of eternal rest, by making the afflictions of the hard-pressed lighter.

And since I too have a property near Chamanene, I ask you to take it under your protection as your own. Do not be surprised if I call my friends' affairs my own; for, along with my other training in virtue, I have also been schooled in friendship, and I remember the wise saying that a friend is another self. The property, then, that belongs to this man I commend to your honour as my own; and I beg you, having looked into the household's difficulties, to grant them some relief for the years that are past, and for the future to make their dwelling-place desirable to them — that dwelling which is now to be shunned and renounced because of the weight of the assessment laid upon it. I shall myself take care, when I have met with your good order, to speak more fully about each particular.
To a Governor.

What I am about to write is almost incredible, yet it shall be written for truth's sake: that, though I had every desire to converse with your nobility of character as often as possible, when I found this occasion of writing I did not run to the godsend, but hung back and shrank from it. The paradox in this is that the very things I prayed might come about, when they came, I would not accept. The reason is that I am ashamed to seem to write not purely for the sake of friendship, but always to be tending some need of my own. But this thought came to me — and I want you, too, to weigh it, so that you may by no means suppose that we hold our conversations in a trading rather than a friendly spirit — that the addresses we make to rulers must have something different about them from those made to private men. For we are not to approach a physician and any chance person in the same way, nor likewise a ruler and a private man; rather we must try to draw benefit from the one through his art, and from the other through his authority, for our own affairs. Just as, then, the shadow follows of necessity those who walk in the sun, even if they do not choose it, so too something of profit follows upon our dealings with rulers — the help given to those in distress.

Let the first cause of the letter, then, be fulfilled by the very act of greeting your magnanimity. This, even when no pretext for writing is added, must itself be reckoned a good chief point. Be greeted, therefore, by us, best of men, and may you be preserved your whole life long, exchanging office for office and benefiting now these, now those, by your governorships. For this is my custom to do, and it is owed to you by all who have experienced, even a little, your excellence in ruling.

After the prayer, receive also the supplication on behalf of the wretched old man, whom an imperial rescript released from public duties; or rather, even before the emperor, old age itself granted him the necessary exemption. And you yourself confirmed the grace from above, out of reverence for nature and, as I think, out of forethought for public affairs, lest, through a man whose mind is failing with age, some of the common business should come to harm.

But by another road, again, how did it escape you, admirable man, that you have brought him back into the midst of affairs? For his grandson, not yet in his fourth year from birth, you have ordered to take part in the council-chamber; and what else is this but to bring the old man, through his grandchild, once more from the beginning into public service? But now we entreat you to take pity on both ages, and to release both, because of the pitiable circumstances belonging to each. The one has not seen his parents, nor known them, but came into this life through others' hands, orphaned of both straight from his swaddling-clothes; the other has been so reserved by life that no form of misfortune has passed him by. For he has looked upon the untimely death of a son; he has seen his house bereft of heirs; and he will now look — unless you yourself devise something worthy of your loving-kindness — upon the only consolation of his childlessness becoming for him the occasion of countless evils. For surely the little child will not pay the councillors' dues, or collect the levies, or furnish the soldiers' rations; rather, the gray hairs of the wretched old man must again be put to shame. Grant, then, a favour both consistent with the laws and in accord with nature: ordering that the one be granted respite until he reaches the age of manhood, and that the other be allowed to await death upon his bed. As for the unbroken press of affairs and the inexorable claim of necessity, let others put these forward. For it is not of your character either to overlook those in distress, or to make light of the laws, or to fail to yield to friends who earnestly entreat you — even were the affairs of men to press hard upon you.
That oaths must not be imposed.

We do not cease, at every synod, to protest, and privately in our meetings to discourse upon the same things — namely, that oaths over the public payments should not be imposed by the collectors upon the country people. It remained also, by letter, to bear witness about the same things before God and men: that it is right for you to cease bringing death upon the souls of men, and to devise some other means of collecting the dues, while allowing men to keep their souls unwounded. We write this to you, not as though you needed exhortation from words — for you have within yourself the grounds for fearing the Lord — but that through you all who give heed to you may be taught not to provoke the Holy One to wrath, nor to drag down a forbidden thing, through evil custom, into a matter of indifference. For these oaths are of no use to the collectors in respect of the dues, while they take upon their souls an admitted evil. For when men have once practised perjury, they no longer press themselves toward payment, but suppose that in the oath they have found a weapon of deceit and an occasion of delay.

Whether, then, the Lord brings swift retribution upon those who have sworn falsely — in which case they will have none left to obey, since those who are liable have been consumed by the punishment — or whether the Master bears with them in long-suffering (which, as I said before, is just why those who have experienced the Lord's forbearance despise His kindness) — let them not transgress to no purpose, nor provoke God against themselves.
We have said what falls to us; those who are disobedient will see to the rest.
To the Governor.

I know that it is the greatest and first concern of your honour to favour justice in every way, and the second, both to do good to your friends and to take up the cause of those who flee to the patronage of your magnanimity. All these, then, have run together to the same point in the present matter. For the affair on whose behalf we make our plea is just; and it is a favour to us, whom you have deigned to number among your own friends; and it is owed to those who call upon your firmness for help in what they have suffered.

Some of those entrusted with the management of public affairs at Berisi have plundered the grain — which was all that our most beloved brother Dorotheus had for the necessary sustenance of life — whether coming to the violence of their own accord, or with others prompting them. In any case, the deed is in no way free of blame to them; for in what is the man who is wicked of himself less guilty than the man who serves the wickedness of others? And to those who have suffered, the loss is the same. This man we ask that he may recover what was taken from him, and that they may not be permitted to lay the blame for their outrages upon others. And by however much it is worth to escape the necessity that comes of want of grain, by so much shall we value the favour from your nobility of soul, if indeed you deign to grant it.
Without address, on behalf of the same persons.

I marvelled how, with you acting as mediator, so great an evil could be dared against our fellow presbyter — that the only resource he had for his livelihood should be plundered; and what is most outrageous of all, that those who dared this lay upon you the blame for what they have done. For you it was fitting not only not to permit such things to happen, but with all your might to prevent them — most of all against all men, but if not, at least against the presbyters, and of these such as are of one soul with us and walk the same road of true religion. If, then, you have any care to give us relief, see that what has been done is quickly set right. For with God's help you can set right both these things and even greater than these, in whatever matters you wish. I have also written to the ruler of our native country, so that, if they are unwilling of their own accord to do what is just, they may be compelled to do it by the action of the courts.
Without address, to a collector of money.

The difficulty of gathering in the commercial gold your honour has come to understand better than anyone; and of our poverty we have no such witness as you, who out of your great loving-kindness have both sympathized with us and borne with us, as far as you could, up to the present, nowhere letting the gentleness of your settled character be moved by the disturbance of those set over you from above. Since, then, there remains to us out of the whole assessment only a little gold still, and this must be gathered from the contribution to which we have urged the whole city, we beg your gentleness to extend our term a little, so that those outside the city, too, may be reminded; for the greater part of those in office are in the country, as you yourself are not unaware. If, then, it is possible for so many pounds to be sent off — for that is what remains to us — we beg that this be done, and the rest will be dispatched afterward. But if there is every necessity that it all be conveyed to the treasury at once, then, as we asked from the beginning, let our term be made wider for us.
To Meletius, bishop of Antioch.

The good God, by affording us pretexts for addressing your honour, soothes the vehemence of our longing. For He Himself is witness of the desire we have to behold your face, and to enjoy your good and soul-profiting teaching. And now, by the most reverent and most diligent brother Dorotheus, our fellow deacon, who is coming to you, we beg you first of all to pray for us, that we may not be a stumbling-block to the people, nor a hindrance to your prayers in moving the Lord. Next, we remind you to be willing to set in order everything through the aforesaid brother; and if anything must be written to those in the West — since letters must of necessity be carried to them by one of our own people also — to dictate the letters yourself. For we, having met with Sabinus, the deacon sent by them, wrote to the Illyrians and to the bishops in Italy and Gaul, and to certain of those who had written to us privately. And it is reasonable that someone be sent, as from the common body of the synod, to carry a second set of letters, which you yourself should order to be drawn up.

And concerning the most reverend bishop Athanasius we remind your perfect wisdom, which knows it exactly, that it is impossible by my letters to make any progress, or to do any of the things that are owed, unless he receives some treatment also from you — from those who at that time deferred his communion. For he himself is said to be very eager to be joined to us, and to contribute what is in his power, but to be grieved that even then he was sent away without communion, and that still now the promises remain unfulfilled.

As for how things stand in the East, this has surely not escaped the ears of your godliness, and the aforesaid brother will himself relate everything more exactly in person. Be so good as to send him off at once after Easter, since he must await the replies from Samosata; welcome his eagerness, and, having strengthened him with prayers, send him forward to the tasks before him.
To the most holy brethren and bishops in the West.

The good God, who ever yokes consolations to afflictions, has given us even now, amid the multitude of our pains, to find some measure of comfort in the letters which our most honoured father, Bishop Athanasius, received from your uprightness and forwarded to us — letters that bear witness to a sound faith and give proof of your unassailable concord and harmony of spirit, so as to show forth shepherds who follow in the footprints of the fathers and who shepherd the people of the Lord with knowledge. All this gladdened us so greatly as to dissolve our despondency, and to bring some little smile into our souls, away from this gloomy condition of affairs in which we are now set.

And the Lord increased our consolation through our son, the most reverent fellow deacon Sabinus, who, by relating accurately the good things among you, fed our souls; and who, having learned our affairs by experience, will report them to you plainly, so that, first of all, by your earnest and laborious supplication to the Lord, you may contend together with us, and, next, may not refuse to bring such comfort as you can to the hard-pressed churches. For things here have grown weary, most honoured brethren, and the Church, under the continual assaults of her adversaries, has given out — like a ship in mid-ocean racked by the successive blows of the waves — unless there come some swift visitation of the goodness of the Lord. As, then, we make your mutual harmony and unity our own good, so we beg you, too, to feel for our divisions, and not, because we are separated by the situation of our places, to cut us off from yourselves, but, because we are united in the fellowship of the Spirit, to take us up into the concord of one body.

The things that afflict us are known, even if we do not speak of them; for by now they have echoed out into the whole world. The doctrines of the fathers are despised; apostolic traditions are set at nought; the inventions of innovating men hold sway in the churches; men now ply a craft of argument rather than do theology; the wisdom of the world wins the first place, having thrust aside the boast of the cross. Shepherds are driven off, and grievous wolves are brought in their stead, tearing apart the flock of Christ. Houses of prayer are bereft of worshippers; the wildernesses are full of mourners. The elders mourn, comparing the old days with the present; the young are more pitiable still, not knowing of what they have been deprived.

These things are enough to move to sympathy those who have been schooled in the love of Christ; yet, set beside the truth of the facts, my account falls far short of their full worth. If, then, there is any consolation of love, any fellowship of the Spirit, any tender mercies of compassion, be moved to come to our aid. Take up a zeal for true religion; deliver us from this storm. Let that good proclamation of the fathers be spoken among us, too, with freedom — the proclamation that overthrows the ill-named heresy of Arius and builds up the churches in sound teaching, in which the Son is confessed to be of one substance with the Father, and the Holy Spirit is numbered together and worshipped together with equal honour: so that the freedom of speech for the truth which the Lord has given you, and the boast that lies in the confession of the divine and saving Trinity, He may grant to us also through your prayers and your cooperation. The particulars the aforesaid fellow deacon will himself report to your love. And to all that has been done canonically by your honour we have given our assent, welcoming your apostolic zeal for orthodoxy.
To Valerian, bishop of the Illyrians.

Thanks be to the Lord, who has granted us to see the fruit of an ancient love in your purity — you who, though separated so far in body, have joined yourself to us by letter, and, embracing us with your spiritual and holy longing, have wrought in our souls an unspeakable affection. For we have learned by deed the force of the proverb: As cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country.

For there is among us a grievous famine of love, most honoured brother. And the cause is plain: because lawlessness has been multiplied, the love of the many has grown cold. For this reason, too, your letter seemed to us of great worth; and we send our reply by the same man, our most reverent fellow deacon and brother Sabinus, through whom we also make ourselves known to you and beg you to keep watch in prayers on our behalf, that the holy God may at length grant calm and quiet to affairs here too, and rebuke this wind and this sea, so that we may have rest from the tossing and the upheaval in which we are now set, ever awaiting that we shall be utterly sunk.

But this the Lord has greatly granted us in the present circumstances: to hear that you are in exact harmony and unity with one another, and that among you the proclamation of true religion is announced without hindrance. For at some point — if indeed the time of this world is not yet closed up, but there still remain days of human life — it must be that through you the faith will be renewed in the East, and that for the good things you received from her, you will at the right time render her the recompense. For the sound part here, that defends the godliness of the fathers, has grown sufficiently weary, the devil in his subtlety having shaken it with many and various assaults of his devices. But by your prayers, of you who love the Lord, may the wicked and people-deceiving heresy of the false doctrine of Arius be quenched, and may the good teaching of our fathers who gathered at Nicaea blaze up again, so that, in harmony with our saving baptism, the doxology may be rendered in full to the blessed Trinity.
To the Italians and Gauls.

To the most God-loving and most holy brethren, our fellow ministers throughout Italy and Gaul, the bishops of one soul with us: Meletius, Eusebius, Basil, Bassus, Gregory, Pelagius, Paul, Anthimus, Theodotus, Bithus, Abramius, Jobinus, Zeno, Theodoretus, Marcian, Barachus, Abramius, Libanius, Thalassius, Joseph, Boethus, Iatrius, Theodotus, Eustathius, Barsumas, John, Chosroes, Iosakes, Narses, Maris, Gregory, Daphnus — greeting in the Lord.

A groan sent up again and again from the depth of the heart brings some comfort to souls in pain, and a tear let fall has often carried off the greater part of an affliction. But for us the recounting of our sufferings to your love holds a comfort beyond what groan and tear afford; for a kindlier hope, too, warms us — that perhaps, if we declare to you the things that grieve us, we may rouse you to come to our aid, which long ago we expected would be given by you to the churches of the East, but which we have not yet obtained. Doubtless God, who governs our affairs in wisdom, according to the unsearchable judgments of His righteousness, has ordained that we be drawn out for a longer time in these trials. For surely you have not been ignorant of our condition, most honoured brethren — the report of which has run out even to the ends of the world; nor are you, anywhere, without sympathy toward the brethren of one soul with you, being disciples of the Apostle, who teaches that love toward one's neighbour is the fulfilment of the law. But, as we said, the just judgment of God has held back your impulse, measuring out to us, to be fulfilled, the affliction appointed for our sins. Yet now at least, both for your zeal for the truth and out of compassion for us, we beg you to rouse yourselves, having learned everything — even all that before this escaped your ears — from our most reverent brother, the fellow deacon Sabinus, who will be able to relate to you from himself whatever escapes the letter. Through him we beg you to put on bowels of compassion, and to lay aside all hesitation, and to take up the labour of love: to reckon as nothing the length of the road, the occupations of home, or any other human consideration.

For the danger is not over one church, nor are two or three the ones that have fallen into this grievous storm. For the evil of the heresy spreads almost from the borders of Illyricum as far as the Thebaid. Its wicked seeds the ill-named Arius first cast down; and, having been rooted deep by the many in the intervening time who industriously cultivated the impiety, it has now sprouted forth its destructive fruits. For the doctrines of true religion are overthrown, and the ordinances of the Church are thrown into confusion. The lust for power of those who do not fear the Lord leaps upon the positions of authority; and now, openly, the chief seat is set forth as the prize of impiety, so that the man who has blasphemed the more grievously is preferred to the oversight of a people. The dignity of the priesthood is gone; there is a failing of those who shepherd the flock of the Lord with knowledge, since those who are greedy of power ever squander the resources meant for the poor upon their own enjoyments and the distribution of gifts. The exactness of the canons is darkened. The licence to sin is great; for those who have come to rule through human exertion repay the favour of that exertion in this very thing — by yielding in everything, for pleasure's sake, to those who sin. Just judgment has perished; every man walks according to the will of his own heart. Wickedness is beyond measure; the people are past admonition; those who preside are without freedom of speech, for they are slaves of those who have given them the favour — those who have gained their dominion for themselves through men. And now the supposed defence of orthodoxy has even been devised by some as a weapon in their war against one another, and, concealing their private enmities, they make a show of being at enmity for the sake of true religion. Others, evading the conviction of their basest deeds, drive the people mad with strife against one another, that by the common evils they may cast a shadow over their own.

For this reason, too, this war is without truce, since those who have wrought wicked deeds look with suspicion upon the common peace as one that exposes the hidden things of their shame. At this the unbelievers laugh; those of little faith are shaken; the faith is in doubt; ignorance is poured out over souls, because those who corrupt the word in their knavery imitate the truth. For the mouths of the godly are silent, while every blaspheming tongue is let loose. Holy things have been profaned; the sound part of the people flee the houses of prayer as schools of impiety, and in the wildernesses lift up their hands, with groans and tears, to the Master in the heavens. For surely there has reached even to you what is happening in most of the cities — that the people, with their wives and children and the old men themselves, pouring out before the walls, perform their prayers in the open air, bearing all the hardships from the weather with great long-suffering, awaiting the aid of the Lord.

What lamentation is worthy of these calamities? What springs of tears will suffice for evils so great? While, then, some still seem to stand, while still a trace of the old order is preserved, before the shipwreck comes utterly upon the churches, hasten to us — hasten now, yes, we beseech you, most genuine brethren; give a hand to those who have been brought to their knees. Let your brotherly bowels be moved over us; let tears of sympathy be poured out. Do not overlook half the world swallowed up by error; do not endure that the faith be quenched among those with whom it first shone forth.

What you must do to come to the aid of affairs, and how you are to show your compassion toward the afflicted, you will by no means need to learn from us; the Holy Spirit Himself will suggest it to you. Only there is need of speed, in order to save those who are left, and of the presence of more of the brethren, so that those who come may make up the full number of a synod — that the credibility for setting things right may rest not only on the dignity of those who send, but also on the number of those present — and that they may renew the faith written at Nicaea by our fathers, proclaim the heresy excommunicate, and address words of peace to the churches, gathering into concord those who hold the same beliefs. For this, indeed, is the most pitiable thing of all: that even what seems to be sound has become divided against itself; and there have beset us, as it seems, sufferings much like those that once encompassed Jerusalem in the siege of Vespasian. For those people were at once pressed by the war from without and consumed by the inner faction of their own countrymen. And for us, besides the open war of the heretics, the rising up of those who seem to be orthodox has brought the churches to the last extremity of weakness. For these things, above all, we have need of your help, so that those who confess the apostolic faith may dissolve the schisms they have devised and submit henceforth to the authority of the Church, that the body of Christ may become whole, restored to wholeness in all its members; and that we may not only count blessed the good things among others — which is what we now do — but may also see our own churches receiving back the ancient boast of orthodoxy. For truly it is worthy of the highest blessedness, the gift granted by the Lord to your godliness: to distinguish the counterfeit from the tried and pure, and to proclaim, without any reserve, the faith of the fathers — which we too have received, and have recognized as formed after the apostolic stamp, giving our assent both to it and to all that has been decreed canonically and lawfully in the synodal document.
To Caesaria, a patrician lady, concerning communion.

To communicate each day, and to partake of the holy body and blood of Christ, is good and beneficial, since He says plainly: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life. For who doubts that to partake continually of life is nothing other than to live in many ways? We ourselves, however, communicate four times each week — on the Lord's day, on Wednesday, on Friday, and on the Sabbath — and on the other days, if there is the commemoration of some saint.

As for being compelled, in times of persecution, when no priest or minister is present, to receive communion with one's own hand, it is superfluous to demonstrate that this is in no way burdensome, since long custom confirms it through the very facts. For all the solitaries who dwell in the deserts, where there is no priest, keep communion at home and partake of it by themselves. And in Alexandria and in Egypt each one of those who are reckoned among the laity, for the most part, has communion in his own house, and partakes of it by himself when he wishes. For once the priest has completed the sacrifice and given it, the one who has received it, as he partakes of the whole at once, taking it each day, must rightly believe that he partakes and receives from the one who gave it. And indeed, in the church too, the priest gives the portion, and the one who receives it holds it with full authority, and so brings it to his mouth with his own hand. It is therefore the same in effect whether one receives a single portion from the priest, or many portions at once.
To Elias, governor of the province.

I myself was minded to come to your honour, so that by my absence I might not stand at any disadvantage against my slanderers; but since bodily illness prevented me, attacking far more violently than usual, I have of necessity had recourse to a letter. I, then, admirable man, when I lately met with your honour, was minded both to share with your prudence all the affairs of my life, and to make some statement on behalf of the churches, so that no room might be left for the slanders that come afterward. But I held myself back, reasoning that it was altogether officious, and ambitious beyond measure, to lay even the cares outside of necessity upon a man who has so great a multitude of affairs hanging upon him. And, at the same time — for the truth shall be told — I shrank from it on another ground as well, lest we should ever come to the necessity, by mutual disputes, of wounding your soul, which ought, in pure reverence toward God, to reap the perfect reward of godliness. For in truth, if we turn you toward ourselves, we shall leave you little leisure for public affairs, and shall do much as if a man were to burden, with an added cargo, a helmsman who is steering a newly built ship in a great swell, when he ought rather to take off some of the load and lighten it as far as he can. Whence it seems to me that the great emperor too, having understood this busy zeal of ours, has left us to administer the churches by ourselves.

Those, however, who trouble your guileless ears, I would have asked: in what is the public welfare the worse for us? Or what, small or great, of the common interests has been diminished by our administration of the churches? Unless one should say that it brings harm to affairs to raise up to our God a house of prayer magnificently built, and around it a dwelling — the one part, a free residence set apart for the chief, the others, ranked below, distributed in order among the servants of the divine, the use of which is common both to you the rulers and to those who attend you. And whom do we wrong in building lodgings for strangers, both for those who visit us in passing and for those who need some tending because of weakness, and in establishing for these the necessary comfort: the nurses, the physicians, the beasts of burden, the escorts? With these there must follow trades as well — both those necessary for living and all that have been devised for a seemly conduct of life — and other buildings, again, suited to the labours; all of which are an ornament to the place and, to our governor, a matter of dignified report, since the praise of them comes back to him. For not even on this account were you forced to take up our oversight, as though you alone sufficed, by the greatness of your judgment, both to take up the works that had fallen into decay, and to people the unpeopled places, and altogether to refashion the wildernesses into cities. To drive off and outrage the man who lends his aid to such things, or to honour and cherish him — which was the more fitting? And do not suppose, best of men, that what we say is mere talk; for we are already at the work, in the meantime collecting the materials.

Such, then, is my defence toward the governor. But what must be answered to the reproaches of fault-finders — as to a Christian and a friend who has cared for our good name — it is necessary for now to leave unsaid, as being both longer than the measure of a letter and, besides, not safe to entrust to lifeless writing. But so that, in the time before our meeting, being led on by the slanders of certain men, you may not be forced to lower somewhat your goodwill toward us, do what Alexander did. For they say that he too, when one of his familiars was being slandered, left one of his ears open to the slanderer, but carefully stopped the other with his hand, showing thereby that the man who is to judge rightly must not be wholly carried off at once by those who speak first, but must keep the half of his hearing unimpaired, as a defence for the one who is absent.
To Eusebius, bishop of Samosata.

Long ago I wrote to your godliness, for the sake of certain other matters and of our meeting one another, but I was disappointed of my hope, since the letter did not reach the hands of your honour. The blessed deacon Theophrastus received our letter, as I was of necessity setting out on a certain visitation; but he did not forward it to your godliness, since he was first overtaken by the illness of which he died. Whence I have come to the writing so much later than the proper time that I cannot hope there will be any use in this letter at all, since the time has been narrowed into the very last extremity. For the most God-loving bishop Meletius, and Theodotus, have charged us to cross over to them, both making the meeting a token of love and wishing that some correction be made of the things that now distress us. They appointed as the time of the meeting the middle of the coming month of June, and as the place the village of Phargamus, distinguished by the renown of its martyrs and by the great concourse of the synod that is held among them each year. And since I had, after my return, to learn of the falling asleep of the blessed deacon, and to find the letters lying idle with us, and so must not keep quiet — there being still thirty-three days left to us before the appointed day — I have sent in haste to the most reverend brother Eustathius, our fellow minister, this letter, so that through him it may be forwarded to your dignity, and that again the replies may be quickly brought back to us. For if it is possible, or otherwise pleasing to you, to be present, we ourselves too will be there; but if not, we shall, God willing, discharge our debt of last year's meeting, unless again some hindrance from our sins comes upon us; and the interview with the bishops we shall defer to another time.
To Sophronius the Master.

And who is so devoted to his city — honouring the country that bore and reared him as he would his parents — as you yourself, who join in praying for the good of the whole city in common and of each man in private, and who not only pray, but confirm your prayers through your own action? For you are able, with God's help, to do such things — and may you be able for the longest time, being so good a man.

And yet, in your day, our native country was rich only as in a dream. It had as the man entrusted with its care such a one as those who know the most ancient things among us say no other before has mounted the seats of authority; but it was quickly robbed of him by the malice of certain men, who made the man's freedom and his refusal to flatter an occasion of war against him, and contrived slanders against him, escaping the notice of your perfect ears. For this reason all of us, throughout the city, are downcast, robbed of a ruler who alone was able to set up again our city, now brought to its knees — a true guardian of justice, accessible to those who are wronged, fearsome to those who break the law, equal toward poor and rich, and, what is greatest of all, restoring the affairs of the Christians to their ancient honour. For the fact that he is the most incorruptible of the men we know, and grants no favour to anyone against justice, we have passed over as a lesser thing than the rest of the man's virtue.

These things we testify late in the day, like those who chant a dirge to console themselves, doing nothing useful for the matter at hand. Yet not even this is useless — that the memory of the man should be laid up in your great soul, and that you should be grateful to him as to a benefactor of his country, and, if any of those who are vexed at not being preferred to justice should set upon him, that you should fight on his behalf and defend him, having made it plain to all that you reckon the man your own, taking as a sufficient ground for that kinship the good testimony concerning him and the experience of affairs — an experience not corresponding to the proportion of the time. For what would not have come about from another even in many years, this has been set right by him in a little while. And it will be a sufficient favour to us, and a comfort for what has befallen, if you both commend him to the emperor and clear away the slanders brought against him. Consider that in this our whole country speaks to you through our single voice, and that it is the common prayer of all that something favourable should be done for the man through your perfection.
To the council of Tyana.

The Lord, who uncovers deep things and makes manifest the counsels of hearts, has given to the lowly, too, an understanding of devices that are, as some suppose, hard to discern. Nothing, then, has escaped us, nor is any of the things that have been done hidden. Yet we ourselves neither see nor hear anything other than the peace of God and all that leads to it. For even if others are powerful and great and confident in themselves, we are nothing, and worthy of nothing; so that we should never take so much upon ourselves as to think that we can prevail over affairs in isolation, knowing exactly that we have more need of the aid of each one of the brethren than the one hand has of the other. For from the very make of our body the Lord has taught us the necessity of fellowship. When I look at these very members of ours, that not one is sufficient of itself for its activity, how shall I reckon that I am sufficient of myself for the affairs of life? For neither could a foot walk safely without the other supporting it together, nor could an eye see soundly without having the other as its partner and striking, in concert with it, upon the things seen. The hearing is more exact that receives the sound through both passages, and the grasp is stronger through the fellowship of the fingers. And, to put it simply, I see nothing — neither of the things accomplished by nature nor of those accomplished by choice — brought to completion without the harmony of one's fellows; since prayer itself, when it has none in agreement, is far weaker than itself, and the Lord has promised to be in the midst between two or three who call upon Him in concord. And the very work of salvation the Lord undertook, that He might make peace through the blood of His cross, whether the things on earth or the things in the heavens.

So that, for all these reasons, we pray to remain in peace for the days that are left to us, and we ask that our falling asleep may be in peace. For this I have resolved to leave undone no labour whatever, to speak or do nothing lowly, to reckon as nothing the length of a journey, to shrink from no other burdensome thing, in order to attain the rewards of peacemaking. And if anyone follows us as we lead the way in these things, that is best, and the prayer attains its end; but if he draws us toward the opposite, I for my part will not even so depart from my own judgment. And each man will, in the day of recompense, recognize the fruits of his own work.
To Eusebius, bishop of Samosata.

Though I was much minded to come to Nicopolis, after receiving the letter from your holiness containing a refusal of the visit, I was relaxed from my eagerness and at the same time put in mind of all my infirmity. There came also into my thought the perfunctoriness of those who had invited me — that, having made their invitation to us a thing of mere passing form through the most reverend brother Hellenius, the surveyor of Nazianzus, they did not deign to send a second man to remind us about the same matters or to guide us. Since, then, we are suspect to them because of our sins, we were afraid lest somehow we should cloud the brightness of their festival by our presence. For with your nobility of soul we do not shrink even from stripping for the great trials; but without you we are not equal even to looking in the face the chance afflictions. Since, therefore, our interview with them was to be for ecclesiastical matters, we let the time of the festival pass by, and deferred the meeting to a time of quiet and undisturbed life; and we have resolved, on reaching Nicopolis, to discuss with the most God-loving bishop Meletius the things necessary for the churches, if he should decline the road to Samosata; but if not, we will run thither together with him, provided this be made plain to us by both — both by him himself, writing back to us about these things (for we have written), and by your godliness.

We were also to meet with the bishops from the second Cappadocia; who, since they were named to another province, supposed that all at once they had become of another race and another tribe toward us — men who have been as ignorant of us as those who have never had any experience of us at all, nor ever come to words with us. There was expected also another meeting with the most reverend bishop Eustathius, which indeed took place. For because he is loudly accused by many of falsifying something in the faith, we came to words with him, and found him, with God's help, following in good will toward all correctness. The letters of the bishops, through the fault of those very men who ought to have forwarded our communications, were not delivered to your honour; but they also escaped me, thrust from my memory by the press of cares.

As for the brother Gregory, I too would have wished him to administer a church commensurate with his nature. But that would be the whole world under the sun, gathered into one. Since, however, this is impossible, let him be a bishop who is not made dignified by his place, but who makes the place dignified of himself. For it is the mark of a truly great man not only to suffice for great things, but also to make small things great by his own power.

But what must be done with Palmatius, who, after so many entreaties of the brethren, still serves Maximus toward the persecutions? Yet not even now do they hesitate to write; for they are not permitted to come, both by bodily weakness and by household occupations.

Know, however, most God-loving father, that our affairs have great need of your presence, and that you must once more set your honoured old age in motion, in order to set firm Cappadocia, which is by now being tossed about and is near to falling.
To Count Terentius.

Though I set great zeal to obey, at least in part, both the imperial command and the friendly letter of your honour — a letter which I have believed to be full, in every word and every thought, of right purpose and good intention — I was not permitted to bring my eagerness into effect. The cause is, first and most truly, my own sins, which everywhere meet me beforehand and trip up my steps; and next, the estrangement from us of the bishop given to us for cooperation.
