For I do not know what came over our most reverend brother Theodotus, who from the beginning had promised to assist us in everything, and who eagerly brought us down from Getasa to Nicopolis: when he saw us in the city, he so abhorred us, and was so afraid of our sins, that he could not endure to admit us either to morning prayer or to evening — doing what was just, indeed, as toward us, and fitting for my way of life, but counselling what was not profitable for the common condition of the churches. And as the reason for this he alleged against us that we had endured to receive the most reverend bishop Eustathius into communion. Yet what was done by us is as follows.

We, having been invited to a synod held by the brother Theodotus, and having set out, for love's sake, to obey the invitation, so as not to seem to make our meeting fruitless and idle, were eager to come to words with the aforesaid brother Eustathius. And we put before him the charges concerning the faith which those about the brother Theodotus bring against him, and asked that, if he follows the right faith, he make it plain to us, so that we might be in communion; but that, if he is otherwise minded, he know exactly that we too shall be otherwise minded toward him. Many words, then, having passed between us, and that whole day having been spent in the examination of these things, when at last evening came on, we parted from one another, having brought the discussion to no agreed conclusion. On the next day, again, sitting down together in the morning, we discussed the same matters, the brother Poemenius, the presbyter of Sebasteia, having now also come and vigorously training the opposing argument against us. Little by little, then, we both freed ourselves from the charges on which we thought to be accused, and brought them on to assent to what we were seeking; so that, by the grace of the Lord, we were found not to differ from one another in even the smallest point. And so, about the ninth hour, we rose for prayers, giving thanks to the Lord, who gave us to think the same thing and to say the same thing. After this I ought to have received some written confession from the man, so that his assent might be made plain to those who oppose him, and that the proof of the man's purpose might be sufficient for the rest. But I myself wished, for the sake of great exactness, to meet first with the brethren about Theodotus and to receive from them a written statement of faith, and to put it before the aforesaid man; that both things might come to pass — that the right faith might be confessed by him, and that they themselves might be satisfied, having no ground for dispute, since their own propositions had been accepted. But before learning for what purpose we had met, and what had been set right by us through the discussion, those about the bishop Theodotus no longer deigned to invite us to the synod. Rather, we turned back from the middle of the road, downcast that they were making our labours for the peace of the churches end in nothing.

After this, then, since the necessity of the road to Armenia came upon us, knowing the man's peculiarity of character, and wishing both to make my own defence for what had been done, before a trustworthy witness, and to satisfy him, I came to Getasa, the estate of the most God-loving bishop Meletius, the aforesaid Theodotus being present with me as well. And so there, since I was accused by him of my union with Eustathius, I told the success of the meeting — that I had received him as agreeing with us in everything. But when he firmly asserted that the man had denied it after our departure, and was firmly maintaining to his own disciples that he had in no point come to agreement with us about the faith, I answered to this (and consider, most admirable man, whether I did not make the most just and irrefutable replies to it): that I, for my part, am persuaded, judging from the man's general steadfastness, that he is not so lightly turned about to the contrary, nor confesses now and then denies what he said — a man who shuns even a falsehood about trivial things as a fearful thing, much less would ever choose to oppose the truth concerning matters so great and so cried abroad among all. But if it should turn out that what is noised about by you is true, then a written statement, containing the full proof of the right faith, must be put before him. If, then, I find him assenting in writing, I will continue in communion with him; but if I find him drawing back, I will withdraw from union with him. When the bishop Meletius and the brother Diodorus, our fellow presbyter, approved this proposal — for they were present at what was done — the most reverend brother Theodotus, having agreed there, and having begged us to come down to Nicopolis, so that we might both inspect his church and have him as a fellow traveller on the road as far as Satala, left us in Getasa; and when we reached Nicopolis, forgetting both what he had heard from me and what he had agreed with us, he put us to shame with those insults and dishonours which I described a little before, and sent us away.

How, then, was it possible for me, most honoured head, to do any of the things that had been commanded, and to give bishops to Armenia, when the partner of my care was so disposed toward me — he from whom I expected to find the suitable men? For in his district there are men both reverent and intelligent and skilled in the language and acquainted with the rest of the customs of that nation; whose names, though I know them, I will willingly pass over in silence, lest some hindrance arise to Armenia's being served at another time at least. And now, having come as far as Satala in such a state of body, I thought, by the grace of God, to set the rest in order: I made peace among the bishops of Armenia, and spoke to them what was fitting, so that they should lay aside their habitual indifference and take up the genuine zeal of the Lord for the churches; and I gave them rules concerning the things done lawlessly and without distinction throughout Armenia, how it befitted them to attend to these. I also received resolutions from the church of Satala, containing a request that a bishop be given them by us. And it became my care to search out, as well, the slander poured over our brother Cyril, the bishop of Armenia; and by the grace of God we found it to have been falsely set in motion through the calumny of those who hate him — which they also openly confessed before us. And we thought we had moderately reconciled the people in Satala to him, so that they should no longer shun his communion. But if these things are small and of no account — still, nothing more was possible to be done by us, because of the discord among ourselves, one with another, arising from the meddling of the devil. These things I ought to have kept silent, lest I should seem to publish my own reproaches; but since it was not otherwise possible to defend myself to your nobility of soul, I came to the necessity of relating the whole truth of what has happened.
To Eusebius, bishop of Samosata.

I saw the letter of your love in the neighbouring country of Armenia as those who sail the sea see a beacon kindled afar off on the open water — especially when the sea happens to be somewhat wild with winds. For while the letter of your dignity is by nature pleasant and full of much comfort, the occasion then most of all increased the grace that came from it — what that occasion was, and how it grieved us, I for my part would not say, having once resolved to forget my sorrows; but our fellow deacon will relate it to your godliness.

My body has utterly failed me, so that I cannot bear even the smallest movements without pain. Nevertheless I pray that my old desire may now at last be fulfilled for me through the help of your prayers — even though this journey abroad has caused me great difficulty, the affairs of our church having been neglected for so long a time. And if God, while we are yet above the earth, should count us worthy to see your godliness in our church, we shall truly have good hopes for the things to come as well, that we are not altogether cast out from the gifts of God. This, at least, if it is possible, we beg may come to pass at the synod which we hold yearly for the commemoration of the blessed martyr Eupsychius, now drawing near, on the seventh day of the month of September. For matters worthy of concern beset us, requiring your cooperation, both for the appointment of bishops and for counsel and consideration about the things being plotted against us by the goodness of Gregory of Nyssa, who is convening synods at Ancyra and leaves no means untried of plotting against us.
A Letter of Consolation

It would have been a thing to pray for, that the first letter I sent you should have a more cheerful occasion for its writing. For then everything would have stood as I would wish, since it is my desire that the whole life of all who have chosen to live in godliness should go forward toward good. But since the Lord who governs our life has, in his unutterable wisdom, ordained that these things should come to pass entirely for the benefit of our souls — by which he has made life painful for you, while leading us, who are bound to you in the love that is according to God, into fellow-feeling — and since we have learned from our brothers the state into which you have come, it seemed necessary to bring you what consolation we can. If indeed it had been possible for me even to travel as far as the place where your nobility happens to be living, I would have valued doing so above all else. But since both the weakness of my body and the multitude of affairs that beset me, and this very journey that I have undertaken at great cost to the churches in my charge, have made that impossible, I was eager to visit your honour by letter, reminding you that these afflictions do not come to the servants of God idly from the Lord who watches over us, but as a testing of our true love toward God who created us. For just as the labours of the contests bring athletes to their crowns, so too the testing that comes in trials leads Christians toward perfection, provided that with the patience that befits us we accept with all thanksgiving what is dispensed to us by the Lord.

All things are governed by the goodness of the Master. We must receive none of the things that befall us as cause for grief, even if for the present it touches our weakness. For though we are ignorant of the reasons by which each of the things that happen is brought upon us by the Master as something good, still we ought to be persuaded of this: that what happens is surely to our advantage, whether for our sake through the reward of patience, or for the sake of the soul that has been taken — that it may not, by lingering longer in this life, be filled with the wickedness that holds sway over this world. For if the hope of Christians were bounded by this life, it would reasonably be thought a grievous thing to be parted from the body too soon. But if the loosing of the soul from these bodily bonds is the beginning of the true life for those who live according to God, why do we grieve, like those who have no hope? Be consoled, then, not to fall beneath your passions, but to show that you stand above them and have risen higher.
To the Citizens of Satala

I, prevailed upon both by your own entreaties and by those of the whole people, both took up the care of your church and promised you in the presence of the Lord that I would leave undone nothing that lay within my power. For this reason I was compelled, as it is written, to touch as it were the apple of my own eye. So far did the surpassing honour you showed me allow nothing else to come into my mind — neither kinship, nor the friendship I have had with the man from childhood — in comparison with what you asked of me. Rather, forgetting all that bound me to him in the way of intimacy, taking no account of the multitude of groans with which the people deprived of his patronage will groan against me, nor of the tears of all his kindred, nor taking to heart the affliction of his aged mother, who is shaken with grief and depends upon his care alone — passing over all such considerations, many and great as they were, I gave myself to one thing only: to adorn your church with the patronage of so great a man, and to come to her aid, who has now been brought to her knees by long want of a leader and needs much and powerful guidance to rise again.

Such, then, is our part. As for yours, we now ask that you appear no less than our hope, and than the promises we have made to the man — that we have sent him to kinsmen and friends, each of you being eager to outdo the other in zeal and love toward him. See, then, that you display this noble rivalry, and that by the abundance of your attention you so encourage his heart that he comes to forget his homeland, to forget his kindred, to forget a people that depended on his patronage as much as a young child upon its mother's breast.

We have sent Nicias ahead, so as to make known to your honourable selves what has been done, and that you may begin to celebrate and to give thanks to the Lord, who through us has counted your prayer worthy to be fulfilled.
To the People of Satala

The Lord has brought to fulfilment the requests of his people, and has given them, through our lowly ministry, a shepherd worthy of the name — not one who, like the many, peddles the word, but one able to please you in surpassing measure, you who love the rightness of the preaching and have embraced the life that is lived according to the commandments of the Lord; and this in the name of the Lord who has filled him with his spiritual gifts.
To Modestus, the Prefect

The very act of writing to so great a man, even if no other occasion be present, is among the greatest honours for those who can perceive it; for converse with men who tower above the rest of the multitude confers the highest distinction on those judged worthy of it. But to me, who am in anguish on behalf of a whole homeland, this approach to your magnanimity is a necessity; and I beg you to bear with it gently and in your own manner, and to stretch out your hand to our homeland, which is now brought to its knees. The matter for which we entreat you is of this kind.

The old census left those consecrated to our God — the presbyters and deacons — exempt from tax. But those who have now made the registration, supposing that they had received no order from your transcendent authority, registered them — except where some happened to have exemption on other grounds, by reason of age. We ask, then, that this be granted to us as a memorial of your beneficence, preserving a good remembrance of you for all time to come, and that, according to the old law, those who serve as priests be released from this assessment. And we ask that the exemption be granted not to the persons of those now in office (for in that way the favour would pass to their successors, who are not in every case worthy to hold the priesthood), but that, after the pattern of the free census, a general concession be made for the clergy, so that exemption may be given by those who administer the churches to whoever are serving at any given time.

This will both preserve for your great nature an immortal glory for your good deeds, and will furnish the imperial house with many who pray for it, and will bring great benefit even to the public revenues — since we provide the relief that comes from exemption not at all to the clergy as such, but to those who are continually worn down with toil; which is just what we do also in the case of the freedmen's census, as anyone who wishes may learn.
To the Deaconesses, the Daughters of Count Terentius

When I came to Samosata I had expected to meet your orderly company; and when I failed of the meeting, I bore the loss with no small distress, considering when it might again be possible for me to draw near to your region, or agreeable to you to come to ours. But let these things lie in the will of the Lord.

For the present, since I found the son Sophronius setting out toward you, I gladly gave him this letter, to carry you a greeting and to make known our mind — that by the grace of God we do not cease to remember you, and to give thanks for you to the Lord that you are good shoots of a good root, fruitful in good works, and truly as lilies among thorns. For that, surrounded by such great perversity on the part of those who corrupt the word of truth, you have not given way to their deceits, nor abandoned the apostolic preaching of the faith to be carried over to the novelty now in fashion — how is this not worthy of great thanksgiving to God, and how does it not most justly earn you great praise? You have believed in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; do not betray this deposit. The Father is the origin of all; the Son is the only-begotten, born from him, true God, perfect from perfect, the living image, showing the whole Father in himself; the Holy Spirit has its existence from God, is the fountain of holiness, the power that bestows life, the grace that perfects, through whom man is adopted as a son and the mortal is made immortal — joined to the Father and the Son in all things, in glory and in eternity, in power and in kingship, in lordship and in godhead, as the tradition of saving baptism also testifies.

But those who call either the Son or the Spirit a creature, or who in any way bring it down into the ministering and servile rank, are far from the truth; their company we should flee and their words we should turn away from as poison to souls. And if the Lord should ever grant us to be together, we shall set out for you more fully the arguments concerning the faith, so that, with proofs from Scripture, you may recognize both the strength of the truth and the rottenness of the heresy.
To a Soldier

Though we have much for which to give thanks to the Lord — among the things of which he counted us worthy during our sojourn — we judged it the greatest good to come to know your honoured self, granted to us by our good Master. For we came to know a man who shows that even in the soldier's life it is possible to preserve the perfection of love toward God, and that the Christian must be marked out not by the dress he wears but by the disposition of his soul.

At that time, then, we met you with all eagerness, and now too, as often as we call you to mind, we enjoy the greatest gladness. Be a man, therefore, and be strong, and be always zealous to nourish and multiply your love toward God, that the supply of good things from him may go forward to you in ever greater measure. That you, for your part, remember us, we need no further proof, having the testimony that comes from your deeds themselves.
To Julitta, a Freewoman

I was much disheartened when I came upon the letter of your nobility, to learn that the same constraints again hem you in. And what is one to do with men who show so changeable a character, saying now one thing and now another, and not abiding by their own agreements? For if, after the promises made before me and the former prefect, he now presses the appointed term as though nothing had been said, the man seems to have lost all sense of shame toward us.

Nevertheless I have written to him, rebuking him and reminding him of his own promises. I have written also to Helladius, the prefect's friend, that through him the prefect may be informed of your situation. For I did not think it fitting for me to presume so far as to address a judge of such rank directly, since I have never yet written to him about any private matter, and I am wary of incurring some censure — for, as you know, great men are easily angered at such things. If, however, anything is to be of use, it will be through Helladius, a man both upright and well-disposed toward us, who fears God and has unbounded freedom of speech with the governor. And the holy God is able to lead you through every affliction, only if we set our hope upon him with a true and sincere heart.
To the Guardian of the Heirs of Julitta

I was astonished to hear that, forgetting those kind promises so befitting your generous spirit, you are now pressing this sister with a most severe and inexorable demand; and I cannot guess from what is reported what to make of it. For I know the great generosity attested of you by those who have had dealings with you, and I remember the promises you made before me and this man — saying that you would set down a shorter term but would in fact allow a longer one, since you wished to accommodate the necessity of the case and to show indulgence to the freewoman, compelled as she was to give up at one stroke so great a sum from her household.

What, then, is the cause of so great a change I cannot understand. But whatever it may be, I beg you — remembering your own generosity, and looking to the Lord who repays good intentions — to grant the time of relief you promised from the first, so that they may be able to sell their property and so discharge the debt. And it is plain that I remember this also, that you promised, if you received the agreed sum of money, to hand over to the said woman all the agreed documents — both those executed before the magistrates and those drawn up privately.

I beg you, then: honour us, and gain for yourself with the Lord a great blessing, calling to mind your own promises, and knowing that you too are a man, and must yourself await the times in which you will have need of the help that comes from God. Do not shut that off from yourself by your present hardness, but prepare the mercies of God for yourself, by showing all kindness and forbearance toward those who are worn down.
To Count Helladius

Though I am most reluctant to be a trouble to your kindness, on account of the greatness of your office, lest I seem to take immoderate advantage of your friendship, yet I am not permitted by necessity to keep quiet. This sister here — who is of our own kin, and is worn down by widowhood, and has the care of the affairs of an orphan child — when I saw her at last held fast by intolerable constraints beyond her strength, I took pity and was grieved at heart, and hastened to beg you that, if there is any power to do so, you would consent to assist the man sent by her, to the end that, having now paid what she promised in our presence, she may be freed from any further harassment. For she promised, by paying the principal, that the interest would be remitted.

But now those of the heirs who manage her affairs are attempting, after the principal, to exact the interest as well. Knowing, then, that it is the Lord who makes the cause of widows and orphans his own, give yourself to this endeavour on behalf of the matter, in hope of the reward that comes from God himself. For I think that the kindly disposed and most admirable prefect, when he learns that the principal has been paid, will himself feel compassion for this now pitiable and wretched household, brought to its knees and no longer able to bear the harassments imposed on it from outside. I beg you, then, both to pardon the necessity for which I have troubled you, and to lend your aid to the matter according to the power which Christ has given you — you who are kind and good in character, and who have used for good the things you have received.
To Modestus, the Prefect

For all the honour and freedom of speech you grant us, consenting in the gentleness of your manner to come down to our level, we pray that as much honour and yet more may come to you, by the increase of your distinction in all your life, from our good Master. As for me, though I had long desired to write and to enjoy the honour you bestow, the reverence I felt before your eminence held me back, since I was afraid I might be thought to take immoderate advantage of such freedom of speech.

But now, both the permission to write that I have received from your matchless greatness, and at the same time the need of those who are worn down, have forced me to take courage. If, then, there is any strength even in the supplications of the small on behalf of the greatest matters, be entreated, most admirable one, with a kindly nod to grant deliverance to a pitiable rural district, and to command that for those who dwell on the iron-bearing Taurus the levy of iron be made bearable, so that they may not be utterly worn out at one stroke, but that their service to the public may continue. That this above all should be your care, we are persuaded by your admirable benevolence.
To Modestus, the Prefect

In other circumstances I would not have presumed to be a trouble to your greatness, knowing how to measure myself and to recognize the powers that be. But since I saw a man, a friend, in great anxiety at being summoned, I made bold to give him this letter, that by presenting it in place of a petition he might meet with some kindness. And surely, even if we ourselves are worth nothing, yet our very moderation is enough to move the most benevolent of prefects to grant us pardon — so that, if the man has committed no fault, he may be saved for the very sake of the truth, and if he has indeed erred, it may be forgiven him for the sake of us who have interceded.
But as to what the affairs here are like, who knows better than you, who both oversee what is unsound in each man and hold all things together by your admirable forethought?
To Andronicus, the Governor

If I were so disposed in body as to be able to endure journeys easily and to bear the hardships of winter, I would not be writing, but would myself be coming to your magnanimity, for two reasons. The first, to pay an old debt of a promise — for I know I agreed to be present at Sebasteia and to enjoy your perfection; which I did, but failed of the meeting, arriving a little behind your goodness. The second, to fulfil in person the embassy which until now I have shrunk from sending, judging myself too small to obtain such a favour, and at the same time reckoning that no one, whether a magistrate or a private man, could persuade another by letters on any matter as well as one present in person — now clearing himself of the charges, now entreating, now begging pardon for some — none of which could easily be done by a letter. Setting, then, against all these one thing — yourself, that divine head, and the thought that it will be enough to make plain to you the mind we have concerning this matter, and that the rest you will supply of your own accord — I did not shrink from the undertaking.

But you see how I go round in circles, hesitating and drawing back from disclosing the reason for which I am making these words. This Domitianus is bound to us by ties going back to our parents, so that he differs in nothing from a brother. For why should one not speak the truth? Then, having learned the cause from which he has suffered these things, we said that he was deserving of such treatment. For let there be no one who, having shown any neglect, small or great, toward your virtue, should escape punishment. But seeing him living in fear and disgrace, and his deliverance lying in your vote, we judged that he has punishment enough. We entreat you to be at once magnanimous and humane in your thoughts concerning him. For to take in hand those who resist is the mark of a man of courage and a true ruler; but to be kind and gentle toward those who have fallen is the mark of one who surpasses all in greatness of mind and in mildness. So that it will be in your power, if you wish, to display in the same act both the magnanimity that avenges and that which saves, as you may choose. This is measure enough of punishment for Domitianus: the fear of what he expects, and the knowledge that he is one who deserves to suffer. We entreat you to add nothing further to his punishment. For consider this also: that many before now have had power over wrongdoers, of whom no account has passed down to later times; but those who in their love of wisdom rose above the many laid aside their anger, and the memory of them has been handed down immortal for all time. Let this too be added to the stories told of you. Grant us, who choose to sing your praises, to surpass the deeds of kindness celebrated in former ages. So too Croesus is said to have laid aside his anger against the slayer of his son, who had surrendered himself for punishment; and Cyrus the Great became, after his victory, a friend to this very Croesus. With these we shall number you, and, as far as our power reaches, we shall proclaim these things — unless we be thought altogether too small to be the heralds of so great a man.

But this, above all, must be said: that we do not punish those who do any wrong for the sake of what has already been done (for what device could there be to make undone what has been done?), but so that either they themselves may become better for the future, or may serve as an example of self-discipline to others. Neither of these, then, can anyone say is wanting in the present case. For he himself will remember these things even after death, and I think the rest are dead with fear, looking to his example. So that whatever we add to the punishment, we shall be thought merely to be glutting our own anger — which I, for my part, would say is far from true of you; and I would not have been moved to speak any of these words, did I not see the favour to be greater for the one who gives than for those who receive it. For the magnanimity of your character will be made plain to no few. For all Cappadocia is watching the future, among whom I would pray to count this too, along with the rest of the good things that belong to you.

I shrink from ceasing to write, thinking that what is omitted may prove a loss to me. Yet this much I will add: that having letters from many who request his pardon, he judged that the one from us was to be preferred to all — though I do not know from where he learned that there is any account made of us with your perfection. So that he may not be deceived in the hopes he has placed in us, and so that we may be able to speak proudly of it before those here, be entreated, matchless master, to assent to the request. And surely you, no worse than any who have ever pursued the love of wisdom, have looked closely at human affairs, and you know what a fair treasure is laid up in advance for one who serves all who are in need.
To the Presbyters of Tarsus

On meeting this man, I gave great thanks to the holy God, both because by his presence he consoled me amid many afflictions, and because through him he plainly showed me your love. For in the resolve of this one man I came to know the zeal of you all for the truth. What we discussed privately with one another he will himself report to you; but what it was fitting that your love should learn from me is this. The present time has great weight toward the ruin of the churches, and this we have for a long time now perceived. But of the building up of the Church, the correcting of faults, compassion toward the weak, the defence of the sound among the brothers — of these there is not one. There is no remedy, no cure for the disease that has already taken hold, no safeguard against the one that is expected. And the condition of the Church now resembles — to use a plain illustration, though it may seem too lowly — an old garment, easily torn at the slightest pretext, and unable to be restored again to its original strength. At such a time, then, there is need of great earnestness and much diligence, that the churches may receive some benefit. And the benefit is this: that what has hitherto been torn apart should be united. And union would come about if we were willing, in matters where we do no harm to our souls, to bear with the weaker. Since, then, many mouths have been opened against the Holy Spirit, and many tongues sharpened for blasphemy against him, we ask you, so far as it lies with you, to reduce the blasphemers to a small number; and to receive into communion those who do not call the Holy Spirit a creature, so that the blasphemers may be left alone, and may either, put to shame, return to the truth, or, persisting in their sin, be discredited through their fewness. Let us, then, seek nothing further, but let us set before the brothers who wish to join with us the faith of Nicaea; and if they assent to it, let us further ask of them that the Holy Spirit ought not to be called a creature, and that those who say so are not to be in communion. Beyond these things I ask that nothing be sought from us. For I am persuaded that, by longer association and by unquarrelsome common exercise, and if anything more should need to be added for clearer understanding, the Lord will grant it — he who works all things together for good to those who love him.
To the People of Tarsus, concerning Cyriacus

How great a good peace is, why should I say to men who are sons of peace? Since, then, this great and wonderful thing, sought after by all who love the Lord, is now in danger of being reduced to a bare name, because lawlessness has been multiplied and love grown cold in the many, I think it ought to be the single endeavour of those who serve the Lord genuinely and truly: to bring back to unity the churches that have been severed from one another in many ways and by many means. In attempting to do this myself, I could not justly incur the charge of being a meddler. For nothing is so proper to a Christian as to make peace; wherefore the Lord has promised us the greatest reward for it. Meeting, then, with the brothers and observing in them much brotherly affection and love toward you, and far more besides their love of Christ and their exactness and vigour concerning the faith, and that they make every effort both not to be separated from your love and not to betray the sound faith — accepting their good resolve, I write to your honoured selves, exhorting you to hold them, with all love, genuinely united to you and sharers in every care of the Church; having pledged to them also your soundness, that they too, by the grace of God, are arrayed for everything in zeal for the truth, however much they may have to suffer for the word of truth.

And there is — as I persuade myself — that which is neither contrary to you, nor insufficient to satisfy the aforesaid brothers, namely this: that you confess the faith set forth by our fathers who once assembled at Nicaea, and that you reject none of the expressions there, but know that the three hundred and eighteen, gathering without contention, did not speak without the working of the Holy Spirit; and that you add to that faith this also, that the Holy Spirit must not be called a creature, and that we are not to be in communion with those who say so, that the Church of God may be pure, having no tare mingled with itself. When this assurance has been offered to them by your tender mercy, they too are ready to render you the submission that befits you. For I myself pledge on the brothers' behalf that they will gainsay nothing, but will display to you every excess of good order, this one thing alone, which is sought of them, being readily granted to them by your perfection.
To Simplicia, a Heretic

Without good counsel do men both hate the better and love the worse. For this reason I too hold my tongue, choking back in silence the reproach for the insults done me. But I will await the Judge above, who knows how to requite all wickedness in the end. For though a man pour out wealth beyond the sands, he harms his soul, having trampled on justice. For God ever seeks sacrifice — not, I think, as one in need, but accepting as a costly sacrifice the godly and just mind. But when a man, transgressing against himself, tramples it down, his prayers are reckoned common.

Remind yourself, then, of the last day, and do not, if you please, teach us. We know more than you, and we are not so choked by the thorns within; nor, amid a few good things, do we mingle a tenfold wickedness. You have stirred up against us lizards and toads — spring creatures, no doubt, yet unclean for all that. But a wing will come from above to feed upon them. For mine is a cause, not as you suppose, but as God knows how to judge. And if there is need of witnesses, no slaves shall stand forth, nor a race of eunuchs, dishonoured and utterly ruined — that very thing: unwomanly, unmanly, mad for women, envious, ill-rewarded, quick to anger, effeminate, slave to the belly, mad for gold, harsh, weeping at dinner, fickle, ungenerous, all-receiving, insatiable, frenzied and jealous; and what more need I say? — condemned to the iron from their very birth. How then can the judgment of these be upright, whose very feet are crooked? These are chaste without reward, by force of the knife; but they rage fruitlessly, through their own shamefulness. Not these shall stand as witnesses of the judgment, but the eyes of the just, and the faces of perfect men — all who shall then see, toward which they now look with understanding.
To Firminus

Your letters are both rare and brief — whether from reluctance to write, or because you are managing in some other way to escape the surfeit that comes from too much, or perhaps because you are training yourself toward brevity. To us, however, nothing is enough; even should it overflow in quantity, it falls short of our desire, because we wish to learn each particular about you: how your body fares, how the matters of your discipline stand, and whether you persevere in the resolutions made from the first, or have changed your mind, shifting your purpose in response to circumstances.

If, then, you had remained the same as yourself, we would not be asking for a quantity of letters, but this much would have sufficed us: "So-and-so to so-and-so: know that we are in health, and farewell." But since we hear what we are ashamed even to mention — that you, abandoning the rank of your blessed forefathers, are deserting to your paternal grandfather, and are eager to become a Brettanius instead of a Firminus — we long to hear these very things, and to learn the reasonings by which you were led to take this road of life. But since you yourself have kept silent out of shame at the design, we exhort you neither to plan anything worthy of shame, and, if anything has crept into your mind, to drive it from your thoughts and to become yourself again; and, bidding a long farewell to military service and arms and the hardships of camp, to take possession of your homeland, judging it enough for security of life and for every distinction to hold sway over the city on equal terms with your forefathers — which we are persuaded will come to you without effort, looking both to your natural fitness for it and to the absence of any who stand in the way. Whether, then, the design never arose at all, or, having arisen, has been cast off again, let us know quickly. But if — which God forbid — the same plans remain, let the calamity come to us as its own messenger; of a letter we have no need.
Without Address, concerning the Ascetic Life

I consider myself in your debt on other grounds, and this present care in which we are engaged necessarily makes us accountable for service in such matters, even were those who give the orders ordinary men — much more you, who are bound to us by many just claims and others besides. There is no need to bring the past under examination; for one might say that we ourselves were the cause of our own troubles, having contended to depart from that good discipline which alone leads to salvation — and so perhaps we were handed over to this trouble as a trial.

But those things have happened and have been deemed worthy of remembrance, that we may not a second time fall into the like. As for what follows, I much wish to assure your reverence that, God permitting, it will be most easily settled for us, since the matter is both lawful and has nothing burdensome in it, and many of our friends in the camp are ready to grant the favour. A petition, then, will be drawn up by us, after the likeness of the document presented to the vicar; and in it, if there be no obstruction, we shall at once send it off, providing the security that comes from the document. And I am persuaded that in such matters our resolve has greater force than imperial commands; and if we display it unchanging and unswerving from the prime of life onward, then, by the help of God, the guarding of virginity will be for us inviolable and secure.
The brother whom you put in our charge we have both gladly received and hold among our intimates, praying that he may prove worthy of God and of your testimony.
To Jovinus, Bishop of Perrha

I have you as my debtor for a good debt. For I lent you a debt of love, which I must recover with interest, since our Lord too does not refuse this kind of interest. Repay it, then, dear head, by visiting our homeland. This, now, is the principal itself. And what is the interest? That you be the one who comes — a man who surpasses us by as much as fathers are better than children.
To Eustathius, Bishop of Sebasteia

Through my most reverend and devout brother Peter I greet your love, begging you, as on every occasion so now too, to pray for me, that, being changed from this blameworthy and harmful way, I may at length become worthy of the name of Christ. And surely, even if I do not speak of it, you two will discuss our affairs with each other, and he will inform you of the exact truth of what has been done, so that you may not accept without scrutiny the wicked suspicions raised against us — such as those are likely to contrive who, both against the fear of God and against the regard of men, have outraged us. For what the noble Basil showed me — he whom I received from your reverence as a safeguard of my life — I am ashamed even to tell; but you will learn each particular, being instructed by our brother. And I say this not to take vengeance on him (for I pray that it may not be reckoned against him by the Lord), but managing that the love I have from you may remain firm to us, which I fear they may shake by the excess of their slanders, such as they are likely to contrive in defence of their own fault. But whatever they may accuse us of, let this be examined by your sagacity: whether they brought any charge against us, whether they sought the correction of the fault they now impute to us, whether they ever made plain at all their grievance against us. But as it is, with a cheerful face and feigned words of love, concealing in their soul an unspeakable abyss of guile and bitterness, they made it plain by their ignoble flight. How great a grief they have caused us by this, and how great a mockery for those who always loathe the devout life in this wretched city, and insist that the appearance of self-control is practised as an art to win trust and a disguise for deceit — all this, even if we do not relate it, is surely known to your understanding; so that no pursuit is now so suspected of wickedness by the people here as the profession of the ascetic life.

How these things ought to be healed, it would be for your understanding to consider. For the charges patched together by Sophronius are no prelude to good things for us, but the beginning of division and separation, and an effort to chill even the love that is among us. We beg, through your tender mercy, that he be restrained from this harmful impulse, and that he try rather, by his own love, to bind together what is being drawn apart, and not to join in widening the separation with those who are bent on division.
To Meletius, Bishop of Antioch

I have received letters from the most God-beloved bishop Eusebius, directing that the Westerns be written to again concerning certain ecclesiastical matters. And he wished the letter to be drafted by us, but signed by all who are in communion. Since, then, I did not find how to write concerning what he enjoined, I have forwarded the memorandum to your godliness, that, having both read it and given heed to what is reported by the most beloved brother Sanctissimus, our fellow-presbyter, you yourself may deign, as seems good to you, to draft something concerning these matters — we being ready both to agree with it and quickly to have it carried round to those in communion, so that the one who is to set out to the bishops in the West may go bearing the signatures of all. Command that what seems good to your holiness be made known to us quickly, so that we may not be ignorant of your decisions.

Concerning the things being contrived, or already devised, against us in Antioch, the same brother will report to your honour, unless the report of what has happened, getting there first, makes the deeds plain. For the expectation of the outcome of these threats is near. I wish your reverence to know that the brother Anthimus has ordained Faustus, the companion of the Pope, as bishop — without even receiving votes — ordaining him to the place of the most reverend brother Cyril, so as to fill Armenia with factions. Therefore, that they may not falsely accuse us, nor that we ourselves be held to blame for the disorder of what has happened, I have made these things known to your honoured self. And it is plain that you too will deign to make them known to the rest. For I think this disorder will grieve many.
To Theodotus, Bishop of Nicopolis

The winter has been severe and prolonged to the utmost, so that not even the consolations that come by letter are easily available to us. Hence I know that I have but seldom both written to your reverence and received letters. But since our most beloved brother Sanctissimus, the fellow-presbyter, has undertaken the journey as far as you, through him I greet your orderly self, and beg you to pray for me and to lend your ear to the aforesaid man, so that you may learn from him in what state the affairs of the churches are, and may bring what diligence you can to the matters before us.

Know, too, that Faustus came to us bearing letters from the Pope, asking that he be made bishop. But when we asked for the testimony of your reverence and of the rest of the bishops, he despised us and went off to Anthimus, and, having received ordination from him, returned without any commendation from us.
To Poemenius, Bishop of Satala

You surely asked the Armenians for letters, when they returned by way of you, and learned the reason why I did not give them the letter. If, then, they spoke truthfully, you granted us pardon at once. But if they concealed it — which I do not suppose — then hear it from us.

The wholly noble Anthimus, who long ago concluded peace with us, when he found an opportunity both to gratify his own vainglory and to procure some grief for us, ordained Faustus on his own authority and by his own hand, without waiting for the vote of any of you, and laughing at us for being scrupulous about such matters. Since, then, he both confounded the ancient good order and despised you also — from whom I was waiting to receive the testimony — and did a thing which I do not know whether it is pleasing to God, for this reason, being grieved at them, I gave no letter to any of the Armenians, nor to your reverence. Nor indeed did I receive Faustus into communion, openly protesting that, unless he brought me letters from you, I would for all time remain estranged from him, and would dispose those of one mind with me to be so disposed toward him.

If, then, what has happened is curable, take pains both to write yourself, bearing witness to him — if you see that the man's life is good — and to urge on the others; but if it is incurable, make this too plain to me, so that I may no longer pay any attention to them at all — even because, as they have shown, they are now bent on transferring their own communion to Anthimus, despising us and this church as worthless for friendship.
To Urbicius, a Monk

You were on the point of coming to us (and the good was near), to cool us at least with the tip of a finger as we burned amid trials. And then? Our sins rose up against us and hindered your impulse, that we might labour without remedy. For as among the waves one subsides, another rises, and another is already darkened with the shudder of breaking, so too of our evils some have ceased, some are present, and some are awaited; and our one relief from evils, for the most part, is to yield to the moment and to withdraw from those who pursue us.

But be present with us — whether to console, or to give counsel, or to send us on our way — and in any case, by the very sight of you, to make us lighter. And, what is greatest, pray, and pray earnestly, that our reasonings too may not be drowned by the evil and the surge, but that in all things we may keep thanksgiving toward God, that we may not be numbered among the wicked servants, who confess him when he does us good, but, when he disciplines us through adversities, do not hold fast to him; rather, that even through hardships themselves we may be benefited, trusting in him the more, the more we have need.
To Theodorus

Some say that those who are caught by the passion of love, when by some more violent constraint they are led away from the objects of their longing, find rest for the vehemence of their passion, if they can look upon an image of the beloved form, through the enjoyment that comes by the eyes. Whether these things are true or not I cannot say; but what has happened to me toward your goodness is not far from what is described. For since a certain disposition arose in me toward your holy and guileless soul — a loving one, so to speak — and since the enjoyment of the objects of my longing, as of no other good, is not easy for us, on account of the hindrance that comes from our sins, I thought that I had seen a most vivid image of your goodness in the presence of our most devout brothers. And if it had befallen me to meet your genuine self apart from these, I would have reckoned that in you I had seen them also; for so great, I say, is the measure of love in each of you, that the rivalry of each to surpass in it shows itself equally. For these things I gave thanks to the holy God, and I pray that, if any time of life still remains, my life may through you be made sweet — since, as things now are, I count the very fact of living a wretched thing and to be fled, parted from the company of those dearest to me. For there is nothing, in my judgment, in which one could take joy, when severed from those one truly loves.
A Copy of the Confession of Faith dictated by the most holy Basil, to which Eustathius, Bishop of Sebasteia, subscribed.

Those who have been preoccupied by another confession of faith and wish to be transferred to fellowship with the orthodox, or who now for the first time desire, in the catechizing of the word of truth, to be instructed, must be taught the faith written by the blessed fathers in the council once convened at Nicaea. This same course would be useful also toward those suspected of being opposed to sound teaching and of cloaking the mind of false doctrine under specious evasions of their own. For these too the faith set down is sufficient. For either they will correct their hidden disease, or, concealing it in the depths, they will themselves bear the judgment of their deceit, while preparing for us an easy defence on the day of judgment, when the Lord will uncover the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of hearts. They must therefore be received when they confess that they believe according to the words set forth by our Fathers at Nicaea, and according to the sound meaning conveyed by those words.

For there are some who, even within this faith, falsify the word of truth and drag the sense of the words in it toward their own purpose. Thus even Marcellus dared — impiously denying the subsistence of our Lord Jesus Christ and interpreting him as a mere word — to allege that he had taken the starting-points of his teaching from there, wrongly interpreting the meaning of the term "of one substance." And some of those who hold the impiety of Sabellius the Libyan, supposing subsistence and substance to be the same, draw from there the occasions for the construction of their own blasphemy, from the fact that it is written in the faith: "But if anyone says that the Son is of another substance or subsistence, the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes him." For there they did not say that substance and subsistence were the same. For if the terms conveyed one and the same notion, what need was there of both? But it is plain that, since some were denying that the Son is of the substance of the Father, while others were saying that he is not of the substance but of some other subsistence, they thus forbade both, as foreign to the mind of the Church. For where they declared their own mind, they said that the Son is of the substance of the Father — no longer adding "of the subsistence." So that the former clause is set down for the rejection of the wicked opinion, while the latter holds the manifestation of the saving doctrine. We must therefore confess the Son to be of one substance with the Father, as it is written; and confess that the Father is in his own subsistence, the Son in his own, and the Holy Spirit in his own, just as they themselves also plainly set forth. For they showed it sufficiently and clearly when they said "light from light" — that the light which begot is one, and the light begotten another, yet light and light all the same; so that the account of the substance is one and the same. Let, then, the very faith written at Nicaea be set before us.

"We believe in one God the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten of the Father, only-begotten, that is, of the substance of the Father; God from God, light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made; of one substance with the Father, through whom all things came to be, both the things in heaven and the things on earth; who for us men and for our salvation came down, and was made flesh, became man, suffered, and rose again on the third day, ascended into the heavens, and is coming to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit. But those who say, 'There was a time when he was not,' and 'Before he was begotten he was not,' and that he came to be out of things that are not; or who assert that the Son of God is of another subsistence or substance, or is changeable or alterable — such persons the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes."

Since, then, here all the other matters have been defined sufficiently and exactly — some for the correction of those who have been harmed, others for guarding against those expected to spring up — but the statement concerning the Spirit lies in passing, deemed worthy of no elaboration, because this question had not yet then been stirred, but the understanding concerning it remained unassailed in the souls of believers; and since, little by little, the wicked seeds of impiety advancing — those that were first sown by Arius, the champion of the heresy, and afterward nurtured to the ruin of the churches by those who succeeded badly to his teachings — the sequence of impiety has burst out into blasphemy against the Spirit: it is necessary, against those who do not spare themselves, nor foresee the inescapable threat which our Lord held out against those who blaspheme against the Holy Spirit, to set forth this — that they must anathematize those who call the Holy Spirit a creature, and those who so think, and those who do not confess that it is holy by nature, as the Father is holy by nature and the Son is holy by nature, but who estrange it from the divine and blessed nature. And the proof of right thinking is not to separate it from the Father and the Son (for we must be baptized as we received it, and believe as we are baptized, and glorify as we have believed — Father and Son and Holy Spirit), but to stand apart from the communion of those who call it a creature, as plainly blasphemous; this being agreed upon (for the notice is necessary, on account of the slanderers): that we neither call the Holy Spirit unbegotten — for we know one unbegotten and one principle of beings, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ — nor begotten; for we have been taught in the tradition of the faith one only-begotten. But having been taught that the Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father, we confess it to be of God, without being created. And we must anathematize also those who call the Holy Spirit "ministering," as by this word bringing it down into the rank of the creature. For the ministering spirits Scripture has handed down to us as creatures, saying, "Are they not all ministering spirits sent forth for service?" And on account of those who confound all things and do not keep the teaching in the Gospels, it is necessary to add this distinction also: that we must flee those who change the order which the Lord handed down to us, as plainly fighting against godliness — those who set the Son before the Father, and put the Holy Spirit before the Son. For we ought to keep the order unmoved and untampered with, which we received from the very voice of the Lord, when he said: "Go, make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit."
The subscription of Bishop Eustathius.

I, Eustathius the bishop, having read it to you, Basil, have understood it, and have assented to what is written above. And I have subscribed in the presence of the brothers who were with me — our own Fronto, and the chorepiscopus Severus, and certain other clergy.
To Atarbius

When we had come as far as Nicopolis, in the hope both of setting right the disturbances that had arisen and of bringing what comfort we could to those whose conduct had been disorderly and contrary to the law of the Church, we were greatly disheartened not to find your Excellency there, but learned instead that you had set off in all haste, and this when the synod you were holding was almost at its midpoint. We were therefore obliged to resort to a letter, by which we remind you to come and meet us, so that you yourself in person may relieve our grief, with which we have been grieved even to death, on hearing that deeds had been ventured in the midst of the Church such as had never until this day come to our ears. And these things, though painful and grievous, are still bearable, because they were done against a man who, having entrusted to God the vindication of what he has suffered, gives himself wholly to peace, and to seeing that no harm comes to the people of God through any fault of his.

But since certain of our honoured brethren, worthy of all credence, reported to us that some innovations were being made by you concerning the faith, and that things were being said by you contrary to sound doctrine, we were on this account more deeply shaken still, and wrestled in great anguish lest, in addition to the countless wounds which the Church has suffered at the hands of those who have sinned against the truth of the Gospel, yet another evil should spring up, with the old heresy of Sabellius, the Church's enemy, being revived — for the brethren reported to us that what was said is akin to it. For this reason we have written, that you would not hesitate to move a short distance and come to us, and, by giving full assurance on these matters, both soothe our pain and comfort the churches of God, which are now grieved beyond endurance, heavily oppressed both by what has been done and by what is rumoured to have been said by you.
To Eusebius, Bishop of Samosata

God, the lover of mankind, who joins to our afflictions consolations of like measure, and comforts the lowly, lest they be unawares swallowed up by excessive grief, has brought us a comfort equal to the disturbances that have lately befallen us at Nicopolis, by setting over us at the right moment the most God-beloved bishop Jovinus; and how opportunely he appeared to us, let him relate himself. For we, sparing the length of the letter, will keep silence, and also lest we should seem, as it were, to brand with a memorial of their fault those who through their change of heart have become dear to us.

But may the holy God grant that you come to our regions, so that we may embrace your reverend dignity and recount each thing in detail. For somehow the things that have grieved us in the experience come to have a certain solace when they are told as stories. Yet, for the way in which the most God-beloved bishop bestirred himself — perfectly as regards his love for us, and above all firmly as regards the strict observance of the canons — praise him, and give thanks to the Lord, that your nurslings everywhere display the stamp of your dignity.
To Eusebius, Bishop of Samosata

I have not yet been able to show in deed, as it deserves, my zeal for the peace of the churches of the Lord; yet I declare that in my heart I have so great a longing for it that I would gladly lay down even my own life, if only the flame of hatred kindled by the evil one might be quenched. And if it were not for my desire for peace, I should not have endured to draw near to the region of Coloneia — may my life never know peace if I lie! Yet it is the true peace, the peace left to us by the Lord himself, that I seek; and what I asked to be given me for my full assurance comes from one who desires nothing else than the true peace, even though certain men, perverting the truth, interpret it otherwise. Let those men, then, use their tongues for whatever they will; for assuredly they will one day repent of these words.

But I beg your Holiness to remember the original propositions, and not to be led astray by accepting other answers in place of the questions asked, nor to give effect to the sophistries of men who, without any power of speech, by mere intent alone do the cruellest violence of all to the truth. For I put forward plain, clear, and easily remembered words: whether we refuse communion to those who do not accept the faith of Nicaea, and whether we cannot endure to share fellowship with those who have the audacity to call the Holy Spirit a creature. But he, instead of answering my questions to the point, recited back to us those things which you sent — and this not from simplicity of mind, as one might suppose, nor from inability to perceive the consequence. Rather he reckons thus: that by denying our proposition he will make himself plain to the people, while by agreeing with us he will fall away from that middle position, than which up to now nothing has been more precious to him. Let him not, then, play the sophist with us, nor, along with the rest, deceive your prudence too; but let him send us a brief reply to the question, either confessing or denying communion with the enemies of the faith. If you persuade him to this and send me answers that are sound and such as I pray for, then I am the one who has erred in all that went before; I take all that blame upon myself; then demand of me a display of humility. But until none of this is done, forgive me, most God-beloved father, since I cannot stand at the altar of God with dissimulation. For if I had not feared this, why was I separating myself from Euippius, a man so accomplished in matters of discourse, so advanced in years, and possessing so many claims upon my friendship? But if those things were done rightly and fittingly for the sake of the truth, it would surely be absurd to be seen joining myself, through the middle position of these clever and charming gentlemen, to men who say the same things as he.

Yet it does not seem to me right wholly to estrange ourselves from those who do not accept the faith; rather we should show some care for these men according to the ancient laws of charity, and write to them with one accord, bringing to bear every appeal with compassion, and, setting before them the faith of the fathers, invite them to union. And if we persuade them, let us be joined with them in common; but if we fail, let us be content with one another, and banish this double-mindedness from our character, taking up the evangelical and guileless manner of life by which those who from the first came to the word once lived. For, it is said, the heart and soul of those who believed was one. If, then, they are persuaded by you, this is best. But if not, make known to us the makers of war, and cease henceforth writing to us about reconciliations.
To Meletius, Bishop of Antioch

I knew that the charge now brought against Apollinaris — who finds it so easy to say anything — would strike your Perfection's ear as strange. For neither was I myself in the time before this aware that he held such views; but now the Sebastenes, having ferreted them out from somewhere, have brought them into the open, and they carry about a treatise on the strength of which they especially condemn us too, as holding the same opinions. It contains expressions such as these: "So that everywhere it is necessary to conceive the first identity as conjoined — rather, as united — with the otherness, and to call the same a second and a third. For what the Father is in the first place, this the Son is in the second, and the Spirit in the third. And again, what the Spirit is in the first place, this is the Son in the second — inasmuch as the Lord too is the Spirit — and the Father in the third, inasmuch as God is Spirit. And, to signify the ineffable in a more forced manner, the Father is paternally Son, and the Son filially Father; and likewise in the case of the Spirit, inasmuch as the Trinity is one God."

These are the things now noised abroad, which I can by no means believe to be fabrications of those who circulate them — though, given their slander against us, I reckon nothing too daring for them. For in writing to certain of their own party, and adding their calumny against us, they appended these things, calling the words those of heretics, but concealing the author of the composition, so that to the many we might be thought to be the writers. Still, their ingenuity would never have gone so far as actually to compose such words — so at least I persuade myself. Therefore, in order both to repel the blasphemy that prevails against us and to show all men that we have nothing in common with those who say such things, we were compelled to make mention of the man, as one who approaches the impiety of Sabellius. And on this matter, so much.

From the imperial court someone has come announcing that, upon the first impulse of the emperor — which those who pour out their slanders against us had stirred up in him — a second resolution has been reached, that we should not be given up to our accusers, nor handed over to their will, as had been decreed from the first, but that some delay should for the present be granted. If, then, either these arrangements stand, or something more humane than these is decided, we shall make it known to your Reverence. But if the former counsels prevail, this too shall not escape you.

The brother Sanctissimus has assuredly been with you for some time, and what he is seeking has been made plain to your Perfection. If, then, the letter to those of the West seems to require anything necessary, deign to draft it and send it to us, so that we may have it signed by those of one mind with us and have the signature ready, set out on a separate sheet which we can attach to the document carried by our brother the fellow-presbyter. For I myself, finding nothing of substance in the memorandum, had nothing about which to write to those in the West. The necessary matters have already been dealt with, and to write what is superfluous is wholly idle. And to trouble them again about the same things — would that not be ridiculous?

But this point seemed to me, as it were, unexercised and to afford scope for a letter: to urge them not to receive without discrimination the communions of those who come from the East, but, having once chosen a single party, to admit the rest on the testimony of those in communion; and not to attach themselves to everyone who writes out a creed under the mere pretext of orthodoxy. For in this way they will be found in communion with men at war with one another, who often put forward the same words, yet fight among themselves as much as those who are furthest apart. In order, then, that the heresy may not be the more inflamed, with men at strife with one another putting forward against each other their respective letters, they should be urged to make discriminating judgements both about the communions of those who come to them and about those granted in writing, according to the practice of the Church.
To Theodotus, Bishop of Nicopolis

Rightly and fittingly you have reproached us, my truly honoured and most beloved brother, that ever since we withdrew at that time, bearing to Eustathius those propositions of yours concerning the faith, we have made known to you nothing at all, neither small nor great, of what concerns him. But I passed over the things he did to us, not as though I held them of little account, but because the report had by now been spread abroad to all men, and no one had any further need of teaching from us in order to learn the man's true purpose. For this he himself contrived, as though afraid he might have but few witnesses to his own opinion, dispatching to every furthest corner the letters he composed against us. From our communion, then, he himself broke away, refusing both to meet us at the appointed place and to bring forward his disciples, as he had promised; nay, he even branded us in public synods, together with Theophilus the Cilician, charging us with bare and undisguised blasphemy, as having sown in the souls of the people doctrines foreign to his own teaching. These things alone were enough to dissolve all our union with him. But when, on coming into Cilicia and meeting a certain Gelasius, he set forth to him a creed which only Arius, or some genuine disciple of his, could have composed, then indeed we were the more confirmed in our separation, reckoning that neither will the Ethiopian ever change his skin, nor the leopard his spots, nor can one bred up in perverse doctrines wash off the evil of his heresy.

He played the bold youth in these matters too, writing against us — rather, composing long discourses full of every kind of abuse and slander; to which for the present we have made no answer, because we have been taught by the apostle not to avenge ourselves, but to give place to wrath; and at the same time, when we considered the depth of the hypocrisy with which he dealt with us all that time, we were held by a kind of speechlessness through astonishment.

But even if none of those things existed, this latest deed of his, the thing he has dared — in whom would it not have stirred a shudder and an utter turning-away from the man? For he has dared, as I hear (if indeed the report is true and not a fabrication put together in slander), even to reordain certain men — something which to this day none of the heretics is found to have done. How, then, is it possible for us to bear such things meekly, and to think the man's sins curable? Do not, therefore, be led astray by false words, nor be persuaded by the suspicions of men who readily take everything in the worst sense, as though we treated such matters as things indifferent. For know, most beloved and honoured of us, that I do not remember ever before admitting into my soul so great a grief as now, when I heard of the confusion of the laws of the Church. Only pray that the Lord may grant us to do nothing in anger, but to keep that love which behaves not unseemly and is not puffed up. For see how those who lack it have been lifted up beyond the measure of men, and behave unseemly in their lives, daring deeds for which the time past holds no precedents.
To Olympius

Truly the hearing of unexpected things is enough to make both a man's ears ring; and this is just what has now happened to me. For though these treatises being circulated against us fell upon ears by now well exercised — since I myself had received the letter before, a letter befitting indeed my sins, yet never expected to be written by those who sent it — nevertheless this second matter appeared to us to contain in itself so great an excess of bitterness as to throw the former into shadow. For how was I not nearly driven out of my own senses, when I came upon the letter to the most reverend brother Dazinas, full of countless insults and unbearable accusations against us, and of charges of rebellion, as though we had been found among the most grievous schemes against the Church? And forthwith proofs that the blasphemies against us were true were adduced from a treatise written, I do not know, by whom. Some parts of it I recognized, I confess, as written by Apollinaris of Laodicea — and these I had never actually read myself, but knew only from the report of others; but I found certain other things written in it which I had never read nor heard anyone else utter; and of this my witness in heaven is faithful. How, then, those who turn away from falsehood, who have been taught that love is the fulfilling of the law, who profess to bear the weaknesses of the powerless — how they have brought themselves to lay these slanders upon us and to condemn us out of other men's writings, I cannot, for all my reasoning, devise the cause, unless, as I said at the outset, I judged this to be a portion of the punishments owed me for my sins, and the grief that goes with them.

For first I mourned in my soul, because truth has grown scarce among the sons of men; and then I feared also for myself, lest, in addition to my other sins, I should fall victim to misanthropy, reckoning nothing in anyone to be trustworthy, if those whom I had trusted in the greatest matters have shown themselves such towards me, and such towards the truth itself. Know therefore, brother, and let everyone who is a friend of the truth know, that the treatises are not mine, nor do they please me, since they were not written according to my mind. And if I once wrote, many years ago, to Apollinaris or to anyone else, I ought not to be accused on that account; for neither do I myself accuse anyone, if some member of a fellowship has split off into heresy (you surely know the men, even though I do not name them), since each man will die in his own sin.

These things I have now answered to the volume that was sent, so that you yourself may know the truth and may make it plain to those who do not wish to hold the truth in unrighteousness. And if it be necessary to make a fuller defence concerning each of the charges brought against us, this too we will do, with God's help. We, brother Olympius, neither speak of three gods, nor are we in communion with Apollinaris.
To Abramius, Bishop of Batnae

All the time since autumn I have been ignorant of where your Reverence was staying. For I found the reports conflicting, some announcing that your Reverence was lodging at Samosata, others in the country, and others affirming that they had seen you about Batnae itself; and for this reason I did not write continually. But now, having learned that you are staying at Antioch, in the house of the most reverend Saturninus the count, I have eagerly given the letter to the most beloved and most reverend brother Sanctissimus, my fellow-presbyter, through whom I greet your Charity, begging you, wherever you may be, to remember above all God, and then us also, whom you chose from the first to love, and to keep numbered among those most your own.
To Peter, Bishop of Alexandria

Of bodily friendship the eyes are the agents, and intimacy formed over a long time confirms it; but true love is established by the gift of the Spirit, which joins together what is widely separated in place, and makes those who love one another known to each other, not through bodily features but through the distinctive marks of the soul. This indeed the grace of the Lord has wrought in our case too, granting us to see you with the eyes of the soul, and to embrace you with true love, and, as it were, to grow together with you and come into one union out of fellowship in the faith. For we are persuaded that you, being the nursling of so great a man, and having had your portion of long association with him, walk by the same Spirit and follow the same doctrines of piety.

Therefore we greet your Honour, and beg you, along with all else, to take up after him the great man's affection towards us; to write to us regularly of your own affairs, and to care for the brotherhood everywhere with the same tenderness and the same eagerness which that most blessed man also showed towards all who love God in truth.
To Paeonius the Presbyter

How greatly you gladdened us by your letter you can surely judge by the very things you wrote; so clearly was the purity of the heart, from which those words came forth, declared out of the letter. For as the channel of water shows its own spring, so the nature of speech marks the heart that produced it. So I confess I have felt something strange and far removed from what one would expect. For though I was always eager to come upon a letter from your Perfection, yet when I took the letter in my hands and read it, I was not so much pleased by what was written as grieved, reckoning how great a loss we had suffered during the time of silence.

But since you have begun to write, do not cease to do so. For you will gladden me more than those who send great riches to lovers of wealth. None of my scribes was at hand, neither of the fine penmen nor of the shorthand-writers. For of those whom I had happened to train, some have run back to their first way of life, and others have given up under the toil, worn out by long sickness.
To Diodorus, Presbyter of Antioch

I have read the books sent by your Honour. With the second I was greatly delighted, not only for its brevity — as was natural for one now sluggish in all things and feeble in condition — but because it is at once dense in its ideas, and in it the objections of the opponents and the answers to them are set out with clarity; and the plainness and unadorned quality of the diction seemed to me fitting for the purpose of a Christian who writes not so much for display as for the common good. But the former book, though it has the same force in its substance, yet being dressed up with more elaborate language and varied figures and the graces of dialogue, seemed to me to require much time to go through, and much labour of mind both to gather its ideas and to retain them in memory. For the calumnies of the opponents and the rejoinders of our own side, thrown in between, though they seem to lend the treatise certain dialectical charms, nevertheless, by introducing leisure and delay, break up the continuity of the thought and slacken the tension of the argumentative discourse.

For your shrewdness has surely perceived this, that even among the philosophers outside the faith, those who composed dialogues — Aristotle and Theophrastus — laid hold at once of the matters themselves, because they were conscious of their own lack of Platonic graces. But Plato, with his command of language, at the same time contends with his doctrines and also ridicules the persons of his speakers: in Thrasymachus assailing his boldness and rashness, in Hippias the lightness and emptiness of his mind, and in Protagoras his arrogance and pomposity.
