But where he brings indeterminate persons into his dialogues, he uses the interlocutors for the sake of clarity in the matters, but introduces nothing further from the persons into his subjects; as he did in the Laws.

It behoves us too, then, who come to writing not out of vanity, but having chosen to leave behind for the brotherhood the foundations of profitable discourse — if we set up some person already proclaimed to all for the wilfulness of his character, to weave into the discourse something also from the quality of that person, if indeed it falls to us at all to assail men, leaving the matters aside. But if the interlocutor is indeterminate, the digressions against the persons break the continuity, and arrive at no useful end.

These things I have said in order to show that you have not sent your labours into the hands of a flatterer, but have shared your toils with a most genuine brother. And I have said them not to correct what is written, but as a safeguard for what is to come. For surely one who has employed such skill and zeal in writing will not shrink from writing on; since those who furnish the subjects do not leave off either. For us it will be enough to read your works; but from being able to write anything ourselves we are so far removed that I am almost ready to say we are removed even from being in health, or from having moderate leisure from affairs.

I have now sent, by the reader, the larger and earlier book, having gone through it as far as I was able. The second I have kept back, wishing to copy it out, but for the present finding no one who writes quickly. For to such poverty have the much-envied possessions of the Cappadocians come.
To Eusebius, Bishop of Samosata

In what condition the good Isaaces found us, he will himself relate to you better than I can, even if his tongue is not adequate to set forth in tragic style the overpowering excess of my sufferings, so great was the magnitude of my illness. And what is likely is clear to everyone who knows me even a little. For if, in my seeming good health, I was weaker for living than those given up for dead, one may judge what I must have been in sickness. And yet it ought to have been (grant pardon to a fever that mocks me) that, since to be ill was natural to me, in this change of condition the better part of health should now have remained to me. But since it is a scourge of the Lord, intensifying my pain with additions proportioned to my deserts, I acquired weakness upon weakness, so that henceforth it is plain even to a child that of all necessity this husk of ours must depart — unless, perhaps, the loving-kindness of God, granting us in his long-suffering time for repentance, should now too, as often before, work some release and a way out from desperate troubles. Let these things, then, be as is pleasing to him and profitable to us.

But as for how the affairs of the churches are perishing and being sold for nothing, while we, for the sake of our own security, overlook our neighbours' concerns and cannot even see this — that with the common misfortune each man's interest too is lost together — what need is there to speak? Especially to a man who, foreseeing each thing from afar, both bore witness beforehand and proclaimed it, and yourself rose up first and roused up the rest as well, writing, coming in person, leaving nothing undone, uttering every cry — things which we remember at each new event, but profit by no longer. And now, had not my sins stood in my way — first our most reverend and beloved brother Eustathius the co-deacon, falling into a grievous sickness, kept me waiting two whole months, watching day by day for his recovery; then all who were with me fell sick, of whom brother Isaaces will recount the remnants; and last of all I myself was held by this disease — else I should long ago have been with your Honour, not that I could be of any use to the common cause, but that I might gain for myself great profit from meeting you. For I had resolved to get beyond the reach of ecclesiastical missiles, because of our defencelessness against the machinations of our opponents. May the great hand of God preserve you to all your life, noble guardian of the faith and watchful champion of the churches; and may he count us worthy, before our departure, of meeting you, for the profit of our souls.
To Antipater

Now above all I think I feel the loss which I endure through being ill, when, with such a man as you governing our country, I am compelled to be absent because of the care of my body. For a whole month now I have been waiting upon the treatment of the naturally hot waters, as though I were to gain some benefit from it. But it seems I am labouring in vain in the wilderness, or even appearing to be matter for laughter to the many, since I will not even heed the proverb which says that there is no benefit from hot springs for the dead.

For this reason, even so, I wish, setting all else aside, to come to your reverend self, both to enjoy the good things in you, and to set in good order, through your uprightness, the affairs of my own household. For the house of our most honoured mother Palladia is my own special concern, a woman to whom not only kinship of family joins us, but whose graciousness of character too has made her a mother to us. Since, then, some trouble has been stirred up about her house, we ask your magnanimity to defer the inquiry a little and to await our coming — not that justice should be corrupted (for I would a thousand times rather die than ask such a favour from a judge who is a friend to the laws and to justice), but that you may learn from my own lips, as I report them, those things which it is not seemly for me to write. For thus you yourself will not fail of the truth, nor shall we suffer anything against our wishes. I beg, then, since the person is in safe keeping and held by the court, that you grant us this favour, free of any burden and free of any cause for envy.
To Eusebius, Bishop of Samosata

What state of soul do you think I was in when I received the letter of your Reverence? For if I looked to the affection in the letter, I straightway set out to fly to the land of the Syrians; but if to the sickness of body by which I lay fettered, I felt myself in want not only of flying but even of turning over on my bed. For this was the fiftieth day I was passing in illness, on which our beloved and most zealous brother Elpidius, the co-deacon, came to us; greatly wasted by the fever which, for want of material to feed it, wrapped itself about this dry flesh as about a burnt-out wick, and brought on a wasting and lingering sickness. And next, my old affliction, this liver of mine, taking over, shut me off from food, drove sleep from my eyes, and held me on the borders of life and death, granting me only so much life as to be conscious of the troubles that come from it. So I had recourse even to naturally hot waters, and submitted to certain attentions from physicians. But this violent malady confounded them all; for if the habit of it is present, another man might bear it, but when it falls on one unaccustomed, no one is so adamantine as to hold out against it.

Long troubled by it, I was never so grieved as now, when I was hindered by it from meeting your true love. For what gladness of heart we were deprived of I know full well, since with the very tip of my finger I tasted last year the sweetest honey of the church among you.

I, moreover, for the sake of other pressing matters too, needed to come together with your Reverence, and to take counsel about many things and to learn many things. For there is no finding here even true love; and even when one finds someone who loves greatly, there is no one able, in a manner approaching your perfect wisdom and the experience which you have gathered from many labours about the churches, to give us counsel concerning what lies before us.

The other matters, then, I could not write; but those things which it is safe to set forth are these. The presbyter Evagrius, son of Pompeianus of Antioch, who once set out with the blessed Eusebius for the West, has now returned from Rome, demanding of us a letter containing word for word the very things written by those of the West (for he brought back to us our own letter, as not having satisfied the more exacting among them there), and that an embassy be at once pressed forward through men of repute, so that the men may have a respectable pretext for our being visited.
Those at Sebasteia who hold our views, having laid bare the festering sore of the false doctrine of Eustathius, demand of us some ecclesiastical attention.

Iconium is a city of Pisidia, in old times the first after the greatest, but now it too presides over a district which, gathered from various sections, has received the administration of its own province. This city calls upon us also for a visitation, to give it a bishop; for Faustinus has died.

Whether, then, one should not shrink from ordinations beyond one's borders, and what answer should be given to the Sebastenes, and how one should be disposed towards the proposals of Evagrius — about all this I needed to be instructed by meeting your Honour in person, of which I have been deprived through my present weakness. If, then, it be possible to come upon someone arriving here quickly, deign to send me answers about everything; but if not, pray that what is pleasing to the Lord may come into my mind. And in the synod bid that mention be made of us, and pray yourself for us, and take the people with you, that we may be counted worthy to serve, during the remaining days or hours of our sojourn, as is pleasing to the Lord.
To the Alexandrians

The report of the persecutions which have taken place at Alexandria and throughout the rest of Egypt reached us long ago, and disposed our souls as was to be expected. For we reflected on the artfulness of the diabolical warfare: which, when it saw the Church multiplied and rather flourishing under the persecutions of the enemy, changed its counsel, and no longer wars openly, but lays hidden snares for us, cloaking its plot under the name which they bear, so that we may both suffer the same things as our fathers, and yet not seem to suffer for Christ's sake, because our persecutors too bear the name of Christians. Reflecting on these things, we sat a long while astounded at the tidings of what had happened. For indeed both our ears rang when we learned of the shameless and misanthropic heresy of those who persecuted you, that they reverenced neither age, nor labours in the service of the state, nor the love of the people; but tortured their bodies, dishonoured them, delivered them to exile, and plundered the possessions of those they could find, neither shamed by the condemnation of men, nor foreseeing the dreadful requital of the just Judge. These things astounded us and nearly drove us out of our senses. And along with these reflections there entered also this thought: has the Lord perhaps utterly forsaken his own churches? Is this perhaps the last hour, and is the apostasy through these things gaining its entrance, so that henceforth the lawless one, the son of perdition, the adversary, may be revealed, who exalts himself above all that is called God or is worshipped?

But whether the trial is for a season, bear it, you noble combatants of Christ; or whether all things are being delivered up to utter destruction, let us not lose heart at what is present, but await the revelation from heaven and the appearing of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ. For if all creation shall be dissolved and the fashion of this world shall be changed, what wonder if we too, being a part of creation, should suffer the common sufferings and be delivered to afflictions which the just Judge brings upon us according to the measure of our strength, not allowing us to be tried beyond what we are able, but giving with the trial also the way out, that we may be able to endure?

The crowns of the martyrs await you, brethren; the choirs of the confessors are ready to stretch out their hands to you and to receive you into their own number. Remember the saints of old, that no one in luxury or in flattery was counted worthy of the crowns of endurance, but all, tried in the fire through great afflictions, displayed their proof. For some had trial of mockings and scourgings, others were sawn asunder, others died by slaughter of the sword. These are the glories of the saints. Blessed is he who is counted worthy of the sufferings for Christ; but more blessed is he who has abounded in the sufferings, because the sufferings of the present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which is to be revealed in us.

If, then, it were possible for me to come in person, I should have preferred nothing to meeting you, that I might both see the athletes of Christ, and embrace them, and share in the prayers and the spiritual gifts among you. But since my body has now been consumed by chronic disease, so that I cannot even come down from my bed, and those lying in wait for us are many, like ravening wolves, watching for a time when they may be able to plunder the sheep of Christ, I have of necessity resorted to a visitation by letter, begging first of all that you would make earnest supplications for me, that I may be counted worthy to serve the Lord, at least for the days or hours that remain, according to the gospel of the kingdom; and then also that you would pardon my absence and this tardiness of my letters. For we have scarcely been able to procure a man able to minister to our desire; I mean our son Eugenius the monk, through whom I beg you to pray for us and for the whole Church, and to write back to us about your affairs, so that, learning of them, we may be more cheerfully disposed.
To the Church of Antioch

Who will give me wings, as of a dove? And I shall fly to you and lay to rest the longing which I have for meeting your love. But as it is, I am in want not of wings only, but of the body itself, long since worn out by lengthy illness, and now utterly crushed by continual afflictions. For who is so adamantine in soul, who so wholly without sympathy and so savage, as to hear the groan that assails us from every side — like some downcast choir sounding forth a common and harmonious lament — and not suffer in his soul, and be bowed down to the ground, and be utterly consumed by these helpless cares? But the holy God is able to give some release from these helpless straits and to grant us some breathing space from our long toils. Therefore I ask that you too have the same comfort, and, rejoicing in the hope of comfort, endure the present pain of your afflictions. For if we are paying the penalty of our sins, the scourges are enough henceforth to win remission of God's wrath against us; or if through these trials we have been called to the contests for piety, the steward of the games is just, and will not allow us to be tried beyond what we are able to endure, but, for what we have already toiled through, will render us the crown of endurance and of hope in him. Let us not, then, grow weary in contending in the struggles for piety, nor through despair cast away what we have laboured for. For not one act of courage nor a brief toil displays the steadfastness of the soul; but he who proves our hearts wishes us, through a long and protracted trial, to be shown forth as wearers of the crown of righteousness.

Only let our purpose be kept unyielding, let the firmness of our faith in Christ be preserved unshaken, and he who will help us will come quickly; he will come and will not delay. For expect affliction upon affliction, hope upon hope, yet a little while, yet a little while. Thus the Holy Spirit knows how to console his own nurslings with the promise of what is to come. For after the afflictions comes hope, and from close at hand the things hoped for are present. For though one should name the whole of human life, it is an utterly tiny span, in comparison with that boundless age which is laid up in our hopes.

As for the faith, we neither accept a newer one written for us by others, nor do we ourselves dare to hand on the offspring of our own thought, lest we make the words of piety merely human; but what we have been taught by the holy fathers, this we declare to those who ask us. There is, therefore, established from the fathers in our church the faith written by the holy fathers who assembled at Nicaea; which we suppose to be on your lips too, but, lest we incur the charge of negligence, we do not refuse to set down the very words in writing. They are these. We believe in one God the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ the Son of God, begotten of the Father, only-begotten — that is, of the substance of the Father; light of light, true God of true God; begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father, through whom all things came to be, both the things in heaven and the things on earth. Who for us men and for our salvation came down; was made flesh, became man, suffered, and rose again on the third day; ascended into the heavens, and is coming to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit. But those who say, "There was once when he was not," and, "Before he was begotten he was not," and that "he came to be out of things that are not," or who affirm that the Son of God is of another hypostasis or substance, or changeable, or alterable — these the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.

In these things we believe. But since the statement concerning the Holy Spirit is left undefined — the fighters against the Spirit not having yet appeared at that time — they were silent about the necessity of anathematizing those who say that the Holy Spirit is of a created and servile nature. For nothing at all of the divine and blessed Trinity is created.
To Eusebius, Bishop of Samosata

I have already received two letters from your divinely inspired and most perfect wisdom, of which one described to us plainly both how we were awaited by the people under the hand of your Holiness, and how greatly we grieved them by being absent from the most holy synod. The other, the older one, as I conjecture from the writing, but delivered to us later, contained an instruction befitting you and necessary for us: not to be negligent of the churches of God, nor little by little to surrender affairs to our opponents, whereby their cause will grow and ours be diminished. And I think I have answered both; but nevertheless even now, since it is uncertain whether those entrusted with the service preserved our answers, I make my defence concerning the same matters. As to the absence, writing a most true reason — of which I think the report has reached even to your Holiness — that I was held by a sickness which brought me down to the very gates of death. And even now, when I was sending about these things, I wrote bearing the remnants of the illness. And these are such as would suffice to be grievous diseases for another man.

But as to its not being through any negligence of ours that the affairs of the churches have been betrayed to our opponents, I wish your Reverence to know that those bishops who are supposedly in communion with us, whether through hesitation, or because they are still suspicious of us and not wholehearted, or through the opposition to good works that comes from the devil, will not endure to lend us their aid. In outward appearance, indeed, the greater number of us are together with one another, the good Bosporius too having been joined to us; but in truth they lend us aid in none of the most necessary matters; so that I too am for the most part hindered, by this very despondency, from recovery, my sicknesses continually returning upon me from my intense grief.

And what could I do alone, since the canons, as you yourself know, do not permit such administrative measures to one man? And yet what remedy have I not tried? Of what judgement have I not reminded them, partly through letters, partly through meeting them? For I went even as far as the city on the report of my death. And when it pleased God that we should be found alive by them, we discoursed to them as was fitting. And when present I am reverenced, and they promise everything fitting; but once we are gone, they run back again to their own opinion. These things we too reap from the common state of affairs, the Lord plainly having forsaken us, who, because lawlessness has been multiplied, have grown cold in love. But for all this let your great and most powerful intercession with God suffice us. For perhaps we may either become of some use to affairs, or, failing of what we strive for, may escape condemnation.
To the Auditor of the Prefects

I gathered together all our brethren the country-bishops at the synod of the blessed martyr Eupsychius, in order to make them known to your Honour. But since you were absent, it is necessary that they be presented to your Perfection by letter. Know, then, that this brother is worthy to be trusted by your prudence, for the fear of the Lord. And whatever he may bring to your good will on behalf of the poor, deign to believe him as one who speaks the truth, and to furnish what aid you can to those who are hard pressed. You will, of course, also deign to inspect the poor-relief work of the company under his charge, and to relieve it altogether of the assessment. For this your colleague too has already agreed to do, to free from public service the small property of the poor.
To Another Auditor

If it were possible for me to be present in person with your Honour, I should certainly have laid before you myself the matters I wished to, and taken up the cause of those who are hard pressed. But since sickness of body and the press of affairs draw me away, I commend to you in my stead this brother the country-bishop, that you may attend to him sincerely and use him as a counsellor, since he is able to give counsel about affairs in a manner both truth-loving and prudent. For the poor-house administered by him, whenever you deign to view it (and you will view it, I know well, and not pass it by, since you are not without experience of the work, but, as someone reported to me, maintain one of those in Amasea out of what the Lord has given you) — whenever, then, you have seen this too, you will furnish him all that he seeks. For your colleague too has already promised me some kindness concerning the poor-houses. And I say this not that you should imitate another (for it is fitting that you should be a leader to others in good works), but that you may know that other men too have been moved to entreat us about these very matters.
To a Secretary of the Prefects

You assuredly know this man from your meeting in the city; yet I commend him to you also by letter, assuring you that he will be useful to you in many of your concerns, because he is able to suggest what should be done both prudently and reverently. And those things which you spoke into my ear — now is the time to show them forth, when the aforesaid brother shall point out to you the affairs of the poor.
To Eusebius, Bishop of Samosata

I know the countless toils you have endured for the churches of God, and I am not ignorant of the multitude of cares you have, managing your stewardship not carelessly but according to the will of the Lord. And I bear in mind the one settled near you as your neighbour, before whom you must, like birds cowering before an eagle, each run not far from your shelter. None of these things has escaped me. But longing is a forceful thing, both to hope for what is not possible and to attempt the impossible; or rather, hope in the Lord is the strongest of all. For not by unreasoning desire, but by the strength of faith, I expect both that a way will appear amid impossibilities, and that you will easily overcome all hindrances, so as to see the most beloved of churches, and indeed to be seen by it — which to it is most precious of all good things, to look upon your face and to hear your voice. Do not, then, leave its hopes unfulfilled. For last year, when I returned from Syria and brought it the promise I had received, how, do you think, I raised it up with hopes! Do not, then, defer its visitation to another time, O admirable man. For even if it be possible to see it sometime, yet it will not be along with us, whom our sickness presses now at last to depart from this painful life.
To Antiochus

I cannot reproach you for sloth or negligence, that, when occasion offered, you kept silence of letters. For the greeting which you sent me by your honoured hand I count more precious than many letters. In return for it, then, I greet you, and beg you earnestly to lay hold of the salvation of your soul, schooling all the passions of the flesh by reason, and keeping the thought of God continually established in your soul as in some most holy temple; and in every action and every word to set before your eyes the tribunal of Christ, so that your particular deeds, gathered together at that exact and dreadful inquiry, may bring you glory on the day of recompense, when you are counted worthy of praise before all creation. And if the great man should consent to make the journey as far as us, it will be no small gain to see you with him in our land.
To Aburgius

I used to think the tale of Homer a fable, when I went through that part of his poetry in which he relates the sufferings of Odysseus. But the misfortune that has befallen the most excellent Maximus has taught us to consider as credible even those things, until now mythical and quite incredible. For he too became governor of a nation by no means the least, just as that man was general of the Cephallenians. And as the one came home stripped, though he had carried off much wealth, so this man too his calamity has so reduced that he is in danger of being seen by those at home in another man's rags. And he has suffered these things, having perhaps provoked the Laestrygonians against himself, and having fallen in with a Scylla in woman's form possessing a dog's inhumanity and savagery. Since, then, it has scarcely been granted him to swim through this inescapable surge, he supplicates you through us, asking you to respect our common nature, and, grieving at his undeserved misfortunes, not to hide his case in silence, but to make it known to those in power, so that, best of all, some help may come to him against the contrived injury; or, if not, that at least the purpose of the one who insolently wronged him may be made public. For it is sufficient comfort to the wronged man that the wickedness of those who plotted against him be brought to light.
To Trajan

It brings much comfort to those who are hard pressed even to be able to bewail their own misfortunes, and especially when they meet with men able, out of the nobility of their character, to feel sympathy with their pains. For this reason the most reverend brother Maximus, who governed our country, having suffered such things as no other man yet has — stripped of all his possessions, both what was his by inheritance and what had been gathered from former labours, and grievously afflicted in body by his wanderings up and down, and not even keeping unharmed the very right of citizenship for which it is the custom of free men to endure all toils — has greatly lamented to us about what has befallen him, and has asked that through us the whole Iliad of evils that has surrounded him be made plain to you in summary. And I, since I could in no other way take away any of his troubles, readily granted this favour: to report to your Excellency a few of the many things I heard from him, since he himself seemed to blush to recount his own misfortunes plainly.

For even if what happened does not establish the man who wronged him as wicked, yet at least it shows the one who suffered to be of the most pitiable lot, since the very fact of falling into heaven-sent evils seems somehow to be a proof of being delivered over to suffering. But it is enough for him, as comfort for what has happened, that you should look upon him with a kindly eye, and that the all-sufficing grace which all enjoy yet cannot exhaust — I mean the grace of your gentleness — should be extended to him also. And that in the courts too your inclination toward him will be a great means to his victory, we are all firmly persuaded. And most just of all is this very man, who sought our letter as something that would be of use to him; whom, along with the rest, may we see extolling your dignity with such voice as he can command.
To Trajan

You yourself set before your eyes the affliction of Maximus, formerly held in esteem but now the most pitiable of all men, who governed our country — would that he had not! For I think the governorship of provinces would become a thing to be deprecated by many, if their tenures of office are to come to such an end. Why, then, need we report each particular, both of what we saw and of what we heard, to a man who, through the great keenness of his mind, is able to conjecture the rest from the few things that were done? Yet, perhaps, in saying this much, I shall not seem to you superfluous: that, many and dreadful as were the things ventured against him before your arrival, those that came after were such as to make the earlier seem an act of kindness. So great was the excess of insolence and loss and bodily affliction in the measures afterwards devised against him by the one in power. And now he comes under guard, to pay out the remnants of his evils here, unless you are willing to stretch out your great hand over the man who is hard pressed. I know that I am doing a superfluous thing in calling upon your goodness to show kindness; nevertheless, since I wish to be useful to the man, I implore your reverend self to add something, for our sake, to your natural zeal for what is good, so that the benefit of our intercession on his behalf may become plain to the man.
To Amphilochius, as from Heraclides

I both remember the conversations we once held with one another, and have not forgotten what I myself said and what I heard from your nobility. And now public life no longer holds me. For though in heart I am the same, and have not yet put off the old man, yet in outward form, and in having removed myself far from the affairs of life, I have seemed at length to have set foot, as it were, on the road of the life that is according to Christ. I sit by myself, like those about to put out to sea, looking off toward what is to come. For those who sail need winds for a fair voyage, but we need one to lead us by the hand and to convey us safely through the salt waves of life. For I reckon that I need, first, a bridle for my youth, and then goads for the course of piety. And the agent of these is plainly reason, now schooling the disorderliness in us, now rousing the sluggishness of the soul. Again I have need of other remedies, to wash off the filth that comes from habit. For you know that we who have long been habituated to the public square are unsparing of our words, and unguarded against the impressions formed in the mind from the evil one. We are conquered too by love of honour, and we do not easily lay aside thinking something of ourselves. For these things I reckon I need a great and experienced teacher. And then too, that the eye of the soul be cleansed, so that, all the darkening that comes from ignorance being removed like some film, it may be able to gaze upon the beauty of the glory of God — this I judge no small work, nor one that brings benefit in small degree.

That your learning both perceives these things, and desires that there should be some help toward it, I know exactly; and if ever God grant that I come together with your reverend self, plainly I shall learn more about the things I must take thought for. For now, through much ignorance, I cannot even recognize of how many things I am in need; except that I have in no way repented of my first impulse, nor does my soul flag toward the goal of the life that is according to God — which you feared on my behalf, doing rightly and fittingly for yourself, lest, turning back, I should become a pillar of salt, as a certain woman suffered, as I hear. But the authorities outside still constrain me, the magistrates seeking me out as though I were some deserter. But what holds me back most of all is my own heart, witnessing to itself those things which I have said.

And since you made mention of agreements, and promised to bring an accusation, you made me laugh in the midst of this dejection of mine, that you are still an orator and do not let go of your rhetorical skill. For I, unless as an ignorant man I altogether miss the truth, think thus: that there is one road leading to the Lord, and that all who journey toward him travel together with one another and walk by one agreement of life. So that where could I go, to be separated from you, and not live with you and serve with you the God to whom we have fled in common? For our bodies will be parted by places, but the eye of God plainly watches over us both in common — if indeed my life too is worthy to be looked upon by the eyes of God; for I have read somewhere in the Psalms that the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous. For I pray to be present in body with you, and with everyone whose choice is like yours, and every night and day to bend the knee with you to our Father who is in the heavens, and with anyone else who worthily calls upon God. For I know that fellowship in prayers brings much gain. But if, every time it falls to me to groan, cast away in some out-of-the-way corner, lying will assuredly follow me, then I have nothing to set against the argument, but already condemn myself as a liar, if I uttered any such thing according to my old indifference, which renders me liable to the judgement of falsehood.

Coming near Caesarea, in order to learn how matters stood, yet not enduring to approach the city itself, I took refuge in the neighbouring poor-house, that I might there learn the things I wished. Then, when the most God-beloved bishop came there according to his custom, I laid before him the things your learning had enjoined upon us. What he answered, it was not possible for me to keep in memory, and it exceeded the measure of a letter; but in summary, concerning the renunciation of property, he said that this is the measure: that each should reduce his possessions to his last garment. And he furnished us with proofs from the Gospel: one, that John the Baptist said, "He who has two coats, let him share with him who has none"; and another, that the Lord forbade his disciples to have two coats. He added to these also this: "If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions, and give to the poor." He said too that the parable of the pearl bears upon this — that the merchant who found the pearl of great price went and sold all his possessions and bought it. He added to these that one ought not even to entrust to oneself the distribution of one's money, but to the one entrusted with administering the affairs of the poor. And this he confirmed from the Acts: that, selling their possessions, they brought and laid them at the feet of the apostles, and from them it was distributed to each, according as anyone had need. For he said that the discernment of the one truly in need from the one who asks out of greed requires experience. And he who gives to the afflicted has given to the Lord, and from him will receive his reward; but he who furnishes to everyone who goes about begging has cast it to a dog — troublesome through its shamelessness, but not pitiable through any want.

But concerning how we ought to live day by day, he had said but little, in proportion to the greatness of the subject; yet I would have you learn it from that man himself. For it is not reasonable that I should obscure the exactness of his teachings. I prayed to come upon him sometime together with you, so that you, keeping in memory exactly what was said, and adding by your own intelligence what is lacking, might supply the rest. For this I remember from the many things I heard, that the teaching about how a Christian ought to live needs not so much discourse as the daily example. And I know that, if the bond of caring for your aged father did not hold you, you yourself would have preferred nothing to meeting the bishop, nor would you have advised me to leave him and wander into deserts. For the caves and the rocks await us, but the benefits to be had from such men do not always remain with us. So, if you will bear with my counsel, you will dispose your father to permit you to withdraw from him for a little, and to fall in with a man who knows much, both from the experience of others and from his own intelligence, and who is able to impart it to those who come to him.
To Eustathius, the court physician

If there is any benefit in my letters, then never let any interval pass without writing to me and rousing me in turn to write. For my own part, I plainly grow happier when I receive letters from men of understanding who love the Lord; and if you too find anything in me worth your attention, that is for you, the readers, to judge. If I were not carried off by the multitude of my occupations, I would not deny myself the constant gladness that comes from writing. But you, whose cares are fewer, soothe me with your letters as often as you can. For wells too, they say, become better for being drawn upon. Yet your counsels drawn from medicine seem to me to go almost beside the point, since it is not I who apply the knife, but those who have become useless and fall away of their own accord.

Now there is the saying of the Stoic: since, he says, things do not come about as we wish, let us wish them as they come about. But I, for my part, do not accept that we should make our judgement conform to circumstances; though I do not condemn a man for doing, against his will, something that necessity demands. For neither do you physicians wish to cauterize the sick man or otherwise to cause him pain; yet often you consent to it, yielding to the gravity of the disease. Nor do sailors willingly throw their cargo overboard, but to escape shipwreck they submit to the jettison, preferring a life of poverty to death. So you must believe that I too bear painfully, and with countless laments, the separation from those who fall away; bear it nonetheless. For to the lovers of truth nothing is more precious than God and the hope set upon Him.
To Victor, the general

If I were failing to write to anyone else, I might perhaps justly incur a charge of negligence or forgetfulness. But how could one forget you, whose name is on the lips of all men? And how could one grow careless of you, who rise above almost all in the world by the height of your dignities? Yet the reason for my silence is plain: I shrink from being a trouble to so great a man. But if, along with the rest of your virtue, you have accepted even this — not only to receive the letters sent by me, but to seek them out when they are wanting — then see, I now write with confidence, and I will write hereafter as well, praying to the holy God that there be granted to you the recompense for the honour you show me. As for the Church, you have anticipated my appeals, having done everything that I would have asked. And you do this not to gratify men, but God, who has honoured you; who has given you some good things in this present life, and will give you others in the age to come, in return for your having walked His way in truth, keeping your heart unswerving in the uprightness of the faith from the beginning to the end.
To Victor, of consular rank

As often as it falls to me to read the letters of your Decorum, so often do I give thanks to God that you continue both to remember me and to let your love be diminished by no slander — the love which once, by the most upright judgement or by a worthy custom, you consented to take up. We pray, then, to the holy God both that you may abide in the same disposition toward me, and that I may be worthy of the honour you show me through your letter.
To Ascholius, bishop of Thessalonica

You have done well, and in accordance with the law of spiritual love, in taking the lead in writing to me and, by your good example, summoning me to a like zeal. For the friendship of the world needs eyes and meeting, that from there a beginning of intimacy may arise; but those who know how to love spiritually do not use the flesh as the broker of their friendship, but are led by the communion of faith to spiritual union. Thanks, then, to the Lord, who has comforted my heart by showing that love has not grown cold in all men, but that there are somewhere in the world those who display the stamp of the discipleship of Christ. And indeed it seemed to me that your situation resembles the stars in their nightly conjunction, shining out in different quarters of the heaven — whose brightness is delightful, but whose unexpectedness, surely, is more delightful still. Such are you also, you luminaries of the churches, altogether few and easily numbered in this gloomy state of things, shining as it were in a moonless dark; and beyond the charm that comes from your virtue, you have besides the quality of being longed for through the rarity of finding you.

Your letter made your disposition sufficiently known to me. For though it was small in the number of its syllables, yet by the uprightness of its thought it gave me a sufficient proof of your purpose. For to have been earnest in the cause of the most blessed Athanasius is the clearest sign of being sound in the greatest matters. In return, then, for the gladness your letter brought, I owe much gratitude to my most honoured son Euphemius; for whom I myself also pray that every help may come from the Holy One. And I beg you to join your prayers with mine, that we may receive him back speedily, together with his most decorous yokefellow, who is our daughter in the Lord. And be entreated yourself not to set the limit of my gladness at its very beginning, but, on every occasion that offers, to write, and by the frequency of our converse to increase your disposition toward me; and to indicate how the affairs of your churches stand as regards their concord. As for affairs here, pray that with us too there may come a great calm, when the Lord has rebuked the wind and the sea.
Without address, concerning a trainer

To the many accusations set down in the letter — the first and only one your Nobility has thought fit to send me — I am at a loss how to make my defence; not for any lack of justice on my side, but because, amid the multitude of charges brought, it is hard to give precedence to the more urgent, and to decide where I ought to begin the cure. Or perhaps I should follow the very order of the things written and meet each one in turn.

Those who set out from here for Scythia I have not, to this day, come to know; nor did any of those of your household remind me, so that I might greet you through them — though I am very much in earnest to address your Honour on every occasion. But that I should forget you in my prayers is impossible, unless I first forget the work to which the Lord has appointed me. For you assuredly remember the proclamations of the Church, being faithful by the grace of God: that we make our prayers in the holy Church both for the brothers who are abroad, and for those serving in the armies, and for those who speak out boldly for the name of the Lord, and for those who display the spiritual fruits — among whom, in most cases, or rather in all, I reckon that your Honour too is included. And how, in private, could I forget you, when I have so many things to move me to remembrance — such a sister, such nephews, a kinship so kindly, so loving toward me, a household, servants, friends, through whom, even against my will, I am of necessity reminded of your good purpose?

Concerning the matter you raise, the brother so-and-so has brought me nothing burdensome, nor has any judgement injurious to him been issued by me. Turn your grief, then, against those who told you what was false, acquitting of all blame both the chorepiscopus and myself. And if the advocate so-and-so is pursuing some lawsuit, he has public courts and laws at his disposal. I ask you, therefore, to lay no blame on us in these things.

As for yourself, all the good you do, you store up for yourself; and whatever rest you grant to those persecuted for the name of the Lord, this you prepare beforehand for yourself against the day of recompense. And you will do well if you send relics of the martyrs to your homeland too, since, as you wrote to me, the persecution there is even now making martyrs for the Lord.
To Evagrius, the presbyter

So far was I from being vexed at the length of your letter, that, because of the pleasure of reading it, the letter even seemed to me short. For what is a sweeter thing to hear than the name of peace? Or what is more becoming to holy men, and more pleasing to the Lord, than to take counsel for such things? To you, then, may the Lord grant the reward of peacemaking, since your purpose is so good and you press so earnestly upon a blessed work. And as for me, honoured friend, believe that, so far as having purposed and prayed to see one day the time when all who are not divided from one another in their thoughts shall make up one assembly, I yield the first place to no one in zeal for these things. For we should be, in truth, the most absurd of all men, if we took delight in the schisms and dissections of the churches, and did not count the joining together of the members of the body of Christ as the greatest of goods. But know that, as great as our desire is, so great is the deficiency of our power. For your perfect understanding is not unaware that disorders strengthened by time first need time for their correction, and then a strong and more vigorous treatment, if one is to reach to their very depth, so as to root out utterly the maladies of the sick. You know what I mean, and, if I must speak more plainly, there is nothing to fear.

Self-love, rooted in souls by long habit, one man is unable to remove, nor one letter, nor a brief space of time. For it is impossible that suspicions and the chafings that come from disputes should be wholly removed, unless someone trustworthy mediates the peace. And if grace flowed upon us, and we were able by word and deed and by spiritual gifts to win over those who are set against us, then we ought to have dared so great an undertaking. Yet perhaps not even then would you have advised that I should come alone to the work of correction, since there is, by the grace of God, a bishop to whom the care of the church belongs first of all; who cannot himself come to me, and for me to travel meanwhile, because of the winter, is not easy, or rather wholly impossible — not only because my body has given out under a long illness, but because the passes over the Armenian mountains become, a little later, impassable even to those in the full vigour of their age. I will not, however, decline to indicate these things to him by letter. Yet I do not expect that anything worth mentioning will come of the letters, both because I take the measure of the man's exactness, and because of the very nature of letters: for the written word, sent off, has no power to win a man over plainly. Much must be said, much must be heard in reply, the objections that arise must be resolved, and counter-arguments brought against the points raised in opposition — none of which the word in a letter can do, lying idle and lifeless, scattered upon the paper.

Nevertheless, as I said, I will not shrink from writing. But know, my truly most reverent and much-longed-for brother, that I have, by the grace of God, no private contention with anyone. Nor have I busied myself to learn the charges to which each man is, or is said to be, liable. So you ought to attend to my mind in this way: that I can do nothing out of partiality, nor am I prejudiced toward slander against anyone. Only, may it be the Lord's good pleasure that all things be done in the manner of the Church and in due order.

But our most beloved son Dorotheus, the fellow-deacon, grieved me by reporting concerning your Reverence that you were reluctant to share in the assembly with him — though such was not what we discussed, if I remember anything. To send anyone to the West is for me wholly impossible, since I have no one suited to this ministry. But of the brothers there, if anyone chooses to take up the labour on behalf of the churches, he knows of course both to whom he will go, and with what aim, and from whom he is to be furnished with letters, and of what kind. For when I have looked all around me, I see no one with me. And I pray indeed to be numbered among the seven thousand who have not bowed the knee to Baal. Except that those who lay their hands upon all men seek my life too. Yet not for that reason shall we fail in any of the zeal we owe to the churches of God.
To Antiochus

How heavily, do you think, did I take it that I missed meeting you during the summer? And yet not even the meeting of the others was such as to come to us in full measure; but still, even to see what one longs for in a dream brings some consolation to those who love. But you do not even write, you are so idle, so that I cannot put down your failure to any other cause rather than to your sluggishness toward journeys undertaken for love's sake. But let this be done with between us. Pray for me, and entreat the Lord not to forsake me, but, as He brought me through the trials that have come, so to deliver me also from those that are expected, to the glory of His name, on which we have set our hope.
To Antiochus

Since my sins have stood in my way, so that I have been unable to bring to fulfilment the desire I have long had to meet with you, I console myself for our being apart at least by letters; and I beg you not to leave off remembering me in your prayers, that, if we live, we may be counted worthy to enjoy your company, and if not, that by the help of your prayers we may, with good hope, depart from this world. The brother in charge of the camels I commend to you.
To Eupaterius and his daughter

How great a gladness your Decorum's letter brought me you may surely guess from the very things you wrote. For what could be sweeter to a man who makes it his prayer always to be in converse with those who fear God, and to share in the gain that comes from them, than such letters, through which the knowledge of God is sought? For if Christ is our life, then in due order our speech too ought to be about Christ, and our thought, and every action, ought to hang upon His commandments, and our soul to be conformed to Him. I rejoice, then, to be questioned about such things, and I rejoice with those who ask. For us, then, to put it in a single word, the faith of the fathers who came together at Nicaea is preferred above all those later devised: the faith in which the Son is confessed to be of one essence with the Father, and to be of the same nature as the One who begot Him. For Light from Light, and God from God, and Good from Good, and all such things, were confessed by those holy men; and by us now, who pray to walk in their footsteps, the same is witnessed.

But since the question that has now risen up from those who are forever attempting innovations was passed over in silence by the men of old, because it was beyond dispute, and so was left undefined — I mean the question concerning the Holy Spirit — we add our word about this, in accordance with the sense of Scripture: that as we are baptized, so also we believe; and as we believe, so also we offer glory. Since, then, baptism has been given to us by the Saviour into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, we offer a confession of faith in keeping with our baptism, and a giving of glory in keeping with our faith, glorifying the Holy Spirit together with the Father and the Son, being persuaded that He is not foreign to the divine nature. For that which is estranged in nature could not share in the same honours. But those who call the Holy Spirit a creature we pity, as falling, by such a word, into the unforgivable sin of the blasphemy against Him. For that the creation is distinct from the Godhead needs no argument for those who have been even a little trained in the Scriptures. For the creation is enslaved, but the Spirit sets free; the creation stands in need of life, but the Spirit is the giver of life; the creation needs teaching, but the Spirit is the teacher; the creation is sanctified, but the Spirit is the sanctifier. And whether you name angels, or archangels, or all the powers above the world, they receive their holiness through the Spirit; but the Spirit Himself has holiness by nature, not received by grace, but united to His being; whence also He has obtained, in a special manner, the title of the Holy. That which is, then, holy by nature, as the Father is holy by nature and the Son is holy by nature, we will not ourselves endure to separate and cut off from the divine and blessed Trinity, nor do we accept those who lightly number it with the creation.

Let this, as in a summary, be said as enough for your Reverence. For from small seeds you will cultivate the greater part of piety, the Holy Spirit working together with you. For give occasion to a wise man, and he will be wiser still. The fuller teaching we will defer to our meeting face to face, by which it is possible both to resolve the objections, and to set out more amply the testimonies from the Scriptures, and to confirm every sound pattern of the faith. For the present, grant pardon to my brevity. For I would not have written at all, had I not thought it the greater harm to deny the request altogether than to grant it imperfectly.
To Diodorus

There has reached me a letter bearing the inscription of Diodorus, but the rest of it more fitting to be some other man's than Diodorus's. For it seems to me that one of the practised sort, slipping into your person, wished thus to make himself trustworthy to his hearers. For when he was asked by someone whether it was lawful for him to take in marriage his wife's sister, his wife being dead, he did not shudder at the question, but bore the hearing of it calmly, and very nobly and combatively helped to carry through the licentious desire. Now if I had the letter by me, I would have sent it back, and you would have been able both to defend yourself and to defend the truth. But since the man who showed it took it away again, and carried it about like some trophy against me — against me who had forbidden the thing from the first — saying that he had the permission in writing, I have now written to you, so that with a double hand we may come against that spurious argument and leave it no strength, that it may not be able easily to harm those who come upon it.

First, then, the greatest point in such matters: the custom that we have to put forward, which has the force of law, because the ordinances were handed down to us by holy men. And it is this: that if anyone, mastered at some time by the passion of uncleanness, falls into unlawful union with two sisters, this is to be reckoned no marriage, nor are they to be received at all into the full body of the Church before they are parted from each other. So that, even if there were nothing else to say, the custom would suffice to guard what is right. But since the writer of the letter has attempted, by a counterfeit argument, to bring so great an evil into life, it is necessary that I too should not hold back the help that comes from reasoning — although, in matters that are exceedingly plain, each man's prior conviction is stronger than argument.

It is written, he says, in Leviticus: You shall not take a woman as a rival to her sister, to uncover her nakedness alongside her, while she is still living. From this, then, he says, it is plain that it is permitted to take her when the sister is dead. To this I will say first this: that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law; since otherwise we shall be subject to circumcision too, and to the Sabbath, and to abstinence from foods. For surely we shall not, whenever we find something that agrees with our pleasures, put ourselves under the yoke of the slavery of the law, but whenever any of the law's requirements seems burdensome, then run off to the freedom that is in Christ. We were asked whether it is written that one may take a woman alongside her sister. We said what is safe for us and true, that it is not written. But to infer the thing left unspoken from the consequence of what follows belongs to one who makes laws, not to one who states the law; since otherwise it will be open to whoever wishes to dare even, while the wife is still living, to take the sister. For this very same sophism fits that case too. For it is written, he says, You shall not take her as a rival — as though the law did not forbid taking her where there is no rivalry. So the man who pleads for the passion will define the character of the sisters as free from jealousy. Once, then, the cause for which the law forbade the living together of both has been removed, what will there be to hinder the taking of sisters? But these things are not written, we shall say. Yet neither are those things laid down; and the notion of the consequence gives licence alike to both cases. He ought, by running back a little to what precedes in the legislation, to have rid himself of his difficulties.

For the lawgiver seems not to include every kind of sin, but to forbid specifically the practices of the Egyptians, from whom Israel had departed, and those of the Canaanites, to whom they were being removed. For the text runs thus: According to the practices of the land of Egypt, in which you dwelt, you shall not do; and according to the practices of the land of Canaan, into which I am bringing you, there you shall not do, and in their statutes you shall not walk. So that this kind of sin was probably not then current among the nations; and therefore the lawgiver did not need to guard against it, but was content with the unschooled custom to denounce the abomination. How, then, having forbidden the greater, did he keep silent about the lesser? Because the example of the patriarch seemed to many of the carnally minded to do harm, as regards living with sisters while they were still alive.

But what must we do? Speak the things written, or further work out the things passed over in silence? For instance, that a father and son ought not to make use of one harlot is not written in these laws, but by the prophet it is thought worthy of the gravest accusation. For son, he says, and father went in to the same girl. And how many other kinds of unclean passions has the school of the demons invented, which the divine Scripture has passed over in silence, not choosing to defile its own dignity with the naming of shameful things, but denouncing the uncleannesses by general names — as the apostle Paul too says: But fornication and all uncleanness, let it not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints — including under the name of uncleanness both the unspeakable acts of males and those of females. So that silence does not, in every case, bring licence to the pleasure-loving.

But I, for my part, say that this matter has not even been passed over in silence, but that the lawgiver has forbidden it very vehemently. For the words, You shall not go in to any near of kin to your flesh, to uncover their nakedness, include also this kind of kinship. For what could be nearer to a man than his own wife, or rather than his own flesh? For they are no longer two, but one flesh. So that through the wife the sister passes into kinship with the husband. For as he will not take the mother of his wife, nor the daughter of his wife, because he may take neither his own mother nor his own daughter, so neither the sister of his wife, because he may not take his own sister. And conversely, neither will it be permitted to the wife to live with the kin of her husband; for the rights of kinship are common to both. But I solemnly declare to everyone who deliberates about marriage that the fashion of this world passes away, and the time is shortened, that those who have wives may be as though they had none. And if anyone reads against me the words Be fruitful and multiply, I laugh at the man who does not distinguish the proper times of the legislations. A second marriage is a remedy against fornication, not a provision for licentiousness. If they cannot contain themselves, let them marry, he says — not that, in marrying, they should also transgress the law.

But these men do not even look to nature — they whose souls are bleared by the passion of dishonour — though nature long ago distinguished the names of kindred. For from what relationship will they name the children born? Will they call them brothers of one another, or cousins? For both names will fit them, because of the confusion. Do not, O man, make the children's aunt their stepmother; nor arm with implacable jealousies the woman who ought to cherish them in a mother's place. For the race of stepmothers alone drives their enmity on even after death. Or rather, those who are otherwise enemies make peace with the dead, but stepmothers begin their hatred after death.

The sum of what has been said: if a man is moved to marriage by law, the whole world is open to him; but if his eagerness is born of passion, for that very reason let him be the more shut out, that he may learn to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honour, not in the passion of lust. Though I was minded to say more, the measure of a letter holds me back. I pray either that our exhortation may prove stronger than the passion, or that this pollution may not take up residence in our land, but may remain in the places where it was dared.
To Amphilochius, on his being ordained bishop

Blessed be God, who in every generation chooses those who are well-pleasing to Him, and marks out the vessels of His choosing, and uses them for the ministry of holy things; who now too, when you were fleeing — not from me, as you yourself say, but from the calling expected through me — has caught you in the inescapable nets of His grace, and brought you into the midst of Pisidia, that you might take men alive for the Lord, and draw up from the deep into the light those who had been taken alive by the devil to do his will. Say, then, you too the words of blessed David: Where shall I go from your Spirit? And from your face, where shall I flee? For such are the wonders that our Master, who loves mankind, works. Asses are lost, that a man may become king of Israel. But he, being an Israelite, was given to Israel; whereas you — she who reared you and raised you to so great a height of virtue does not have you, but sees her neighbour glorying in her own ornament. Yet since all who have set their hope on Christ are one people, and those who are Christ's are now one Church, even if it is named from different places, your homeland too rejoices and is glad in the dispensations of the Lord, and counts that it has not lost one man, but that through one man it has gained whole churches. Only may the Lord grant us, when present, to see, and, when absent, to hear of your progress in the Gospel and of the good order of the churches.

Be a man, then, and be strong, and go before the people whom the Most High has entrusted to your right hand. And, like a man of understanding, steering your course, rising in mind above every storm that is raised by the heretical spirits, keep the ship unsunk by the salt and bitter waves of false doctrine, awaiting the calm that the Lord will make, when there is found a voice worthy to rouse Him to rebuke the spirits and the sea. And if you wish to visit me, now hard pressed by long illness toward the necessary departure, wait neither for an occasion nor for any signal from me, knowing that to a father's heart every season is fitting for embracing a beloved child, and that the disposition of the soul is greater than any words.

Do not lament a burden that exceeds your strength. For if you yourself were the one who would have to bear this load, even so it would not merely be heavy, but altogether unbearable. But if the Lord is the one who bears it with you, Cast your care upon the Lord, and He Himself will act. Only be entreated to keep this watch in all things: not yourself to be carried along with corrupt customs, but, by the wisdom given you from God, to change what has been wrongly received into what is useful. For Christ sent you not to follow others, but yourself to lead those who are being saved. And we beg you to pray for us, that, if we are still in this life, we may be counted worthy to see you together with your church; and if we are commanded henceforth to depart, that we may see you there with the Lord — her flourishing like a vine in good works, and you, like a wise husbandman and a good servant, giving to your fellow-servants their measure of food in due season, receiving the reward of a faithful and prudent steward.
All who are with me greet your Reverence. May you be in health and good cheer in the Lord; may you be kept, holding good repute in the gifts of the Spirit and of wisdom.
To Eusebius, bishop of Samosata

This, it seems, both makes me hesitant to write, and again shows the writing to be necessary. For whenever I look to the debt of my own coming to you, and reckon the benefit of meeting, I am very much inclined to think little of letters, as not able to fulfil even the account of a shadow set beside the truth. But when, again, I reflect that the only consolation, for one who has missed the greatest and first things, is to address so great a man, and to entreat him, as my custom is, not to forget me in his prayers, then I come to judge the matter of letters no small thing. The hope of my coming, then, I do not myself wish to cast out of my soul, nor would I have your Godliness despair of it. For I should be ashamed not to show myself, through your prayers, so confident as even to become young again out of an old man, if there were need of it — not to say merely a little stronger, out of one who is weak and altogether failing, such as I now am.

The causes of my not being present already are not easy to set out in words — not only because I am shut out by my present weakness, but because I never had such power of speech as to declare plainly a sickness so manifold and various. Only that from the day of Pascha until now fevers and fluxes, and risings of the bowels, like waves washing over me, do not allow me to keep my head above water. What my condition was, and of what kind, the brother Barachus too could tell, even if not worthily of the truth, yet enough to bear witness to the cause of the postponement. And I am fully persuaded that, if you would truly pray together with me, all my difficulties would readily be loosed.
To Jovinus, the count

I saw your soul in your letter. For in truth no painter can take off the stamp of a body so exactly as speech can portray the secrets of the soul. For the word in your letter sufficiently delineated for me the steadiness of your character, the genuineness of your honour, and the integrity, in all things, of your mind; whence too it brought me a great consolation for your absence. Do not, then, leave off using every occasion that offers to write, and to grant me this converse across the distance; since the weakness of my body now makes me despair of meeting face to face. How great that weakness is the most God-beloved bishop Amphilochius will tell you, who has come to know it through having been long in my company, and is able to set before you in words what he has seen. And I wish my difficulties to be known not for any other reason than for pardon hereafter, that I may not incur a charge of negligence if I fail to visit you. And yet for this loss I need consolation rather than excuse. For if it were possible for me to be with your Gravity, I would have set this far above me before all that others busy themselves over.
To Ascholius, bishop of Thessalonica

With how great a gladness your Holiness's letter filled me I could not easily show, my words being too weak for the plain truth; but you ought yourself to guess it within you, judging by the beauty of what you wrote. For what did your letter not have? Did it not have love for the Lord? The wonder concerning the martyrs, sketching the manner of their contest so vividly as to bring the events before our eyes? The honour and disposition toward me? Anything that one might name of the noblest things? So that, when I received the letter into my hands, and read it many times, and learned the grace of the Spirit teeming in it, I thought I had been born in the ancient times, when the churches of God were in flower, rooted in faith, united in love, as in one body, where there is one breath of life among the different members; when the persecutors were plain, and plain too the persecuted; when the peoples, though warred upon, grew more numerous, and the blood of the martyrs, watering the churches, nourished many times as many champions of piety, those who came after stripping for the contest in zeal for those who had gone before. In those days we Christians kept peace with one another — that peace which the Lord left to us, of which now not even a trace is left to us, so harshly have we driven it away from one another. Yet our souls returned to that ancient blessedness, when a letter came from far away, in flower with the beauty of love, and a martyr came to us from the barbarians beyond the Ister, proclaiming through himself the exactness of the faith that is followed there. Who could recount the gladness of our souls at these things? What power of speech could be conceived able to declare plainly the disposition in the hidden chamber of our heart? And when we saw the athlete, we counted his trainer blessed, who too will receive from the just Judge the crown of righteousness, having strengthened many for the contest on behalf of piety.

And since you brought to our remembrance the blessed man Eutyches, and exalted our homeland as having itself supplied the seeds of piety, you gladdened us by the reminder of old things, but grieved us by the reproof of what we see. For none of us is near to Eutyches in virtue — we who are so far from taming barbarians by the power of the Spirit and the working of the gifts that come from Him, that by the excess of our sins we have made savage even those who were gentle. For we reckon to ourselves and to our sins the cause that the power of the heretics has been poured out so far. For there is scarcely any part of the world that has escaped the burning of the heresy. But your tales are of athletic struggles, bodies torn for the sake of piety, barbarian fury despised by hearts that are not dismayed, the manifold tortures of the persecutors, the steadfastness in all things of the contenders, the wood, the water, the things that perfected the martyrs. But what are our affairs like? Love has grown cold; the teaching of the fathers is being ravaged; shipwrecks of the faith are frequent; the mouths of the godly are silent; the peoples, driven out of the houses of prayer, raise their hands in the open air to the Master in heaven. And the afflictions are heavy, yet there is martyrdom nowhere, because those who ill-treat us bear the same name as ourselves. For these things pray to the Lord yourself, and take all the noble athletes of Christ into your prayer on behalf of the churches, that, if indeed there still remain some seasons for the world's existence, and all things are not being driven on toward the contrary motion, God, being reconciled to His own churches, may bring them back to their ancient peace.
To Ascholius, bishop of Thessalonica

The holy God has fulfilled an old prayer of mine, in counting me worthy to read the letters of your true Godliness. For the greatest thing, and worthy of the greatest eagerness, would be to see you yourself and to be seen by you, and to enjoy in person the gifts of the Spirit that are in you; but since the distance of place takes this away, and the circumstances that hold each of us privately, it is worth a second prayer that my soul be nourished by frequent letters of your love in Christ. And this has now fallen to me, when I received into my hands the letter of your Understanding; for I was made more than doubled in the enjoyment of what you wrote. For it was truly possible to behold even your very soul, showing through, as it were through some mirror of words. And it made my gladness many times greater not only that you are such as the testimony of all presents you to be, but that the good things in you are the boasts of our homeland. For like some flourishing branch, springing from a noble root, you have filled the land beyond the border with spiritual fruits. So that our homeland fittingly delights in her own offspring. And when you were striving through the contests for the faith, she glorified God, hearing that the good inheritance of the fathers was kept safe in you.

And what are your present doings too? By a martyr, lately a contender against the barbarian who is your neighbour, you honoured the land that bore you, like some grateful husbandman sending the firstfruits of his harvest to those who supplied the seeds. Truly the gifts are fitting for an athlete of Christ: a witness of the truth who has just bound on the crown of righteousness; whom we received with joy, and glorified God, who has now fulfilled in all the nations the Gospel of His Christ. And be entreated to remember in your prayers us also who love you, and earnestly to pray to the Lord for our souls, that we too may one day be counted worthy to begin to serve God along the way of His commandments, which He gave us for salvation.
To Eusebius, bishop of Samosata

Honoured by me in all things, and among the truest of friends, our most reverend brother Eupraxius showed himself more honoured still and more genuine through his disposition toward you; for even now he has hastened to your Godliness (to use David's words) as a deer, cooling a great and unbearable thirst at a fresh and pure spring. And blessed is he who has been counted worthy to draw near to you; and more blessed still is he who, by sufferings for Christ and by sweats for the truth, has set such a crown upon them, which few of those who fear God have obtained. For you did not display your virtue untested, nor did you sail rightly and steer the souls of others only in a time of fair weather, but you shone out amid the hardships of trials, and rose above your persecutors by nobly removing from the land that bore you.

And others have their fathers' ground, but we the city above; others perhaps our throne, but we Christ. O the bargain — what things we have despised, what things we have gained! We have passed through fire and water; and I believe that we shall come out also into a place of refreshment. For God will not forsake us to the end, nor overlook the right doctrine when it is persecuted; but according to the multitude of our pains His comforts will gladden us. This, then, we both believe and pray. And you, I beg, pray for our lowliness, and as often as the occasion offers, do not be reluctant to bless us by letter, and to make us of better cheer by making known your own affairs — which you have now thought fit to do.
To Eusebius, bishop of Samosata

Both by writing and by remembering you gladden me, and, what is greater than this, by blessing me in your letters. As for us, if we were worthy of your sufferings and of your contest for Christ, we should have been counted worthy, by coming as far as you, to embrace your Godliness and to take a pattern of endurance in suffering. But since we happen to be unworthy of this, held fast as we are by many afflictions and occupations, we do what is second best: we address your Perfection, and ask that you not grow weary of remembering us. For it is not only a benefit to us to be counted worthy of your letters, but also a boast before the many and an ornament, that there is some account of us with a man so great in virtue and of so great a closeness to God, that he can make others, too, close to Him, both by word and by example.
To Antiochus the presbyter, his nephew, who was with him in exile

As much as I lament the church bereft of the oversight of such a shepherd, so much do I count you blessed who have been counted worthy, in such a time, to be with a man who is fighting the great contest for piety. For I am persuaded that the Lord will count you too worthy of the same portion, who nobly anoint him and rouse his eagerness. And how great a gain it is, in deep tranquillity, to enjoy a man who has gathered so much both from learning and from the experience of affairs — so that I am persuaded that you have now come to know the man, how great he is in understanding. For in time past his mind too was divided among many things, and you had no leisure from the affairs of life, so as to give yourselves wholly to the spiritual stream that pours forth from the man's pure heart. But may the Lord grant that you be a comfort to him, and that you yourselves have no need of the consolation of others — which indeed I am persuaded is true of your hearts, judging both by my own experience, which for a little while I had of you, and by the great teaching of your good guide, one day's company with whom is a sufficient provision for salvation.
Basil to Gregory

You have undertaken a mild and gentle and humane task in gathering up the captives of that contemptible Glycerius (for so, for the present, I write of him), and in covering over, as far as you could, our common disgrace. But your Reverence ought nonetheless, having learned the facts about him, so to undo the dishonour.

This Glycerius, now so haughty and grave in your eyes, was ordained by me a deacon of the church at Venesa, to minister to the presbyter and to take care of the work of the church. For the man, though otherwise of difficult temper, is not without skill at his task. But when he was appointed, he neglected the work so much as though it had never come about at all; and, gathering up some wretched virgins by his own authority and self-will — some who came running to him willingly (you know how ready the young are for such things), others against their will — he undertook to act as their flock-leader, and, putting about himself the name and dress of a patriarch, he suddenly grew insolent — having come to this not from any orderly course and piety, but having set it up as a means of livelihood, as another man might some other thing. And he has all but turned the whole church upside down, despising his own presbyter, a man venerable both in conduct and in age, despising the chorepiscopus and me as worthy of nothing, and forever filling the city and the whole body of clergy with disturbances and tumults.

And at last, that he might not be even slightly rebuked in word by me and the chorepiscopus, so as not to despise us (for he was training the young men too into the same folly), he conceived a very bold and inhuman plan. Plundering as many virgins as he could, and watching for night, he became a runaway. These things will seem very dreadful to you. Consider too the occasion.
