The synod there was being held, and a great multitude, as was likely, was streaming in from every quarter. But he led out in opposition his own troupe, following young men and dancing around, stirring up much dejection in the godly, and much laughter in the unrestrained and those readier with the tongue. And this is not enough, great as it is in its enormity; but, as I learn, the parents of the virgins, unable to bear their childlessness, and wishing to bring back the scattered flock, falling, as was likely, with laments before their own daughters — these the admirable young man, with his band of brigands, insults and dishonours.

Let these things not seem bearable to your Reverence; for the laughter falls on us all in common. But above all, command him to return with the virgins; for he might meet with some kindness if he came back with letters from you. But if not, at least send the virgins back to their mother, the church. But if not, at least do not allow those who wish to be tyrannized to remain so, but order them to return to me. Otherwise, we call you to witness, before God and men, that these things are not rightly done, nor according to the ordinances of the church. As for Glycerius, if he returns with discretion and the fitting steadiness, that is best; but if not, let him be stopped from his ministry.
To Glycerius

How long will you be senseless, and counsel ill for yourself, and trouble me, and shame the common order of the monks? Return, then, with confidence in God and in me, whose love for mankind we imitate. For though we rebuked you as a father, we will also pardon you as a father. This comes to you from me, since many others entreat me, and before the others your own presbyter, whose grey hairs and tender heart I respect. But if you keep yourself far from me, you have wholly fallen from your rank, and you will fall also from God, together with your followers and with the garb in which you lead the young women — not to God, but into a pit.
To Gregory

I wrote to you a while ago, too, about Glycerius and the virgins. But they have not even to this day returned, but still delay — I do not know whence or how. For I would not suspect of you that you do this to my discredit, either yourself feeling something against me, or to gratify others. Let them come, then, fearing nothing; be yourself their surety for this. For we feel pain at the cutting off of our members, even if they were rightly cut off. But if they resist, the burden is on others, and we wash our hands of it.
To Sophronius the bishop

How greatly you gladdened me with your letter I need not write; for you may surely guess it from the very things you wrote, such as they were. For the first fruit of the Spirit, love, you showed me through your letter. And what could be more precious to me than this in the present state of the times, when, because lawlessness has been multiplied, the love of the many has grown cold? For nothing is now so rare as the meeting with a spiritual brother, and a word of peace, and spiritual communion — which, finding in your Perfection, I gave great thanks to the Lord, praying that I may share also in the perfect gladness over you. For if your letters are such, what must the meeting be? And if you charm me so from afar, how much will you be worth when you appear to me close at hand? And know well, that if a multitude of countless occupations did not beset me, and these inescapable necessities to which I am bound, I would myself hasten to your Perfection. And yet this old illness of the body is a great hindrance to my movements; but even so I would not have reckoned it a hindrance, for the sake of the benefit I expect. For to be counted worthy to meet a man who thinks the same things and holds the faith of the fathers — as the report of our honoured brothers and fellow-presbyters has it — is truly to return to the ancient blessedness of the churches, when those who were diseased about questionings were few, and all were in tranquillity, being workers of the commandments who need not be ashamed, serving the Lord through a simple and uncurious confession, and keeping inviolate and uncurious the faith in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.
To Theodora the canoness

What makes me reluctant to write is that I am not persuaded that my letters are delivered to your Love at all, but that, through the negligence of the carriers, countless others encounter them first — and especially now, when the affairs throughout the world are so troubled. For this reason I am, in a way, waiting to be blamed and to have my letters demanded of me by force, that I may use this very thing as proof of my having sent them. Whether writing, then, or keeping silence, we have one work in our hearts: to keep the memory of your Decorum, and to pray to the Lord to grant you to finish the course of the good life that you have chosen. For in truth it is no small contest, for one who has professed it, to carry through to the end the consequences of the profession. For to choose the way of life according to the Gospel is open to everyone; but to carry one's observance even to the smallest things, and to overlook nothing of what is there written, this has been rightly achieved by very few of those who have come to our knowledge: so as to use a tongue that is bridled and an eye that is schooled according to the will of the Gospel, and to work with the hands according to the aim of pleasing God, and to move the feet, and to use each of one's members as our Maker ordered from the beginning; decorum in dress, reserve in meetings with men, contentment in food, and freedom from superfluity in the possession of necessities. All these things, though they seem small when stated thus simply, yet need a great contest for their accomplishment, as we have found in truth itself. And further, perfection in lowliness of mind — so as neither to remember the distinction of one's ancestors, nor, if some advantage belongs to us by nature, whether in body or in soul, to be lifted up by it, nor to make the opinions others hold of us an occasion of being lifted up and puffed up — these things belong to the evangelical life: vigour in self-control, diligence in prayers, sympathy in love of the brethren, fellowship toward the needy, a humbled spirit, contrition of heart, soundness of faith, evenness in dejection, our thought never failing to keep the memory of that fearful and inexorable tribunal, toward which we all are hastening, but of which very few are mindful and dread the issue that comes from it.
To a free woman

I, though greatly wishing to write continually to your Nobility, have always held myself back, lest I should seem to stir up some trials for you, because of those disposed to be our enemies and, as I hear, driving their enmity even to such lengths as to inquire busily whether anyone, anywhere, receives a letter of mine. But since you yourself, doing well, took the lead in writing, and wrote to me what was fitting, communicating about the affairs of your soul, I was moved to write back, at once making good what was left undone in time past, and at once answering what was written by your Nobility.

Blessed is the soul that, night and day, turns over no other care than how, on the great day, on which the whole creation will stand around the Judge, rendering account of its deeds, it too may be able lightly to lay down the account of its life. For he who sets that day and that hour before his eyes, and ever rehearses his defence at that tribunal which cannot be deceived — such a man will sin either not at all or very little, since sinning comes to us through the absence of the fear of God. But those to whom the expectation of the things threatened is present and vivid — to such men the indwelling fear will give no opportunity to fall into unwished-for actions or thoughts.

Remember God, then, and keep His fear in your heart, and take all men into the fellowship of your prayers. For great is the help of those who are able to win God's favour. And do not leave off doing these things. For while we live this life in the flesh, prayer will be a good helper, and when we depart from here, a sufficient provision for the age to come. And as care is a good thing, so again despondency and despair and being without hope of salvation are among the things that harm the soul. Set your hope, then, on the goodness of God, and await His help, knowing that, if we turn to Him rightly and genuinely, He will not only not cast us off utterly, but, while we are still speaking the words of prayer, He will say: Behold, I am here.
To Magnenianus the count

A while ago your Gravity wrote to me, charging me expressly to write certain things and, among them, about the faith. But I, for my part, admire your earnestness about the matter, and pray to God that the choice of good things may dwell in you unshaken, and that you, ever advancing, may be perfected both in knowledge and in good works. Yet because I do not wish to leave behind a treatise on the faith, nor to write differing creeds, I have refrained from sending what you sought.

But it seems to me that you are being deafened by those there, men who do nothing, who, to discredit me, say certain things, thinking thereby to establish themselves, if they fasten the most shameful falsehoods upon me. For time past has shown those men for what they are, and the experience that comes will make them plainer still. But we exhort those who have set their hope on Christ to busy themselves about nothing beyond the ancient faith, but, as we believe, so also to be baptized, and as we are baptized, so also to give glory. And it is enough for us to confess those names which we have received from holy Scripture, and to flee the innovation that goes beyond them. For our salvation is not in the inventing of titles, but in the sound confession concerning the Godhead in which we have believed.
To Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium

May the holy God grant that this letter of ours reach your hands while you are sound in body, free from every distraction, and prospering in all your affairs, so that the request we make may not be made in vain. We ask you now to appear in our city, to add solemnity to the festival which our church is accustomed to hold each year in honour of the martyrs. For be assured, my most honoured and truly beloved friend, that our people, who have made trial of many men, hold to no acquisition so firmly as to your presence; such a sting of love did you leave behind from that brief meeting. Therefore, that the Lord may be glorified, that the people may rejoice, that the martyrs may be honoured, and that we old men may receive from a true son the attention that is owed us, consent to make the journey to us without delay, and to come ahead of the days of the assembly, so that we may meet one another at leisure and find mutual comfort through the sharing of spiritual gifts. The day is the fifth of September. We ask you, therefore, to be here three days beforehand, so that by your presence you may also do great honour to the memory of the poorhouse. May you be kept safe for me and for the Church of God, sound and cheerful in the Lord, and praying earnestly for me, by the grace of the Lord.
To Sophronius the Master

It is not easy to list all those who through us have been benefited by your magnanimity; so many do we know to have been helped by us through that great hand of yours, which the Lord has granted us as an ally in our gravest hours of need. And the most deserving of all is the man now commended to you by our letter, the most reverend brother Eusebius, who has fallen victim to an unaccountable slander, which it lies with your uprightness alone to scatter. We ask you, therefore — both as one who gives to justice its due, and as one who looks with regard to our common humanity, and as one who grants us your accustomed favours — to be everything to this man, and to stand by him in the cause of truth. For he has no small ally in the justice of his case; and if the present crisis does not work it harm, that justice will very easily be shown to be clear and beyond dispute.
To Aburgius

I know that I have often commended many men to your honour, and that in the gravest hours of need I have been of considerable help to those in distress. Yet I am not aware of having previously sent to your excellency anyone dearer to me, or one contending for greater things, than my most beloved son Eusebius, who now places this letter of ours in your hands. In what sort of affair he has become entangled he will himself relate to your dignity, should he find the occasion. What it is fitting for us to say is this: that the man should not be swept away, nor, because many have been shown to be guilty of the most serious offences, should he too come to share in any part of the suspicion that falls upon the many; but that he should obtain a trial, and that his life should be brought to examination. For in this way the slander will most readily be made plain, and the man, having obtained the most just protection, will be a perpetual herald of the kindnesses done him by your gentleness.
To Arinthaeus

That you are a lover of freedom and a lover of mankind we are well taught both by the nobility of your nature and by your fellow-feeling toward all. We therefore make our appeal with confidence on behalf of a man who is illustrious from of old and through his ancestors, but who deserves still greater honour and respect on his own account, for the gentleness of character that is native to him. We ask, then, that at our request you stand by him as he contends in a lawsuit which, as far as the truth is concerned, is contemptible, but which is otherwise full of peril because of the gravity of the slander. For it would weigh greatly in the balance toward his safety if you would consent to utter some kind word on his behalf — granting it first of all to justice, and then granting in this matter also to us, who are among those especially yours, your accustomed honour and favour.
To Sophronius the Master, on behalf of Eumathius

Having met a man of worth caught in an intolerable predicament, I was grieved in soul. For how, being a man myself, could I fail to share the pain of a free man entangled, beyond his deserts, in such troubles? And taking thought how I might be of use to him, I found one remedy for the difficulty that holds him fast — to make it known to your excellency. The rest, then, is yours: to extend to him also that zeal of yours which, with us as witnesses, you have shown toward many.

The matter itself will be made known by the petition he has presented to the emperors, which we ask you to take into your hands and, as far as you are able, to help the man forward. For you will be doing a favour to a Christian, a man of noble birth, and one who carries the dignity that great learning confers. And if we add that we too receive a great favour through the kindness done to him, then surely — even though our own weight is otherwise slight — since your dignity always deigns to hold our affairs in account, what is granted to us will appear no small thing.
To Otreius of Melitene

I know that the departure of the most God-beloved bishop Eusebius touches your reverence as deeply as it touches us ourselves. Since, then, we both stand in need of comfort, let us become consolation to one another. Do you send us word of what comes from Samosata, and we will report whatever we learn from Thrace. For to know of the people's steadfastness brings me no small relief amid present sorrows, while to your goodness it will be a comfort to learn how our common father fares. Indeed, even now we have no need to give word by letter; for we have presented to you the very man who knows the matter exactly, and who reports in what circumstances he left him, and how he bears what befalls. Pray, then, both for him and for us, that the Lord may speedily bring about the release from these hardships.
To the presbyters of Samosata

As much as we grieve when we consider the desolation of the church, so much do we count you blessed for having reached this measure of the contest — which may the Lord grant you to pass through with patient endurance, so that for the faithful stewardship and the noble steadfastness you have displayed on behalf of the name of Christ you may receive the great reward.
To the magistrates of Samosata

When I consider that the trial has now been poured out over the whole inhabited world, and that the greatest of the cities of Syria have made trial of sufferings equal to your own, but that nowhere is the council of magistrates so well approved and so distinguished for good works as yours is now famed to be for its zeal in good works, I am near to being grateful for what has been ordained. For had this affliction not come about, your worth would never have been made manifest. So it seems that what the furnace is to gold, this is the affliction endured for the hope set on God to those who lay claim to any virtue.

Come then, admirable men, see that to the labours already accomplished you add a sequel worthy of them, and that you may be seen to set upon a great foundation a still more notable summit; gather around the shepherd of the church, whenever the Lord grants him to appear once more upon his own throne, each of you relating some one of the things you have done as citizens on behalf of the Church of God; and on the great day of the Lord may each of you receive from the bountiful God a recompense in proportion to your labours. And by remembering us and writing whenever it is possible, you will both do what is just in repaying us in kind, and at the same time will gladden us not a little, sending us through your letters clear tokens of your voice, which is most sweet to us.
To Eustathius, bishop of Himmeria

I know that bereavement is a gloomy thing and full of cares, since it brings desolation through the loss of those who lead. Hence I suppose that your reverence too, grieving over what has befallen, does not write to us, and is at the same time now caught up in greater pressing affairs, going about among the flocks of Christ because of the assaults of enemies on every side. But since the consolation of every sorrow is converse with those of like soul, deign to write to us as often as you are able; and may you yourself find rest in speaking to us, and console us by sharing with us your own words. This too we shall be eager to do, as often as circumstances permit. And do you yourself pray, and earnestly urge the whole brotherhood to entreat the Lord, that he may at last show us release from the dejection that surrounds us.
To Theodotus, bishop of Beroea

I know that, even if you do not write to us, yet in your heart the memory of us abides. And this I infer, not because I myself am worthy of any favourable remembrance, but because your soul is rich in the abundance of love. Still, as far as you are able, use whatever occasions arise to write to us, so that we too may take better heart on learning your news, and may find occasion ourselves to make our own affairs known to you. For this is the mode of converse for those so far separated in body — the converse by letter — of which let us not deprive one another, so far as circumstances permit. And may the Lord grant us also a meeting face to face, that we may increase our love and multiply our thanksgiving to our Master for his still greater gifts.
To Antipater, the governor

How noble a thing philosophy is — in other respects, and in this too, that she does not even allow her foster-children to be cured at great expense; for with her one and the same thing is both a relish and enough for health. For I have learned that you restored your failing appetite with cabbages pickled in vinegar — cabbages which formerly I used to find distasteful, both on account of the proverb, and because they were a reminder of the poverty in which I was reared.

But now I think I shall both bring myself round to another mind and laugh at the proverb, seeing that the cabbage is so good a nurse, since it has brought our governor back to vigour. And henceforth I shall consider nothing comparable to it — not the Homeric lotus, no, nor even that ambrosia, whatever it may have been, which feeds the dwellers on Olympus.
Antipater to Basil

"Cabbage twice over is death," says the spiteful proverb. But I, having asked for it many times, shall die only once — and certainly I shall die even if I do not ask for it. So, since die I must, do not shrink from eating a relish that is pleasant, and has been reviled by the proverb to no purpose.
First Canonical Letter: To Amphilochius, concerning the canons

"To a fool who asks a question," it is said, "wisdom shall be reckoned." But the question of a wise man, it seems, makes even the fool wise; which by the grace of God befalls us whenever we receive the letters of your industrious soul. For we become more attentive and more thoughtful than we were through the very asking, learning many things of which we were ignorant; and the care of answering becomes our teacher. So indeed now, having never before given thought to your questions, we have been compelled to examine the matter carefully, both to recall whatever we heard from our elders, and to reason out for ourselves whatever was akin to what we had been taught.

Now the question concerning the Cathari has been treated before, and you rightly recalled that one must follow the custom of each country, because those who in former times deliberated on these matters were of differing minds concerning their baptism. But the case of the Pepuzeni seems to me to admit of no argument at all; and I was surprised that so great an authority on the canons as Dionysius overlooked it. For the ancients laid down that the baptism to be accepted is the one which departs in no respect from the faith. Hence they named some bodies heresies, others schisms, and others irregular congregations: heresies, those wholly broken off and estranged in the very faith itself; schisms, those who, on account of certain ecclesiastical causes and curable questions, have fallen out with one another; and irregular congregations, the assemblies held by insubordinate presbyters or bishops and by untaught peoples. For example, if someone, examined for a fault, has been suspended from the ministry and has not bowed to the canons, but has claimed for himself the presidency and the ministry, and certain others have departed with him, leaving the Catholic Church — that is an irregular congregation. And it is schism, to be at variance over repentance with those who belong to the Church. But heresies are such as those of the Manichaeans, the Valentinians, the Marcionists, and these very Pepuzeni; for here at once the difference touches faith in God itself. It seemed good, therefore, to those who lived in the beginning, to reject the baptism of heretics altogether; to accept that of those who had separated in schism, as still belonging to the Church; and as for those in irregular congregations, when they had been amended by a notable repentance and conversion, to join them again to the Church — so that often even those in a clerical grade, who had gone off with the insubordinate, when they repented, were received again into the same rank. The Pepuzeni, then, are plainly heretics; for they blasphemed against the Holy Spirit, lawlessly and shamelessly applying the name of the Paraclete to Montanus and Priscilla. Whether, then, as making gods of men, they are to be condemned; or whether, as outraging the Holy Spirit by comparing him with men, they are in this way liable to eternal condemnation, since the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit cannot be forgiven. What reason is there, then, that the baptism of these people should be approved, who baptize into Father and Son and Montanus or Priscilla? For those baptized into things not delivered to us have not been baptized at all. So that, even if this escaped the great Dionysius, we must not preserve the imitation of his error. For the absurdity is at once plain, and evident to all who possess even a little share of reasoning.

The Cathari too are themselves among the separated. Nevertheless it seemed good to the ancients — I mean those around Cyprian and our own Firmilian — to subject them all to one verdict: Cathari, Encratites, and Hydroparastatae; because the beginning of the separation came about through schism, and those who departed from the Church no longer had the grace of the Holy Spirit upon themselves, for its communication failed when the continuity was broken. For the first to depart had their ordinations from the fathers, and through the laying on of their hands they held the spiritual gift; but those who were broken off, having become laymen, had no authority either to baptize or to ordain, being no longer able to confer on others the grace of the Holy Spirit from which they had themselves fallen away. Therefore, regarding those baptized among them as baptized by laymen, they ordered that, when they came to the Church, they should be cleansed afresh with the true baptism of the Church. But since it has seemed good to some in Asia, for the sake of managing the multitude, to accept their baptism, let it be accepted.

But we must understand the mischief of the Encratites: that, in order to make themselves unacceptable to the Church, they have henceforth attempted to forestall it with a baptism of their own, and thereby they have falsified even their own custom. I think, therefore, since nothing is plainly declared about them, that it becomes us to reject their baptism; and if anyone has received it from them, he is to be baptized when he comes to the Church. If, however, this is going to prove an impediment to the general policy, then again we must use custom, and follow the fathers who have managed our affairs. For I am afraid that, while we wish to make them slack about baptizing, we may hinder those who are being saved by the severity of the requirement. But if they keep our baptism, let this not abash us; for we are not bound to render them a return of grace, but to serve the strictness of the canons. By all means, however, let it be laid down that those who come over from their baptism are to be anointed in the presence of the faithful, and so approach the mysteries. I know that we received into the rank of bishops the brothers around Izois and Saturninus, who were of that order. So that we can no longer separate from the Church those joined to their company, since by receiving their bishops we have, as it were, set forth a kind of canon of communion with them.

She who has procured an abortion by design is liable to the penalty of murder. With us there is no precise distinction of the formed and the unformed embryo. For here vengeance is taken not only for what was to be born, but also for her who plotted against her own self; because for the most part the women die in such attempts. There is added to this also the destruction of the embryo, a second murder, at least in the intent of those who dare these things. We must not, however, prolong their reconciliation to the hour of death, but accept the measure of ten years; and define the cure not by time, but by the manner of the repentance.

A deacon who has committed fornication after entering the diaconate shall be cast out of the diaconate; but, being thrust down into the place of the laity, he shall not be debarred from communion. For there is an ancient canon that those who have fallen from a grade are subjected to this one mode of punishment only; the ancients following, as I suppose, that law, "Thou shalt not take vengeance twice for the same offence." And there is another reason: that those in the lay order, when cast out from the place of the faithful, are again taken up into the place from which they fell; whereas the deacon has, once for all, the abiding penalty of deposition. So that, since the diaconate is not restored to him, they fixed upon this one penalty alone. These, then, are the prescriptions of the canons. But more truly, in general, the remedy is the abandonment of the sin. So that he who through the pleasure of the flesh rejected grace will give us full proof of his cure if, through contrition of the flesh and every subjection of himself in self-restraint, he withdraws from the pleasures by which he was overthrown. We must, then, know both things — what belongs to strictness and what belongs to custom; and in the case of those who do not accept the extreme rule, we must follow the form that has been handed down.

Concerning those married three times and many times, they have laid down the same canon, in proportion, as for those married twice; for a year is assigned for the twice-married, though others assign two years; and the thrice-married they exclude often for three or four years. They call such a state no longer marriage, but polygamy, or rather a chastened fornication. Hence the Lord too said to the Samaritan woman, who had changed five husbands, "He whom you now have is not your husband" — as if those who have exceeded the measure of a second marriage are no longer worthy to be called by the name of husband or wife. We have found as custom, for the thrice-married, a separation of five years; not from the canons, but from the practice of our predecessors. But we must not wholly bar them from the Church, but admit them to the hearing of the Scriptures for some two or three years; and after that allow them to stand with the faithful, but to abstain from the communion of the Good; and so, when they have shown some fruit of repentance, restore them to the place of communion.

Heretics who repent at the point of death must be received; received, however, clearly not without examination, but testing whether they show true repentance, and whether they have the fruits that bear witness to their zeal for salvation.

The fornications of those vowed to the canonical life are not to be reckoned as marriage, but their union is to be broken up by every means. For this is profitable both for the security of the Church, and it will not give the heretics a handle against us, as though they drew people to themselves through the licence to sin.

Those who corrupt males and those who corrupt animals, and murderers, and sorcerers, and adulterers, and idolaters, have been judged worthy of the same condemnation. So the form you have for the others, keep for these too. As for those who have repented for thirty years over the uncleanness which they committed in ignorance, we ought not even to hesitate to receive them. For their ignorance makes them worthy of pardon, as does the voluntary character of their confession and the prolongation over so great a length of time. For they were given over to Satan for almost a whole generation of man, that they might be taught not to behave shamefully. So command them now to be received without delay, especially if they also have tears that move your compassion, and show a life worthy of sympathy.

He who in anger used an axe against his own wife is a murderer. You have done well, and worthily of your own discernment, to remind me to speak more fully about these matters; for there are many distinctions in the voluntary and the involuntary. For it is wholly involuntary, and far removed from the one who initiated it, that a man who has thrown a stone at a dog or a tree should strike a person. For his impulse was to ward off the beast, or to shake down the fruit; but the passer-by came of his own accord under the blow as he went along — so that such a thing is involuntary. And it is also involuntary if someone, wishing to correct another, strikes him with a strap or a rod that is not hard, and the one struck dies; for here the intention is regarded, that he wished to better the one in fault, not to destroy him. Among the involuntary cases is also this: that one defending himself in a fight with a stick or his hand should bring the blow unsparingly upon a vital spot, so as to hurt him, not so as to destroy him utterly. But this now approaches the voluntary. For one who used so great an instrument in self-defence, or who brought down the blow without sparing, is plainly, because mastered by passion, unsparing of the man. Likewise also one who used a heavy stick, or a stone too large for human strength, is reckoned among those who kill involuntarily, having intended one thing and done another. For through anger he brought such a blow as to destroy the one struck; though his aim was perhaps to crush him, not to kill him outright. He, however, who used a sword, or any such thing, has no excuse — and least of all one who has hurled an axe. For he is shown not even to have struck with his hand, so that the measure of the blow might rest with him, but he hurled it, so that, by the weight of the iron, and its edge, and its passage over so great a distance, the blow necessarily became deadly.

Again, it is wholly voluntary, and admits of no doubt, such as the deed of robbers and of attacks in war. For these slay for money, fleeing examination; and those who go to slaughter in wars choose openly neither to frighten nor to chasten, but to destroy their adversaries. And further, even if for some other meddlesome reason a person mixes a drug and kills, we count such a thing voluntary; as women often do, who attempt by certain incantations and binding-spells to draw men to their own love, and give them drugs that produce a darkening of the mind. Such women, then, who have killed — even if they intended one thing and did another — are yet, because of the meddlesome and forbidden character of the practice, reckoned among those who kill voluntarily. And so too the women who give drugs to cause abortion are themselves murderers, as are those who receive the poisons that kill the embryo. So much for these matters.

The pronouncement of the Lord — that it is not lawful to depart from marriage except for the cause of fornication — applies equally, according to the sequence of the thought, to men and to women. But the custom is not so; rather, in the case of women we find much strictness, the Apostle saying, "He that is joined to a harlot is one body," and Jeremiah, "If a wife belong to another man, she shall not return to her husband, but being defiled she shall be defiled," and again, "He that keeps an adulteress is foolish and impious." But custom enjoins that adulterous men, and men living in fornication, be retained by their wives. So that I do not know whether the woman who lives with a husband who has been dismissed can be called an adulteress; for here the charge touches the woman who has divorced her husband, on what ground she withdrew from the marriage. For if she was beaten and could not bear the blows, she ought rather to have endured than to be separated from her husband; or if she could not bear the loss to her property, that pretext is not worthy of regard either. And if it is because he lives in fornication, we do not have this observance in the custom of the Church; rather, a wife was not commanded to separate even from an unbelieving husband, but to remain, because of the uncertainty of the outcome: "For how do you know, woman, whether you shall save your husband?" So that the woman who has left her husband is an adulteress if she has gone to another man. But the husband who has been left is to be pardoned, and the woman who lives with such a man is not condemned. If, however, the husband, having withdrawn from his wife, has gone to another, he is himself an adulterer, because he makes her commit adultery; and the woman who lives with him is an adulteress, because she has drawn another woman's husband to herself.

Let those who have sworn not to accept ordination, when they forswear themselves, not be compelled to commit perjury. For even if there seems to be a canon which permits such men this, yet we have learned by experience that those who break their oaths do not prosper. One must consider also the form of the oath, and the words, and the disposition in which they swore, and the precise additions in the wording; so that, if there is no relief from any quarter, one must let such men entirely alone. But the affair concerning Severus — that is, the presbyter ordained by him — seems to me to admit of some such relief, if it also seem good to you. Command that farm which lies near Mesteia, to which the man was assigned, to belong to the parish of Vasodae; for in this way he too will not be forsworn by not departing from his post; and Longinus, having Cyriacus with him, will not leave the church desolate, nor condemn his own soul by idleness; and we shall seem to do nothing contrary to the canons in accommodating Cyriacus, who swore to remain with the people of Minda, but accepted the transfer. For the return will be a keeping of the oath; and his yielding to the dispensation will not be reckoned to him for perjury, since it was not laid down in the oath that he would not depart even for a short time from Minda, but that he would remain henceforth. And to Severus, who pleads forgetfulness, we shall grant pardon, saying that he who knows the hidden things will not overlook his own Church being injured by such a man — one who from the beginning acted uncanonically, who bound men by an oath contrary to the Gospels, who taught perjury by the transfer he made, and who now lies in feigning forgetfulness. Since, however, we are not judges of hearts, but judge from what we hear, let us leave the vengeance to the Lord, and let us ourselves receive him without distinction, granting pardon to the forgetfulness as a human weakness.

He who has committed an involuntary murder has paid the penalty sufficiently in eleven years. For it is plain that in the case of those struck we shall observe the rule of Moses; and the man who, after being laid up by the blows he received, then walked again with the aid of his staff, we shall not reckon to have been murdered. But if he did not rise again after the blows — still, by reason of his not having chosen to kill him, the one who struck is a murderer indeed, but an involuntary one because of his intention.
The canon has wholly excluded the twice-married from the ministry.

Killings in war our fathers did not reckon among murders, granting pardon, it seems to me, to those who defend chastity and piety. But perhaps it is well to advise that, since their hands are not clean, they abstain for three years from communion alone.
He who takes interest, if he consents to spend the unjust gain on the poor, and henceforth to be freed from the disease of avarice, is acceptable to the priesthood.

I am surprised that you demand grammatical precision of Scripture, and reckon that the language of the translation is constrained, giving out its own sense, but not transferring what is properly signified by the Hebrew expression. Yet since one must not pass idly over a problem raised by an inquiring man — the fowls of the heaven and the fishes of the sea also obtained the same origin in the creation of the world. For both kinds were brought forth from the waters; and the reason is that both have the same characteristic property. For the one swims through the water, the other swims upon the air. For this reason, then, they were mentioned together. But the form of the expression, though incongruously applied as regards the fishes, is yet very fitting as regards all that lives in the waters. For the fowls of the heaven are subjected to man, and the fishes of the sea; and not these alone, but all that pass through the paths of the seas. For not everything that lives in water is a fish, such as the sea-monsters — whales, hammer-fish, dolphins, seals, and besides, sea-horses, and dogfish, and saw-fish, and sword-fish, and the sea-cows; and, if you like, sea-nettles too, and scallops, and all the shellfish, none of which is a fish — and all that pass through the paths of the seas; so that there are three kinds: fowls of the heaven, fishes of the sea, and all those creatures of the water which, being distinct from the fishes, themselves also pass through the paths of the seas.

But Naaman was not great before the Lord, but before his own lord; that is, he was among those who shared power with the king of the Syrians. Give close heed, then, to the Scripture, and from it itself you will find the solution of the question.
To Eustathius the chief physician.

The practice of your art is, for all of you who pursue medicine, a love of mankind. And it seems to me that whoever, among all the pursuits men are zealous for in life, sets your science first, would arrive at a fitting judgement and not fail of what is proper; since the most precious thing of all, life itself, is to be shunned and full of pain unless one can possess it together with health — and the giver of health is your art. But in your case the science is exceptionally accomplished, and you make the bounds of your love of mankind wider for yourself, not confining the favour of your art to bodies alone, but devising also the correction of the soul's ailments. And I say this, not only following the report of the many, but taught by my own experience, in many other matters, and especially now in the indescribable malice of our enemies — a malice which, like an evil flood pouring down upon our life, you skilfully drained away, dispersing this grievous inflammation of our heart by pouring over it the comforting flow of your words. For I, looking to the repeated and varied assaults of our enemies against us, thought I ought to keep silent and receive in quiet what was brought upon me, and not to answer those armed with falsehood — that evil weapon, which often through the very appearance of truth thrusts in its point. But you, doing well, urged me not to betray the truth, but to refute the slanderers, that the many might not be harmed by falsehood prevailing over truth.

Now those who have taken up against us this groundless hatred seem to me to do something very like the fable of Aesop. For just as that fabulist made the wolf bring certain charges against the lamb — ashamed, as it were, to appear to destroy without just cause one who had done him no prior injury — and, when the lamb easily dissolved every accusation brought against him by slander, made the wolf abate nothing of his fury, but, beaten in the matter of justice, conquer with his teeth; so those for whom hatred of us has been pursued as though it were one of the good things, blushing perhaps to seem to hate without cause, fabricate causes and charges against us. And they do not abide to the end by any of the things they say, but allege now this, and a little later another, and again yet a third as the ground of their hostility toward us. Their malice rests on nothing; but when they have shaken off one charge, they fasten upon another, and from that again they take up a third; and even if all the charges are dissolved, they do not desist from hating. They accuse us of professing three Gods, and they ring this in the ears of the many, and do not cease persuasively to build up this slander. But the truth fights on our behalf, both publicly before all and privately before those we meet, as we show that everyone who speaks of three Gods has been anathematized by us, and is not even judged to be a Christian. But when they hear this, Sabellius is ready to hand against us, and the disease that springs from him is rumoured against our teaching. Again, against this too we put forward our customary weapon, the truth, showing that we shudder at such a heresy as much as at Judaism.

What then? After so many attempts, have they grown weary and rested? It is not so. But they bring against us a charge of innovation, framing the accusation against us in this way: they charge us with confessing three hypostases, and with speaking of one goodness, and one power, and one Godhead. And this, they say, is not outside the truth; for we do say it. But in bringing the charge they object that their custom does not have this, and that Scripture does not compose it so. What, then, do we say to this as well? We do not think it just to make the custom prevailing among them a law and a canon of right doctrine. For if custom has force as a proof of rightness, then it is certainly permitted to us also to bring forward in opposition the custom prevailing among us. And if they cancel ours, neither are we bound to follow theirs. Let the divinely inspired Scripture, then, be our arbiter; and with whomsoever the doctrines are found to agree with the divine words, on their side will the verdict of truth certainly fall. What, then, is the charge? For two things at once have been brought forward in the accusation against us: one, that we distinguish the hypostases; the other, that we no longer number any of the names befitting God in the plural, but, as has been said, declare the goodness and the power and the Godhead, and all such things, in the singular. Now toward the distinction of the hypostases those who teach a difference of essences in the divine nature could have no quarrel; for it is not likely that those who speak of three essences should not also speak of three hypostases. Therefore this alone stands in the charge: that we proclaim in the singular the names applied to the divine nature.

But our answer to this is ready and clear. For he who condemns those who speak of one Godhead must of necessity agree either with him who speaks of many, or with him who speaks of none. For it is not possible to conceive anything besides what has been said. But the divinely inspired teaching does not permit us to speak of many; for wherever it makes mention, it makes mention of the Godhead in the singular, as, "In him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead," and elsewhere, "For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead." If, then, to extend the number of Godheads into a multitude belongs only to those sick with the polytheistic error, while to deny the Godhead altogether would belong to the atheists, what argument is it that slanders us for confessing one Godhead? But they uncover more plainly the aim of their argument: in the case of the Father they consent that he is God, and that the Son likewise is honoured with the name of Godhead, but the Spirit, when numbered with Father and Son, they no longer include in the conception of Godhead; rather, halting the power of the Godhead at the Son, they cut off the nature of the Spirit from the divine glory. We too, therefore, must make our defence, as far as we are able, briefly, against this notion as well.

What, then, is our argument? When the Lord delivered the saving faith to those who are made disciples by the word, he joined to the Father and the Son also the Holy Spirit. And what has once been joined, we say, holds the conjunction throughout all. For it is not the case that, ranked with them in one respect, it is fenced off in others. But in the life-giving power, by which our nature is transformed from a corruptible existence to immortality, the power of the Spirit is taken up together with Father and Son; and in many other respects too — as in the conception of the good, and the holy, and the eternal, the wise, the upright, the sovereign, the powerful, and everywhere, evidently — it has its inseparability in all the names understood in the better sense. We hold, therefore, that it is right to think that what is joined to Father and Son in so many lofty and God-befitting conceptions is separated from them in nothing. For we do not know of any difference of better and worse among the names conceived of the divine nature, so that it should be holy to suppose that, while we grant the Spirit a share in the lower names, we judge it unworthy of those that are more exalted. For all the conceptions and names that befit God stand equal in honour with one another, in that they do not disagree at all concerning the signification of the subject. For the appellation "good" does not lead the mind to one subject, and that of "wise" and "powerful" and "just" to another; but whatever names you may speak, the thing signified through all of them is one. And if you say "God," you have pointed to the same one whom you conceived through the rest of the names. But if all the names applied to the divine nature are of equal force with one another in pointing to the subject, leading our mind to the same thing under different emphases, what argument is it that grants the Spirit fellowship with Father and Son in the other names, but fences it off from the Godhead alone? For it is altogether necessary either to grant the fellowship in this too, or not to allow it in the rest either. For if it is worthy in those, it is surely not unworthy in this. But if, by their argument, it is too small for the fellowship of the name of Godhead with Father and Son to reach it, then it is not worthy to share in any other of the names befitting God either. For when the names are learned thoroughly and compared with one another through the emphasis contemplated in each, they will be found to fall in no way short of the appellation of God. A proof is that by this name many even of the lower things are named; or rather, the divine Scripture does not spare this shared use of the name, not even in the case of things utterly out of keeping, as when it names the idols with the appellation of God. For "the gods," it says, "who did not make heaven and earth, let them be taken away, and let them be cast beneath the earth," and, "All the gods of the nations are demons." And the woman with the familiar spirit, conjuring up for Saul by her sorceries the souls he sought, says that she has seen gods. But Balaam too, being a soothsayer and a diviner, who carried his divinations in his hand, as the Scripture says, and who had perfected for himself through the meddlesome art of augury the teaching that comes from demons, is recorded by the Scripture to be counselled by God. And there are many such things one might collect and set forth from the divine Scriptures, to show that this name in no way takes precedence over the rest of the appellations befitting God, since, as has been said, we find it spoken in a shared sense even of things out of keeping. But the name of the holy, and of the incorruptible, and of the upright, and of the good, we have nowhere been taught by Scripture to make common with what is unbefitting. If, then, in the names piously spoken of the divine nature alone and in a special way they do not deny that the Holy Spirit has fellowship with the Son and the Father, what argument is it to maintain that it is excluded from this name alone, of which even the demons and the idols were shown to partake by a certain shared use?

But they say that this appellation indicates nature, and that the nature of the Spirit has no fellowship with Father and Son, and that therefore it does not share in the fellowship of this name. Let them show, then, by what means they came to know the difference of nature. For if it were possible for the divine nature itself to be contemplated in itself, and to find through what appears both what is proper to it and what is foreign, then we should certainly have no need of arguments or other proofs for the apprehension of what is sought. But since it is too high for the comprehension of the things sought, and we reason from certain proofs about the things that escape our knowledge, it is altogether necessary that we be led by the operations to the investigation of the divine nature. If, then, we see that the operations performed by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit differ from one another, we shall conjecture from the difference of the operations that the natures which operate are also different. For it is not possible that things separated according to the principle of nature should be brought together with one another in the form of their operations — fire does not cool, nor does ice make warm — but by the difference of their natures the operations that come from them are also distinguished from one another. But if we understand the operation of Father and Son and Holy Spirit to be one, differing or varying in nothing, then we must, from the identity of the operation, infer the unity of the nature.

The Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit alike sanctify, and give life, and enlighten, and comfort, and do all such things. And let no one assign in a special way the sanctifying authority to the operation of the Spirit, having heard the Saviour in the Gospel saying to the Father concerning the disciples, "Father, sanctify them in your name." And in the same way all the rest is performed equally upon the worthy by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit: every grace and power, the guidance, the life, the comfort, the change to immortality, the passage into freedom, and whatever other good descends to us. But the dispensation above us also, both in the intelligible creation and in the sensible — if one must, from the things known to us, conjecture also about the things that lie above us — this too is not set outside the operation and power of the Holy Spirit, each receiving a share of the benefit according to its own worth and need. For even if the ordering and governance of the things above our nature is unseen by our perception, yet from the sequence one would more reasonably conclude, through the things known to us, that the power of the Spirit is active among them too, than that it is excluded from the dispensation among the higher beings. For he who says the latter puts forward a bare and unsupported blasphemy, establishing the absurdity by no reasoning; but he who holds that the things above us also are dispensed, together with Father and Son, by the power of the Spirit, supports his assertion about these things by the clear proof drawn from his own life. Therefore the identity of the operation in the case of Father and Son and Holy Spirit clearly shows the unchangeableness of the nature. So that, even if the name of Godhead signifies nature, the community of essence requires that this appellation be properly applied to the Holy Spirit as well.

But I do not know how those who would establish everything bring the appellation of Godhead to the indication of nature, as though they had not heard from the Scripture that a nature does not come into being by appointment. But Moses was appointed god of the Egyptians, when he who gave the oracle spoke to him thus: "I have given you as a god to Pharaoh." Therefore the appellation indicates some authority, whether of oversight or of operation. But the divine nature, in all the names conceived of it, remains, as it is in itself, unsignified, as our argument holds. For learning of a benefactor, and a judge, the good and the just, and whatever other such names, we have been taught differences of operations; but of the nature of the one who operates we are no more able to gain knowledge through the comprehension of the operations. For when one gives an account of each of these names, and of the nature itself about which the names are spoken, he will not give the same account of both. And of things whose account is different, the nature is also different. Therefore the essence is one thing, of which no defining account has yet been found; and the signification of the names spoken of it is another, the names being given from some operation or worth.

We find, then, that there is no difference in the operations, from the fellowship of the names; but of any variation according to nature we grasp no clear demonstration, since, as has been said, the identity of the operations indicates the community of the nature. Whether, therefore, Godhead is a name of operation, then, just as we say there is one operation of Father and Son and Holy Spirit, so we say there is one Godhead; or whether, according to the opinions of the many, the name of Godhead is indicative of nature, then, because we find no variation in the nature, we not unreasonably define the holy Trinity to be of one Godhead.
To Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium.

Worthily of your own graciousness and zeal, of which I am ever an admirer, you have taken thought for the affairs of the church of the Isaurians. That it would be in every way more advantageous for the charge to be divided among several bishops is, I think, plain at once even to a chance observer; nor did this escape your discernment, but you both noted it rightly and made it known to us. But since it is not easy to find worthy men, may it not happen that, while we wish to have the credit that comes from numbers, and to make the Church of God more carefully administered by a greater number, we unawares, through the unfitness of those called, drag the matter down into cheapness and breed in the peoples a habit of indifference? For you yourself know that, whatever sort the leaders are, such for the most part the characters of those they rule are wont to become. So perhaps it is better to put forward one approved man, if even this is easy, as protector of the city, and to entrust to his own responsibility the administration of each matter — provided only that he be a servant of God, a workman not ashamed, not seeking his own interest, but that of the many, that they may be saved; one who, if he knows himself too small for the care, will take to himself workmen for the harvest. If, then, we find such a man, I confess that the one is worth many, and that it is more advantageous for the churches, and less dangerous for us, thus to manage the care of souls. But if this is not easy, let us be zealous first to give leaders to the small towns, or rather small villages, which from of old have held the throne of bishops; and then we will set up the bishop of the city, lest the one put forward become an impediment to our subsequent administration, and we straightway begin to be at war with our own household, because he wishes to rule over more and will not accept the ordinations of bishops. But if this is burdensome, and the time does not permit, let your discernment be zealous for this: to make the bishop of the Isaurians limit his own circuit, so that he may ordain some of the neighbouring places. And the rest will remain stored up for us, so that at the proper time we may give to all the others bishops whom we ourselves judge to be more worthy, having tested them by much examination.

We questioned George, as your reverence commanded, and he said what your piety also reported, in face of which we must keep quiet, casting upon the Lord the care of the house. For I trust the holy God that he will give understanding, so as to deliver us from our needs in some other way, and to procure for us a life free from grief. If, then, this does not seem good, do you yourself deign to send me a memorandum, as to what office I should bring zeal to bear upon, that we may begin to ask each of our influential friends for this favour, whether without payment, or at a moderate price, as the Lord shall prosper us.

I have written to brother Valerius, as you directed. The affairs of Nyssa are similar to those left by your piety, and they advance toward the better through the cooperation of your prayers. Those, however, who at that time broke away from us — some of them have gone off to the camp, others remain, awaiting the report from there. But the Lord is able both to make their hopes vain and to render the others' return fruitless.

Philo, interpreting the manna, said — as though taught from some Jewish tradition — that its quality was such that it was blended according to the imagination of the eater; and that in itself it was like a grain of millet boiled in honey, but that it furnished now the taste of bread, now of meat — and meat of this or that kind, whether of bird or of land animal — now of a vegetable, and of the vegetable each one desired, and of fish, so that the proper character of the quality of each kind was exactly preserved in the taste of the eater.

The Scripture knows of chariots having warriors of the third rank as riders, because the rest of the chariots had two riders, the driver and the man-at-arms; but those of Pharaoh had two who fought, and one who held the reins of the horses.

Simplicius wrote to us a kindly letter, and one of fellowship, to whom we, in reply, have sent the letter to your reverence, so that, when you have fully approved it, you may command it to be sent to him — with the addition, of course, of your own letter as well.
May you be granted to me, sound and cheerful in the Lord, praying earnestly for me, and to the Church of God, by the lovingkindness of the Holy One.
To Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium.

On reading the letter of your reverence, we gave much thanks to God, because we found traces of the ancient love in the words of your letter. For you did not suffer what the many suffer, nor did you set yourself contentiously against being the first yourself to begin the loving converse; but, as one schooled in the greatness which comes to the saints out of humility, you so chose to be shown, by taking the second place, ahead of us. For this too is the law of victory among Christians, and he who consents to have the lesser part is crowned. That we may not, then, be left behind in this good rivalry, behold, we too answer your dignity, and show our purpose: that, since by the grace of God our agreement in the faith stands firm, there is nothing else that hinders us from being one body and one spirit, as we were called in one hope through our calling. It belongs, then, to your love to render also what follows upon this good beginning: to gather around yourself those of like soul, and to make known both the time and the place of our meeting, so that, when by the grace of God we have thus recovered one another, we may administer the churches in the ancient manner of love, receiving as our own members the brethren who travel from each side, sending them on as to our own people, and receiving them again as from our own people. For this was once the boast of the Church, that, furnished with small tokens, the brethren from each church travelling from the ends of the inhabited world to the ends found everywhere fathers and brothers. But now, along with the rest, the enemy of the churches of Christ has taken this too from us, and we have been confined within our cities, and each of us holds his neighbour in suspicion. And what else have we done but grow cold in that love by which alone our Lord said his own disciples are marked? And if you think it good, do you first make yourselves known to one another, that we may know with whom our agreement will be. And so, by common consent, choosing some place not burdensome to both, and a time suitable for the journeys, we will hasten to one another, and the Lord will prosper our way. May you be sound and cheerful, praying earnestly for me, and may you be granted to me by the lovingkindness of the Holy One.
To Sophronius the Master.

If you yourself received a double favour, in that, with your unsurpassable eagerness for good works, you wrote to us — one favour in receiving our letter, a second in supplying our need — how great a favour must we be reckoned to have, both in meeting with the letter of that most sweet voice, and in seeing the need we sought so quickly fulfilled? So that, having gladly received what was sent for its own nature's sake, we welcomed it far more gladly because you were the one who presided over its provision. And may the Lord grant us to see you soon, so that we may acknowledge the favour by word of mouth, and enjoy all the good things in you together.
To Meletius the chief physician.

We have not so much as the cranes have, the power to escape the hardships of winter; but as for foreseeing the future, we are perhaps no worse than the cranes, while in the freedom of our way of life we fall as far short of the birds as we do, very nearly, of the power to fly. For first, certain engagements with the affairs of life held me back; then continuous and violent fevers so wasted my body that something even thinner than I appeared — namely, I myself; and after that, attacks of quartan fever lasting for more than twenty cycles. And now, when I think I am rid of the fevers, I am so reduced by weakness that in this I fall nothing short of a spider's web. Hence every road is impassable to me, and every gust of wind brings me more danger than the great waves bring those who sail. There is no choice, then, but to be hidden under a small roof, and to await the spring — if indeed we are able to hold out until it, and do not perish first from the malady that has settled in our inward parts. But if the Lord preserves us with his great hand, most gladly will we make our way to your retreat, and most gladly will we embrace you, that head so dear to us. Only pray that our life may be ordered to the soul's advantage.
To Zoilus.

What are you doing, admirable man, outdoing us in the measure of humility? For, being such in education, and knowing so well how to write, as your letter shows, you yet ask, as though for some bolder undertaking exceeding your worth, to obtain pardon from us. But, leaving aside this irony, write to us on every occasion. For whether we have any share in eloquence, we shall most gladly read the letters of a learned man; or whether — taught by Scripture how great a good love is — we count of all worth the converse of a man who loves us. And may it be yours to write of the good things we pray for you, health of body and prosperity of your whole house.

But know that our own affairs are no more endurable than usual. It is enough to say this much, and to indicate to you the weakness of our body. For the present excess of sickness that holds us is neither easy to indicate in words, nor to be believed by deeds, if anything more than those things which you yourself knew has been found in us toward sickness. But it is the work of the good God to give us strength to bear with patience the blows brought upon our body for our profit by the Lord who does us good.
To Euphronius, bishop of Colonia in Armenia.

Because Colonia, which the Lord has given to be guided under you, lies far from the travelled roads, often, even when we write to the other brethren throughout Lesser Armenia, we are slow to send a letter to your reverence, having no hope of anyone to carry it as far as those parts. But now, expecting either that you yourself will be present, or that the letter will be forwarded by the bishops to whom we have written, we both write to your reverence and greet you by letter — signifying at once that we still seem to be above the earth, and at the same time asking you to pray for us, that the Lord may lessen our afflictions, and may carry away from us, like some cloud, this great weight of grief that now lies upon our hearts. And this will come to pass if he grants a swift return to the most God-beloved bishops who are now in the dispersion, paying the penalty on behalf of true religion.
To Aburgius.

That you flash like the stars, rising now in one part of the barbarian land, now in another — now furnishing provisions to the soldiers, now appearing before the emperor in splendid array — the report that is herald of good things does not cease to announce to us. And we pray God that, your enterprise advancing according to reason, you may come to greatness, and at last appear in your homeland. As for us, we are still above the earth, and draw in this air; for we have so much share in life as is enough only to breathe.
To Ambrose, bishop of Milan.

Great always and many are the gifts of our Master, and neither is their greatness to be measured, nor their multitude to be numbered. And one of the greatest gifts, for those who receive his graces with sensitive hearts, is this present one: that, separated as we are by the very position of our places by the greatest distance, he has granted us to be joined to one another through the address of letters. He has bestowed on us a twofold manner of knowing one another: the one through a meeting, the other through the converse of a letter. Since, then, we have come to know you through what you have spoken — and we have come to know you, not by stamping upon our memory your bodily features, but by learning the beauty of the inner man through the richness of your words, since each of us speaks out of the abundance of his heart — we glorified our God, who in every generation chooses out those who are well-pleasing to him; who formerly raised up a ruler for his people from the flocks of sheep, and, having empowered Amos from the herd of goats through the Spirit, exalted him to be a prophet; but now has drawn a man from the imperial city, one entrusted with the rule of a whole nation, lofty in mind, illustrious in birth, distinguished in life, mighty in eloquence, conspicuous in all the things of this life, to the care of the flocks of Christ; who, having cast away all the advantages of this life and counted them as loss that he might gain Christ, has been entrusted to take the helm of that great and far-famed ship — the Church of Christ, founded upon faith in God. Come then, man of God, since it was not from men that you received or were taught the Gospel of Christ, but the Lord himself transferred you from the judges of the earth to the throne of the apostles: fight the good fight, correct the ailments of the people, if indeed the disease of Arian madness has touched any of them; renew the ancient footsteps of the fathers; and the foundation of love toward us which you have laid, be zealous to build upon by the constancy of your greetings. For thus we shall be able to be near one another in spirit, even if in our dwelling upon the earth we are separated by a vast distance.

Your generosity and zeal concerning the most blessed bishop Dionysius bear witness to all your love toward the Lord, your honour toward those who have gone before, your zeal for the faith. For one's disposition toward the well-disposed among one's fellow-servants refers back to the Master whom they have served; and he who honours those who have contended for the faith is plainly possessed of the same zeal for the faith — so that this one act bears the testimony of much virtue. And we make known to your love in Christ that the most diligent brethren, who were chosen by your reverence for the ministry of this good work, first of all brought praise upon the whole clergy by the gracefulness of their manners; for in their own seemly conduct they made plain the steadfastness common to all. Then, employing all zeal and diligence, they dared an impassable winter, and persuaded with all earnestness the faithful guardians of the blessed body to yield up to them the safeguards of their own life. And know that neither the authorities nor the powers of men could ever have forced those people, had not the earnestness of purpose of these brethren prevailed upon them to consent. And what contributed most of all to the accomplishment of what was sought was the presence of our most beloved and most reverend son Therasius, our fellow-presbyter, who, of his own accord taking upon himself the labour of the journey, stilled the vehemence of the impulse of the faithful there, and, having by reasoning persuaded those who held back, took up the relics with fitting reverence, in the presence of presbyters and deacons and many others who fear the Lord, and brought them safe together with the brethren. Receive them, then, with as much joy as the grief with which those who guarded them sent them forth. Let no one make distinctions; let no one doubt: this is that unconquered athlete. These bones the Lord knows, which contended together with the blessed soul. These he will crown together with it on the day of his just recompense, according to what is written: that we must stand before the judgement-seat of Christ, that each may receive according to what he has done through the body. One coffer it was that received that precious body; no one lay near it; the burial was conspicuous; the honour, that of a martyr. Christians it was who received him as a guest and laid him with their own hands then, and took him up now. These wept as men deprived of a father and a protector, yet sent him forth, counting your joy more precious than their own consolation. Reverent, then, are those who delivered him; exact, those who received him. Nowhere is there falsehood, nowhere deceit. We bear witness; let the truth be free from slander among you.
To Eusebius, bishop of Samosata.

After the letter brought to us by the officials, I received one other afterwards sent to us. We ourselves have written — not many letters, indeed, because we did not even succeed in finding people travelling to you, but yet more than four — among which we forwarded to the most reverend brother Leontius, the assessor of Nicaea, those letters brought to us from Samosata sealed under the first writings of your piety, asking through him that they be conveyed to the steward of the house of the most reverend brother Sophronius, so that he might take charge of their delivery to you. Since, then, the letters pass through many hands, it is likely that the engagements or negligence of some one person became the cause of your reverence not receiving them. So pardon us, we beg, for the scarcity of letters.

As for the fact that, when it was needful to send someone from among ourselves, we did not do this — you yourself, with your own discernment, rightly inquired after it and reproached us; but know that the winter in our parts was so severe that all the roads were closed until the days of Easter, and that we have no one of bold disposition toward the hardships of the journey. For even though our clergy seems somehow to be numerous, yet they are men unpractised in travel, since they neither engage in trade nor choose to dwell abroad, but most of them handle the sedentary crafts, having from there their means of daily life. So, for instance, this brother whom we have now sent to your reverence — we summoned him from the country and made use of him as bearer of the letters to your holiness, that he may both clearly announce our affairs, and convey to us, by the grace of God, plainly and quickly, the news from there. And our most beloved brother Eusebius the reader, who has long been eager to go to your piety, we have kept back, awaiting the mildness of the weather. And even now I am in no slight anxiety, lest his being unaccustomed to travel produce some strain on him, and provide a cause of sickness to a body easily disposed toward weakness.

As for the innovations in the East, it is superfluous for us to indicate them by letter, since the brethren themselves are well able to report them of their own knowledge. But know, head most honoured by me, that when I was writing these things, I was so wretchedly disposed that henceforth all my hopes of living had failed. For it is not even possible to recount the multitude of the symptoms that came upon me, and the weakness, and the greatness of the fevers, and how malignant they were; only that out of all of them one conclusion is gathered: that the time of our sojourning in this wretched and painful life is at last fulfilled.
Second Canonical Letter: To Amphilochius, concerning the canons.

Long ago, having answered the questions put to us by your reverence, I did not send off the letter, partly being occupied by a long and dangerous illness, and partly through the lack of those who might serve as bearers. For few among us are both experienced in travel and prepared for such services. So, learning the reasons for the delay, grant us your pardon.

We marvelled at your love of learning together with your humility, that you both consent to learn, though entrusted with the rank of teacher, and to learn from us, who have nothing great in the way of knowledge. But nevertheless, since for the fear of God you consent to do a thing not easily done by another, we too must support your eagerness and good zeal even beyond our power.

You asked us concerning Bianor the presbyter, whether he is acceptable into the clergy on account of the oath. Now I know that I have already set forth a certain common ruling concerning all who took the oath together with him among the clergy of Antioch: namely, that they abstain from the public assemblies, but privately perform the functions of presbyters. And this same thing gives him also leave for his own ministry, since the priesthood is not in Antioch, but in Iconium — which, as you yourself wrote to us, he exchanged for Antioch as his dwelling. That man, then, is acceptable, being required by your reverence to repent of the lightness of the oath which he swore in the presence of the unbeliever, being unable to bear the trouble of that small peril.

Concerning virgins who have fallen — those who have professed to the Lord the life of holiness, and then, through yielding to the passions of the flesh, set at naught their own undertakings — our fathers, dealing simply and gently with the weaknesses of those who slip, laid down that they be received after a year, ranking them in likeness to those married twice. But it seems to me that, since by the grace of God the Church, advancing, becomes stronger, and the order of virgins is now multiplied, we must give close heed both to what the matter shows according to reflection, and to the meaning of Scripture, which it is possible to find out from what follows. For widowhood is less than virginity; therefore the sin of widows is far inferior to that of virgins. Let us see, then, what is written to Timothy by Paul: "But the younger widows refuse; for when they have begun to wax wanton against Christ, they will marry, having condemnation, because they have set at naught their first faith." If, then, a widow is liable to a most grievous condemnation, as having set at naught her faith toward Christ, what must we reckon concerning the virgin, who is a bride of Christ and a sacred vessel dedicated to the Master? It is a great sin even for a slave-woman to give herself to secret marriages and to fill the house with corruption, and through an evil life to outrage her owner; but far more grievous, surely, is it for the bride to become an adulteress, and, dishonouring her union with the bridegroom, to give herself over to licentious pleasures. Therefore the widow is condemned as a corrupted slave, but the virgin is liable to the condemnation of the adulteress. Just as, then, we name the man who joins himself to another's wife an adulterer, not receiving him into communion before he has ceased from the sin, so plainly we shall be disposed also toward the man who has the virgin. But this it is necessary for us first to agree upon: that she is named a virgin who has voluntarily presented herself to the Lord, and renounced marriage, and preferred the life of holiness. And we approve the professions from the time when the age has the completion of reason. For it is not fitting to regard the utterances of childhood as wholly binding in such matters, but she who has passed sixteen or seventeen years, being mistress of her own thoughts, after being examined at length and then persisting, and beseeching with entreaties to be received — she must then be enrolled among the virgins, and the profession of such a one confirmed, and the setting at naught of it punished without reprieve.
