For parents and brothers and some of the relatives bring forward many girls before the age, not set in motion of themselves toward the celibate life, but managing some worldly affair of their own. Such we must not readily receive, until we have plainly searched out their own mind.

Of the professions of men we have known nothing, except that some have enrolled themselves in the order of monks; who, in their silence, seem to have accepted celibacy. But even in their case I think this ought to come first: that they be questioned, and that an express profession be taken from them, so that, when they change to the flesh-loving and pleasure-loving life, they may be brought under the penalty of fornicators.

As for all the women who, while in heresy, professed virginity, and then afterwards chose marriage instead, I do not think these should be condemned. For "whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law." But those who have not yet come under the yoke of Christ do not even recognize the law-giving of the Master. So they are acceptable to the Church, together with all things, having forgiveness for these matters also through faith in Christ. And in general, what was done in the catechumen's life is not brought to account. But these, of course, the Church does not receive without baptism. So that the privileges of the new birth are most necessary in their case.

If a man living with a wife, when, not content with marriage, he falls into fornication, we judge such a one a fornicator, and we prolong him further in the penalties; we have, however, no canon to subject him to the charge of adultery, if the sin be committed against a woman free from marriage; because of the adulteress it is said, "Being defiled, she shall be defiled, and shall not return to her husband," and "He that keeps an adulteress is foolish and impious." But he who has committed fornication shall not be debarred from living with his own wife. So that the wife shall receive her husband when he returns from fornication, but the husband shall send away the defiled woman from his house. The reason of these things is not easy; but custom has so prevailed.

Those who have wives by abduction: if they have carried off women betrothed to others, they must not be received before the women are taken from them and placed at the disposal of those who first betrothed them, whether they wish to take them or to withdraw. But if anyone carry off a woman unattached, the woman must be taken away and restored to her own people, and the matter committed to the judgement of her relatives, whether they be parents, or brothers, or whoever are guardians of the girl; and if they choose to give her to him, let the union stand; but if they refuse, let no force be used. As for the man who has a wife by corruption, whether secret or more violent, he must of necessity submit to the penalty of fornication. And the penalty fixed for fornicators is in four years. In the first year they must be cast out of the prayers, and weep at the door of the church; in the second, be received to the hearing; in the third, to repentance; in the fourth, to standing with the people, while abstaining from the offering; then they are to be permitted the communion of the Good.

Concerning those who marry two sisters, or women who marry two brothers, a little letter of ours has been issued, of which we have sent a copy to your reverence. But he who has taken his own brother's wife shall not be received before he withdraws from her.

A widow enrolled in the number of widows — that is, one supported by the Church — the Apostle judged should be overlooked if she marries. But upon a man who has lost his wife no law is imposed, but the penalty of those twice-married is enough for such a one. The widow, however, who has reached sixty years, if she choose to live again with a husband, shall not be deemed worthy of the communion of the Good, until she ceases from the passion of uncleanness. But if we number her before sixty years, the charge is ours, not the woman's.
He who keeps as a wife the woman corrupted by himself shall undergo the penalty for the corruption, but shall be permitted to have the woman.

Fornication is not marriage, nor even the beginning of marriage. So that, if it be possible for those joined in fornication to be separated, this is best. But if they cleave in every way to the union, let them acknowledge the penalty of fornication, but let them be left alone, lest something worse happen.

Concerning the presbyter who through ignorance was entangled in an unlawful marriage, I have defined what was necessary: that he share in the seat, but abstain from the rest of the functions. For pardon is enough for such a one. But for him to bless another, who is bound to tend his own wounds, is inconsistent. For a blessing is the imparting of sanctification; and he who does not have this, because of the fall arising from ignorance, how shall he impart it to another? Let him, then, bless neither publicly nor privately, nor distribute the body of Christ to others, nor perform any other ministry; but, content with the presidency, let him weep to the Lord that the transgression arising from ignorance may be forgiven him.

This, indeed, seemed to me laughable: that someone had vowed to abstain from swine's flesh. So deign to teach them to abstain from untaught prayers and vows; but allow the use to be a matter of indifference. For no creature of God is to be rejected, if it is received with thanksgiving. So the vow is ridiculous, and the abstinence is not necessary.

As for rulers swearing to do harm to their subjects, this too ought by all means to be remedied. And the remedy of these things is twofold: one, that they be taught not to swear rashly; the other, that they not persist in their evil judgements. So let one who has been caught beforehand by an oath into harming another show repentance for the rashness of the oath, but let him not, under the pretext of piety, confirm his own wickedness. For it did not profit Herod to keep his oath, who, that he might not be forsworn forsooth, became the murderer of the prophet. The oath is once for all forbidden; but far more, surely, is it likely that one made for an evil purpose has been condemned. So the man who swears must change his mind, not be zealous to confirm his own impious act. For examine the absurdity more broadly. If someone should swear to gouge out his brother's eyes, would it be good for him to bring such a thing to deed? If someone should swear to murder? If someone, in general, should swear to transgress some commandment? "For I have sworn and resolved" — not to commit sin, but "to keep the judgements of your righteousness." And just as the commandment must be confirmed by unalterable resolves, so sin must in every way be annulled and made to disappear.

Concerning those who carry off women, we have no ancient canon, but we have made our own judgement: that they themselves, and those who help them in the abduction, be excluded from the prayers for three years. But what is done without violence is not punishable, when no corruption nor theft has preceded the act. And the widow is her own mistress, and it rests with her whether to follow. So we need not concern ourselves with appearances. The woman who, when her husband has withdrawn and is missing, before she is assured of his death, lives with another, commits adultery.

Clergy who commit a sin unto death are degraded from their grade, but are not excluded from the communion of the laity; for "you shall not take vengeance twice for the same offence." The woman who has given birth on the road and neglected the offspring shall be subject to the charge of murder.

Women who have committed adultery and confess it for piety's sake, or are in any way convicted, our fathers commanded not to be made public, lest we provide a cause of death to those convicted; but they ordered them to stand without communion until the time of repentance be completed.

In the case of the husband abandoned by his wife, one must consider the cause of the abandonment; and if it appear that she withdrew without reason, he is worthy of pardon, but she of penalty. And the pardon will be given to him for the communion of the Church.

Soldiers' wives who have married while their husbands are missing are subject to the same principle as those who, on account of their husbands' being away from home, did not wait for their return; except that the matter has some pardon here, because the suspicion of death is greater.
The man who marries a woman after she has been taken away from another will be charged with adultery as regards the first, but as regards the second will be free from blame.

Girls who follow a man against their father's will commit fornication; but when the parents are reconciled, the deed seems to receive healing. They are not, however, at once restored to communion, but shall be under penalty for three years.
The woman who lives with an adulterer is an adulteress the whole time.

The woman who gives herself to a man against the will of her master committed fornication; but she who afterwards made use of an open marriage was married. So that the former is fornication, but the latter is marriage. For the agreements of those under authority have nothing binding.

The woman who in her widowhood has authority over herself is without blame in living with a man, if there is no one to break up the union; the Apostle saying, "But if her husband die, she is free to be married to whom she will, only in the Lord."

Marriages without those in authority are fornications. So that, while a father or master is living, those who join together are not free from blame. But when the masters consent to the union, then it receives the validity of marriage.
He who has given a deadly blow to his neighbour is a murderer, whether he began the blow or defended himself.

The deaconess who has committed fornication with a Greek is acceptable to repentance, but shall be received to the offering in the seventh year — that is, if she lives in purity. But the Greek who, after the faith, returns again to sacrilege turns back to the vomit. We, however, no longer permit the body of the deaconess, as consecrated, to be in fleshly use. If anyone, having taken the name of Christianity, outrages Christ, he gets no profit from the appellation.

The woman who, in ignorance, married the man abandoned for a time by his wife, and was then dismissed because the former wife returned to him, committed fornication, but in ignorance. She shall not, therefore, be barred from marriage. But it is better if she remain as she is.

Encratites and Sackcloth-wearers and Apotactites are not subject to the same principle as the Novatians, because concerning the latter a canon has been issued, though a different one; but the matters concerning these have been passed over in silence. We, however, by one principle rebaptize such people. But if the rebaptism is forbidden among you, as indeed it is among the Romans, for the sake of some policy, yet let our principle have force. For since their heresy is, as it were, an offshoot of the Marcionists, who abhor marriage and turn away from wine, and say that the creation of God is defiled, we do not receive them into the Church unless they are baptized into our baptism. For let them not say, "We were baptized into Father and Son and Holy Spirit," who suppose God to be the maker of evils, on a par with Marcion and the rest of the heresies. So that, if this be agreeable, several bishops must come together in one place and so set forth the canon, that both the one who acts may be without danger, and the one who answers may have credit in his answer concerning such matters.

The woman abandoned by her husband, in my judgement, ought to remain. For if the Lord said that "if anyone forsakes his wife except for the cause of fornication, he makes her commit adultery," by naming her an adulteress he excluded her from fellowship with another. For how can the husband be liable, as the cause of adultery, while the woman is blameless — she who has been called an adulteress by the Lord on account of her fellowship with another man?
Corruptions that come about by compulsion shall be without blame. So that even the slave-woman, if she was forced by her own master, is without blame.

There is no law of third marriage. So that a third marriage is not contracted by law. Such things we regard as defilements of the Church; but we do not subject them to public condemnations, as being preferable to unrestrained fornication.
To Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium.

One illness after another comes upon us, and the pressing demands both of ecclesiastical affairs and of those who do violence to the churches have held us fast through the whole winter, and through the time up to the present letter. For this reason it has not been possible for us either to send anyone to your reverence or to visit you. And we guessed that your circumstances too were similar — not as regards illness, I mean; God forbid! For may the Lord grant your body health enough for the service of his commandments — but because the care of the churches casts the same distraction upon you as well. And even now I was about to send someone for this very purpose, to make known to us how your health stands. But since our most beloved son Meletius, escorting the new recruits, reminded us that it was possible to address you through him, we gladly took up the occasion of writing, and we hastened to make him the bearer of our letters — a man who is sufficient even to stand in place of a letter, both for the truth-loving character of his manner and because he is ignorant of nothing concerning our affairs. Through him we ask your reverence first of all to pray for us, that the Lord may grant me release from this burdensome body, and to his churches peace, and to you quiet and leisure so that, when you have set in apostolic order the affairs of Lycaonia, as you have begun, you may visit the affairs here also — whether we are still at home in the flesh, or are already bidden to depart to the Lord — that you yourself, as your own (which indeed they are), may take charge of the places under us, and may strengthen what is unsound, rouse what is sluggish, and, by the grace of the Spirit who is in you, set all in order anew toward what is well-pleasing to the Lord.

And our most honoured sons Menetius and Melitius, whom you know from of old and judge to be your own, keep as a trust, praying for them; for this is sufficient for them toward all security. Deign also to greet on our behalf those who are with your holiness, and all the clergy, and the people shepherded under you, and our most God-beloved brethren and fellow-ministers. Remember the commemoration of the most blessed martyr Eupsychius, and do not wait for a second reminder, nor be eager to make your visit at a fixed later date, but to come beforehand and gladden us, if indeed we are still upon the earth. Until then, may you be kept safe for us and for the churches of God, sound in the Lord and praying earnestly for us, by the grace of the Holy One.
To Amphilochius, Bishop of Iconium.

I long to meet you for many reasons: that I might take your counsel about the matters now in hand, and, in short, that after so long a separation the sight of you might give me some consolation for the parting. But since one and the same thing has held us both back — the illness that has befallen you and the older infirmity of mine, which has not yet let me go — let us, if you are willing, grant pardon to each other for it, so that of ourselves we may release one another from the charge.
To Amphilochius, Bishop of Iconium.

To meet your Reverence is at all times worth a great deal, but now most of all, when the business that brings us together is of such a kind. But since the remnants of my illness are such as to allow me not even the slightest movement — for in trying to travel by carriage the road as far as the shrines of the martyrs I came near to relapsing once more into the same sickness — I must needs ask your pardon. If it should be possible to postpone the matter for a few days later, then I shall be with you, by the grace of God, and shall share in your deliberations. But if what is being urgently pursued cannot wait, then carry out with God's help the tasks that lie to your hands, and count me in among yourselves as though present and laying my own hand upon the good that is being done. May you be kept strong and cheerful in the Lord, praying earnestly for me, and preserved by the grace of the Holy One for the Church of God.
To the Bishops of the Seaboard.

I have often had a strong impulse to meet with you, but always some hindrance has arisen to stand in the way of my eagerness. For either the weakness of my body has held me back — and you cannot be wholly ignorant how great a measure of it has been with me from my earliest years down to this old age, having grown up alongside me and disciplined me, according to the just judgment of God who orders all things in wisdom — or else the cares of the churches, or the struggles against those who rise up against the word of truth. And so up to the present I pass my days in much affliction and grief, conscious that what I owe toward you has been left undone. For I have heard from God — who for this very reason consented to His sojourn in the flesh, that by examples of what we ought to do He might give rule to our life, and by His own voice announce to us the gospel of the kingdom — that "By this shall all know that you are My disciples, if you love one another"; and I have heard that, as a parting gift to His own disciples, when He was about to complete His dispensation in the flesh, the Lord left them His own peace, saying, "Peace I leave with you, My peace I give to you." I cannot persuade myself that, without love for one another, and without being at peace with all so far as it lies in me, I can be counted worthy to be called a servant of Jesus Christ. For I waited a long time, in case some visitation might come to us even from your charity. For you are not unaware that, set out in public before all, like the rocks that stand forth into the sea, we receive the fury of the heretical waves, and as they break around us they do not flood what lies behind us. When I say "we," I refer not to human strength, but to the grace of God, who shows His own power in the weakness of men, as the prophet says, speaking in the person of the Lord: "Will you not fear Me, who set the sand as a boundary to the sea?" For by the weakest of all things and the most contemptible, by the sand, the Mighty One bound fast the great and heavy sea. Since, then, our case too is something of this kind, it was fitting that from your charity some of your genuine brethren should constantly be sent to visit us in our distress, and that letters of love should come to us more frequently, both to strengthen our resolve and to set us right wherever we go astray. For we do not deny that we are subject to countless errors, being men and living in the flesh.

But since in the time before this, either because you did not perceive what was fitting, you left undone what was owed to us, most honored brethren, or because you were prepossessed by certain persons into the slanders against us, you did not think us worthy of a loving visitation — behold, now we ourselves take the lead in writing, and we declare that we are ready to strip ourselves bare before you of the charges brought against us; only let those who insult you consent to stand face to face with us before your Reverence. For if we too are convicted, we shall acknowledge our sin; and you, after the proofs, will find pardon with the Lord for withdrawing yourselves from communion with us sinners; and those who have proved the charge will have their reward for having brought to light our hidden wickedness. But if you condemn us before the proofs, we for our part shall have suffered no wrong, except the loss of that possession most precious of all to us, your love; while you, having no power to make us suffer even this, will also be seen to fight against the gospel which says:

"Does our law judge a man unless it first hears him and knows what he does?" But he who pours out his abuse upon us, and yet brings no proof of what he says, will be shown to have fastened an evil name upon himself by the unfitting use of his words. For how else ought we to call the slanderer than by giving him the very name his own conduct earns? Let not, then, the one who reviles us be a "devil" but an accuser; or rather, let him not even receive the name of accuser, but let him be a brother admonishing us in love, and bringing his proof for the sake of correction. And do not you become listeners to abuse, but examiners of proofs; nor let us be left without remedy, our sin remaining unrevealed to us.

For do not let this reasoning take hold of you — that those who dwell on the seaboard are outside the common affliction, and need no help from others; so what need have we of fellowship with others? For the Lord has separated the islands from the mainland by the sea, but He has bound the islanders to the men of the mainland by love. Nothing separates us from one another, brethren, unless of our own choice we submit to separation. We have one Lord, one faith, the same hope. Whether you reckon yourselves the head of the Church universal, the head cannot say to the feet, "I have no need of you"; or whether you rank yourselves in some other order of the Church's members, you cannot say to us who are set in the same body, "We have no need of you." For the hands need one another, the feet support one another, and the eyes have the clearness of their perception only in concert. We, for our part, confess our own weakness and seek your fellowship of spirit. For we know that, even though you are not present in the body, by the help of your prayers you will furnish us great benefit in the most pressing seasons. But for you to use such words — words that not even the nations who do not know God have used — is neither seemly among men nor pleasing to God. Indeed, we hear that those nations, even when they occupy a land sufficient for all their needs, nevertheless, on account of the uncertainty of the future, welcome alliance with one another and pursue intercourse as a thing that holds some gain. But we, who are of those fathers who laid down by law that through small tokens the symbols of communion should be carried about from the ends of the earth to its ends, and that all should be fellow citizens and members of one household with all — we now cut ourselves off from the inhabited world, and are neither ashamed of our isolation, nor count the rending of concord to be a loss; nor do we shudder that the fearful prophecy of our Lord reaches even to us, who said, "Because iniquity shall abound, the love of the many shall grow cold."

Not this, most honored brethren — do not endure this; but for what has passed, encourage us with peaceful letters and loving greetings, soothing as it were by some gentle touch the wound of our heart, which by your past neglect you have made in us. And whether you wish to come to us yourselves and search out our infirmities in person — whether they are really such as you hear, or whether by the additions of falsehood our faults are reported to you as heavier than they are — let this be done; we are ready with open hands to receive your coming, and to set ourselves forth for an exact testing; only let love govern all that is done. Or whether you wish to appoint among yourselves some place where we may come and both pay you the debt of visitation that is owed, and offer to you what trial of ourselves is possible, so as both to heal what has gone before and to leave henceforth no room for slanders — let this too be done. For assuredly, even if we carry about a weak flesh, yet so long as we draw breath we are bound to leave nothing undone of what builds up the churches of Christ.

Do not, then, set at naught this our entreaty; do not bring us to the necessity of declaring our grief even to others. For up to now, you know, brethren, we hide our sorrow within ourselves, ashamed to announce to our fellows who are far from us your estrangement toward us, lest we should grieve them too and bring joy to those who hate us. These things I have written alone for now; but I have sent them with the consent of all the brethren in Cappadocia, who also urged me not to employ any chance person as bearer of the letter, but a man who could supply, by his own understanding which he has from the grace of God, all that we have passed over in the letter, fearing lest we should let our discourse run on into great excess. I mean our most beloved and most reverend brother Peter, my fellow presbyter, whom receive in love and send forward to us in peace, that he may be to us a messenger of good things.
To the Neocaesareans.

For a long time we have kept silence toward one another, most honored and most longed-for brethren, like men who have risen up in anger. And yet who is so deeply embittered and so hard to reconcile with the one who has grieved him that he would prolong the wrath born of hatred over nearly a whole generation of a man's life? Yet this is what may be seen happening in our case, though no just occasion of estrangement exists — none, at least, so far as we ourselves know; but on the contrary, while many great things were present from the beginning to draw us toward the closest friendship and union. The first and greatest is the commandment of the Lord, who said plainly, "By this shall all know that you are My disciples, if you love one another"; and again the Apostle, who clearly sets before us the beauty of love, both where he declares that love is the fulfilling of the law, and where he places the beauty of love above all great things together, in the words: "If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and have all faith so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing. And if I dole out all my goods, and give up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing" — not that any of the things enumerated could ever be performed apart from love, but because the Holy One wished, by this extreme manner of speaking, to bear witness to the surpassing supremacy of the commandment above all things.

Second, that if it is any great thing toward union to have shared the same teachers, the same men are teachers of the mysteries of God both to you and to us, and our spiritual fathers, those who from the beginning laid the foundations of your Church. I mean the great Gregory, and all who in succession to him inherited the throne of your episcopate, one after another rising like so many stars, who trod in the same footsteps, so as to leave to those who wished the discernible signs of a heavenly citizenship. And if the bonds of kinship of the body too are not to be cast aside, but contribute much toward an unbroken union and a fellowship of life, these claims too were ours toward you. For what reason, then, O most venerable of cities — for through you I address the whole city — comes there from you no gentle letter, no friendly voice, but your ears are opened to those who attempt to slander? So that I am bound to groan the more, the more I see their endeavor succeeding; since the work of slander has for its evident leader the one who, well known from many wrongdoings, is characterized above all by this wickedness, so that even his name has become "sin." Yet bear with my frankness: opening both your ears to those who slander us, you receive all things into your souls without examination; and there is no one to sift the false from the true. Who was ever at a loss for wicked charges when he contended alone? Who was ever convicted of lying when the one he maligned was not present? What word is not plausible to its hearers, if the reviler insists that it is indeed so, while the one reviled is neither present nor hears the blasphemies? Does not the very custom of life teach you in these matters, that one who is to be a fair and impartial hearer must not be wholly carried off by the one who spoke first, but must wait also for the defense of the accused, that so, by the setting of both speeches side by side, the truth may be made plain? "Judge righteous judgment" is one of the most necessary of the commandments unto salvation.

And I say these things not because I have forgotten the apostolic words — that he, fleeing human tribunals, reserved his whole life for the scrutiny of that court which cannot be deceived — in which he says: "To me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you, or by man's day." But nevertheless, since false slanders that came before have taken hold of your ears, and our life has been slandered, and our faith concerning God has been slandered — knowing that the slanderer inflicts harm upon three persons at once: for he wrongs the one he maligns, and those to whom his words are addressed, and himself — I would indeed have kept silence about the harm to myself, you may be sure, not from any contempt for the esteem you hold me in (for how could that be, when it is precisely that I may not be deprived of it that I write these things and contend now?), but because I see that of the three who are harmed, I am the one who suffers the least loss. For I am deprived of you, but you are robbed of the truth; and the author of these things separates me from you, but estranges himself from the Lord — because it is not possible to be made God's own out of what is forbidden. It is therefore for your sake rather than my own that I make these words, and to deliver you from a harm not to be borne. For what greater evil could a man suffer than to be deprived of the most precious of all things that are, the truth?

What then do I say, brethren? Not that I am without sin, nor that my life is not full of countless defects. For I know myself, and I do not cease to let fall the tear over my faults, if by any means I might be able to propitiate my God and escape the threatened punishment. But I say that he who passes judgment on us — if he affirms that he has a clean eye, let him pluck the mote from ours; for we confess that we need much care from the healthy. But if he could not say this — and the cleaner he is, the less he will say it, since it is the mark of the perfect not to exalt themselves, else they will surely become liable to the boastfulness of the Pharisee, who, justifying himself, condemned the publican — let him seek the physician along with me, and let him not judge before the time, until the Lord come, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of the hearts. Let him remember too Him who said, "Judge not, that you be not judged," and "Condemn not, that you be not condemned." And altogether, brethren, if our faults are curable, why does he not obey the teacher of the churches who says, "Reprove, rebuke, exhort"? But if our lawlessness is incurable, why does he not stand against us to our face, and, publishing our iniquities, free the churches from any harm we might do? Do not, then, endure the abuse muttered against us under the breath. For this even a single serving-girl from the mill might do, or anyone from the marketplace might display to excess, those whose tongue is whetted for every abuse. But there are bishops: let them be summoned to a hearing. There is a clergy in every parish of God: let the most approved be gathered. Let whoever wishes speak with frankness, that what is done may be a proof and not abuse. Let him bring to view the hidden things of my wickedness; but let him not even then hate, but admonish me as a brother. We sinners deserve rather to be pitied by the blessed and sinless men than to be treated harshly.

But if the fault concerns the faith, let the writing be shown to us; again let an equal and common tribunal be seated. Let the charge be read. Let it be examined whether it seems to be a charge rather through the ignorance of the accuser, or whether the document is condemned by its own nature. For many good things do not seem such to those who do not possess an exact tribunal of judgment in the mind. Since even weights of equal heaviness do not seem equal when the scales do not balance evenly against each other. And honey has already appeared bitter to some, whose sense of taste was corrupted by disease. And again an eye that is not in health has failed to see many things that exist, and has supposed many things that do not exist. And so too in the power of words I often see the same thing happen, when the judge falls short of the writer's competence. For the one who judges words and the one who writes them must set out from nearly the same training. Or rather — the works of agriculture the man who is not a farmer is not able to judge, and the unmusical and musical in rhythms he will not discern who does not possess the science of music; but a judge of words anyone who wishes will straightway be, though he can show neither teacher of his own, nor time in which he learned, nor any understanding at all, small or great, of what pertains to words. But I see that even in the oracles of the Spirit it was not permitted to everyone to apply himself to the examination of what is said, but to him who has the Spirit of discernment, as the Apostle taught us, saying in the divisions of the gifts of grace: "For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another the workings of powers; to another prophecy, to another discernings of spirits." So that if our writings are spiritual, let him who wishes to judge ours show himself to have the gift of the discernment of spiritual things; but if, as he himself reviles, they are from the wisdom of this world, let him show himself experienced in the wisdom of the world, and then we will entrust to him the votes of judgment. And let no one suppose that these things are devised by us to escape the proofs. For I entrust it to you, most beloved brethren, to make for yourselves the examination of the charges brought against us. Are you so slow of understanding that you need a host of advocates to find the truth? But if the matter appears to you, by yourselves, beyond dispute, persuade the wranglers to abandon all contentiousness; and if anything seems to you to have some ambiguity, question us through some mediators able faithfully to convey our case; or, if you think fit, demand of us our proofs in writing. But in every way be earnest by all means not to leave these things unexamined.

And of our faith what plainer proof could there be than that we were reared by a blessed woman, a nurse who came from among you? I mean the renowned Macrina, by whom we were taught the words of the most blessed Gregory, as many as, preserved to her by an unbroken memory, she herself guarded, and with which, while we were yet children, she molded and formed us in the doctrines of piety. And when we ourselves had received the power of reasoning, the faculty being completed in us through age, having traversed much land and sea, if we found any walking in step with the rule of piety that had been handed down, these we both inscribed as fathers and made guides of our souls in the journey toward God. And up to this very hour, by the grace of Him who called us with a holy calling to the knowledge of Himself, we know of no word hostile to sound teaching that we have received into our hearts, nor were our souls ever defiled by the ill-named blasphemy of the Arians. But if at any time we received into communion any who set out from that teacher, who concealed the disease that lay in the depths and spoke pious words, or at least did not contradict what was said by us, we received them thus, not entrusting to ourselves the whole judgment concerning them, but following the verdicts already pronounced about them by our fathers. For I, having received letters from the most blessed father Athanasius, the bishop of Alexandria — which I both hold in my hands and put forward to those who seek them, in which he plainly declared that if anyone from the heresy of the Arians wished to change over, confessing the faith of Nicaea, this man should be received, drawing no distinction against him — and having as partners with me in this doctrine all the bishops of Macedonia and Achaia, thinking it necessary to follow so great a man because of the trustworthiness of those who laid down the rule, and at the same time longing to receive the reward of peacemaking, I enrolled those who confessed this faith in the portion of those in communion.

And it is more just that our affairs be judged not by one or two who do not walk uprightly toward the truth, but by the multitude of bishops throughout the inhabited world who are joined with us by the grace of the Lord. Let there be examined the Pisidians, Lycaonians, Isaurians, both the Phrygias, as much of the Armenians as borders on you, the Macedonians, Achaeans, Illyrians, Gauls, Spaniards, all Italy, the Sicilians, the Africans, the healthy part of Egypt, whatever remnant of Syria — all who both send letters to us and again receive them from us. From these things you may learn, both from the letters brought from there and from those sent back in turn to them, that we are all of one soul, holding the one mind. So that whoever flees fellowship with us, let it not escape your exactness that he tears himself away from the whole Church. Look about you, brethren, with whom your communion is. When you are not received by us, who henceforth will recognize you? Do not bring us to the necessity of taking some grievous counsel concerning our most beloved church. Do not make me speak the things I now hide in my own heart, groaning to myself and lamenting the wickedness of the time — that, with no cause existing, the greatest of the churches, which from of old held toward one another the rank of sisters, now stand divided. Do not make me lament these things to all in communion together. Do not force me to utter words which up to now I keep within myself, held back by the bridle of reason. It is better that we be put out of the way and that the churches be of one mind with one another, than that, through our boyish small-mindedness, so great an evil be brought upon the peoples of God. Ask your fathers, and they will tell you that, even if the parishes seemed divided by the position of their place, yet in mind they were one, and were governed by a single judgment. Continual were the minglings of the people; continual the visits of the clergy; and the shepherds themselves had so great a measure of love toward one another that each of them used the other as teacher and guide in the things that pertain to the Lord.
To Elpidius the Bishop.

Once again we have set in motion our beloved fellow presbyter Meletius, to carry our greetings to your Charity. And although we had quite resolved to spare him on account of the weakness which he has willingly brought upon himself, bringing his flesh into bondage for the gospel of Christ, nevertheless, judging it fitting for ourselves to address you through such men — men able readily to supply from themselves whatever escapes the letter, and to become, as it were, a living letter in place of a written one, both to the writer and to the receiver — and at the same time fulfilling his own longing, which he ever cherishes for your Perfection, ever since he came to know by experience the good things in you, we now entreated him to come to you. Through him we both discharge the debt of visitation, and we urge you to pray for us and for the Church of God, that the Lord may grant us to lead a calm and quiet life, delivered from the malicious assaults of the enemies of the gospel.

And if it appears to your good sense to be fitting and necessary that we should come together with one another, and meet also the rest of our most honored brethren, the bishops who dwell along the seaboard, do you yourself appoint for us both a place and a time at which this shall be, and write to the brethren, so that, leaving each at fixed dates the business in hand, we may be able to do something for the building up of the Church of God, and to remove the griefs that now arise among us toward one another out of suspicions, and to ratify that love without which the Lord Himself has determined for us that the working of every commandment is incomplete.
To Elpidius the Bishop, a Letter of Consolation.

Now most of all do I feel my body's weakness, when I see how greatly it hinders me from the benefit of the soul. For if matters went according to my mind, I should not be addressing you by letters nor through intermediaries, but should myself in person both discharge the debt of love and enjoy at close quarters the spiritual gain. But as it is, I am so situated that I gladly undertake even the journeys about my native land, which we make of necessity in visiting the parishes throughout our country. But may the Lord grant both to you strength and readiness, and to me, along with the eagerness I now have, the power as well, so that, as I entreated you, you may arrange for us the enjoyment of meeting, when you have come to the district of Comana.

But I am afraid for your good order, lest somehow grief over your own household become a hindrance to you. For I have learned that the death of a little child has distressed you. The loss of him is naturally painful to you as a grandfather; but to a man who has already advanced so far in virtue, and who knows the nature of human things both from his experience over time and from spiritual teaching, it follows that the parting from those nearest is not altogether hard to bear. For the Lord does not require the same of us as of ordinary men. They live by custom, but we have for the rule of our conduct the commandment of the Lord, and the examples of the blessed men who went before, whose greatness of mind was displayed especially in critical seasons. Therefore, that you too may leave to life an example of courage and of a true disposition toward the things we hope for, show yourself not bent down by passion, but higher than what grieves, enduring in affliction, rejoicing in hope. Let none of these things, then, become a hindrance to the meeting we hope for. For to infants their age is sufficient for blamelessness; but we are bound to render to the Master the services appointed to us, and to be ready in all things for the stewardship of the churches, for which our Lord has reserved great rewards to the faithful and prudent stewards.
To the Clergy of Neocaesarea.

The harmony of the hatred against us, and the fact that all to the last man follow the leader of the war against us, would have persuaded me to keep silence alike toward all, and to begin neither a friendly letter nor any conversation, but to digest my grief in quiet. But since one must not keep silence in the face of slanders — not that we may avenge ourselves by contradiction, but that we may not allow the falsehood to prosper, nor leave those who have been deceived in their harm — it seemed necessary to me to set this too before all, and to write to your good sense, even though, when lately I wrote in common to the whole presbytery, I was not thought worthy of any answer from you. Do not flatter, O brethren, those who bring evil doctrines upon your souls; nor consent to look on, with your knowledge, while the people of God is overthrown by impious teachings. Sabellius the Libyan and Marcellus the Galatian alone of all men dared both to teach and to write these things, which now among you those who lead the people attempt to bring forward as their own discoveries, stammering with their tongue, and not even capable of leading these sophisms and false reasonings into a plausible construction. These men declaim against us, things speakable and unspeakable, and avoid in every way meeting us. For what reason? Is it not because they suspect the proof against their wicked doctrines? They who have been so shameless toward us as even to fabricate certain dreams against us, slandering our teachings as harmful. But even if they take upon their own heads all the phantoms of the leaf-shedding months, they will not be able to fasten any blasphemy upon us, since there are many in every church who bear witness to the truth.

And if they are asked the cause of this truceless and implacable war, they speak of psalms and a manner of singing that differs from the custom prevailing among you, and such things, for which they ought rather to hide their faces. And we are accused because we have men who are ascetics of piety, who have renounced the world and all the cares of life — which the Lord likens to thorns that do not allow the word to come to fruit. Such men carry about the dying of Jesus in the body, and taking up their own cross they follow God. For my part, I would prize above my whole life that these wrongdoings were mine, and that I had with me men who under my teaching had chosen this ascetic discipline. But now I hear that in Egypt there is such virtue among men; and perhaps some in Palestine too are accomplishing the gospel way of life; and I hear that there are certain perfect and blessed men also in Mesopotamia. But we are children in comparison with the perfect. And if there are also women who have chosen to live according to the gospel, preferring virginity to marriage, bringing into bondage the mind of the flesh, and living in the mourning that is called blessed — they are blessed in their choice, wherever on earth they may be. But among us these things are small, with men still being trained and led toward piety. And if they bring some charge of unseemliness against the life of the women, I do not undertake to make a defense for them; but this I solemnly testify to you, that the things which up to now Satan, the father of lies, has not consented to utter, these the fearless hearts and unbridled mouths are forever speaking without dread. But I wish you to know that we pray to have companies of men and of women whose citizenship is in the heavens, who have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires, who are not anxious about food and clothing, but, being undistracted and well attendant upon the Lord, continue night and day in their prayers; whose mouth does not speak the works of men, but they sing hymns to our God without ceasing, working with their own hands, that they may have to share with those in need.

As to the charge concerning the psalmody, by which especially those who slander us frighten the simpler folk, this I have to say: that the customs now prevailing are in accord and agreement with all the churches of God. For with us the people rise while it is still night and go to the house of prayer, and in labor and affliction and contraction of tears making confession to God, at last they rise from their prayers and pass over to psalmody. And now, divided into two parts, they sing in answer to one another, thereby at once strengthening the study of the oracles, and at the same time securing for themselves attention and the undistractedness of their hearts. Then again, entrusting to one the leading of the chant, the rest sing the response; and so, having spent the night in the variety of psalmody, praying in between, as day now begins to dawn, all in common, as from one mouth and one heart, offer up the psalm of confession to the Lord, each making the words of repentance his own. If for these things, then, you shun us, you will shun the Egyptians, you will shun both the Libyans, the Thebans, the Palestinians, the Arabs, the Phoenicians, the Syrians, and those settled by the Euphrates, and in short all among whom vigils and prayers and common psalmody are held in honor.

But, he says, these things were not so in the time of the great Gregory. No — neither were the litanies which you now practice. And I do not say this to accuse you; for I would wish that all of you lived in tears and continual repentance. For we too do nothing but pray earnestly for our sins; only not with human words, as you do, but with the oracles of the Spirit we propitiate our God. And that these things were not so in the time of the wonderful Gregory, what witnesses have you, who have preserved nothing of his down to now? Gregory did not veil his head at prayer. How should he, the genuine disciple of the Apostle who said, "Every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head," and, "A man ought not to cover his head, being the image and glory of God"? That pure soul, worthy of fellowship with the Holy Spirit, shunned oaths, content with the Yes and the No, because of the command of the Lord who said, "But I say to you, do not swear at all." He could not bear to call his brother a fool, for he feared the threat of the Lord. Wrath and anger and bitterness did not go forth from that mouth. He hated reviling as a thing that does not bring a man into the kingdom of heaven. Envy and arrogance were driven far from that guileless soul. He would not have stood at the altar before being reconciled with his brother. A false and artful word, contrived for the slander of someone, he so abhorred, knowing that falsehood comes from the devil, and that "the Lord will destroy all who speak lies." If none of these things is in you, but you are pure of them all, you are in truth disciples of the disciple of the Lord's commandments. But if not, take care that you are not straining out the gnat, being exact about the sound of the voice in psalmody, while loosening the greatest of the commandments. The necessity of self-defense has brought me to these words, that you may be taught to cast out the beam from your own eyes, and then to remove the motes of others. Yet we forgive everything, even though nothing is unexamined with God. Only let the chief things be sound, and silence your innovations concerning the faith. Do not set aside the hypostases. Do not deny the name of Christ. Do not misinterpret the words of Gregory. But if not, then as long as we breathe and are able to speak, it is impossible for us to keep silence over so great a destruction of souls.
To Eulancius.

You have kept silence a long time, and that too, being a man most fond of talk, who have made it your study and your art always to be saying something and to display yourself through your words. But it seems that Neocaesarea is the cause of your silence toward us. And it seems that, in place of a favor, we receive the boon of not being mentioned among those there — since the memory of us is not a good thing, according to the talk of those who hear it. But you were long ago among those hated for our sake, not among those who endure to hate us for the sake of others. Be then the same man, both writing wherever you may be, and remembering us as is fitting, if you have any care for justice. For it is surely just that those who began with love be repaid in equal measure.
Without Address, by Way of Defense.

You have been allotted a share in the griefs and in the struggles on our behalf. This affords proof of a youthful and vigorous soul. For God, who orders our affairs, provides for those who are able to bear great contests the greater occasions of good repute. And you, then, have set forth your own life as a test of your virtue toward your friends, as the furnace is a test for gold. We pray to God, therefore, that the rest may become better, and that you may remain like yourself, and may not cease to bring such charges as you now brought, alleging the lack of letters against us as a very great injustice. For the complaint is a friend's complaint; and wait patiently while you demand such debts. For I am not so absurd a debtor of friendship.
To the Most Learned Men of Neocaesarea.

In general I had no need at all to publish my purpose to you, nor to tell the reasons why I am now in these parts. For I am not one to seek the limelight, nor is the matter worthy of so many witnesses. But, I suppose, we do not do what we wish, but what those who lead us provoke us to. For my part, to be wholly unknown has been more an object of zeal to me than to be conspicuous is to the lovers of glory. But since, as I hear, the ears of all in your city have been filled with rumors, and there are certain tale-spinners, fabricators of falsehood, hired for this very purpose, who interpret my affairs to you, I did not think I ought to overlook your being instructed by a wicked mind and a foul voice, but to tell myself how my affairs stand. I, both because of my familiarity with this place from childhood (for here I was reared in the house of my own nurse), and because of my long residence here afterwards, when, fleeing the tumults of the city, I came to know this place as suited for the pursuit of philosophy through the quiet of its solitude, spent many years here in succession; and now, because of the brethren who dwell here, having obtained a brief breathing-space from the cares that hold us, I came gladly to this remote spot, not in order to make trouble for others from here, but in order myself to satisfy my own longing.

What need, then, to take refuge in dreams, and to hire dream-interpreters, and to make us the subject of a drunken tale at the public banquets? For my part, even if the slanders were among certain others, I would have put you forward as witnesses of my purpose. And now I ask each of you to recall those old days, when the city was calling us to the care of the young, and an embassy of the chief men among you was present; and after that, how all in a body, thronging about us — what did they not offer? what did they not promise? — yet they were unable to keep us. How then should I, who when called at that time did not obey, now attempt to thrust myself in uninvited? And how should I, who fled from those who praised and admired me, now be pursuing those who slander me? Do not suppose it, good men; our affairs are not so cheaply bought. For no one in his right mind would step aboard a ship without a helmsman, nor would he venture into a church in which the very men who sit at the helm work up the surge and the storm. For whence has the city become full of tumult, when some were fleeing though no one pursued, and others were slipping away though no one came upon them, and oracle-mongers and dream-interpreters were frightening everyone like bogeys? Whence else came these things? Or is it not plain even to a child that it was from the leaders of the multitude? The causes of whose enmity it is not seemly for me to tell, but for you it is very easy to perceive. For when the bitterness and the dissension admit no excess in harshness, while the account given of the cause is utterly insubstantial and ridiculous, then plainly the sickness of the soul is revealed — a sickness that comes upon them at the good fortune of others, but is the proper and chief evil of him who possesses it. To which there is added still another charming feature. For though they are torn and pained in the depths, they are not permitted by shame to utter forth their misfortune. This affliction of their soul is known not only from their conduct toward us, but also from the rest of their life; and if it were unknown, it would be no great loss to the matter. But the truest cause for which they make our company a thing to be shunned, which perhaps escapes the many of you, I will teach. But listen.

A perversion of the faith is being practiced among you, hostile to the apostolic and evangelical doctrines, hostile to the tradition of the truly great Gregory and of those who followed from him down to the blessed Musonius — whose teachings are still ringing in your ears even now, no doubt. For the evil of Sabellius, long ago set in motion but quenched by the tradition of the great Gregory, these men now attempt to renew — they who, from fear of the proofs, fabricate the dreams against us. But do you, leaving the wine-heavy heads — which the vapor rising from the debauch, then surging within, fills with phantoms — bidding them farewell, hear of your harm from us who are awake, and who because of the fear of God are unable to be at rest. Sabellianism is Judaism, brought in under the guise of Christianity into the gospel proclamation. For he who says that one thing of many faces is Father and Son and Holy Spirit, and sets forth one hypostasis of the three, what else does he do but deny the pre-eternal existence of the Only-begotten? And he denies also His dispensational sojourn among men, His descent into Hades, the resurrection, the judgment; he denies also the distinctive operations of the Spirit. But among you now I hear of things ventured even more boldly than by the empty-minded Sabellius. For they assert, so those who have heard them say — your wise men insist and say — that the name of the Only-begotten has not been handed down, but is the name of the adversary; and over this they exult and pride themselves greatly, as over a discovery of their own. For it is said, he claims: "I am come in the name of My Father, and you received Me not; if another shall come in his own name, him you will receive." And because it is said, "Make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit," it is plain, they say, that there is one name. For it is not said "into the names," but "into the name."

These things I wrote to you blushing, because those guilty of them are of our own blood; and I groan over my own soul, because I am compelled, like men boxing against two adversaries, parrying with proofs and beating down the deviations of the argument on either side, to render the proper strength to the truth. For from this quarter the Anomoean tears at us, and from the other, as it seems, Sabellius. But I exhort you not to give heed to these abominable sophisms, which can pervert no one, but to know that the name of Christ, the name that is above every name, is this very thing, that He is called the Son of God; and, according to the word of Peter: "Neither is there any other name under heaven given among men whereby we must be saved." But as to the saying "I am come in the name of My Father," this must be understood — that He says these things because He inscribes the Father as His source and cause. And if it is said, "Going, baptize into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit," it is not on this account to be supposed that one name has been handed down to us. For as he who said "Paul and Silvanus and Timothy" said three names, but bound them together by the conjunction "and," so he who said "the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit," saying three, wove them together with the connective, teaching that to each name its own signification is attached, since names are significant of things. And that the things have their own distinct and self-complete existence, no one who has even a small share of understanding doubts. For of Father and Son and Holy Spirit the nature is the same and the Godhead one; but the names are different, presenting to us defined and complete notions. For it is impossible, unless the mind, dwelling without confusion upon the peculiar properties of each, can fulfill the doxology to Father and Son and Holy Spirit. If, then, they deny that they say these things, or teach thus, what we are striving for has been accomplished. Yet I see that the denial is hard for them, because they have many witnesses of these words. But we do not look at what is past; only let the present be sound. But if they persist in the same things, we must needs cry out your misfortune to other churches also, and cause letters from a greater number of bishops to come to you, breaking down this magnitude of impiety being built up in secret. For either there will be some advancement of our zeal, or at all events the present protestation will free us of the charge before the tribunal.

And already they have laid down these words in writings of their own, which they first sent to the man of God, Bishop Meletius, and, having received from him the fitting answers, like the mothers of monsters who are ashamed at the deformities of nature, so they too, hiding their shameful labor-pains in the fitting darkness, nurse them. And they let down a certain test by letter to our like-minded brother Anthimus, bishop of Tyana, as though Gregory had said in an Exposition of Faith that Father and Son are two in thought but one in hypostasis. But that this was not said doctrinally, but controversially, in the disputation against Aelianus, those who count themselves blessed for the fineness of their wits were unable to perceive. In that disputation there are many errors of the copyists, as we ourselves will show from the very words, if God wills. Then too, persuading the pagan, he did not think it necessary to be precise about the words; but there are places where he even concedes something to the custom of his opponent, so as not to oppose him on the essential points. And so you will find there many expressions which now furnish the heretics their greatest strength — such as "creature" and "thing made" and the like. And many things said about the union with man, those who hear the writings without instruction refer to the discourse concerning the Godhead; of which kind is also this which is bandied about by these men. For one must know well that, just as he who does not confess the commonness of the essence falls into polytheism, so he who does not grant the distinctness of the hypostases is carried away into Judaism. For our mind must, as it were, leaning upon some object and imprinting its clear characteristics, so come to a perception of what is sought. For unless we have conceived the fatherhood, nor reflected on Him to whom this property is marked off, how is it possible to receive the notion of God the Father? For it is not enough to enumerate differences of persons, but one must confess each person to exist in a true hypostasis. Since not even Sabellius declined the unsubstantial fashioning of the persons, saying that the same God, being one in substrate, is transformed to meet the needs that fall out from time to time, and discourses now as Father, now as Son, now as Holy Spirit. This error, long ago quenched, the inventors of this nameless heresy now renew — they who set aside the hypostases and deny the name of the Son of God. Whom, unless they cease speaking unrighteousness against God, one must lament along with the deniers of Christ.

These things we have of necessity set forth to you, that you may guard yourselves against the harms from wicked teachings. For in truth, if one must liken wicked doctrines to deadly drugs, as your dream-interpreters say, these are hemlock and aconite and any other man-slaying drug. These are the poisons of souls — not our words — which the wine-stricken brains cry out, full of phantoms because of their passion. If these men were sober, they ought to know that the gift of prophecy shines forth upon souls that are undefiled and cleansed of every stain. For neither can a dirty mirror receive the reflections of images, nor can a soul preoccupied with the cares of life and darkened by the passions that come from the mind of the flesh receive the illuminations of the Holy Spirit. For not every dream is straightway prophecy, as Zechariah says: "The Lord made a vision, and a winter rain, because they that speak forth spoke labors, and dreamed false dreams." But these men are ignorant also of this — they who, according to Isaiah, dream and love to slumber in bed — that often a working of error is sent upon the sons of disobedience. And there is a lying spirit, which, coming upon the false prophets, deceived Ahab. Knowing these things, they ought not to have been so exalted as to bear witness to prophecy in themselves, who are shown to fall short even of the exactness of Balaam the soothsayer. He, summoned by the king of the Moabites with the greatest of gifts, would not consent to utter a word against the will of God, nor to curse Israel, whom the Lord does not curse. If, then, their visions in sleep run together with the commandments of the Lord, let them be content with the Gospels, which need no help from dreams toward their trustworthiness. But if the Lord left us His own peace, and gave us a new commandment that we love one another, while the dreams suggest fighting and dissension and the abolition of love, let them not give occasion to the devil to mount upon their souls through sleep, nor make their own phantoms more authoritative than the saving teachings.
To Olympius.

Both on reading the letter of your Honor I became more cheerful and more contented than I had been, and on coming to converse with your most beloved sons I seemed to behold you yourself. Finding my soul greatly afflicted, they so disposed it that I forgot the hemlock among you, which the dream-mongers and dream-peddlers, for the favor of those who hired them, carry about against us. As for letters, some I have sent, and others I will give later, if you wish. Only may there be some benefit from them to those who receive them.
To Hilarius.

What do you think I felt, or what was my state of mind, when I came to Dazimon and learned a few days after our arrival that your Eloquence had departed? For not only because of the admiration I have had for you from childhood — having always, from our studies together, set a high value on your conversation — but also because nothing is now so precious as a truth-loving soul that possesses a sound judgment of affairs; which we believe is preserved in you. For of the rest we see the greater part, as at the horse-races, divided, some for these, some for those, and joining in the shout with the factions. But you, being higher than fear and flattery and every ignoble passion, are likely with a healthy eye to behold the truth. Indeed, I perceive that you do not take a careless view of the affairs of the churches, since you even sent us a letter about these matters, as you showed in your recent letter; and who it was that received it to convey it, I would gladly learn, so as to know the one who wronged me. For I have not yet met with any letters of yours to us about these things.

For how much, do you think, would I purchase your conversation, that I might make known to you the things that grieve me — for it brings, as you know, a certain relief to those in pain even to speak out — and that I might receive your answer about the matters in question; not entrusting it to lifeless letters, but myself in person plainly telling each thing and going through it. For living words have a more effective persuasion; and as to being easily attacked and easily caught by slander, they are no longer like the written ones. For nothing now is beyond anyone's daring, since even those to whom we entrusted the greatest things — whom we perceived, when we saw them among men, to be something more than human — these consented to pass off as ours some writings of one person or another, whatever they happened to be, and to slander us on the strength of them to the brotherhoods, so that nothing henceforth is more to be shunned by the devout than our name. For having from the beginning made it my study to be unknown — as I know not who else of those who have observed human weakness has done — now, as though I had chosen the opposite, to make myself known to all men, I am thus everywhere on earth (and I will add, on sea as well) bruited about. For both those who practice the utmost limit of impiety, and bring the godless doctrine of the Unlikeness upon the churches, wage war against me; and those who drive the middle course, as they suppose, and who set out from those same first principles, but, because of what is offensive to the ears of the many, do not allow themselves to follow the consequence of their reasonings, are vexed at us and wash us in their abuse, so far as they are able, and abstain from no plot, even though the Lord has made their undertakings come to nothing. How are these things not grievous? How do they not make my life a thing of pain? I who set down as the one consolation of my evils the weakness of the flesh, by which I am persuaded that I shall not remain long in this wretched life. And of these things let so much suffice.

But you, amid the sufferings of the body, I exhort to be disposed nobly and worthily of the God who has called us; who, if He sees us receiving the present circumstances with thanksgiving, will either remit the things that grieve us, as in the case of Job, or will reward us with the great crowns of endurance in the condition that follows after this our life.
Without Address, to a Pious Man.

May the Lord who afforded me swift succor in my afflictions Himself grant you the succor of that refreshment with which you have refreshed us by the visitation of the present letter, repaying the reward of our humility for the comfort you have given with the true and great gladness of the spirit. For it happened that my soul was somehow ill-disposed, when in a crowded assembly I had observed a certain brutish and altogether irrational sluggishness in the people, and an old and hard-to-correct habit of evil in those who lead them. But when I saw your letter and the treasure of love in it, I recognized that He who orders our affairs had caused to shine upon us, who live in bitterness, a sweet consolation. For this reason I send my answering greeting to your Holiness, beseeching your customary comfort, that you not cease to pray for my pitiable life, lest, sunk in the phantom of this life, I forget the God who raises the poor man from the earth, and, suffering some uplifting of pride, I fall into the judgment of the devil; or, growing slack in my stewardship, be caught sleeping by the Master; or, by harmful works, even striking the conscience of my fellow servants, or being found among the drunken, suffer in the righteous judgment of God the things threatened against the wicked stewards. I beseech you, therefore, in every prayer to ask of God that we be sober in all things, that we may not become a shame and a reproach to the name of Christ in the revealing of the hidden things of our heart on the great day of the appearing of our Savior Jesus Christ.

And know that I am in expectation of being summoned to the camp through the malice of the heretics, on the pretext, forsooth, of peace; and that this bishop here, having heard of it, has earnestly written to us to be present in Mesopotamia, and there, having gathered those of like mind who maintain the affairs of the churches, to set out with them to the emperor. For me, perhaps my very body will not be equal to the journey in winter; and meanwhile the matter has not seemed even necessary, unless you yourself advise it. For I shall await also the counsel of your Godliness, that my purpose may be confirmed. Therefore I beg that what occurs to your Perfection and inspired good sense be made known to us speedily, through one of the earnest brethren.
To Count Terentius.

When we heard that your Excellency had again been forced into the management of public affairs, we were at once troubled (for the truth shall be told), reflecting how contrary it is to your wish, after having once been released from public cares and given leisure to the care of your own soul, to be compelled again to return to the same things. Then, coming to the thought that perhaps the Lord, wishing to grant this one consolation amid the countless griefs which now beset our churches, has ordered that your Dignity should again appear in affairs, we became even more cheerful, as men who were going to meet your Honor at least once more before departing this life.

But again another report took hold of us, that you were residing at Antioch and administering, together with the great authorities, the business in hand. And besides this report, there came to our hearing that the brethren of the party of Paulinus are discoursing with your Uprightness about union with us — I mean us, those of the portion of the man of God, Bishop Meletius. They, I hear, now carry about letters of the Westerners, entrusting to them the episcopate of the church at Antioch, and misrepresenting the most admirable bishop of the true Church of God, Meletius. And I do not wonder at this. For some are wholly ignorant of the affairs here; and others, though they seem to know them, expound them more from contentiousness than from truth. But of those men it is nothing strange either to be ignorant of the truth, or even to conceal the cause for which the most blessed bishop Athanasius came to write to Paulinus. But your Perfection, having with you those able to recount exactly the things that passed between the bishops in the reign of Jovian, we beseech to be fully informed by them. But since we accuse no one, and pray to have love toward all, and especially toward those of the household of the faith, we rejoice with those who have received the letters from Rome. And if those letters bear some grand and great testimony to them, we pray that this may be true and confirmed by the very deeds. Yet not for this reason can we ever persuade ourselves either to ignore Meletius, or to forget the church under him, or to count as small the questions over which the division arose from the beginning, and to suppose them to have little bearing on the aim of piety. For I — not only would I never consent to draw back because some man, having received a letter from men, prides himself on it; but not even if one came from the very heavens, yet did not walk in step with the sound word of the faith, could I count him a partaker with the saints.

For consider, O admirable man, that the falsifiers of the truth, who brought the Arian schism in upon the sound faith of the fathers, put forward no other cause for not accepting the pious doctrine of the fathers than the meaning of the term "of one essence," which they themselves wickedly and for the slander of the whole faith interpret, saying that the Son is called by us "of one essence" according to hypostasis. If we give them any occasion for this, by the bandying about of those who, through simplicity rather than malice, say these things or things like them, nothing prevents us too from giving against ourselves indisputable handles, and from establishing the heresy strongly for those whose one study it is, in their discourses before the church, not to establish their own positions, but to slander ours.

And what could be harder than this slander, and more able to unsettle the many, than if some of us should appear saying that of Father and Son and Holy Spirit there is one hypostasis — even though they should very clearly teach the distinction of the persons? For by the fact that Sabellius anticipated the saying of this same thing — that God is one in hypostasis, but is given different persons by Scripture according to the peculiarity of the need that underlies each occasion: now investing himself with the fatherly utterances, when it is the time for that person; now with those befitting the Son, when He descends to the care of us or to certain other dispensational operations; and now putting on the mask of the Spirit, when the occasion demands the utterances proper to such a person — if, then, among us too some should appear saying that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are one in substrate, while confessing three complete persons, how will they not seem to furnish a clear and indisputable proof of the truth of what is said about us?

And as to the fact that hypostasis and essence are not the same, even the brethren from the West, as I think, hinted at this, when, suspecting the poverty of their own language, they handed over the word "essence" to the Greek tongue, in order that, if there were any difference of meaning, it might be preserved in the clear and unconfused distinction of the terms. But if we too must say in brief what seems to us, we will say this: that the relation which the common has to the particular, this the essence has to the hypostasis. For each of us both partakes of being by the common account of the essence, and is this or that man by the properties belonging to him. So also there the account of the essence is common — such as goodness, or Godhead, or whatever else may be conceived — while the hypostasis is contemplated in the property of fatherhood, or of sonship, or of the sanctifying power. If, then, they say the persons are without hypostasis, the statement has its absurdity at once; but if they grant that they exist in a true hypostasis, as they confess, let them also number them, that both the account of "one essence" may be preserved in the unity of the Godhead, and the recognition of true religion concerning Father and Son and Holy Spirit may be proclaimed in the complete and entire hypostasis of each of the persons named. Nevertheless, of this I wish your Excellency to be persuaded, that both you, and everyone who like you takes thought for the truth and does not dishonor those who contend for piety, ought to await the lead in this union and peace from the leaders of the churches, whom I count as the pillars and bulwark of the truth and of the Church; and I revere them so much the more, the farther they are driven into exile, the separation being brought upon them in place of punishment. I beg you, then, keep yourself for us free of prejudice, that we may have at least you to rest upon, whom God has granted us in all things as a staff and support.
To Dorotheus the Presbyter.

As soon as I obtained an opportunity, I wrote to that most admirable man Count Terentius, considering it less open to suspicion to write to him about the matters before us through strangers, and at the same time wishing that no delay should come to the affair of our most beloved brother Acacius. So I gave the letter to the inspector of the prefects' staff, who was traveling by the public post, charging him also to show the letter first to you. But how it is that no one has reported to your good sense that the road to Rome is in winter wholly impassable, the country between Constantinople and our borders being filled with enemies, I do not know. And if we must use the sea, there will be a time for it — only if the most God-beloved bishop Gregory, the brother, will consent both to the voyage and to the embassy on behalf of such matters. For I neither see those who would go along with him, and I know him to be wholly inexperienced in the affairs of the churches; and to a well-disposed man his company is venerable and of much worth, but to one who is lofty and high-flown, sitting somewhere up aloft, and for this reason unable to hear those who from below speak the truth to him, what benefit could come to the common cause from the conversation of such a man, whose character is a stranger to mean flattery?
To Meletius, Bishop of Antioch.

Many other journeys also have led us away from our native land. For we crossed even as far as Pisidia, in order, with the bishops there, to put in order the affairs concerning the brethren in Isauria. And from there the journey to Pontus succeeded, since Eustathius had sufficiently disturbed Dazimon, and persuaded many there to separate themselves from our church.
