We went even as far as the little dwelling of our brother Peter, which, because it draws near to the region of Neocaesarea, both gave occasion for much disturbance to those there, and procured for us the pretext of much insult. For they were fleeing, though no one pursued, while we were supposed, out of a desire for the praises among them, to be thrusting ourselves in uninvited.

But when we returned, having gathered much sickness from the rains and the despondencies, immediately letters from the East overtook us, signifying that the party of Paulinus had received certain letters from the West — like, as it were, the tokens of some primacy — and that the factious men of that quarter were greatly elated and exulting in the letters, and that they were then putting forward a creed, and on the basis of it were ready to be united to our church. Besides these things, this too was reported to us: that they had won over to their cause that altogether excellent man Terentius; to whom I quickly wrote, restraining him, so far as it was possible for me, from his impulse, and instructing him in their deceit.
CANONICAL LETTER III. To Amphilochius, concerning the Canons.

Having returned from a long journey (for I went as far as Pontus on account of the needs of the churches and to visit my friends), and having brought back my body broken, and being moderately ill in soul, when I took into my hands the letter of your Reverence, I straightway forgot all things, receiving the tokens of the voice that is sweetest of all to me and of the hand most dear. Since, then, I became so glad from your letters, you ought to imagine how great a value I set upon meeting you, which may the Holy One bring about, when it shall be without burden and you yourself shall summon us. For it is not hard for me, if you reach the house at Euphemias, to come together there, both escaping the troubles here and hastening to your unfeigned love. And perhaps the sudden withdrawal of the most God-beloved bishop Gregory makes the journey as far as Nazianzus necessary for me on other grounds as well — a withdrawal which, with what cause it came about, is unknown until now. As for the man about whom I too had spoken to your Perfection, and whom you now hoped to have ready, know that, having fallen into a long illness, and being now afflicted in his very eyes from his old ailment and the sickness that lately befell him, he has remained altogether useless for ordinary activities. And there is no other with us. So that it is better, even if they entrusted the matter to us, that one of those very men be put forward. For one must consider that these are the words of necessity, but that their soul wishes that which they sought from the beginning — that the leader be one of their own. And if there is one of the newly enlightened, whether it seem good to Macedonius or not, let that one be put forward. And you will form him to what is needful, the Lord working with you in all things and supplying the grace for this.

Concerning the clergy the canons have set forth without distinction, ordaining that one punishment be appointed for those who fall, namely, expulsion from the ministry, whether they hold a degree, or persevere in a ministry that is without imposition of hands.

She who has neglected her offspring on the road: if, being able to save it, she despised it, either thinking thereby to conceal her sin, or having used altogether a brutish and inhuman reasoning, let her be judged as for murder. But if she was not able to protect it, and through the desert and the lack of necessities the newborn perished, the mother is to be pardoned.

The widow who is a slave perhaps did not greatly err in choosing a second marriage under the appearance of abduction. So that on this account she ought not to be accused. For it is not the outward forms that are judged, but the purpose. But it is plain that the penalty of bigamy remains upon her.

The distinctions of involuntary homicides I know that I formerly wrote to your Godliness, so far as it was possible for me, and I can say nothing more than those things. But it belongs to your good sense, according to the peculiarity of the circumstance, to extend the penalties, or even to lessen them.

Those who go out against robbers, if they are laymen, are kept from the good of communion; but if they are clergy, they are deposed from their degree. For "everyone," it says, "who takes the sword shall die by the sword."

He who has killed willingly, and afterward repented, shall be without communion in the holy things for twenty years. And the twenty years shall be ordered for him thus: for four years he ought to weep, standing outside the door of the house of prayer, and beseeching the faithful who enter to make prayer on his behalf, confessing his own transgression. After the four years he shall be received among the hearers; and for five years he shall go out with them. For seven years he shall go out, praying with those in the rank of prostration. For four years he shall stand only with the faithful, but shall not partake of the offering. When these are fulfilled, he shall share in the holy things.

He who has killed involuntarily shall be without communion in the holy things for ten years. And the ten years shall be ordered for him thus: for two years he shall weep, for three years he shall continue among the hearers, for four years prostrating, and for one year he shall stand only; and the next year he shall be received into the holy things.
The adulterer shall be without communion in the holy things for fifteen years: weeping for four years, hearing for five, prostrating for four, standing for two without communion.

The fornicator shall be without communion in the holy things for seven years: weeping for two, hearing for two, prostrating for two, and standing only for one; in the eighth year he shall be received into communion. She who has professed virginity and fallen from her promise shall fulfill the time appointed for the sin of adultery in the ordering of her own life. The same also for those who have professed the monastic life and fallen.

The thief, if of his own accord, repenting, he accuse himself, shall be hindered from the communion of the holy things for one year only; but if he be convicted, for two years. And the time shall be divided for him into prostration and standing; and then let him be deemed worthy of communion.
He who commits indecency with males shall be ordered according to the time of one who transgresses in adultery.
He who confesses his impiety with irrational beasts shall be subject to the same time, making confession.
The perjurer shall be without communion for ten years: weeping for two years, hearing for three, prostrating for four, standing only for one year; and then being deemed worthy of communion.
He who confesses sorcery or the use of drugs shall make confession for the time of the murderer, being ordered in the same way, as having convicted himself in that sin.

The violator of tombs shall be without communion for ten years: weeping for two, hearing for three, prostrating for four, standing for one year; and then being received. Incest with a sister shall be confessed for the time of the murderer.
The union of men in marriage of a forbidden kinship, if it be detected as having been formed amid sins, shall receive the penalties of adulterers.

A reader, if before his marriage he has had intercourse with his betrothed, shall, after being suspended for a year, be received to read, remaining without advancement. But if he has had clandestine intercourse without betrothal, he shall be made to cease from his ministry. The same also for a subdeacon.

A deacon who has been defiled in the lips and confesses that he has sinned only to this extent shall be suspended from the liturgy; but he shall be deemed worthy to partake of the holy things with the deacons. The same also for a presbyter. But if anyone be detected having sinned anything more than this, in whatever degree he may be, he shall be deposed.
He who has been conscious of each of the aforesaid sins, and has not confessed, but been convicted, shall himself be under penalty for as long a time as the worker of those evils has been penalized.
He who has given himself over to diviners, or to any such persons, shall himself also be ordered for the time of the murderer.

He who has denied Christ and transgressed the mystery of salvation ought, during the whole time of his life, to weep, and is bound to make confession, being deemed worthy of the holy thing at the time when he departs from life, in faith of the lovingkindness that is from God.

If, however, each of those who have been in the aforewritten sins becomes earnest in confessing, he who has been entrusted by the lovingkindness of God to loose and to bind, if he becomes more lenient, seeing the exceeding measure of the confession of the one who has sinned, in lessening the time of the penalties, will not be worthy of condemnation; since the history in the Scriptures makes known to us that those who confess with greater labor quickly lay hold of the lovingkindness of God.

He who has been defiled with his own sister by father or by mother shall not be permitted to be present in the house of prayer until he departs from the unlawful and impious deed. And after coming to a sense of that fearful sin, let him weep for three years, standing at the door of the houses of prayer, and beseeching the people who enter for prayer, so that each with compassion may make on his behalf earnest supplications to the Lord. After this let him be admitted to hearing alone for another three years; and hearing the Scriptures and the teaching, let him be put out, and not be deemed worthy of prayer. Then, if with tears he has sought it and fallen down before the Lord with contrition of heart and strong humility, let prostration be granted to him for another three years. And so, when he has displayed worthy fruits of repentance, in the tenth year let him be received into the prayer of the faithful without the offering; and after standing two years with the faithful at the prayer, let him then at last be deemed worthy of the communion of the good thing.
The same rule also concerning those who take their own daughters-in-law.

He, however, who leaves the wife lawfully joined to him and takes another is subject, according to the sentence of the Lord, to the judgment of adultery. And it has been ordained by our fathers that such persons weep for one year, hear for two years, prostrate for three years, and in the seventh stand with the faithful; and so be deemed worthy of the offering, if with tears they repent.
And let the same rule prevail also concerning those who take two sisters into cohabitation, even if at different times.
Those who are mad after their own stepmothers are subject to the same canon as those who are mad after their own sisters.

Polygamy the fathers passed over in silence, as a brutish thing and altogether foreign to the race of men. But to us it appears that the sin is something more than fornication. Therefore it is reasonable that such persons be subjected to the canons: namely, that after weeping for one year and prostrating for three, they be thus received.

And since many in the incursion of the barbarians transgressed their faith in God, performing pagan oaths, and tasting certain unlawful things offered to them among the magical idols, let these be ordered according to the canons already set forth by our fathers. For those who endured a harsh necessity from tortures, and not bearing the pains, were dragged toward denial, shall be unreceived for three years, and shall hear for two; and after prostrating for three, they shall be thus received into communion. But those who without great necessity betrayed their faith in God, and touched the table of demons, and swore Greek oaths, shall be cast out for three years, and shall hear for one; and after praying in prostration for three years, and standing for another three with the faithful in the prayer, they shall be thus received into the communion of the good thing.

And concerning those who have perjured themselves: if from force and necessity they transgressed their oaths, they are subject to lighter penalties, so as to be received after six years; but if without necessity they betrayed their own faith, after weeping for two years, and hearing for two, and praying in prostration for five, and being admitted for another two years to the communion of prayer without the offering, then at last, having displayed, that is, a notable repentance, they shall be restored to the communion of the body of Christ.

Those who practice divination and follow the customs of the nations, or bring certain persons into their own houses for the discovery of drugs and for purification, let them fall under the canon of six years: weeping for one year, hearing for one year, and prostrating for three years, and standing one year with the faithful, let them be thus received.

And all these things we write so that the fruits of repentance may be tested. For we do not judge such things wholly by the time, but we attend to the manner of the repentance. But if they are hard to draw away from their own habits, and wish to serve the pleasures of the flesh rather than the Lord, and do not accept the life according to the gospel, there is no common ground between us and them. For we, among a disobedient and gainsaying people, have been taught to hear that "in saving, save your own soul." Let us not, then, consent to perish together with such men; but, fearing the heavy judgment, and having before our eyes the fearful day of the Lord's recompense, let us not be willing to perish together for the sins of others. For if the fearful things of the Lord have not instructed us, nor have such great blows brought us to perception — that because of our lawlessness the Lord abandoned us and gave us into the hands of the barbarians, and the people was led away captive into the enemies' land and given over to dispersion, because those who bear the name of Christ dared these things; if they have not known, nor understood, that for these things the wrath of God has come upon us — what common ground have we with these men? But we ought to bear witness to them, both night and day, both publicly and privately; yet let us not consent to be led away with them in their wickednesses, praying above all to gain them and to deliver them from the snare of the evil one; but if we cannot do this, let us be earnest at least to save our own souls from eternal condemnation.
To Amphilochius, Bishop of Iconium.

The business for which brother Aelianus came he settled by himself, needing no help from us; but to us he gave a double favor, both by bringing letters of your Godliness and by furnishing us an occasion for writing to you. We greet, then, through him your true and inimitable love; and we beseech you to pray for us, who now, if ever, stand in need of the help that comes from your prayers. For my body, broken by the journey to Pontus, is held by sickness past bearing. And there is this too which I have long wished to make known to your good sense (not that, hindered by some prior cause, I forgot it); but now I remind you of it, that you would deign to send an earnest man into Lycia, to inspect who they are that hold the right faith. For perhaps they ought not to be overlooked, if what one of the devout men who came to us from there recounted is true: that, being altogether estranged from the Asian way of thinking, they consent to enroll us as their fellows in communion. And if anyone is going to go there, let him seek out at Corydalla Alexander, a bishop from among the monks; and at Limyra Diotimus; and at Myra the presbyters Tatianus and Polemo and Macarius; at Patara the bishop Eudemus; at Telmessus the bishop Hilarius; at Phellus the bishop Lollianus.

These, and yet more, someone made known to us as sound concerning the faith; and I had much thanks to God, if any at all in the Asian region are outside the harm of the heretics. If, then, it be possible, let us for the present inspect them without letters; and being persuaded, we will thereafter send a letter, and be earnest to summon one of them to a meeting with us. And may all things be in season concerning the church of Iconium, most beloved to you. We greet, through you, all the honored clergy and those who are with your Godliness.
To the Clergy of Samosata.

The Lord, who defines all things for us by measure and weight, and who brings upon us trials that do not exceed our strength, but proves through circumstance the contenders for piety, and does not allow them to be tried beyond what they can endure, and who gives the cup of tears in measure to those who ought to be taught whether in their afflictions they keep their thankfulness toward God — He has especially in the stewardship of your affairs made manifest His own lovingkindness, not permitting the persecution from the enemies to be brought upon you of such a kind as to be able to overturn or unsettle any from the faith in Christ. For having yoked you with light and easily-vanquished adversaries, in the victory over them He has prepared for you the prize of endurance. But the common enemy of our life, who by his own devices fights against the goodness of God, when he saw you despising, like a strong wall, the assault from without, has devised, as I hear, that there should arise among you yourselves certain griefs and small-mindednesses toward one another; which at the first are small and easily cured, but as time goes on, increasing through contentiousness, naturally fall away into what is altogether incurable. Therefore I have set out to entreat you through this letter. If it were possible, I myself would have come and supplicated you in person; but since the times do not permit this, we hold out this letter to you in place of a suppliant's olive-branch, that, out of reverence for our entreaties, you may put away all your contentiousness toward one another, and quickly send me the good news that you have forgiven one another your grievances.

For this I wish your good sense to know: that he is great with God who has humbly submitted himself to his neighbor and without shame taken upon himself the charges, even though they are not true, in order to grant the great benefit of peace to the Church of God. Let there be, then, among you a good rivalry, who shall first be deemed worthy to be called a son of God, having won for himself this dignity through peacemaking. The most God-beloved bishop has written to you what is fitting, and will write again what falls to him. But we too — because it has been granted us still to be nearer to you — cannot neglect your affairs. Hence, when the most reverend brother Theodore the subdeacon came and said that the church was in grief and disturbance, being sorely crushed and stricken in heart with deep pain, we could not bear to be silent; but we have entreated you, casting away all pleading of your rights against one another, to accomplish peace, that you may neither give pleasure to the adversaries, nor betray the boast of the Church, which is now noised abroad into all the inhabited world — that all of you, as ordered by one soul and heart, so pass your life in one body. All the people of God, both those in dignities and civic powers and the whole fullness of the clergy, we greet through your Reverence, and we beseech them to remain like themselves. For we seek no addition, since they have anticipated all excess by the display of their good works and shut it out.
To Those in Beroea.

The Lord has given a great consolation to those who are deprived of meeting face to face, namely, converse through a letter, by which one may learn not the bodily form, but the very disposition of the soul itself. Hence now too, having received the letter of your Reverence, we both recognized you at once, and took up the love of you into our hearts, not needing long time to build up acquaintance in us. For from the very mind laid up in the letter we were kindled to a fondness for the beauty of your soul. For besides the things written, being of such a kind, the fitness of the brethren who mediated showed us your affairs still more clearly. For our most beloved and most reverend fellow presbyter Acacius, recounting more than what was written, and bringing before our eyes your daily contest and your vigorous stand on behalf of piety, wrought in us so great an admiration, and roused so great a longing for the enjoyment of the good things in you, that we pray to the Lord that there may at some time be an opportunity to know your affairs also through our own experience. For he reported to us not only the exactness of you who have been entrusted with the ministry of the altar, but also the harmony of the whole people, and the nobility of character of those who lead the city and govern it, and the genuineness of their disposition toward God, so that we counted blessed the church filled out of such men, and pray that now still more there be given to you spiritual calm, that the things you have displayed in this time of contest you may in the time of rest reap the enjoyment of. For somehow the things difficult in the experience naturally bring pleasure to those who remember them. But for the present we beg you not to grow weary, nor to give up before the continuance of the afflictions. For the crowns are near, and near is the succor of the Lord. Do not pour away what you have labored for in advance; do not render useless the toil that is noised abroad through all the inhabited world. Short-lived are the conditions of human affairs: "All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withered, and the flower fell away; but the word of the Lord abides forever."

Holding fast the abiding commandment, let us despise the passing phantom. Many churches has your example set upright. Much reward, in secret, you have gathered for yourselves, by which you have summoned the more inexperienced to the like zeal. Rich is the rewarder, able to grant you the prizes worthy of your contests.
To Those in Beroea.

We came to know you beforehand, most beloved, from your far-noised reverence and from the crown of your confession in Christ. And perhaps one of you might say: And who is it that has carried these things abroad to a distant land? The Lord Himself, who, setting those who are devout toward Him, after the manner of a lamp upon the lampstand, makes them shine over all the inhabited world. Or is it not the prize of victory that is wont to proclaim the champions of the contests, and the contrivance of the work that proclaims the engineers? But if for these and such things the memory remains unforgotten, those who are devout toward Christ — concerning whom the Lord Himself says, "Those who glorify Me I will glorify" — how will He not make them known and conspicuous to all, joining the brightness of their flashing radiance to the rays of the sun?

But again you have implanted in us a greater longing for you by deeming us worthy of a letter, and a letter of such a kind, in which, besides your former wrestlings on behalf of piety, you have lavishly poured out a rich and more vigorous steadfastness of soul on behalf of the true faith. In which we rejoice with you, and join in praying that the God of all — whose is the contest, and whose the arena, and through whom are the crowns — may work in you readiness, may furnish strength of soul, and may bring your work to perfect good repute in His sight.
To the Chalcidians.

The letter of your Reverence, appearing in a time of affliction, became to us such as often comes to contending horses, when in the steady noonday, gasping with violent breath as they draw in the dust in the midst of the course, water is poured upon their mouths. For we drew breath again from the continuance of the trials, and at once we were strengthened by your words, and by the memory of your contests we became more vigorous for bearing without yielding the contest that is set before us. For the conflagration, which has fed upon much of the East, is now creeping over ours as well, and, having burned all around, strives contentiously to lay hold even of the churches in Cappadocia, which until now the smoke from the neighborhood moved to tears. Henceforth, then, it hastens to lay hold even of us — which may the Lord turn back by the breath of His mouth, and cut through the flame of this wicked fire. For who is so cowardly and unmanly, or so untrained for the labors of the athlete, as not to be strengthened for the contest by your cheering cries, and to pray to be proclaimed a wearer of the crown along with you? For you stripped first in the arena of piety, and beat off many trials of heretical wrestlings, and endured the great burning heat of the trials — both you who are the chief men of the church, to whom the service of the altar has been entrusted, and the individuals of the people, and the more powerful. For this above all is admirable in you and worthy of all acceptance, that you are all one in the Lord, some leading toward the good, others following with one accord. Therefore you are also stronger than the assault of the adversaries, giving from no member any handle to those who contend against you.

For this reason we pray night and day to the King of the Ages, that He guard the people in the soundness of the faith, and guard for him the clergy, like a head set unimpaired upon the height, and furnishing of itself forethought to the members of the body beneath. For when the eyes do their proper work, the labors of the hands are skilled, the movements of the feet are without stumbling, and no part of the body is deprived of the fitting providence. Wherefore we beg you, what you do and will do, to hold fast to one another, and that you who have been entrusted with the care of souls should hold together the individuals, and cherish them as beloved children, while the people preserve toward you the reverence and honor owed to fathers, so that in the good order of the church both your strength may be preserved, and the firmness of the faith in Christ, and the name of God may be glorified, and the beauty of love may abound and multiply. And may we, hearing of it, rejoice at your advancement according to God; and if we are still bidden to sojourn in this world through the flesh, may we see you at some time in the peace of God; but if we are bidden henceforth to depart from this life, may we see you in the splendor of the saints, crowned among those who are of good repute through endurance and every display of good works.
To Eustathius of Sebaste.

"There is a time to be silent, and a time to speak," says the word of Ecclesiastes. And so now too, since the time of silence has been sufficient, it is at last seasonable to open the mouth for the disclosure of the truth about the things that are not known. For the great Job too bore his misfortunes a long time in silence, displaying his courage in this very thing, by holding out under the most grievous sufferings; but when he had sufficiently contended in silence, and had continued, holding down the pain in the depth of his heart, then opening his mouth he uttered those things which all know. And to us, then, this third year of silence made enviable the boast of the prophet who says, "I became as a man that hears not, and that has no reproofs in his mouth." Therefore we shut up in the depth of our heart the pain that came upon us from the slander. For in truth "slander humbles a man, and slander harasses the poor." If, then, so great is the evil from slander, that it brings down even the perfect (for this the word hints at through the title "man") from his height, and the poor too — that is, the one who is deficient in the great doctrines (as also seems good to the prophet when he says, "Perhaps they are poor; therefore they will not hear. I will go to the great men" — calling "poor" those who are deficient in understanding; and here, plainly, those who are not yet perfected in the inner man, nor have advanced to the perfect measure of stature, these the proverb says are tossed about and shaken) — nevertheless I thought I ought to bear the painful things in silence, awaiting some correction through the very deeds. For I supposed that those things were said against us not from any malice, but from ignorance of the truth.

But since I see the enmity advancing together with time, and that they neither repent of what was spoken from the beginning, nor take any thought how they might heal the past, but work it out further, and are marshaled toward the aim they set up from the beginning, contriving to injure our life and to stain our reputation among the brethren, no longer does the safety of silence appear to me. But there came upon me the word of Isaiah, who says, "I have kept silence; shall I also always keep silence and forbear? I have endured like a woman in travail." And may it be granted to us both to receive the reward for the silence, and to take some power for the proofs, so that, having reproved, we may dry up this bitter torrent of the false speech that has flowed against us, so that we too may say, "Our soul has passed through the torrent"; and the words, "If the Lord had not been among us, when men rose up against us, then they had swallowed us up alive, then the water had drowned us."

I, having spent much time on vanity, and having wasted nearly all my youth in the vain labor I had in occupying myself with the acquisition of the learning of the wisdom that has been made foolish by God, when at last, as though rising up from a deep sleep, I looked toward the wonderful light of the truth of the gospel, and beheld the uselessness of the wisdom of the rulers of this age that are being brought to nothing — having greatly bewailed my pitiable life, I prayed that a guiding hand might be given me toward the introduction to the doctrines of piety. And above all it was my care to make some correction of my character, which had been perverted for a long time by association with the worthless. And so, having read the Gospel, and having seen there a very great occasion toward perfection in the selling of one's possessions, and the sharing with the needy among the brethren, and altogether the having no anxious thought for this life, and the turning of the soul by no sympathy toward the things here, I prayed to find some one of the brethren who had chosen this way of life, so as to pass over with him this brief surge of life.

And indeed I found many in Alexandria, and many throughout the rest of Egypt, and others in Palestine, and in Coele-Syria and in Mesopotamia; whose self-control in their manner of living I admired, and admired their steadfastness in labors; I was astonished at their vigor in prayers, how they mastered sleep, bent down by no natural necessity, ever preserving the mind of the soul lofty and unenslaved, in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, not turning toward the body, nor consenting to spend any anxious thought upon it, but as though passing their life in a flesh that was another's, they showed by deed what it is to sojourn among the things here, and what it is to have one's citizenship in heaven. Having admired these things, and counted blessed the life of those men, because they show by deed that they carry about the dying of Jesus in the body, I prayed myself also, so far as it was attainable for me, to be an emulator of those men.

For this reason, then, having seen certain men in my own country attempting to emulate those men, I thought I had found some help toward my own salvation, and I made the things seen a proof of the things unseen. Since, then, the things in secret of each of us are uncertain, I considered the lowliness of clothing a sufficient indication of lowliness of mind, and the coarse cloak was enough for my full conviction, and the girdle, and the sandals of untanned leather. And though many drew me away from association with them, I would not endure it, seeing them prefer the steadfast life to the life of enjoyment; and because of the strangeness of their conduct I was jealously attached to them. Hence neither did I admit the slanders concerning their doctrines, although many affirmed that they did not hold right opinions about God, but, having been disciples of the leader of the present heresy, were secretly sowing his teachings; of which, since I never became a direct hearer, I considered those who reported them to be slanderers. But when at last I was called to the leadership of the church, the guards and watchers of my life given to me, forsooth, under the pretense of help and loving fellowship — I pass them over in silence, lest I should seem either, by saying unbelievable things, to slander myself, or, by being believed, to put into those who believe an occasion of misanthropy. This very nearly happened to me too, had not the compassions of God quickly forestalled me. For I nearly fell into suspicion of all men, considering nothing in anyone to be trustworthy, having been stricken in soul by the treacherous wounds. But nevertheless there seemed for a while to be some appearance of my association with them. And there were assaults upon us concerning doctrines, once and twice; and we seemed not to be at variance, having come to agreement. But when they found us uttering the same words concerning the faith in God which throughout all the time they had heard from us. For even if our other things are worthy of groans, yet this one thing I dare to boast in the Lord, that I never held mistaken opinions about God, or, thinking otherwise, learned differently afterward. But the notion of God which I received from childhood from my blessed mother and my grandmother Macrina, this I held in myself, grown greater; for I did not take up one thing after another in the completion of my reason, but I brought to perfection the principles handed down to me by them. For just as the seed, growing, becomes greater from small, but is the same in itself, not changed in kind, but perfected by growth, so I reckon that the same reasoning has grown in me through advancement, and that the present one has not come to be in place of the one that existed from the beginning. So let them search their own conscience, and let them consider the tribunal of Christ, whether they ever heard from us anything other than what we now say — those who now have noised us abroad for wrong belief, and, by the denunciatory letters which they composed against us, have made every ear ring. Hence we too have come to the necessity of this defense.

For we are accused of blasphemy against God, though we can be convicted neither from any writing which we ourselves first put forth concerning the faith, nor from words, as many as we have always, without writing, by mouth, openly discoursed in the churches of God. But neither has any witness been found who says he heard from us any of the impious things uttered in a corner. Whence then are we judged, if we neither write impiously, nor declaim harmfully, nor in our conversations at home pervert those who meet us? O the strange drama! "So-and-so," he says, "in Syria wrote certain things not piously; and you wrote to him twenty years ago and more. Therefore you are a partner of the man, and let his accusations become yours too." But, O man, friend of truth, you who have been taught that falsehood is the offspring of the devil, how were you persuaded that that letter was mine? For you neither sent, nor inquired, nor were taught by me, who am able to tell you the truth. And even if the letter is mine, whence is it plain that this writing now fallen into your hands is contemporary with my letter? Who told you that the composition is twenty years old? Whence is it plain that the composition is that man's, to whom my letter too was sent? And even if he is the writer, and I wrote to him, and the time is one of both my letter and the composition, that I received it in my mind and have within me that opinion — what is the proof?

Ask yourself: how often did you visit us at the monastery on the Iris river, when the most God-beloved brother Gregory was present with me, pursuing the same aim of life as I? Did you hear anything of the kind? Or did you get an impression, small or great? How many days at the village on the opposite bank, with my mother, where, living together as friends, words were stirred between us both by night and by day? Were we found to have anything kindred in our minds? And when we visited the blessed Silvanus at the same time, did not the road hold our words about these things? And at Eusinoe, when, about to set out with several bishops to Lampsacus, you summoned me, were not the words about the faith? Were not your shorthand-writers present all the time, as I dictated the things against the heresy? Were not the most genuine of your disciples present with me all the time? Did I not, while visiting the brotherhoods, and spending the nights with them in prayers, speaking and hearing always the things about God without contention, furnish exact proofs of my own thought? How then has the experience of so long a time appeared inferior to so rotten and feeble a suspicion? And what witness ought there to be of my disposition before you? The things spoken by us at Chalcedon concerning the faith, the things at Heraclea many times, the things earlier at Caesarea in the suburb — are they not all in harmony from us? Are they not all agreeing with one another? Except, as I said, that some growth is observed in what is said, through advancement — which is not a change from worse to better, but a filling out of what was lacking by the addition of knowledge. And how do you not consider this too, that "a father shall not bear the sin of a son, nor a son bear the sin of a father, but each shall die in his own sin"? But to me the one slandered by you is neither father nor son. For he has become neither my teacher nor my disciple. But if the sins of parents are to become charges against the children, far more justly should the things of Arius be laid against his disciples; and if anyone begot Aetius the heretic, the charges of the child should mount to the head of the father. But if it is not just for anyone to be accused on their account, far more justly surely should we not undergo accounting for things in no way belonging to us — if indeed they sinned at all, if anything worthy of condemnation has been written by them. For I am to be pardoned for disbelieving the things said against them, since the experience against me establishes the readiness of the accusers for slander.

For even if, deceived, and thinking me a partner of the opinion of those who wrote those words of Sabellius which they themselves bandy about, they came to the slander against me — not even thus were they worthy of pardon, casting before clear proofs straightway with their blasphemies, and wounding those who had done no wrong — not to say also those bound to them in the closest friendship — and the fact that they have false opinions within them is a proof that they are not led by the Holy Spirit. For one who is going to cut himself off from the friendship of a brother must take much thought, and pass many sleepless nights, and with many tears seek out the truth from God. For if the rulers of this world, when they are about to condemn one of the malefactors to death, draw aside the curtains, and call the most experienced for the consideration of the matters at hand, and spend much time, now looking at the severity of the law, now shamed by the fellowship of nature, and after many groans and laments over the necessity, become public before all in serving the law under necessity, not bringing in the condemnation according to their own pleasure — how much more must one consider as worthy of greater earnestness and care and the counsel of many, the one who is going to break off from the friendship of brethren, a friendship confirmed over much time? But there is one letter, and that itself doubtful. For they could not say that they recognized it from the tokens of the signature, since it was not the one first written but the one transcribed that came into their hands. From one letter, then, and that an old one. For it is twenty years up to the present time since anything was written to that man. And in the time between I have no such witness of my own purpose and life as those who now stand over me as accusers.

But the letter is not the cause of the separation; the ground of the division is another, which I am ashamed to tell, and would have kept silent the whole time, had not the things now done made the disclosure of their whole purpose necessary for me, because of the benefit of the many. The good men supposed that fellowship with us was a hindrance to them toward the assumption of power. And since they were anticipated by a certain signature of the faith, which we had held out to them — not that we ourselves disbelieved their mind (for I confess it), but wishing to heal the suspicions about them which many of our like-minded brethren had — in order that nothing from that confession should seem to meet them as a hindrance toward being received by those now in power, they renounced fellowship with us; and this letter was devised as the ground of the rupture. And the clearest sign of what is said is this: that, having proscribed us, and having composed the censures they wished against us, before sending them to us, they sent the letters around everywhere. For seven days before it came into my hands, the letter appeared among others, who, receiving it from some, were going to pass it on to others. For they devised thus to hand it from one to one, that the distribution might be swift for them throughout the whole country. And these things were said even then by those who reported their affairs to us most clearly; but we decided to keep silence, until He who reveals the deep things should publish their affairs by the clearest and most indisputable proofs.
To Genethlius the Presbyter.

I received the letter of your Reverence, and I praised the title which you aptly gave to the book composed by them, calling it a "bill of divorcement." What defense those who composed it (in order to stand away from our love) have prepared for it at the tribunal of Christ that cannot be deceived, I am unable to conceive. For having set forth an accusation against us, and run us down vehemently, and recounted the things they wished, not such as the truth holds — fashioning for themselves much humility, and laying upon us a mass of arrogance, as though we had not received those sent from them — all false, or at least the greater part of them, that I may not speak too dangerously — persuading men, and not God, and seeking to please men, and not God, with whom nothing is preferable to the truth, thus they composed it. Then they appended to the letters against us heretical words, hiding the author of the impiety, in order that the many and simpler folk, from the accusation set first against us, might suppose the appended matter to be ours, because by those who artfully slander us the name of the father of the wicked doctrines is passed over in silence, and there is left to the suspicion of the more guileless that we are the ones who either conceived or wrote these things. Knowing these things, then, we beg you both not to be disturbed yourselves, and to silence the tumults of those who are shaken; even though we know that our defense is hard to accept, because of the fact that the wicked blasphemies against us have been prepossessed by persons of credit.

As to the fact, then, that the things bandied about as ours are not ours, I think that, even though the anger against us greatly darkens their reasonings against perceiving what is profitable, nevertheless, if they were asked by you yourselves, they would not come to such a degree of hardness as to dare to utter the falsehood with their own mouth and say that the writings are mine. But if they are not mine, why am I judged for what is another's? But they will say that I am a partner of Apollinaris, and that I have the perversion of such doctrines within me. Let the proofs be demanded of them. For if they know how to search out the heart of a man, let them confess this, and then know their truthfulness about everything; but if from things visible and plain to all they convict my fellowship, let them show either canonical letters sent from me to him, or from him to me, or the intercourse of the clergy with us, or whether we ever received any of them into the fellowship of prayer. But if they bring forward a letter written to him some twenty-five years ago, from a layman to a layman, and not even this as written by me, but altered — by whom, God knows — recognize from this very thing the injustice, that no one in the episcopate is accused if he wrote anything indifferently in the lay life without careful observance, and this too not concerning the faith, but a bare letter bearing a friendly greeting. And perhaps those men too appear to have written to both Greeks and Jews and yet have no charge against them. For up to today no one has been judged on such a matter as that for which we are condemned by those who strain out the gnats. That we neither wrote those things, nor composed them, but even anathematize those who hold that wicked opinion of the confusion of the hypostases, in which the most impious heresy of Sabellius was renewed — this, then, is known to God who knows the hearts, and known too to all the brotherhood which has come to experience of our lowliness. And let those very men, who now are our vehement accusers, search their own conscience, and they will know that from childhood we have been far from such doctrines.

But what our opinion is, if anyone seeks it out, he will know from the very document on which their signature is in their own hand. Which they, wishing to set aside, hide their own change of mind under the slander of us. For they do not confess that they repented of signing the book given to them by us; but they bring against us charges of impiety, thinking it is not known that their withdrawal from us is a pretext, but that in truth they have withdrawn from the faith which, having often confessed in writing before many, they at last received also when given by us, and signed — things which all may read, and from the very writings learn the truth. And their purpose will be made known, if anyone, after the signature which they gave to us, reads the creed which they gave to Gelasius, and knows how great the difference of that confession is from this. Those, then, who so easily turn to the opposite, let them not search out the motes of others, but cast out the beam in their own eye.

And more fully, in another letter, we both make our defense and instruct concerning all things, which will fully satisfy those who seek the more. But you, for the present, having received these letters of ours, put away all grief, and ratify your love toward us, for the sake of which I strongly hold fast to union with you. And it is the greatest grief to us, and an inconsolable pain to our heart, if the slanders against us so prevail with you as to cool your love and estrange us from one another. Farewell.
To Demosthenes, as from the Community.

We always have much thanks to God, and to the emperors who care for us, whenever at any time we see the government of our country entrusted to a man who is first a Christian, then upright in character, and an exact keeper of the laws by which we order human affairs. And especially on the occasion of your visit have we acknowledged this favor to God and to the God-loving emperor. But perceiving that certain of the enemies of peace were going to trouble your august courts against us, we expected to be summoned by your Magnanimity, so as to be taught the truth from us; if indeed your great prudence would consent to make the examinations of ecclesiastical matters your own concern. But since the court overlooked us, while your authority, moved by the revilings of Philochares, ordered that our brother and fellow minister Gregory be carried off — and he obeyed the order (for how should he not?), but, being held by a pleuritic affection, and at the same time, from the chill that came upon him, the sickness of the kidneys having risen up as usual, he was compelled, being inexorably held by the soldiers, for the care of his body and the relief of his unbearable pains, to be removed to a place that had quiet — for this reason we have all come to supplicate your Greatness, not to be at all displeased at the postponement of the meeting; for neither did any of the public affairs fare the worse from our delay, nor was any of the ecclesiastical matters harmed on this account.

But if the matter concerns money, as though it had been embezzled, his own treasurers of the sacred funds are ready to give account to whoever wishes, and to show the slander of those who have ventured against your exact hearing; for it is easy for them, from the very writings of the blessed bishop, to make the truth plain to those who seek it. But if there is anything else, of a canonical kind, that needs examination, and your Magnanimity consents to undertake the hearing and the judgment of this too, we all have need of it; because if anything has been left undone of the canonical requirements, those who ordained him are responsible, not he who was forced by every necessity to undertake the ministry.

So that we supplicate you to preserve for us the hearing in our own country, and not to drag us into exile, nor to bring us to the necessity of meeting with bishops from whom we have not yet settled the matters concerning the ecclesiastical questions. And at the same time we beg you to spare our old age and our weakness. For you will know by the experience itself, if God wills, that nothing small or great has been omitted of the canonical requirements in the establishment of the bishop. We pray, then, that under your government both concord and peace toward our brethren may be brought about; for, this not yet having come to pass, even the matter of meeting is grievous to us, because many of the simpler folk are harmed in our division from one another.
To the ascetics under his charge.

The holy God is able to grant us also the joy that comes from meeting in person, since we long both to see you always and to hear how you fare; for in nothing else do we find rest for our souls than in your progress and in your perfection through the commandments of Christ. But as long as this is not granted to us, we count it necessary to visit you through brothers who are most genuine and who fear the Lord, and to converse with your love by letter. For this very reason we have sent our most reverent and most genuine brother and fellow-worker in the Gospel, Meletius, my fellow-presbyter, who will set before you the longing we have for you and the care we feel for your souls; for night and day we beseech the Lord on behalf of your good standing, that we too may have boldness on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ through your salvation, and that you may shine out in the splendour of the saints, when your work has been tested by the righteous judgement of God.

At the same time the hardship of this present season fills us with much anxiety, a season in which all the churches have been shaken and all souls are being sifted. For certain men have opened their mouths without restraint against their fellow-servants. Falsehood is spoken without fear; the truth is kept concealed. Those who are accused are condemned without trial, while those who accuse are believed without examination. Hence I too, hearing that many letters are being circulated against me, branding us and pillorying us and accusing us on matters for which we have our defence ready at the tribunal of truth, was at first inclined to keep silent—as indeed I did; for this is now the third year in which, struck by these slanders, I bear the lashes of the accusation, content that I have the Lord, who knows what is hidden, as witness of the calumny. But since I see that many have already taken our silence as a confirmation of the slanders, and have supposed that we keep silent not out of forbearance but because we have no mouth to open in defence of the truth, for this reason I have undertaken to write to you, urging your love in Christ not to accept as true, without qualification, the slanders that come from one party only; for, as it is written, the law judges no one unless it first hears him and learns what he is doing.

And yet, for a fair-minded judge the facts themselves are enough to make the truth plain. So that, even if we keep silent, you are able to look closely at what is being done. For those who charge us with false doctrine have now plainly shown themselves to be joining the party of the heretics; and those who condemn us on account of the writings of others are seen to be contradicting their own confessions, which they deposited with us in writing. Consider the habit of those who dare such things: that it is always their custom to go over to the stronger side, to trample on those of their friends who are weak, and to court those who are in power. For these men who composed those notorious letters against Eudoxius and his whole party, and sent them round to all the brotherhoods, solemnly charging them to flee from communion with them as the ruin of souls, and who for this reason would not accept the votes brought forward for their deposition, because those votes had been cast by heretics—as they then persuaded us—these same men have now forgotten all this and have gone over to them. And no denial is left open to them; for they have plainly disclosed their own purpose by warmly embracing, at Ancyra, communion with them in private houses, since they had not yet been received by those very men into public communion. Ask them, then: if Basilides, who is in communion with Ecdicius, is now orthodox, why, on their return from Dardania, did they overthrow his altars in the territory of the Gangrenes and set up their own tables? And why even now do they make incursions into the churches of Amasea and Zela and install presbyters and deacons of their own? For if they hold communion with them as orthodox, why do they fall upon them as heretics? And if they have taken them to be heretics, how is it that they do not turn away from communion with them? Are not these things plain even to a child's understanding, most honoured brothers—that always, looking to their own advantage, they set about either to slander certain men or to commend them?

From us too, then, they have separated themselves—not out of vexation that we did not write back to them (for this is the chief thing on account of which they say they were provoked), nor because we did not receive the chorbishops whom they say they sent. And yet those who contrive this will give account to the Lord. For a certain Eustathius was sent, and after delivering letters to the office of the Vicar, and spending three days in the city, and being about to set off for his own home, late one evening, when I was already asleep, he is said to have come near our dwelling. But hearing that I was asleep, he went away and did not approach us again the next day; rather, having thus discharged his duty toward us, he departed. And this is the offence in which we did them wrong; and these long-suffering men did not weigh against this fault our former service, the service we rendered them in love, but they so heaped up their anger against us over this sin that, so far as it lay with them, they made us proscribed in all the churches throughout the world.

Yet this is not in truth the cause of the division. Rather, since they thought they would gain favour at that time with Euzoius if they estranged themselves from us, they devised for themselves those pretexts, in order that they might find some standing with them through their war against us. These men now also slander the faith of Nicaea, and call us 'consubstantialists,' because in that faith the only-begotten Son is confessed to be of one substance with God the Father—not as though from a single substance divided into two kindred parts (far from it; for that holy and God-loving synod did not understand it so), but in the sense that what the Father is according to substance, this the Son too must be understood to be. For so those very men explained it to us when they said, 'light from light.' And this is the faith of Nicaea, brought by them from the West, which they delivered to the synod at Tyana, by which also they were received. But they have a certain clever doctrine for such changes of theirs: that they use the words of the faith as physicians do, according to the occasion, adapting them now in one way, now in another, to the conditions before them. The unsoundness of this sophistry it is not for me to expose, but for you to perceive. For the Lord will give you understanding to recognize which is the straight word and which is the crooked and perverted one. For if at one time one creed must be composed, and at another another, and they must change with the times, then false is the declaration of him who said: 'One Lord, one faith, one baptism.' But if these words are true, let no one deceive you with these empty arguments. For they slander us as innovating concerning the Holy Spirit. Ask, then, what the innovation is. For we confess what we have received, that the Comforter is ranked with the Father and the Son, and is not numbered with the creation. For we have believed in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; and we are baptized into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. For this reason we never separate the Comforter from his conjunction with the Father and the Son. For our mind, enlightened by the Spirit, looks up to the Son, and in him, as in an image, beholds the Father. Neither, then, do we devise names of our own, but we name him Holy Spirit and Comforter, nor do we consent to set aside the glory due to him. These are our beliefs, declared with all truth. On these let the accuser accuse; let him who persecutes us persecute; let him who believes the slanders against us prepare himself for the trial. The Lord is near; let us be anxious for nothing.

If anyone writes in Syria, this is nothing to us. For 'by your words you will be justified,' he says, 'and by your words you will be condemned.' Let my own words judge me; but let no one condemn us for the faults of others, nor bring forward, as proof that we are now in communion with those who composed those writings, the letters written by us twenty years ago. For we, before those writings, being laymen, wrote to laymen, before any such suspicion against them was even stirred up; and we wrote nothing about the faith, nor anything of the kind that these men now circulate to our slander, but bare forms of address, fulfilling an affectionate greeting. For we equally shun and anathematize, as impious, both those who are sick with the doctrines of Sabellius and those who champion the dogmas of Arius. If anyone says that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are the same, and supposes one thing with many names, and one hypostasis uttered under three appellations, such a man we rank in the party of the Jews. Likewise, if anyone says that the Son is unlike the Father in substance, or brings down the Holy Spirit to a creature, we anathematize him, and we hold that he is near to the error of the Greeks. But to stop the mouths of those who accuse us by our writings is impossible; rather it is more likely that they will be provoked the more by our defences and contrive against us greater and harsher charges. To guard your ears, however, is not difficult. So, what lies in your power, do this. Keep your heart pure for us and free from prejudice against the slanders; and concerning the charges brought forward, demand from us the reckoning. And if you find the truth with us, give no place to falsehood; but if you perceive us to be powerless in our defence, then believe our accusers as speaking the truth. Those men are wakeful to do us harm; this we do not require of you. Carrying on a trader's life, they make our slander a side-trade; but you we exhort to remain at home and to live becomingly, fulfilling the work of Christ in quietness, and to shun their gatherings, which are made deceitfully for the ruin of those who hear them—so that you may both keep your love toward us pure, and preserve unbroken the faith of the fathers, and appear approved before the Lord as friends of the truth.
A letter of consolation to the clergy at Coloneia.

And what is so beautiful and so esteemed in the sight of God and of men as perfect love, which we have been taught by the wise Teacher to be the fulfilment of all law? Therefore I commend the ardour of your devotion toward your shepherd. For neither is the loss of a good father bearable to a child who loves his father, nor is the departure of a shepherd and teacher endurable to a church of Christ. So that you give proof of a fine and good disposition in your surpassing affection for your bishop. But this kindness of yours, this heartfelt feeling toward your spiritual father, is acceptable when it is exercised with measure and reason; when it passes beyond bounds, it no longer remains worthy of the same approval.

A good arrangement has been made concerning your most God-beloved brother and fellow-minister Euphronius by those who have been entrusted with the management of the churches—an arrangement necessary for the occasion, profitable both to the church to which he has been transferred and to you yourselves from whom he was taken. Do not think this a human contrivance, nor that it was set in motion by the calculations of men who mind earthly things; rather be assured that those who have the care of God's churches laid upon them did this by the familiar guidance of the Spirit, and take this impulse into your minds, and be eager to bring it to completion. Receive, then, quietly and with thanksgiving what has been done, persuaded of this: that those who do not accept from the churches of God the measures appointed for the churches set themselves against the ordinance of God. Do not contend at law against your mother, the church in Nicopolis. Do not be harsh toward those who have taken up the care of your souls. For while the affairs of Nicopolis hold firm, your portion too will be preserved with it; but if any storm strikes that church, though you should have ten thousand guardians, your portion will be consumed along with the whole. As, then, those who dwell beside rivers, when they see men far off building bulwarks against the streams, know that their own safety is being secured in advance by the warding off of the rivers' assaults, so too those who have now taken up the weight of care for the churches secure your immunity in the guarding of the others; and you will be under shelter from every disturbance, while others receive the onsets of the war. And you ought to consider this also, that he has not cast you off, but has taken on others besides. For we are surely not so envious as to compel a man able to share his gifts with others as well to shut up the grace within you alone and confine it to your own region only. For neither he who walls round a spring and spoils the outflow of water, nor he who prevents an abundant teaching from spreading further, is free from the disease of envy. Let him have, therefore, the care of Nicopolis too, and let your church be an addition to the concerns there. For more labour has come upon the man, but the attention given you is in no way diminished.

But this grieved me greatly and seemed to go beyond all measure: that it was said that, if we fail to obtain what we seek, we will resort to the law-courts and set men over these matters for whom the overthrow of the churches is the sum of their prayers. Let no one, then, carried away by senseless anger, persuade you to utter anything in public, and so let some overthrow arise from this, and the weight of what is done fall back upon the heads of those who furnished the occasion. Rather receive our counsel too, offered to you with a father's heart, and the arrangement of the most God-beloved bishops, made according to the will of God. And wait for us also, who, when we are present—if the Lord works with us—will exhort your reverence in person concerning all that could not be conveyed by letter, and will try to bring you, through the deeds themselves, what consolation is possible.
To the magistrates of Coloneia.

I received the letter of your excellency, and I gave thanks to the all-holy God that, busy as you are with the care of public affairs, you do not treat the concerns of the churches as a secondary matter; rather each of you has been anxious as for his own affair, one that holds together his very life. And you wrote to us in distress at the departure of your most God-beloved bishop Euphronius, whom Nicopolis has not taken from you; for, were she to plead her case, she would say that she has received back her own; but, treated kindly, she will speak to you a word befitting an affectionate mother—that she will hold the father in common with you, who will share his grace with both parties in turn, and will neither allow those others to suffer anything from the assault of the adversaries, nor deprive you of your accustomed care. Considering, then, both the hardship of the times and learning with prudent judgement the necessity of the arrangement, forgive the bishops who have come to this way of settling the churches of our Lord Jesus Christ; and counsel yourselves to do what befits men who possess a mature mind of their own, yet know also how to accept the suggestions of those who love them. For it is likely that you are unaware of much that is afoot, because you are placed at the far edge of Armenia; whereas we, who have entered into the midst of affairs and are struck on all sides every day by reports of churches being overthrown, are in great anguish lest the common enemy, envying the long peace of your life, should be able to sow his own tares in your regions too, and the Armenian portion become the prey of the adversaries. But for now keep quiet, having consented, as it were, to hold the use of a good vessel in common with your neighbours; and a little later, if the Lord grants our coming, you shall receive a fuller consolation for what has happened, should this appear necessary to you.
To the clergy of Nicopolis.

Even a work carried out by one or two devout men assures us that it is done by the counsel of the Spirit. For when nothing human lies before the eyes, and holy men press toward their actions with no aim of personal enjoyment, but set before themselves only what is well-pleasing to God, it is plain that the Lord is the one who directs their hearts. And where spiritual men take the lead in the deliberations, and the people of the Lord follow them in agreement of mind, who will doubt that the decision was reached by the fellowship of our Lord Jesus Christ, who poured out his blood for the churches? Hence you yourselves rightly judged that our most God-beloved brother and fellow-minister Poemenius was moved according to God, who both stood by you at the right moment and came to this manner of consolation. And I praise not only his discovery of what was profitable, but I also admire the nobility of his judgement, in that he did not draw the matter out into delays—which would have slackened the zeal of those who were seeking, given time for self-defence to the claimants, and stirred up the plots of those lying in wait—but at once brought the good plan to its end. May the Lord, by his grace, keep him and all his household safe, so that the church may remain true to itself in the equally honoured succession of its predecessor, and give no place to the evil one, who now, if ever, is vexed at the stability of the churches.

As for the brothers in Coloneia, we have exhorted them much by letter, and you too ought to receive their disposition with goodwill rather than provoke them, as men slighted on account of their small numbers, nor by contempt drive them into rivalry. For somehow those who fall into rivalry tend to become more imprudent, and to manage much of their own affairs badly for the sake of grieving their opponents. And no one now is so small that he cannot furnish an occasion for great evils to those who want an occasion. And we say this not by guesswork, but taught by the experience of our own troubles—which may God turn aside through your prayers. And pray together with us for a good journey, that when we are present we may rejoice with you over your present shepherd, and be comforted together over the departure of our common father.
To the magistrates of Nicopolis.

The arrangements concerning the churches are made by those entrusted with their oversight, but they are confirmed by the people. So that what lay with the most God-beloved bishops has been fulfilled; what remains now looks to you—if you will be willing to cling fervently to the bishop given you, and to repel strongly the attempts of those outside. For nothing so abashes either the rulers or the rest, all who envy your peaceful condition, as harmony in love toward the one given you and firmness of resistance. For it brings them to despair of every wicked undertaking, if they see neither clergy nor people accepting their designs. The judgement, then, that you hold concerning the good, make it common to the city; and address the people and all who dwell in the region, strengthening their good resolves, so that the genuineness of your love toward God may be proclaimed among all. And if we ourselves should ever be counted worthy to come and visit the church that is the nurse of piety, which we honour as the mother-city of orthodoxy—because from of old it has been governed by men most honoured and chosen of God, who hold fast to the faithful word according to the teaching, of whom you have judged the man now brought forward to be worthy, and we have agreed—
Only may you be kept safe by the grace of God, who undoes the wicked counsels of the enemies and works in your souls strength and vigour for the keeping of what has been rightly decided.
To Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium.

I find few occasions for writing to your Reverence, and this grieves me not a little. For it is as if, even when it were possible to see you often and to enjoy your company, I did so only rarely. But I cannot write, for want of those who travel from here to you; since otherwise nothing would prevent my letters from being, as it were, a daybook of my life, announcing to your love the things that befall me day by day. For it brings me relief to share my affairs with you, and I know that you are anxious about nothing so much as about us. But now Elpidius, hastening to his own master to clear himself of the slanders falsely contrived against him by certain enemies, asked us for this letter. Through him we also greet your Reverence, and we commend the man to you, both because in justice he is worthy of your protection and for our sake; for even if we have nothing else to testify on his behalf, yet because he counted it a great thing to become the bearer of our letters, keep him among your own people, and remember us, and pray for the church.

Know, too, that our most God-beloved brother is in exile, unable to bear the harassments of the shameless. And Doara is storm-tossed, the fleshy monster throwing everything there into confusion. As for us, our enemies are brewing their plots at the imperial court, as those who know report; but the hand of the Lord is so far with us. Only pray that we be not utterly forsaken. For indeed the brother lives at ease; and Doara has taken back its old muleteer, though it has nothing more; and the Lord will scatter the counsels of our enemies. The release, however, from all our troubles, both present and expected, would be to behold you. So if it ever becomes possible for you, while we are still above the earth, count us worthy to see you.

The book on the Holy Spirit has been written and finished by us, as you yourself know; but the brothers with me prevented me from sending it written on papyrus, saying that they had instructions from your nobility to have it written in a small volume. So that we might not seem to do anything contrary to your command, we have held it back for now, but we will send it a little later, only if we light upon some suitable bearer. May you be granted to me, and to the Church of God, in good health and good cheer, praying to the Lord for us, through the loving-kindness of the Holy One.
To Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium.

Every day that holds a letter from your Reverence is a festival to us, and the greatest of festivals. And when it carries with it tokens of festival as well, what else must we call it but a festival of festivals, just as the ancient law was wont to name them 'Sabbaths of Sabbaths'? We give thanks, then, to the Lord, having learned that you are well in body and that you have kept the commemoration of the saving dispensation in a church at peace.

But we have been shaken by certain disturbances; nevertheless we have not passed our days without dejection, since our most God-beloved brother has been driven into exile. Yet for him, pray that God may grant him one day to look upon his own church healed of the wounds of the heretics' bitings; and us count very worthy to be visited, while we are still on the earth. Do a deed in keeping with yourself, and to us worthy of the greatest prayer. One may marvel, too, at the meaning of the gifts you sent, that in riddles you wished us a vigorous old age. For you showed that by the carriage-lamps you rouse us to nightly labours, and by the sweetmeats you assure us that we are braced in every part. For chewing is not for me, given my age, since my teeth were long ago worn away both by time and by sickness. To the questions you raised, however, certain answers have been put in the memorandum, such as I was able to give, and as the occasion allowed.
To Amphilochius, who had asked a question.

I too have heard of this, and I recognize the contrivance of these men. What, then, shall we say to it? That the mind is a good thing, and in it we have that which is according to the image of the Creator; and that the activity of the mind is a good thing; and that, being ever in motion, it often forms impressions of things that do not exist as though they did, and often is borne straight to the truth. But since, in our understanding—we who have believed in God—two powers have grown up alongside it, the one evil, the power of the demons, drawing us along into its own apostasy, the other more divine and good, leading us up to the likeness of God: when the mind abides by itself, it perceives little, and only things proportioned to itself; but when it gives itself over to those that deceive it, it obliterates its own faculty of judgement and consorts with monstrous impressions. Then it considers wood to be not wood but God, and judges gold to be not money but an object of worship. But if it inclines toward the more divine portion and receives the graces of the Spirit, then it becomes able to apprehend the more divine things, so far as is proportioned to its nature.

There are, then, three conditions of life, as it were, and the activities of our mind are equal in number to these. For either our pursuits are evil, and evil accordingly are the motions of our mind—such as adulteries, thefts, idolatries, slanders, quarrels, fits of anger, factions, self-conceit, and all that the apostle Paul enumerated among the works of the flesh; or they are good; or the activity of the soul is some middle thing, having in it nothing either to be condemned or to be praised—as is the practice of those mechanical arts, which we call middle arts, since by their own account they incline neither to virtue nor to vice. For what vice is there in piloting a ship or in medicine? Yet these are not themselves virtues either, in and of themselves, but they incline toward one or other of the opposing portions according to the moral choice of those who use them. But the mind that has been mingled with the deity of the Spirit—this is at last able to contemplate the great visions, and beholds the divine beauties, yet only so far as grace bestows and its own constitution can receive.

So, leaving aside those dialectical questions, let them examine the truth not maliciously but with reverence. The faculty of judgement of the mind has been given us for the understanding of the truth. And our God is the very Truth itself. So that it is the primary task of the mind to recognize our God—to recognize him, however, in such a way as the infinitely great can be made known by the very smallest. For not even because the eyes are appointed for the perception of visible things does it follow that all visible things are brought under sight. For not even the hemisphere of the heaven is perceived at a single glance; rather an impression of sight surrounds us, while in truth many things in it—not to say all—are unknown to us: the nature of the stars, their magnitudes, their distances, their motions, their conjunctions, their separations, and all their other relations, the very substance of the firmament, the depth from the hollow circumference to the convex surface. And yet we would not say that the heaven is invisible because of the things unknown, but visible by reason of our moderate perception of it. So it is also with God. If the mind has been harmed by demons, it will fall into idolatry, or be turned aside to some other form of impiety; but if it has given itself to the help of the Spirit, it will recognize the truth and will know God. And it will know him, as the apostle said, in part, and in the life after this more perfectly; for when that which is perfect comes, that which is in part shall be done away. So that the faculty of judgement of the mind is both good and given for a useful end—the perception of God—working, however, only so much as it is able to contain.
To the same, on another question.

Do you worship what you know, or what you do not know? If we answer, 'What we know, this we worship,' their reply comes at once: 'What is the substance of the one you worship?' And if we confess that we do not know the substance, again they turn upon us and say: 'Then you worship what you do not know.' But we say that to know has many meanings. For we say that we know the greatness of God, and his power, and his wisdom, and his goodness, and the providence by which he cares for us, and the justice of his judgement—but not his very substance. So the question is captious. For he who says he does not know the substance has not confessed that he does not know God, since our conception of God is gathered from the many things we have enumerated. 'But God is simple,' he says, 'and whatever you reckon among the things known of him belongs to his substance.' But this is a sophism that holds countless absurdities. Of all these things enumerated, are they all names of one substance? And is his terribleness of equal force with his loving-kindness, his justice with his creative power, his foreknowledge with his recompensing, his majesty with his providence? Or, whichever of these we name, do we declare the substance?
