If indeed they say this, let them not ask whether we know the substance of God, but let them inquire of us whether we know God to be terrible, or just, or loving toward men. These things we confess that we know. But if they say that the substance is something else, let them not cheat us by appeal to his simplicity. For they themselves have confessed that the substance and each of the things enumerated are different. But the activities are various, while the substance is simple. We, however, say that we know our God from his activities, but we do not promise to draw near to his very substance. For his activities come down to us, but his substance remains inaccessible.

'But if you do not know the substance,' he says, 'you do not know him.' But you, reverse it: if you say you know the substance, you do not know him. For neither does the man bitten by a mad dog, who sees the dog in the cup, see more than those who are healthy; rather he is pitiable for this reason, that he supposes he sees what he does not see. Do not, then, marvel at him for his profession, but judge him pitiable for his derangement. Know, therefore, that it is the talk of triflers: 'If you do not know the substance of God, you worship what you do not know.' But I, that he exists, I know; what the substance is, I set above the reach of thought. How, then, am I saved? Through faith. And faith is sufficient to know that God exists, not what he is, and that he becomes a rewarder to those who seek him out. The knowledge, then, of the divine substance is the perception of his incomprehensibility; and what is to be reverenced is not the apprehension of what the substance is, but that the substance exists.

And let them be questioned in turn thus. 'No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him.' What did the only-begotten declare of the Father—the substance or the power? If the power, then so much as he declared to us, so much we know. If the substance, tell me, where did he declare the substance of his unbegottenness? When did Abraham worship—was it not when he believed? And when did he believe—was it not when he was called? Where, then, here was an apprehension testified to him by Scripture? And when did the disciples worship him—was it not when they saw the creation made subject to him? For from the sea and the winds obeying him they recognized his deity. From his activities, then, comes knowledge; and from knowledge, worship. 'Do you believe that I am able to do this?' 'I believe, Lord'—and he worshipped him. So worship follows upon faith, and faith is confirmed from power. But if you say that he who believes also knows, then from the things he believes, from these also he knows; or, conversely, from the things he knows, from these also he believes. And we know God from his power. So that we believe in him who has been known, and we worship him who has been believed.
To the same, on another question.

Which comes first, knowledge or faith? We say that, in general, in the case of the disciplines faith goes before knowledge, but in our doctrine, even if someone says that knowledge takes the lead before faith, we do not dispute it—meaning, however, the knowledge that is proportioned to human apprehension. For in the disciplines one must first believe that a letter is called alpha, and, having learned the characters and the pronunciation, afterward grasp also the exact understanding of the power of the element. But in faith concerning God, the conception that God exists leads the way, and this we gather from his works. For wise, and powerful, and good, and all his invisible things we recognize by perceiving them from the creation of the world. So too we accept him as our own Master. For since God is the maker of the whole world, and we are part of the world, then God is the maker of us also. Upon this knowledge faith follows, and upon such faith, worship.

But now, since the word 'knowledge' has many meanings, those who mock the simpler folk, and who display themselves alike with their paradoxes—like those who in the theatres, before the eyes of all, palm the counting-stones—snatch up the whole by a question put in general terms. For since the word 'knowledge' extends widely, and a thing is known in one way according to number, in another according to magnitude, in another according to power, in another according to its manner of existing, in another according to the time of its coming to be, in another according to substance—these men, taking up the whole in a single question, if they catch us confessing that we know, demand of us the knowledge of the substance; but if they see us cautious about the assertion, they turn upon us the reproach of impiety. But we confess that we know what is knowable of God, while to know again something that escapes our apprehension is impossible. So, just as, if you ask me whether I know what sand is, and I answer that I do, you will plainly be slandering me if you straightway demand also its number—because your first question bore upon the nature of the sand, but your second, a slander, was turned about its number. This sophism is like the one that says: 'Do you know Timothy? Then, if you know Timothy, you know also his nature; but you have confessed that you know Timothy; render to us, then, the account of Timothy's nature.' But I both know Timothy and do not know him—not, however, in the same respect and in the same regard. For it is not in the respect in which I know him that I also do not know him, but in one respect I know him, in another I am ignorant of him. For I know him by his appearance and his other characteristics, but I am ignorant of his substance. Indeed, in this way I both know and am ignorant of myself by the same reasoning. For I know myself, who I am, but I do not know myself in so far as I am ignorant of my substance.

Let them explain to us, then, how Paul said, 'For now we know in part.' Do we know his substance in part, as though we know parts of his substance? But this is absurd, for God is without parts. Or do we know the whole of it? How, then, 'When that which is perfect comes, that which is in part shall be done away'? And on what charge are the idolaters accused? Is it not that, knowing God, they did not glorify him as God? Or the foolish Galatians—why are they reproached by Paul, when he says, 'But now, having known God, or rather having been known by God, how is it that you turn again to the weak and beggarly elements?' And how was God known in Judaea? Is it because in Judaea his substance, whatever it was, came to be known? 'The ox,' it says, 'knew its owner'—so then, by your account, the ox knew the substance of its master; 'and the ass its master's crib.' The ass, then, also knew the substance of the crib! 'But Israel,' it says, 'did not know me.' This is charged against Israel, on your account—that they did not come to know the substance of God, whatever it is. 'Pour out,' it says, 'your wrath upon the nations that do not know you'—that is, that have not apprehended your substance. But knowledge is manifold, as we have said. For there is the understanding of him who created us, and the perception of his wonders, and the keeping of his commandments, and intimacy with him; but these men, thrusting all this aside, drag knowledge to a single meaning, the contemplation of the very substance of God. 'You shall place it,' it says, 'before the testimonies, whence I will be known to you from there.' Does 'I will be known' stand for 'I will reveal my substance'? 'The Lord knew those who are his.' Did he, then, know the substance of his own, but is ignorant of the substance of the disobedient? 'Adam knew his wife.' Did he, then, come to know her substance? And of Rebecca it says, 'A virgin; a man had not known her'; and, 'How shall this be, since I do not know a man?' Did no one, then, come to know the substance of Rebecca? And does Mary mean this—that I have not perceived the substance of any man? Or is 'knew' what Scripture is accustomed to use of marital unions? And 'God shall be known from the mercy-seat'—that is, he shall be made manifest to those who serve him. And 'The Lord knew those who are his'—that is, he received them, through their good works, into intimacy with himself.
To the same Amphilochius.

The saying in the Gospel about our Lord Jesus Christ being ignorant of the day of the end and the hour has already been a matter of inquiry among many, and is especially put forward continually by the Anomoeans for the overthrow of the glory of the Only-begotten, as proof of his being unlike in substance and of an inferiority in dignity—as though one who does not know all things could not have the same nature, nor be conceived in a single likeness, with him who comprehends the knowledge of all things by his foreknowing power that reaches out to things to come. This question has now been put to us by your discernment as something new. The things, then, that we heard from childhood from the fathers, and that, from love of what is good, we accepted without scrutiny, these we are able to say—not as untying the shamelessness of the enemies of Christ (for what argument could be found stronger than their impulse?), but as furnishing, perhaps, sufficient assurance to those who love the Lord and possess, in their preconception from faith, something stronger than proof from argument.

The word 'no one' seems to be universal, so that not even a single person is excepted by this expression; yet it is not so used in Scripture, as we have observed in the case of 'No one is good except one, God.' For not even there does the Son say this in order to set himself outside the nature of the good; rather, since the Father is the first good, we believe that 'no one' is said with 'first' understood. So too 'No one knows the Son except the Father.' For not even there does he charge the Spirit with ignorance, but he testifies that the knowledge of his own nature belongs first to the Father. So too we hold that 'No one knows' is said in the sense of referring the first knowledge, both of things present and of things to come, to the Father, and of pointing men through all things to the first cause. For how else can the saying agree with the rest of the testimonies of Scripture, or accord with our common notions—we who have believed that the Only-begotten is the image of the invisible God, and an image not of bodily form but of the very deity, and of the greatnesses conceived as belonging to the substance of God, an image of power, an image of wisdom, in the sense in which Christ is called the power of God and the wisdom of God? And knowledge is plainly a part of wisdom, which he would not image forth in its entirety if he fell short in any matters. And how is it that the Father, through whom he made the ages, did not show him the smallest part of the ages, that day and that hour? Or how is the maker of all things lacking in the knowledge of the smallest part of the things created by him? And he who says that, near the end, such and such signs shall appear in the heaven and in the regions of the earth—how is he ignorant of the end itself? For when he says, 'The end is not yet,' he speaks not as one in doubt but as one who knows and defines. And again, to one who considers fairly, the Lord says many things to men from the human side: for example, 'Give me to drink' is a voice of the Lord fulfilling a bodily need. And yet he who asked was not flesh without a soul, but deity making use of ensouled flesh. So too now, if anyone takes the matter of ignorance as belonging to him who took all things upon himself by the dispensation, and who advanced before God and men in wisdom and grace, he will not be carried outside a reverent understanding.

It would be a task for your diligence to set forth the sayings of the Gospel and to compare with each other those of Matthew and of Mark. For these alone appear to be in agreement with each other on this passage. Now the text of Matthew runs thus: 'But concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, except the Father alone.' And that of Mark: 'But concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, except the Father.' What, then, is worthy of note in these passages? That Matthew said nothing about the Son's not knowing, but seems to agree with Mark in meaning, by saying, 'except the Father alone.' We, however, hold that 'alone' is said by way of contrast with the angels, and that the Son is not included with his own servants in respect of ignorance.

For he who said, 'All things that the Father has are mine,' does not lie. And one of the things he has is the knowledge of that day and hour. Passing over, then, his own person in silence in the text of Matthew, as a thing agreed upon, the Lord said that the angels do not know, but that the Father alone knows—saying, by what is left unspoken, that the Father's knowledge is also his own, because he has said in another place, 'As the Father knows me, I also know the Father.' And if the Father knows the Son wholly and through and through, so as to know all the wisdom laid up in him, then in equal measure he will also be known by the Son—that is, together with all the wisdom that is in him and the foreknowledge of things to come. We claim, then, this consolation for the words that stand in Matthew, 'except the Father alone.' But as for Mark's text, since it plainly seems to cut off the Son also from knowledge, we understand it thus: that 'no one knows, neither the angels of God, nor even the Son knew, except the Father'—that is, the cause of the Son's knowing is from the Father. And this interpretation is without strain for one who hears fairly, since 'alone' is not added, as it is in Matthew. The sense, then, in Mark is this: but concerning that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels of God, nor would the Son have known, except the Father; for from the Father the knowledge was given to him as his own. And this is a most reverent and God-befitting thing to say concerning the Son: that from him whose substance he shares he has also his knowing, and his being beheld in all the wisdom and glory befitting his deity.

Concerning Jechoniah, whom the prophet Jeremiah says was made an outcast from the land of Judaea when he said, 'Jechoniah was dishonoured like a vessel for which there is no use,' and that he was cast out, both he and his seed, and there shall not rise from his seed one sitting on the throne of David, a ruler in Judah—the explanation is plain and clear. For when Jerusalem had been destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, the kingdom was dissolved, and there were no longer hereditary successions of the rulers as there had been before; but at that time the descendants of David spent their lives from the beginning in captivity. And when those of Salathiel and Zerubbabel returned, they led the people in a more popular manner, the rule having passed thereafter to the priesthood, because the priestly and the royal tribe were mingled together. Hence the Lord is both king and high priest in the things pertaining to God. And the royal tribe did not fail until the coming of Christ, yet the seed of Jechoniah no longer sat upon the throne of David. For by 'throne' is plainly meant the royal dignity. And you surely remember the history, that all Judaea was tributary to David, and the land of Idumaea and the Moabite country, and as much of Syria as bordered on it and what lay farther off as far as Mesopotamia; and on the other side as far as the river of Egypt. If, then, none of those who came after appeared in so great a dignity, how is the word of the prophet not true, that none from the seed of Jechoniah shall any longer sit on the throne of David? For no one from him appears to have taken hold of this dignity. The tribe of Judah, however, did not fail, until he came for whom it was reserved—who himself did not sit upon the bodily throne either, the Jewish kingdom having passed thereafter to Herod, the son of the Ascalonite Antipater, and to his children, who divided Judaea into four governments, while Pilate was governor and Tiberius held the whole power of the Roman empire. But by the throne of David, on which the Lord sat, Scripture means the indestructible kingdom. For he is the expectation of the nations, not of the smallest part of the world; 'For there shall be,' it says, 'the root of Jesse, and one who rises to rule the nations; on him shall the nations hope.' 'For I have set you as a covenant of the race, as a light of the nations.' And 'I will establish,' it says, 'his seed forever and ever, and his throne as the days of heaven.' So, then, he remained a priest also, even if he did not take up the sceptres of Judaea, and God is king of all the earth, and the blessing of Jacob was confirmed: 'And in his seed shall all the tribes of the earth be blessed, and all nations shall call Christ blessed.'

To the subtle Encratites, in answer to their solemn problem—why do we not also eat all things?—let this be said: that we even loathe our own bodily wastes. For in respect of worth, meat is to us as the herbs of the field; but in respect of distinguishing what is beneficial, just as among herbs we separate the harmful from the suitable, so among meats we distinguish the harmful from the useful. For hemlock is a herb, just as vulture's flesh is meat; yet no one in his right mind would eat henbane, nor touch a dog unless great necessity pressed him—though one who did eat would not break the law. As for those who say that human affairs are governed by fate, do not seek arguments from us, but wound them with the proper barbs of rhetoric; for the problem is longer than my present infirmity allows.

Concerning the rising up in baptism, I do not know what led you to ask, if indeed you accepted that the immersion fulfils the figure of the three days. For it is impossible to be baptized three times without rising up as many times.
The word 'glutton' we accent on the penult.

Substance and hypostasis have this difference, which the common has to the particular—as, for example, animal has to such-and-such a man. For this reason we confess one substance in the deity, so that we may not give a varying account of being, but a particular hypostasis, in order that our notion of Father and Son and Holy Spirit may be in us unconfused and made clear. For if we do not conceive the distinct characters belonging to each—such as fatherhood and sonship and sanctification—but confess God from the common notion of being, it is impossible to render the account of the faith soundly. We must, then, adding the particular to the common, confess the faith thus: the deity is common, fatherhood is particular; and joining them together, say, 'I believe in God the Father.' And again, in the confession of the Son, do the like, joining the particular to the common, and say, 'I believe in God the Son.' Likewise also concerning the Holy Spirit, shaping the utterance according to the sequence of the expression, say, 'I believe also in the divine Holy Spirit'—so that throughout both the unity may be preserved in the confession of the one deity, and the particularity of the persons may be confessed in the distinction of the properties conceived as belonging to each. But those who say that substance and hypostasis are the same are compelled to confess only different persons, and, in shrinking from saying three hypostases, are found not to escape the evil of Sabellius, who himself also, confounding the notion in many places, undertakes to divide the persons, saying that the same hypostasis is transformed to meet each need that arises.

And concerning the things you asked—how the middle and indifferent things are dispensed in our regard, whether by some chance occurrence or by the just providence of God—we say this: that health and sickness, wealth and poverty, glory and dishonour, in so far as they do not make their possessors good, are not among the natural goods; but in so far as they furnish some ease to our life, the preferred ones are more choiceworthy than their opposites, and have a certain value when so reckoned. These things, however, are given by God to some for the sake of a dispensation, as to Abraham and to Job and such men; but to the baser sort they are a summons to be improved in their conduct, since one who, after so great a welcome from God, persists in his wrongdoing, undeniably renders himself liable to condemnation. The just man, however, neither turns toward wealth when it is present, nor seeks it when it is absent; for he is not one who enjoys what is given, but one who administers it. And no one with sense rushes into the burdensome business of distributing the goods of others, unless he looks to the glory of the many, who admire and envy those established in some position of power. But sickness the just receive as a contest, awaiting great crowns for their endurance. And to set some other power over the management of these things is not only out of harmony but also impious.
To Eusebius, bishop of Samosata.

I both wrote to your Reverence through the vicar of Thrace, and I wrote other letters by a certain superintendent of the treasuries at Philippopolis who was crossing from our country into Thrace, and I asked him to take them up when he set off. But the vicar did not receive our letters. For while we were going round on visitation through the parish, he reached the city in the evening and rode away again at deep dawn, so that the stewards of the church did not learn of the man's arrival, and so the letters remained with us. And the superintendent, perhaps held back by some unwished-for circumstance, set off without either taking up the letters or seeing us. And there was no one else to be found. Hence we remained in distress, that we can neither write to you nor receive letters from your Reverence. And yet I wished, if it were possible for me, to announce to you the things that befall us day by day. For so many and so strange are these matters that they require the record of a daybook—which indeed I have composed, be assured, except that, by the continual press of what befalls me, my reckonings are knocked off the things before me.

A vicar arrived among us—the first and greatest of our troubles. Whether the man is also a heretic in mind, I do not know (for I think him without experience of any argument, and that he has no zeal or study about such matters; for I see him occupied in other things, soul and body, night and day), but he is at any rate fond of heretics, loving them no more than he hates us. For he convened, in the middle of winter, a synod of men who set the faith aside, in Galatia; and he expelled Hypsis and set up Ecdicius in his place. And he ordered my brother to be brought in by force, accused by a single man, and that an obscure one. Then, after busying himself a little about the imperial court, he came upon us again breathing anger and slaughter, and with one voice handed over all the clergy of the church in Caesarea to the council; and at Sebasteia he sat for many days dividing men by class, naming as councillors those who are in communion with us, and condemning them to the service of public duties, while he surrounded those attached to Eustathius with the greatest honours.

Again he ordered a synod of Galatians and Pontics to be convened near Nyssa. And they obeyed, and, running together, sent to the churches a man whom I would not choose to describe, but your prudence may guess what kind of man it is likely to be who serves the purposes of such men. And now, as I write this, this same body has set off for Sebasteia, to join Eustathius and with him to overthrow the affairs of the Nicopolitans. For the blessed Theodotus has fallen asleep. And for a while they repelled the vicar's first assaults nobly and stoutly; for he tried to persuade them to receive Eustathius and through him to take a bishop; but when he saw that they would not willingly yield, he is now trying to install the one given them with a more violent hand. And there is a rumour, too, of an expected synod, at which they intend to summon us and either receive us into communion or use their accustomed methods. Such, then, is the state of the churches. As for myself, how I am in body, I think it better to be silent than to write, since by telling the truth I shall grieve you, and to lie I cannot endure.
To the presbyters of Nicopolis.

I received the letter of your Reverence, and I had nothing newer to learn from it than what I already knew. For the report had reached the whole surrounding region, proclaiming the shame of the man who has fallen among you, who, out of desire for empty glory, gathered to himself the most disgraceful dishonour, and was found, through his self-love, to have fallen away from the rewards that come from the faith; yet he does not even hold that wretched bit of glory, in desire of which he sold himself to impiety, since, by the justice of God, he is hated by those who fear the Lord. But that man brought forth, by his present choice, the clearest proof of his whole life: that he never lived in hope of the promises laid up for us with the Lord, but if he ever contrived for himself anything human, both the words of faith and the pretence of reverence—all this was practised for the deceiving of those he met.

But you—why does what happened distress you? In what have you become worse than yourselves because of it? One has dropped out of your number; and if some one or two others departed with him, these are pitiable for their fall, but your body is whole by the grace of God. For what was made useless has flowed away, and what remains has not been maimed. And if it grieves you that you have been cast out of the walls, yet you will lodge under the shelter of the God of heaven, and the angel who is the overseer of the church departed with you. So they recline among empty things each day, by the dispersal of the people preparing for themselves a heavy judgement. And if there is any labour in the matter, I am persuaded in the Lord that this will not turn out in vain for you. So that the more you are placed amid more trials, the more costly is the reward you may await from the just judge. Neither, then, be downcast at the present, nor grow weary in hope. For yet a very little while, and he who takes your part will come to you, and will not delay.
To Eusebius, bishop of Samosata.

The Lord has granted us now too, through our most longed-for and most reverent brother Antiochus, my fellow-presbyter, to greet your Holiness, and to exhort you to do what is customary, to pray for us, and to find for ourselves some consolation for the long separation in the converse that comes through a letter. And in your prayers we exhort you to ask of the Lord first and above all this: that we be delivered from the absurd and wicked men who have so prevailed over the people that we now reflect nothing other than the events of the capture of the Jews. For the more the churches slip away into weakness, the more men's love of rule grows strong. And the name of the episcopate has now passed to wretched house-bred slaves—no one of God's servants choosing to put himself forward in their place, but only the desperate, such as those now sent in by Anysius, the nursling of Euippius, and by Ecdicius of Parnassus, whose appointer left him in the churches as an evil provision for himself in the life to come. These men have now driven my brother out of Nyssa and brought in his place a man—or rather a slave worth a few obols, but in his corruption of the faith a match for those who appointed him. And to the village of Doara they sent a corrupt man, the servant of orphans, who had run away from his own masters, and who, through the flattery of a godless little woman—who formerly used George for her own will, and now has this man as his successor—they have sent, doing outrage to the pitiable name of the episcopate. And as for the affairs of the Nicopolitans, who could lament them as they deserve—when the wretched Fronto, who formerly pretended, forsooth, to be an advocate for the truth, in the end shamefully betrayed both the faith and himself, and received as the wages of his treachery a name of dishonour? For he received from them the dignity of a bishopric, as he supposes, but by the grace of God he has become the common abomination of all Armenia. Only there is nothing they dare not attempt, nor do they lack fellow-workers worthy of them. As for the rest of the affairs of Syria, the brother Antiochus both knows and will relate them better than we.

As for those from the West, you yourself met with them earlier, when the brother Dorotheus had related everything. What kind of letters must I give him again as he departs? For perhaps he will share the journey with the excellent Sanctissimus, who has great zeal and is going about the East, collecting from each of the notable men subscriptions and letters. What, then, must be written through them, or how I am to agree with those who write—I myself am at a loss; but if you quickly find people coming to us, count us worthy to be informed. For to me it comes to mind to say the saying of Diomedes: 'Would that you had not entreated him'; because, he says, 'the man is overbearing.' For in truth haughty characters, when courted, are wont to become more disdainful. For if the Lord is propitiated to us, what other addition do we need? And if the wrath of God persists, what help to us is the Western brow? Those men neither know the truth nor endure to learn it, but, preoccupied with false suspicions, they now do those things which they did before in the case of Marcellus—quarrelling with those who reported the truth to them, while they confirmed the heresy by themselves. For I myself wished to write to their chief apart from the common form: nothing about ecclesiastical matters, except so far as to hint that they neither know the truth of our affairs nor accept the way by which they might learn it; but in general, that one must not set upon those humbled by trials, nor judge pride a dignity—a sin sufficient by itself to make enmity with God.
To the presbyters of Nicopolis.

You did well both in writing to us and in writing through such a man, who, even without a letter, would have sufficed to give us ample consolation in our cares and to make an exact instruction about affairs. For there was much that we sought to learn from one who knew most clearly, because the reports came across to us in distorted form; all of which our most longed-for and most honoured brother Theodosius, the fellow-presbyter, related to us steadily and with full knowledge. The things, then, that we counsel ourselves, these we also write to your Reverence: that these things which have happened to you have happened to many, and not in the present time only, but in the time past also there are countless examples of such things; some the histories have left in writing, and others we have received by the unwritten memory of those who knew them—that trials, both upon each man individually and upon cities, encompassed those who had set their hope on the name of the Lord, for that name's sake. But nevertheless all passed away, and none of the grievous things had an immortal pain. For just as hailstorms and torrents and all the sudden evils easily harm and ruin what is soft, but, meeting with what resists, suffer rather than do, so too the furious trials stirred up against the Church have been shown to be weaker than the firmness of faith in Christ. As, then, the cloud of hail passed by, and the torrent flowed away down the gully (for the one was dissolved into clear sky, and the other vanished in the deep, leaving dry and waterless the channel through which it ran), so too the things that now buffet us will, a little later, be no more—only if we consent not to look at the present, but to gaze with our hopes at things a little farther off.

Whether, then, the trial is heavy, brothers, let us endure the toils; for no one is crowned who has not been struck in the contests and covered with dust. Or whether these are the devil's light playthings, and those sent against us are troublesome, because they are his servants, yet contemptible, because God has joined weakness to their wickedness, let us guard against condemnation, as men lamenting great things over small sufferings. For there is one thing worthy of grief: the destruction of that very man, who, for the sake of temporary glory (if indeed we must call it glory to behave disgracefully in public), deprived himself of the eternal honour of the just. You are children of confessors, and children of martyrs, of those who resisted sin to the point of blood. Let each use his own examples for his stand on behalf of piety. None of us has been torn with stripes, no one's house has been confiscated, we have not lived in exile, we have not known the prison. What dreadful thing have we suffered? Unless perhaps this is grievous, that we have suffered nothing, nor were thought worthy of the sufferings for Christ. And if it grieves you that such-and-such a man holds the house of prayer, while you worship the Master of heaven and earth in the open air, consider that the eleven disciples were shut up in the upper room, while those who crucified the Lord were fulfilling the Jewish worship in the renowned temple. For Judas, who preferred death by hanging to living with shame, showed himself, perhaps, a more choiceworthy man than those who now have lost all shame before every condemnation of men, and on that account are shamelessly disposed toward what is base.

Only do not be deceived by their false words, when they profess rightness of faith. For such men are traffickers in Christ, and not Christians, always preferring what is profitable to them in this life to living according to the truth. When they thought to acquire this empty office, they joined the enemies of Christ; when they saw the people growing fierce, they again put on the appearance of orthodoxy. I do not acknowledge as a bishop, nor would I number among the priests of Christ, one who has been put forward for office by profane hands for the overthrow of the faith. This is my judgement. And you, if you have any portion with us, will plainly think the same as we. But if you take counsel by yourselves, each is master of his own judgement, and we are innocent of this blood. And I have written these things not because I distrust you, but to steady the wavering of some by making known my own mind—that no one may be forestalled into communion, nor, having received the laying-on of their hands, afterward, when peace has come, force himself to be numbered with the priestly body. We greet, through you, all the clergy, both of the city and of the parish, together with all the people who fear the Lord.
To Eusebius, bishop of Samosata.

It is not to multiply our despondencies that we often do not spare the recital of our difficulties in our letters to your Honour, but in order both to give ourselves some consolation through our groanings—which somehow are wont, when they come, to scatter the pain that lies in the depths—and to spur on your magnanimity to a more earnest prayer for the churches. For Moses too prayed continually for the people, as is plain; but when the contest against Amalek was joined for him, he did not let down his hands from morning until evening; rather the stretching out of the holy man's hands was completed together with the end of the battle.
To those in the West.

Since the holy God has promised to those who hope in him a way out of every affliction, even though we have been caught in the midst of a sea of troubles, and are tormented by the great waves stirred up against us by the spirits of wickedness, nevertheless we hold out in Christ who strengthens us, and we have not relaxed the strain of our zeal for the churches, nor, as in a storm when the surge runs high, have we despaired of our salvation and now await dissolution; rather we still hold to the zeal that is possible for us, knowing that he too who was swallowed by the sea-monster, because he did not despair of himself but cried out to the Lord, was counted worthy of salvation. So we ourselves too, though come to the extremity of troubles, do not let go of our hope in God, but look about on every side for his help. Hence we have looked also to you now, our most honoured brothers, whom we have often expected to appear to us in the season of our afflictions. But falling away from that hope, we too said to ourselves: 'I waited for one to grieve with me, and there was none, and for comforters, and I found none.' For such are our sufferings that they have reached even the ends of our world; and if, when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it, it surely befitted your compassion too to be affected together with us, who have laboured for a long time. For it is not nearness of place, but the conjunction in spirit, that is wont to produce that intimacy which we have believed to exist between us and your love.

Why, then, has there been no letter of comfort, no visitation of brothers, nor any other of the things owed to us by the law of love? For this is now the thirteenth year since the heretical war rose up against us, in which the afflictions of the churches have become greater than any recorded since the Gospel of Christ has been proclaimed. To relate to you each of these in detail we decline, lest the weakness of our speech should enfeeble the vividness of the evils; and at the same time we do not think that you need instruction, having long ago been taught the truth of these matters by report. But the sum of the evil is this: the people, abandoning the houses of prayer, gather in the deserts, a pitiable sight—women, and children, and old men, and others who are weak, in the most violent rains, and in snow and winds and the frost of winter, and likewise in summer under the blaze of the sun, suffering miserably in the open air. And they suffer this because they will not consent to become part of the wicked leaven of Arius.

How could speech set these things vividly before you, unless the very experience and the sight through the eyes should move you to compassion? So we exhort you now at least to stretch out a hand to the churches of the East, already bent to their knees, and to send some men to remind us of the rewards laid up for the endurance of sufferings for Christ. For the familiar word does not work so powerfully as a strange voice produces consolation, especially when it comes from men everywhere known by the grace of God for their highest virtues, such as report proclaims you to be among all men—men who have remained unwounded in the faith, who have kept the apostolic deposit inviolate. But our affairs are not so; rather we have certain men who, from desire of glory and from that self-conceit which most of all overthrows the souls of Christians, have grown bold with certain innovations of words, whence the churches, weakened, like loosened vessels, have received the heretical corruption that flowed into them. But you, our beloved and most longed-for, be physicians to the wounded and trainers of the healthy, healing what is sick and anointing what is sound for piety.

To the bishops of Italy and Gaul, concerning the condition and confusion of the churches. To the truly most God-beloved and most longed-for brothers and like-minded fellow-ministers, the bishops throughout Gaul and Italy, Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, who consented to call the whole Church of God his own body, and showed us, each one, to be members of one another, granted to us all to have intimacy toward all, according to the harmony of the members. Therefore, even if we are very widely separated from one another in our dwellings, yet by the principle of conjunction we are near to one another. Since, then, the head cannot say to the feet, 'I have no need of you,' surely you too will not endure to disown us, but will sympathize with our afflictions, to which we have been delivered for our sins, as much as we rejoice with you who are glorified in the peace that the Lord has granted you. Already, indeed, at other times we have cried out to your love for our succour and sympathy; but doubtless, because the vengeance has not yet been fulfilled, you were not permitted to rouse yourselves to the succour we seek. For we desire above all that, through your Reverence, our confusion should be made plain even to him who rules over your part of the world; and, if this is difficult, at least that some should come from you to visit and console the afflicted, in order that they may set before your eyes the sufferings of the East, which it is impossible to take in by hearing, since no words can be found to set our condition vividly before you.

A persecution has overtaken us, most honoured brothers, and the heaviest of persecutions. For shepherds are persecuted, that the flocks may be scattered. And the heaviest thing is this: that those who are ill-treated neither receive their sufferings in the full assurance of martyrdom, nor do the people honour the contestants in the rank of martyrs, because the name of Christians is attached to the persecutors. There is one charge now severely prosecuted: the exact keeping of the traditions of the fathers. For this reason the pious are driven from their homelands and removed to the deserts. Gray hairs are not respected by the judges of injustice, nor the practice of piety, nor a way of life according to the Gospel carried through from youth to old age. But while no malefactor is condemned without proofs, bishops have been convicted on mere calumny, and, with no proof brought forward for the charges, are handed over to punishments. Some have neither known their accusers, nor seen courts, nor were even slandered to begin with, but, violently seized in the dead of night, were driven into exile, delivered over to death by the hardships of the wilderness. And the things that follow upon these are known to all, even if we keep silent: flights of presbyters, flights of deacons, and the plundering of all the clergy. For one must either worship the image or be handed over to the wicked flame of the scourges. There are groanings of peoples, continual weeping both in houses and in public, while all lament to one another what they suffer. For no one is so stone-hearted that, bereft of his father, he bears his orphanhood meekly. There is a sound of mourners in the city, a sound in the fields, in the roads, in the deserts. One voice from all, uttering pitiable and gloomy things. Joy and spiritual gladness are taken away. Our festivals have been turned into mourning; the houses of prayer have been shut up; idle are the altars of spiritual worship. No longer are there gatherings of Christians, no longer the presidency of teachers, no saving instructions, no festal assemblies, no nightly hymn-singing, no longer that blessed exultation of souls which comes upon the souls of those who believe in the Lord at the assemblies and the communion of spiritual gifts. To us it is fitting to say: 'There is in this time no ruler, nor prophet, nor leader, nor offering, nor incense, no place to bring fruit before the Lord and to find mercy.'

These things we write to those who know them, because there is no part of the world that has not by now learned of our calamities. So that you ought not to think we make these statements for the sake of instruction, nor to remind your harmonious selves. For we know that you would never forget us, no more than a mother forgets the offspring of her womb. But since those held fast by some overwhelming pain are wont somehow to lighten their pains through groanings, this we too do; we, as it were, unload the weight of our grief by announcing to your love our manifold calamities—if perhaps, moved more vehemently to your prayers on our behalf, you may beseech the Lord to be reconciled to us. If, then, afflictions alone were what wore us down, we might have counselled ourselves to keep quiet and to rejoice in our sufferings for Christ, since 'The sufferings of the present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us.' But as it is, we fear lest the evil, growing—like some flame that travels through burning matter and, when it has consumed what is near, lays hold also of what is far off—since the evil of the heresy spreads, and there is fear lest, having devoured our churches, it creep at last upon the healthy part of your region also. Perhaps, then, because sin abounded among us, we were the first to be handed over for devouring to the raw-eating teeth of the enemies of God; or perhaps—what is even more likely to conjecture—because the Gospel of the kingdom, beginning from our regions, went out into all the world, for this reason the common enemy of our souls strives to spread the seeds of apostasy, taking their beginning from these same regions, into all the world. For upon those on whom the illumination of the knowledge of Christ shone, upon these he contrives that the darkness of impiety should come too.

Reckon our sufferings, then, as your own, as genuine disciples of the Lord. It is not for money, nor for glory, nor for any other of the temporary things that we are fought against, but for the common possession, the ancestral treasure of sound faith, that we stand contending. Suffer along with us, O lovers of the brethren, that the mouths of the pious are shut among us, while every bold and blasphemous tongue of those who speak injustice against God is opened. The pillars and the support of the truth are in dispersion, while we, overlooked because of our smallness, are without freedom of speech. Be in anguish for the peoples; and do not look to your own case only, that you are anchored in calm harbours, the grace of God having granted you every shelter from the tempest of the spirits of wickedness. But stretch out a hand also to the storm-tossed churches, lest, being forsaken, they utterly suffer the shipwreck of the faith. Groan over us, that the Only-begotten is blasphemed, and there is no one to gainsay it. The Holy Spirit is set at naught, and he who is able to refute is driven away. Polytheism has prevailed. With them there is a great God and a small one. The name 'Son' is held to be not a name of nature, but an appellation of a certain honour; the Holy Spirit is held to be not the completion of the Holy Trinity, nor a sharer in the divine and blessed nature, but one of the things that come from the creation, thrown in at random and as it chanced with the Father and the Son. Who will give water to my head, and to my eyes a fountain of tears? And I will weep for the people many days, the people who are being thrust toward destruction by these wicked teachings. The ears of the simpler are swept away; they have come at last into the habit of the heretical impiety. The infants of the Church are reared up together with the words of impiety. For what shall they do? Baptisms are with them, funeral processions for the departing, visitations of the sick, consolations of the grieving, helps for the worn-down, succours of every kind, communions of the mysteries—all of which, performed by them, becomes a bond to the peoples of concord with them; so that, when a little time has gone by, even if some freedom should come, there is no longer hope that those held fast by the long-standing deception can again be called back to the knowledge of the truth.

For these reasons many of us ought to have hastened together to your Reverence, and each to become an expositor of his own affairs. But as it is, let this very thing be a proof to you of the hardship in which we live: that we are not even masters of our own travel. For if anyone should withdraw even for the briefest time from his own church, he will leave the people surrendered to those lying in wait. But by the grace of God we have sent one in place of many, our most reverent and beloved brother Dorotheus, the fellow-presbyter; who is able, by his own narration, to fill up whatever has escaped our letters, since he has followed all things with exactness, and is a zealot for the right faith. Receive him in peace and send him back to us quickly, bearing us good tidings of the zeal you have for the succour of the brotherhood.
To Patrophilus, bishop of the church at Aegae.

I read your letter, which you sent through our brother Strategius the fellow-presbyter, and I read it with pleasure. For how could I not, when it was written both by a man of understanding and from a heart taught, by the commandment of the Lord, to perfect love toward all? And I came near to recognizing the cause of your silence in the time past. For you seemed to be at a loss and astounded, that the Basil who from boyhood had served so-and-so in such a way, who had done this in such circumstances and that, who had taken up the war against the many for the sake of serving the one—that this man had now become another out of another, and had taken up war in place of love; and all the other things you wrote, sufficiently showing the bewilderment of your soul at the unexpected change of affairs. And if you also rebuked us in anything, I did not take this with displeasure. For I am not so beyond admonition as to be offended at the loving rebukes of the brethren. So far am I from being vexed at what you wrote, that I almost laughed at it—that, when so many and so great were the things which seemed to confirm our friendship for one another before, you yourself, over small matters that had reached you, wrote that you had suffered so great a bewilderment. Have you, then, suffered what the many suffer, who, leaving aside the examination of the nature of things, attend to the men whom the discussions concern, and become not examiners of the truth but assayers of the difference of persons, forgetting the exhortation that 'To recognize a person in judgement is not good'?

But since God does not accept the person of a man in judgement, the defence that I have prepared for the great tribunal, this I will not refuse to make known to you also. That nothing on our part, from the beginning, neither small nor great, became the cause of the separation; but men who hate us, for reasons which they themselves know (for it is not for me to say anything about them), made continual slanders, and once and twice we put these off; but as the thing was endless, and there was no use in continual defence—we being settled far away, while the false speakers had near at hand a heart easy to overcome and not taught to keep the other of its ears pure for the absent one, when it was wounded by their slanders against us—when the Nicopolitans demanded some assurance of faith, which surely you yourselves did not fail to know, it seemed good to us to undertake the service of the letter. For we reckoned to accomplish two things at once: both to persuade the Nicopolitans not to think ill of the man, and to stop the mouths of those who slandered us, since the agreement in the faith would shut out the calumnies from both sides. And indeed the creed was composed, and it was offered by us; and it was subscribed as it was subscribed, and a place for a second synod was indicated, and another time, in order that our brothers throughout the parish too, coming together, might be united with one another, and that the communion might be genuine and guileless for the future.

We, then, met at the appointed time, and the brothers with us, some were present and others kept flowing in, all of them bright and eager, as men running to peace; and there were letters from us, and day-runners signalling that we were present; for the place appointed for the reception of those who hastened together was ours. But when from the other side there was no one, neither running ahead nor announcing the coming of those expected, and those sent by us came back relating much dejection and grumbling on the part of those there, as though a new creed had been proclaimed by us; and they were said to be declaring firmly that they would by no means permit their bishop to cross over to us; and someone came bringing us also a letter, a perfunctory one, having no mention of the things agreed upon from the beginning. And the brother Theophilus, worthy of all my reverence and honour, sending one of those with him, made known certain things which he thought it fitting for him to say and proper for us to hear. For he did not see fit to write—not so much suspecting the proof from letters as taking care not to come into the necessity of addressing us as bishops; except indeed that the words were vehement, and brought forth from a heart heated. At these things we broke up, put to shame and fallen in spirit, having nothing to answer to those who asked. And not much time was in between, and a journey as far as Cilicia, and from there a return. And letters at once, holding a renunciation of communion with us.

And the cause of the rupture: that 'You wrote to Apollinaris,' he says, 'and you have our fellow-presbyter Diodorus in communion.' But I never considered Apollinaris an enemy, and there are matters in which I even respect the man; yet I did not so join myself to the man as to take his charges upon myself; since I myself have something to charge against him, having met with some of his writings. But concerning the Holy Spirit I do not know of any book that I either asked him for or received when sent. But I hear that he has become the most prolific of all writers, while I have met with few of his writings; for I have no leisure to search out such things, and at the same time I am somewhat reluctant toward the reception of newer authors, I whose body does not even allow me to persevere diligently, and in the manner one ought, in the reading of the divinely inspired Scriptures. What, then, is this to me, if someone has written something that does not please so-and-so? And yet, if one man must give account for another, let him who charges me on Apollinaris' behalf make his defence to us on behalf of Arius, his own teacher, and on behalf of Aetius, his own disciple. But we have neither been taught anything by, nor were disciples of, the man whose charges they turn upon us.

Diodorus, as a nursling of the blessed Silvanus, we received from the beginning; and now we both love and honour him for the grace of speech that belongs to him, through which many of those who meet him become better.

Disposed by this letter as was likely, and astounded at so unreasonable and sudden a change, I was unable even to make a reply. For my heart was bound fast, my tongue was paralysed, my hand was numbed; and I suffered the suffering of an ignoble soul (for the truth shall be told, though it deserves pardon): I almost fell into misanthropy, and every character seemed to me suspect, and the beauty of love seemed not to be in human nature, but to be a fine-faced word furnishing a kind of adornment to those who use it, while in truth this disposition does not exist in the heart of man. For if one who seemed from boyhood to deep old age to have made care of himself was so easily made savage from such pretexts, taking no account of any of our doings, nor setting the experience of the past as more authoritative than so worthless a slander, but, like some uncolted, untamed foal not yet taught to bear its rider well, from a small suspicion reared up and shook off and threw to the ground those in whom he formerly gloried—what must one suspect concerning others, toward whom we have neither so many pledges of friendship nor such a display of care for their conduct on their part? Unrolling these things by myself in my soul, and continually turning them over in my heart—or rather being turned over in heart by them, so did they bite and prick me through memory—I made no reply to that letter, having kept silent not out of disdain (do not think this, brother; for we make our defence not to men, but we speak before God in Christ), but out of bewilderment and helplessness and having nothing to say worthy of the grief.

While we were in this state, there overtook us another letter, written ostensibly to a certain Dazizas, but in truth sent to all men, as their so swift distribution shows—so that in a few days it was scattered over all Pontus and overran Galatia. And some say that the messengers of these good tidings, passing through Bithynia, reached as far as the Hellespont itself. What the things sent against us to Dazizas were, surely you know. For they do not place you so far from their friendship as to leave you alone unrewarded with that honour. But if the letter did not reach you, I am sending it to you. In it you will find us accused of deceit and trickery, of corruption of churches and destruction of souls, and—what they consider the truest of all—that we made that offering of the creed as a put-up job, not serving the Nicopolitans, but having ourselves guilefully contrived to obtain a confession. Of these things the Lord is judge; for what clear proof could there be of the reckonings in the heart? But this I marvelled at in them: that, whereas over the book offered by us they have made use of so great a divergence as to mix together both what is and what is not for the assurance of those who accuse them, yet they do not consider that in Rome a written confession of theirs of the faith of Nicaea is laid up; nor that with their own hand they delivered to the synod at Tyana the book from Rome, which is laid up with us, holding this same faith. And they have forgotten their own public speech, which, standing forth then in the midst, they made—lamenting the deception by which they were led to consent to the tome composed by the company of Eudoxius; because they devised this defence of that error: that, having gone to Rome, they received from there the faith of the fathers, so that the harm they did to the churches by their agreement with the evil they might set right by the introduction of the better. But those who undertook the longest journeys for the faith, and made these wise speeches, now revile us as going deceitfully, and as doing the deeds of plotters under the appearance of love. And the things now being circulated show that they have condemned the faith of Nicaea. For they saw Cyzicus, and came back with another faith.

And why do I speak of the changeableness in their words, when I have far greater proofs, from the very facts, of their turning to the opposite? For those who would not yield to a decree of five hundred bishops brought forth against them, nor consent to withdraw from the administration of the churches, when so many agreed in the judgement of their deposition—because, they say, those bishops were not partakers of the Holy Spirit, nor administering the churches by the grace of God, but had snatched the offices of presidency by human power and desire of empty glory—these same men now receive as bishops those ordained by them. Ask them in my stead: if they despise all men also, as having neither eyes, nor ears, nor a perceiving heart, at least enough to be able to see the inconsistency of what has been done—what thought do they have in their own heart? How can there be two bishops, both the one deposed by Euippius and the one ordained by him? For both are the work of the same hand. And if he did not have the grace given to Jeremiah, to pull down and to build up, to root out and to plant, he would neither have rooted out the one nor planted the other. But if you grant him the one, you will concede to him the other also. But there is one aim, it seems: to seek their own everywhere, and to consider a friend the one who works together with their desires, but to judge an enemy, and to spare no slander against him, the one who resists their desires.

For such, too, are their present administrations against the Church. Fearful, because of the easy-going temper of those who do them; pitiable, because of the insensibility of those who suffer them. Children of Euippius and grandchildren of Euippius, summoned back from exile through a trustworthy embassy to Sebasteia, were entrusted with the people. They took over the altar; they became a leaven to the church there. By these men we are persecuted as consubstantialists. But Eustathius, who carried in the papyrus from Rome as far as Tyana the term 'consubstantial,' he is now mingled with them—even though he could not be received into their much-desired communion, either because they feared the multitude of those who had agreed against him, or because they were ashamed of the trustworthiness of those witnesses. For who those gathered were, and how each was ordained, and from what kind of former life he came now to this power, may I never have so much leisure as to recount their deeds. For I have learned to pray: 'That my mouth may not speak the works of men.' But you, searching it out, will learn; and even if it escapes you, it will surely not escape the Judge. The suffering I suffered, however, I will not refuse to tell to your love as well: that last year, falling sick with a most violent fever, and coming as far as the very gates of death, then recalled by the loving-kindness of God, I was reluctant to return, reckoning into what evils I was coming again; and I pondered within myself what at last it could be that was laid up in the depth of the wisdom of God, on account of which days of life in the flesh were granted me again. But when I considered these things, I reckoned that the Lord wished us to see the churches ceasing from the storm which they had suffered before this, at the separation of those who were trusted in everything because of their assumed dignity. Or perhaps the Lord wished to brace my soul and make it more watchful for what lay ahead, so as not to attend to men, but to be perfected through the evangelical commandments, which change neither with the seasons nor with the circumstances of human affairs, but remain the same, as they were brought forth from the truthful and blessed mouth, so abiding forever.

But men are like the clouds, borne now to one part of the air, now to another, according to the changes of the winds. And these especially, of whom is our discourse, have appeared the most shifty of all who have come within our experience. Whether also in the other affairs of life those who lived with them might have something to say, what at any rate appeared to me, the changeableness about their faith, I do not know to this day whether I have ever in others either myself observed or heard from others. They followed Arius from the beginning; they went over to Hermogenes, who was diametrically the enemy of the false doctrine of Arius, as the very creed of Nicaea shows, which was uttered by that man at the beginning. Hermogenes fell asleep, and again they went over to Eusebius, a leading man of the Arian circle, as those who tried them say. Falling away from there for whatever reasons, again they ran back to their homeland, and again they hid the Arian opinion. Having come to the episcopate—to pass over the things in between—how many creeds they set forth: at Ancyra one, another at Seleucia, another at Constantinople, the much-talked-of one, another at Lampsacus, after that the one at Nice in Thrace, now again the one at Cyzicus; of which I do not know the rest, but I hear this much, that, having silenced the term 'consubstantial,' they now bring forward 'like in substance,' and compose, together with Eunomius, blasphemies against the Holy Spirit. And of these creeds which I have enumerated, even if they are not all contrary to one another, yet they likewise establish the changeableness of their character, because they have never stood by the same words. These things are true, while countless others are left unsaid.

But since they have now crossed over to you as well, we ask you to write back through the same man (I mean our fellow-presbyter Strategius), whether you have remained the same toward us, or whether you too have been altered by the meeting. For neither was it likely that those men would keep silent, nor that you yourself, who wrote such things to us, would not use your freedom of speech toward them as well. If, then, you should remain in communion with us, this is best and worthy of the highest prayer; but if they have transferred you to themselves, this is grievous. For how is it not the separation of such a brother? Yet, if nothing else, at any rate we have been sufficiently trained, by those very men, to bear such losses.
To Theophilus the bishop.

Having long ago received the letter from your love, I waited to write back through a trustworthy person, so that the bearer of the letter might fill up whatever should escape the letter. Since, then, our most longed-for and most reverent brother Strategius has come to us, I thought it just to make use of him as my agent, since he both knows our mind and is able to deliver our message both genuinely and reverently.

Know, then, most longed-for and most honoured of men, that we count of great worth our love toward you—from which, so far as the disposition of the soul is concerned, we are not conscious of having departed for a single hour, even though many and great occasions for reasonable grief have arisen. But we judged this, as in a balance, setting the more agreeable things against the more unpleasant, to attach our mind to the inclination of the better. But since affairs have been altered by those by whom least of all it ought to have happened, forgive us too, who have not altered our mind, but have changed our position. Or rather, we remain in the same position, while it is others who are continually shifting, and who now even openly desert to the adversaries—men whose communion we counted of how great worth, while they were on the sound side, you yourself are not ignorant. But now, if we neither follow those men nor turn away from those who think the same as they, we should justly obtain pardon, setting nothing before the truth and our own safety.
To the Nicopolitans.

When I see both the evil prospering and your Reverence wearied and giving out before the continuance of the outrages, I am filled with despondency. But when again I consider the great hand of God, and that he knows how to set upright those who have been broken down, and to love the just, but to crush the proud and bring down the mighty from their thrones, then, changing, I become lighter in my hopes, and I know that, through your prayers, the Lord will quickly show us calm. Only do not grow weary in praying; but of those things of which you are teachers in word, be eager, in the present season, to set before all visible examples in deed.
To the Nicopolitans.

When I read the letter of your Holiness, how I groaned and lamented that with my own ears I had received these evils too: blows and outrages against your very selves, the sacking of houses, the desolation of the city, the overturning of a whole homeland, the persecution of the church and the flight of the priests, the rising up of wolves, and the scattering of the flocks. But when I had ceased from my groaning and my tears, looking to the Master in the heavens, I know and am persuaded—what I wish you also to know—that the help will be swift, and the forsaking will not be to the end. For what we have suffered, we have suffered because of our sins; but his help the lover of mankind will show, because of his love and tender mercy toward his churches.

Nor, indeed, while we were present, did we fail to entreat those in power, and to write to those who love us at the imperial court, that the raging man's wrath might be checked. And I think condemnation will come upon him from many, unless perhaps the season, being full of tumult, gives no leisure for these matters to those in charge of affairs.
To Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium.

When we look to our own desire, we are grieved at being so far separated from your Reverence; but when we look to the peacefulness of your way of life, we give thanks to the Lord, who has snatched your Reverence from this conflagration, which has consumed more of our region. For the just judge gave us, according to our works, an angel of Satan, sufficiently buffeting us, and vehemently championing the heresy; and he has carried the war against us so far as not even to spare the blood of those who have believed in God. For surely it did not escape your love that a certain Asclepius, because he would not choose communion with Doeg, being struck by them, died under the blows—or rather, through the blows was translated to life. And consider all the rest to follow upon that: persecutions of presbyters and teachers, and all the other things that men would do who use the power that comes from office for their own will. But the release from these things the Lord will give us by your prayers, and the endurance also, so that we may bear the weight of the trials worthily of our hope in him.

And do you yourself count us worthy to write to us continually about your own affairs. And if you find anyone of those faithful to you who is able to convey the book we have laboured over, count us worthy to send for it, so that, taking courage from your judgement, we may send it abroad into the hands of others as well. In good health, in good cheer in the Lord, praying earnestly, may you be granted to me and to the Church of the Lord, by the grace of the Holy One.
Without address, on behalf of a devout man.

I rejoice with this brother, both that he is being delivered from the tumults here and that he is reaching your Reverence. For he has chosen for himself a good provision for the age to come, a good way of life among those who fear the Lord. We commend him to your Honour, and I beg you to pray, through him, for our pitiable life, that, delivered from these trials, we may begin to serve the Lord according to the Gospel.
To Patrophilus, bishop of the church at Aegae.

Late, indeed, I received the answers to my earlier letter, yet I received them nevertheless through the most longed-for Strategius, and I gave thanks to the Lord that you remain the same in your love toward us. And the things you have now seen fit to write concerning the same subject hold proof of your good purpose, that you think what is fitting and counsel us what is profitable.

But, since again I see my discourse becoming longer for me, if I should mean to answer each of the things written by your discernment, I say only this: that the good of peace, if it is circumscribed in the name of peace alone, is ridiculous—to choose this man and that man, and to share the keeping of peace with these alone, but to shut out countless others from fellowship in the good. And if agreement with the harmful, under the appearance of peace, makes those who receive them do the work of enemies, consider who they are with whom they have mingled themselves. It is not those who hated us with unjust hatred, but those of the party of those who are out of communion with us; for I have no need now to mention them by name. These men were both invited by them to Sebasteia, and took over the church, and ministered at the altar, and shared their own bread with all the people, being proclaimed bishops by the clergy there and throughout the whole country, and sent on their way by them as holy men and in communion. If one must choose their party, it is ridiculous to begin from the claws and not to converse with their very heads.

If, then, one must in general consider no one a heretic, nor turn away from anyone, for what reason, tell me, do you separate yourself and withdraw from communion with certain men? But if there are some to be avoided, let them tell us, by the rule of strictness—they who are exact in all things—of what party are those whom they brought to themselves from Galatia.

If, then, these things appear to you worthy of grief, reckon the separation to the authors of them; but if you judge them indifferent, forgive us for not consenting to become part of the leaven of those who teach otherwise. So that, if it seems good, leaving aside those fair-faced arguments, with all freedom of speech refute those who do not walk uprightly toward the truth of the Gospel.
To the People of Euaesae

Although the mass of affairs that surround us is great, and our mind is held fast by countless cares, yet we have never cast from our memory our concern for your love, praying to our God that you may continue in the faith in which you stand and in which you boast in hope of the glory of God. For in truth it has become hard to find, and altogether rare, to see a Church that is pure, in no way harmed by the difficulty of the times, but preserving the apostolic teaching whole and unbroken — such as He who in every generation shows forth those who are worthy of His calling has shown your Church to be in these present times.

And may the Lord grant you the good things of the Jerusalem that is above, in return for your having sent back upon the heads of the liars the false slanders they uttered against us, refusing to give them entrance into your hearts. And I know and am persuaded in the Lord that your reward is great in heaven for this deed also. For you reasoned this wisely among yourselves — and it is so in truth — that those who repay me evil for good, and hatred in return for my love toward them, now slander me on the very points for which they themselves are found to have set down written confessions.

And they fell into this contradiction not only by bringing forward their own written accusations against you, but also in that, having been deposed by unanimous vote of those who assembled at Constantinople, they did not accept their deposition, calling those men a synod that set the canons at nought, and refusing to grant them the title of bishops, so that they might not ratify the verdict pronounced against themselves. And they added, as the reason these men were not bishops, that they presided, so they say, over a wicked heresy. But this took place not quite seventeen full years ago. Now the leaders of those who deposed them were Eudoxius, Euippius, George, Acacius, and the rest of their party; and those who now hold those Churches are their successors, some ordained in their place, others advanced by those very men.

Now then, let those who charge us with false doctrine tell us this: how were those men heretics, whose deposition these refused to accept, and how are these men orthodox, who were advanced by those men and who preserve the same mind as their fathers? For if Euippius is orthodox, how is Eustathius, deposed by him, not a layman? And if that man was a heretic, how is the one now advanced by his hand in communion with Eustathius? But these are games, played against the Churches of God, by men who set about both to slander people and again to restore them, as suits their own advantage.

Eustathius, passing through Paphlagonia, overturned the altars of Basilides the Paphlagonian, and ministered at his own tables; and now he is a suppliant of Basilides, asking to be received. He excluded our most reverent brother Elpidius for his association with the people of Amaseia; and now he is a suppliant of the people of Amaseia, seeking their fellowship. And you yourselves know how dreadful were the things proclaimed against Euippius. And now he exalts as orthodox those who hold that man's views, provided only that they assist in his eagerness for his own restoration. But we are slandered — not because we do any wrong, but because he thought this would bring him credit with the people of Antioch. As for the men whom they summoned last year from Galatia, supposing that through them they could recover the open standing of their episcopate, they are such as even those who have spent a little time with them know them to be. May the Lord never grant me such leisure as to reckon up their deeds! Yet, escorted by the most honoured of their bodyguard and fellow-initiates, they passed through their whole country, receiving the honours and attentions due to bishops; and they were brought conspicuously into the city, holding assembly with full authority. For the people were handed over to them, the altar was handed over to them. And when, having advanced as far as Nicopolis, they could accomplish none of the things they had promised, how they returned, and how they appeared on their return, those who were present know. So they are always seen to do everything for their own advantage. But if they say that they have repented, let them show their repentance in writing, with an anathema upon the faith set forth at Constantinople, and a separation from the heretics, and let them not deceive the simpler folk. And such are their affairs.

But we, beloved brethren, small and lowly though we are, yet ever the same by the grace of God, have never altered ourselves with the changes of circumstances. With us there is not one faith at Seleucia and another at Constantinople, and another at Zela, and another at Lampsacus, and yet another at Rome; and the faith now in circulation is not different from those before, but always one and the same. For as we received from the Lord, so we are baptized; as we are baptized, so we believe; as we believe, so also we give glory — neither separating the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, nor setting It before the Father, nor saying that the Spirit is older than the Son, as the tongues of the blasphemers contrive. For who is so reckless that, thrusting aside the Lord's own ordinance, he dares to invent his own order for the names? But neither do we say that the Spirit, ranked together with the Father and the Son, is created, nor do we dare to call servile that which is sovereign. And we exhort you, mindful of the threat of the Lord who said, "Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven to men; but the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come," — guard yourselves against the teachings that are harmful to the Spirit. Stand fast in the faith; look round upon the whole inhabited world, and see that this diseased part is small, but all the rest of the Church, which from end to end of the earth has received the Gospel, abides in this sound and undistorted teaching. From their communion we too pray that we may not fall away, and we join in praying that you may receive your portion on the righteous day of our Lord Jesus Christ, when He shall come to render to each according to his deed.
To the Bishops of the Pontic Diocese

The honours paid to the martyrs are an earnest concern for all who have set their hope upon the Lord, but especially for you who lay claim to virtue, who through your disposition toward those of your fellow-servants who are held in good esteem display your goodwill toward our common Master — all the more because the life lived with exactness has a certain kinship with those who were perfected through endurance. Since, then, the most distinguished of the martyrs, Eupsychius and Damas and the company around them — whose memory is celebrated throughout the year by our city and by all the surrounding country — call you to mind, the Church, which is their own proper adornment, exhorts you through our voice to take up again the ancient custom of visiting her. Therefore, since a great work lies before you among a people that seeks the building-up you can give, and since a reward is laid up for you in the honour shown to the martyrs, receive our exhortation and consent to the favour, conferring on us a great benefit at the cost of a little labour.
To the Presbyters of Antioch
