The care which you have for the Churches of God will in part be set at rest by our most beloved and most reverent brother Sanctissimus, our fellow-presbyter, who has recounted the love and disposition toward us of the whole West; and in part it will rouse you up and stir you on the more, when he sets plainly before you in his own person how much diligence the present circumstances demand. For while each of the others reported to us, as it were by halves, both the opinions of the men there and the state of affairs, he himself — being competent both to grasp the purpose of men and to investigate accurately the state of affairs — will tell you everything, and will guide your good zeal toward every task. So you have matter befitting that perfect purpose of yours which you have always shown in your cares for the Churches of God.
To Pelagius, Bishop of Laodicea in Syria

May the Lord grant that I too may one day come into the presence of your true godliness, and that we may supply by our presence all that we have left wanting in our letter. For we have begun to write late, and we have great need of an excuse. But since our most beloved and most reverent brother Sanctissimus, our fellow-presbyter, is present, he himself will recount to you everything, both our affairs and those from the West. In these latter he will indeed gladden you; but in telling of the troubles that have held us fast, he will perhaps add some grief and care to those already laid up in your good heart. Yet it is not without use that you, who are able to move the Lord by your supplication, should grieve; for your care will turn out to our profit, and I know that we shall obtain help from God, having the cooperation of your prayers. And if you join in praying for us that we may be delivered from our cares, and ask for some increase to the strength of our body, the Lord will give us a prosperous way, so that our desire may be fulfilled and we may come into the presence of your good order.
To Vitus, Bishop of Carrhae

Would that it were possible for me to write to your reverence every single day! For ever since I came to know your love by experience, I have a great longing — above all to live together with you, but if that may not be, at least to write and to receive letters, so that I may both make known my own affairs and learn how it is with you. But since we do not have all that we wish, but only what the Lord gives, and these things we ought to receive with thanksgiving, we have given thanks to the holy God, who has provided us with an occasion for writing to your reverence: the arrival of our most beloved and most reverent brother Sanctissimus, our fellow-presbyter, who, having endured great toil in his journey, will recount to you with exactness all that he found in the West. For these things too we ought to give thanks to the Lord and to worship Him, that He may grant the same peace to us also, and that we may receive one another in freedom. Greet from us all the brotherhood in Christ.

To his most beloved and most reverent brethren, his fellow-presbyters Acacius, Aetius, Paul, and Silvanus, and to the deacons Silvinus and Lucius, and to the rest of the monastic brethren, Basil the bishop.

When I heard of that grievous persecution raised against you, and that, immediately after Easter, those who had fasted only for quarrels and brawls fell upon your dwellings and gave your labours to the fire — for you preparing the house in heaven not made with hands, for themselves storing up that fire which they used to harm you — I groaned at what had happened, not, brethren, out of grief for you (far from it!), but for those so plunged beneath wickedness as to stretch their own malice to such lengths. And I expected that you would all run at once, as to a ready refuge, to our lowliness; and I held it in hope that the Lord would grant me a respite from my continual pains by my embracing you, and that, receiving upon this idle body of mine the noble sweat which you shed for the truth, I might have some share in the prizes laid up for you by the Judge of truth. But since this never even came into your minds, and you did not expect to find any rest with us, I longed at least to find continual occasions for letters to you, so that, like those who shout encouragement to athletes contending, I too might cry out to you something through letters to spur on your good struggle. But not even this was easy for us, for two reasons: one, that we did not know where you were living; the other, that there are not many who set out from us to come to you.

But now the Lord has brought to us our most beloved and most reverent brother Sanctissimus, our fellow-presbyter, through whom we both greet your love and exhort you to pray for us, rejoicing and exulting that your reward is great in heaven, and — since you have boldness toward the Lord — not to cease crying out to Him night and day, that this tossing of the Churches may cease, that the shepherds may be restored to their peoples, and that the Church may return to her proper dignity. For I am persuaded that, if a voice be found to move the Good One by supplication, He will not be long in showing His mercies, but will at last grant us, together with the trial, also the way out, that we may be able to endure it. Greet from us all the brotherhood in Christ.
To the Monks Harassed by the Arians

The things I said within myself when I heard of the trial brought upon you by the enemies of God, these I thought it well to make known to you by letter: that in a time supposed to be one of peace you have won for yourselves the blessedness laid up for those who are persecuted for the name of Christ. For because a name gentle and mild is laid upon those who work wickedness, we ought not for that reason to suppose that their deeds also are not the deeds of enemies. For I judge war from one's own kindred to be the more grievous, in that it is easy to guard against enemies openly proclaimed, but against those mingled among us we must of necessity be exposed to every harm — which is what you too have suffered. For our fathers also were persecuted, but by idolaters; their substance was plundered, their houses overturned, and they themselves driven into exile, by those who warred openly against us for the name of Christ. But the persecutors who have now appeared hate us no less than those did, yet for the deceiving of the many they put forward the name of Christ, so that the persecuted may not even have the consolation that comes from confession — since the many and simpler folk acknowledge indeed that we are wronged, but do not reckon to us death for the truth as a martyrdom. Therefore I am persuaded that a greater reward is laid up for you from the righteous Judge than for the martyrs of old, seeing that those had as well the acknowledged approval of men, and were awaiting the reward from God, whereas for you, for equal achievements, the honours from the peoples do not exist. So it is likely that a recompense many times greater is laid up in the age to come for your toils on behalf of true religion.

Therefore we exhort you not to lose heart in your afflictions, but to renew yourselves in the love of God, and day by day to add to your zeal, knowing that in you the remnant of true religion must be preserved, which the Lord at His coming will find upon the earth. And if bishops have been driven from the Churches, let not this shake you; if traitors have sprung up from among the clergy themselves, let not even this unsettle your trust in God. For it is not the names that save us, but our purposes and our true love toward Him who created us. Consider that in the plot against our Lord also it was the chief priests and scribes and elders who contrived the treachery, and that few of the common people were found who genuinely received the word; and that it is not the multitude that is saved, but the elect of God. So let no crowding of a multitude ever dismay you — men who, like the water of the sea, are carried this way and that by the winds. For even if one alone be saved, as Lot in Sodom, he ought to abide by the right judgment, holding unshaken his hope in Christ, since the Lord will not forsake His holy ones. Greet from me all the brotherhood in Christ. Pray genuinely for my pitiable soul.
To Epiphanius the Bishop

What was long ago foretold by the prediction of the Lord, and is now at last confirmed by the experience of events — that because lawlessness is multiplied the love of the many shall grow cold — has by now prevailed among us; and so it seemed good to break open the letter that was brought from your honour. For it is no ordinary token of love, first to have remembered us, who are so small and worthy of nothing, and then to have sent brethren to visit us, men fit to be ministers of letters of peace. For there is no rarer sight than this, now that all are disposed toward all with suspicion. For nowhere is there compassion, nowhere fellow-feeling, no brotherly tear for a brother in distress. Neither persecutions for the truth, nor Churches groaning all together, nor this long catalogue of hardships that beset us, can move us to care for one another. But we leap upon the fallen, we scrape afresh the wounds, we who seem to share the same mind heighten the outrages of the heretics; and those who agree in the most vital matters are nonetheless divided from one another by some single point. How then shall we not marvel at the man who, amid such circumstances, displays a pure and guileless love toward his neighbours, and across so great a sea and continent as separates us bodily, bestows upon our souls such care as is possible?

I marvelled at this too in you, that you received with grief the dissension of the brethren on the Mount of Olives, and wish that some reconciliation may come about between them; and that not even the things contrived by certain persons, which brought disturbances upon the brotherhood, escaped you, but you took up the care for these matters also — and this I welcomed. But that other thing I no longer judged worthy of your good sense: to entrust to us the correction of matters so weighty — to men neither led by the grace of God, because we live with sins, nor possessing any power in argument, because, though we have gladly withdrawn from vain things, we have not yet taken up the proper habit in the doctrines of the truth. We have therefore already written to our beloved brethren on the Mount of Olives, to our own Palladius and to Innocent the Italian, in answer to what they wrote to us, that we can add nothing to the faith of Nicaea, not even the slightest thing, except the glorifying of the Holy Spirit, because our fathers mentioned this part only in passing, the question concerning it not having been stirred up at that time. But the doctrines woven on afterward to that faith, concerning the Lord's incarnation, as being deeper than our comprehension, we have neither examined nor accepted, knowing that, once we have disturbed the simplicity of the faith, we shall find no end of arguments, the controversy ever leading us on to more, and we shall throw into confusion the souls of the simpler folk by the introduction of strange notions.

As for the Church at Antioch — I mean that part which agrees in the same mind — may the Lord grant us one day to see it united. For this above all is in danger of having received the snares of the enemy, who bears it a grudge because it was there that the name of Christians was first given. And the heresy is cut off from the orthodox; but orthodoxy too is cut, even against itself. As for us, since the first to speak boldly for the truth and to contend that noble contest in the times of Constantius was the most reverend Meletius the bishop, and since my Church held him in communion, loving him exceedingly for that firm and unyielding constancy, we hold him in communion to this present day by the grace of God, and we will hold him so, if God will. For the most blessed Pope Athanasius too, when he came from Alexandria, greatly wished that communion with him should be brought about; but through the malice of advisers their union was put off to another time — as it ought not to have been. But of those who entered last we have not yet admitted any to communion — not judging them unworthy, but having nothing of which to convict them. And indeed we have heard many things from the brethren, but we did not admit them, because the accused did not stand face to face with their accusers, according to that which is written, "Does our law judge a man unless it first hear him and know what he does?" So we cannot yet write to them, most honoured brother, nor ought we to be compelled to this. But it would befit your peaceful disposition not to join the one and tear apart the other, but to bring what is divided into the union already existing. So first pray, and then, with all your power, exhort them to cast ambition out of their souls, and, for the sake of restoring strength to the Church and bringing down the arrogance of the enemies, to come to terms with one another. That too greatly comforted my soul which was added by your exactness to the rest that was nobly and exactly stated in theological terms: that it is necessary to confess three hypostases. So let the brethren at Antioch also be taught this by you — though surely they have been taught it already; for plainly you would not have chosen communion with them, had you not secured above all this part of their belief.

As for the nation of the Magousaeans — concerning which you deigned to inquire of us in the other letter — they are many among us, scattered over almost the whole country, settlers brought in to us of old from Babylonia. They follow peculiar customs, holding no intercourse with other men; and to use reason with them is altogether impossible, inasmuch as they have been taken captive by the devil unto his will. For they have neither books nor teachers of doctrines, but are reared in a senseless custom, the son receiving the impiety in succession from the father. Apart, then, from these things which are seen by all, they refuse the sacrifice of animals as a defilement, slaughtering by others' hands the animals they need for use; they are mad for unlawful marriages; they hold fire to be God; and the like. But as for any descent from Abraham, none of the Magi has down to the present told us any such tale; rather they name a certain Zarnouas as the founder of their race. So I have nothing further to write to your honour concerning them.
To Palladius and Innocent, Monks

How much I love you, you ought to guess from the love you yourselves bear toward us. I have always desired to be an arbiter of peace, and when I fail in this I am grieved — how could I not be? Yet I cannot for this reason bear enmity toward any, knowing that long ago the blessing of peace was taken away from us. And if the cause of the division lies with others, may the Lord grant that those who make the dissensions may cease. Nor indeed do I ask for your continual presence among us; so do not on this account even make excuses to me. For I know that men who have chosen the life of toil, and who always provide themselves the necessities by their own hands, cannot be long absent from their own homes. But wherever you may be, remember us, and pray for us, that we at least may have peace with ourselves and with God, no disturbance dwelling in our thoughts.
To Optimus the Bishop

Even apart from this I look gladly upon your good young men, both for the steadiness of their character beyond their years, and for their close attachment to your reverence — from which one may expect something great in them. But since I saw them coming to me with letters from you as well, I doubled my affection for them. And when I read the letter and saw in it both the providence of your disposition for the Churches and your diligence in the reading of the divine Scriptures, I gave thanks to the Lord, and I prayed for good things upon those who brought us such a letter, and before them upon the one who wrote it to us.

You inquired what solution there is to that much-discussed text, bandied about by everyone up and down: "Everyone who slays Cain shall loose seven vengeances." By this, for the present, you have first commended your own self, keeping exactly what Paul handed down to Timothy — for it is plain that you give heed to reading; and then you have roused up even us, who are old and already grown numb both with age and with the weakness of the body and with the multitude of afflictions, which, many of them now stirred up about us, have weighed down our life. Yet you have stirred us up, and, fervent in spirit, you bring us, frozen as we are like animals lying in their dens, back to a moderate wakefulness and a vital activity.

This text, then, can be understood simply, and can also admit of a manifold interpretation. The simpler sense, which can present itself readily to anyone, is this: that Cain must render a sevenfold punishment for the sins he committed. For it is not the part of a just judge to fix recompenses equal to equal, but the one who began the evil must of necessity pay what is owed with an addition, if he himself is to be made better by the punishments, and to make the rest more prudent by the example. Since, then, it has been ordained that Cain shall pay the penalty for his sins seven times over, "he who slays him," it says, "shall loose" this sentence decreed against him by the divine judgment. This is the meaning that falls to us here from the first reading.

But since the mind of the more diligent is apt to search out the depths, it asks how justice is fulfilled in the sevenfold, and what the "vengeances" are — whether the sins are seven, or whether the sin is one and the punishments seven upon the one. Now Scripture always limits the number of forgiveness of sins within seven. "How often," it says, "shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him?" (It is Peter speaking to the Lord.) "Until seven times?" Then the answer of the Lord: "I do not say to you, until seven times, but until seventy times seven." For the Lord did not pass on to another number, but, multiplying seven, set in it the bound of forgiveness. And after seven years the Hebrew was released from slavery; and seven weeks of years made the famous jubilee among the ancients, in which the land kept sabbath, debts were remitted, there was deliverance from slavery, and a new life was as it were established afresh from the beginning, the old in a manner receiving its consummation in the seven-fold number. And these things are figures of this present age, which, cycling round through the seven days, runs past us; in which the payments are made for the more moderate sins, according to the loving care of the good Master, that we may not be delivered over to the endless age for punishment. The "seven times," then, is on account of the kinship with this world — since those who love the world ought to be chastised most by the very things for the sake of which they chose to do wickedly. And as for the "vengeances," whether you take them as the sins committed by Cain, you will find seven; or as those brought upon him by the judge, in that case too you will not fail of the meaning. Now in the things ventured by Cain the first sin is envy at the preference of Abel; the second is the guile with which he conversed with his brother, saying, "Let us go out into the plain"; the third is the murder, an addition of evil; the fourth, that it was also the murder of a brother, a greater intensification; the fifth, that Cain was also the first murderer, leaving an evil example to life; the sixth wrong, that he made grief for his parents; the seventh, that he lied to God — for being asked, "Where is Abel your brother?" he said, "I do not know." Seven, then, were the vengeances that were to be loosed by the slaying of Cain. For when the Lord said, "Cursed is the earth, which opened to receive your brother's blood," and "Groaning and trembling shall you be upon the earth," Cain says: "If you cast me out today from the earth, and I shall be hidden from your face, and I shall be groaning and trembling upon the earth, then everyone who finds me shall kill me." To this the Lord says: "Not so; everyone who slays Cain shall loose seven vengeances." For since Cain thought he was easy prey for everyone, because he had no security upon the earth (for the earth was cursed because of him) and was bereft of help from God, who was angry with him for the murder, so that no succour was left him either from earth or from heaven — "Everyone who finds me," he says, "shall kill me" — the word convicts him of his error, saying "Not so," that is, "you shall not be slain." For death is a gain to those who are punished, bringing release from sorrows. But you shall be kept alive, that the chastisements may be meted out to you according to the desert of your sins. And since "that which is avenged" is understood in two ways — both the sin for which the vengeance is taken, and the manner of the punishment by which the vengeance is taken — let us see whether seven kinds of torments were brought upon the one who did the wickedness.

The seven sins of Cain, then, the argument reckoned up in what went before. Now we inquire whether there are seven punishments brought upon him for chastisement, and we say thus. After the question of the Lord, "Where is Abel your brother?" — which the loving Master brought forward not wishing to learn, but to provide him an occasion for repentance, as the very words show — for when he denied it, the Lord makes the conviction swift, saying, "The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me." So the "Where is Abel your brother?" gave that man an occasion for the awareness of his sin; it did not become for God the means of instruction. For if he had not met with God's visitation, he would have had a pretext, as one forsaken and given no occasion for repentance. But now the physician appeared to him, that the sick man might flee to him. Yet he not only does not hide the sore, but works another besides, joining a lie to the murder: "I do not know. Am I my brother's keeper?" From here, then, count the punishments. "Cursed is the earth because of you." One punishment. "You shall till the earth." This is the second. For an unspeakable necessity was yoked to him, driving him to the tilling of the earth, so that not even when he wished was he permitted to rest, but he was forever to be wearied at his hostile earth, which he himself made cursed for himself, defiling it with a brother's blood. "You shall till the earth" — a dread punishment, the life among those who hate, to have an enemy for a housemate, a foe that never ceases. "You shall till the earth"; that is, strained by the labours of husbandry, you shall have no respite at any time, released from your toils neither by night nor by day, but having an unspeakable necessity harsher than some bitter master, rousing you to the work. "And it shall not yield to you its strength." And yet, even if the ceaseless labour had borne some fruit, the toil itself was no slight torment to one forever strained and wearied. But since the toil about the earth is both ceaseless and fruitless (for it did not give its strength), this is the third punishment, the fruitlessness of his toils. "Groaning and trembling shall you be upon the earth." He added two others to the three: continual groaning, and a trembling of the body, the limbs no longer having the support that comes from strength. For since he had used the power of the body wickedly, its vigour was taken from him, so that he shook and was convulsed, able neither easily to bring bread to his mouth nor to convey drink — the wicked hand, after the unholy deed, being no longer permitted to minister even to the body's own necessary needs. Another punishment, which Cain himself revealed, saying: "If you cast me out now from the earth, I shall also be hidden from your face." What is "If you cast me out from the earth"? That is, if you separate me from the benefit it gives. For he was not removed to another place, but estranged from its good things. "And I shall be hidden from your face." The heaviest punishment to the right-minded is separation from God. "And it shall be," he says, "that everyone who finds me shall kill me." He conjectures from the consequence of what went before: if I have been cast out from the earth, if I shall be hidden from your face, it remains for me to be slain by everyone. What then says the Lord? "Not so." But He set a sign upon him. This is the seventh punishment, that the punishment is not even hidden, but is proclaimed beforehand to all by a manifest sign, that this is the worker of unholy deeds. For to one who reasons rightly the heaviest of punishments is shame, which we have learned concerning the judgment as well: that "these shall rise to eternal life, and these to shame and everlasting reproach."

There follows upon this a kindred question, that which was said by Lamech to his wives: "I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt; for if Cain was avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy times seven." And some think that Cain was slain by Lamech, as having lasted to that generation, in order that a longer punishment might be given. But this is not true. For he is shown to have committed two murders, from his own account. "I have slain a man and a young man"; the man to a wound, and the young man to a hurt. So a wound is one thing and a hurt another; and a man is one thing and a young man another. "For if Cain was avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy times seven." I am liable to undergo four hundred and ninety punishments, if the judgment of God upon Cain is just, so that he should pay seven chastisements. For he, as he did not learn to murder from another, so neither did he see a murderer undergoing punishment; but I, having before my eyes the one groaning and trembling and the greatness of the wrath of God, was not made prudent by the example. Therefore I am worthy to pay four hundred and ninety chastisements.

Some have ventured upon such an interpretation, not out of tune with the doctrine of the Church: that from Cain to the flood seven generations passed, and the punishment was brought upon all the earth, because of the great outpouring of sin. But the sin of Lamech does not need a flood for its cure, but Him who takes away the sin of the world. Reckon, then, from Adam to the coming of Christ the generations, and you will find, according to the genealogy of Luke, that the Lord was born in the seventy-seventh succession.

These things, then, have been examined to the best of my power, many of the points that might be examined being passed over, that we may not carry the discourse beyond the measure of a letter; but for your understanding even a few seeds suffice. For "give occasion to the wise," it says, "and he will be wiser," and "the wise man, receiving a word, will praise it and add to it."

The words of Symeon to Mary have nothing manifold or deep. "For Symeon blessed them, and said to Mary his mother: Behold, this one is set for the falling and the rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that is spoken against. And a sword shall pass through your own soul also, that the reasonings of many hearts may be revealed." In which I marvelled at this: how, passing by the foregoing as clear, you inquired after this one thing, "And a sword shall pass through your own soul also." And yet to me it seems no less perplexing how the same one is set for falling and rising, and what the sign that is spoken against is, than, thirdly, how a sword shall pass through Mary's soul.

I hold, then, that the Lord is set for the falling and rising — not of some falling and others rising, but of the worse in us falling down and the better rising up. For the appearing of the Lord is destructive of the bodily passions and rousing of the properties of the soul. As when Paul says, "When I am weak, then I am strong," the same one both is weak and is strong, but he is weak in the flesh and strong in the spirit. So too the Lord does not provide to some the occasions for falling and to others for rising. For those who fall, fall from the standing in which they once were. And it is plain that the unbeliever never stands, being always dragged along the ground with the serpent whom he follows. He has therefore nothing from which to fall, because he has been already cast down by his unbelief. So the first benefit is for the one standing in sin to fall and to die, then to live to righteousness and to rise, faith in Christ granting us both. Let the worse fall, that the better may find occasion for the rising. If fornication does not fall, chastity does not rise; if irrationality is not crushed, the rational part in us will not flourish. So then, "for the falling and rising of many."

"And for a sign that is spoken against." We have learned that in Scripture the cross is properly called a sign. For "Moses set the serpent upon a sign," that is, upon a cross. Or a sign is what indicates some marvellous and unseen thing, seen by the simpler, but understood by those quick in mind. Since, then, men do not cease wrangling about the incarnation of the Lord — some defining that He took a body, others that His coming was bodiless; some that He had a body capable of suffering, others that He fulfilled the dispensation through a body only in some appearance; and some that the body was earthy, others that it was heavenly; and some that His existence was before the ages, others that He had His beginning from Mary — for this reason He is "for a sign that is spoken against."

By "sword" he means the testing word, the discerner of thoughts, which pierces even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and is a discerner of thoughts. Since, then, every soul at the time of the Passion was subjected, as it were, to a certain discrimination, according to the saying of the Lord, who said, "You shall all be made to stumble in me," Symeon prophesies concerning Mary herself: that standing by the cross and seeing the things done and hearing the voices, after the testimony of Gabriel, after the ineffable knowledge of the divine conception, after the great display of the miracles, there will come, he says, a certain tossing about your soul too. For the Lord had to taste death for every man, and, becoming a propitiation for the world, to justify all in His blood. You too, then, who have been taught from above the things concerning the Lord — some discrimination shall touch you; that is, the sword. "That the reasonings of many hearts may be revealed" — he hints that, after the stumbling that came about at the cross of Christ both to the disciples and to Mary herself, a swift healing will follow from the Lord, confirming their heart in the faith toward Him. For so we saw Peter too, after stumbling, holding more firmly to the faith in Christ. The human, then, was shown to be unsound, that the strength of the Lord might be displayed.
To the People of Sozopolis

I have read your letter, most honoured brethren, which you sent concerning your affairs. And that you have taken us as partners in care, for the attention to matters necessary and worthy of zeal among you, we gave thanks to the Lord. But we groaned on hearing that, in addition to the disturbance brought upon the Churches by the Arians, and to the confusion which they have made concerning the doctrine of the faith, yet another novel utterance has appeared among you, casting the brotherhood into great distress — men, as you wrote to us, introducing things new and strange to the ears of the faithful, as though from the teaching of the Scriptures. For you wrote that there are certain ones among you who, as far as in them lies, dissolve the saving dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ, and set aside the grace of the great mystery, which was kept silent from the ages but made manifest in its own times, when the Lord, having gone through all that pertains to the care of the human race, at the last bestowed upon us His own coming. For He benefited His own creature, first through the patriarchs, whose lives were set forth as examples and rules for those who wish to follow in the footsteps of the saints and, by a zeal like theirs, to attain the perfection of good works. Then He gave the law as a help, ordaining it through angels by the hand of Moses; then prophets, foretelling the salvation that was to be; judges, kings, righteous men, working mighty deeds by a hidden hand. After all these, in the last of the days, He Himself was made manifest in the flesh, born of a woman, born under the law, that He might redeem those under the law, that we might receive the adoption.

If, then, the coming of the Lord in the flesh did not take place, the Redeemer did not give the price for us to death, nor did He break through the kingdom of death by Himself. For if what was ruled by death was one thing, and what was assumed by the Lord another, then death would not have ceased working its own works, nor would the sufferings of the God-bearing flesh have become our gain; He did not slay sin in the flesh; we who died in Adam were not made alive in Christ; what had fallen was not refashioned, what had been broken down was not set upright, what had been estranged through the deceit of the serpent was not made akin to God again. For all these things are done away with by those who say that the Lord came having a heavenly body. And what need was there of the holy Virgin, if the God-bearing flesh was not to be assumed from the lump of Adam? But who is so reckless as now to renew, through sophistical phrases and a supposed witness from the Scriptures, the doctrine of Valentinus, long ago silenced? For this impiety is no newer than the docetic heresy, but began long ago from the vain-minded Valentinus, who, having torn away a few phrases of the apostle, contrived for himself an impious fabrication — saying that the Lord took the form of a servant, and not the servant himself, and saying that the Lord came to be in fashion, but not that He Himself assumed the man. To these men these others seem to utter kindred things — men whom one should bewail, as they bring upon you these newfangled disturbances.

But to say that the sufferings of the man pass over to the Godhead itself is the work of those who in no way preserve consistency in their reasonings, and who do not know that the sufferings of flesh are one thing, of ensouled flesh another, and of a soul making use of a body another. For proper to flesh is to be cut and diminished and dissolved; and again, proper to ensouled flesh is to be wearied and to feel pain, to hunger and thirst and be overcome by sleep; while of a soul making use of a body are griefs and distresses and cares and the like. Of these, some are natural and necessary to the living being, while others, brought in through an ill-disposed will, arise from a life ill-trained and unexercised toward virtue. Hence the Lord is seen to have accepted the natural sufferings, for the confirmation of His true and not merely apparent incarnation, but to have put away the sufferings that come from vice — all that befoul the purity of our life — as unworthy of the undefiled Godhead. For this reason it is said that He was made in the likeness of sinful flesh — not in the likeness of flesh, as these men suppose, but in the likeness of sinful flesh — so that He took our flesh with its natural sufferings, but committed no sin. But as death, which is in the flesh, transmitted to us through Adam, was swallowed up by the Godhead, so also sin was utterly consumed by the righteousness that is in Christ Jesus; so that in the resurrection we recover the flesh, neither liable to death nor subject to sin.

These, brethren, are the mysteries of the Church; these are the traditions of the fathers. We solemnly charge every man who fears the Lord and awaits the judgment of God not to be carried away by various teachings. If anyone teaches otherwise and does not consent to the sound words of the faith, but, thrusting aside the oracles of the Spirit, makes his own teaching more authoritative than the evangelical doctrines, beware of such a one.

And may the Lord grant that we may one day come together with one another, so that all that has escaped our discourse we may supply through meeting face to face. For we have written to you few things out of many, not wishing to go beyond the measure of a letter, and at the same time being persuaded that for those who fear the Lord even a reminder in few words suffices.
To Urbicius, a Monk

You did well in writing to us, for you showed no small fruit of love; and do this continually. But do not suppose that you have any need of excuse when you write to us. For we know ourselves, and we know that for every man there is by nature an equality of like honour toward all, and that the points of superiority among us are not according to family, nor according to abundance of money, nor according to the frame of the body, but according to the superiority of the fear of God. So what hinders you, who fear the Master more, from being in this very respect greater than we? Write to us continually, then, and let us know how the brotherhood about you fares, and which members of the Church among you are in health — that we may know to whom we should write, and on whom we may rest. And since I hear that there are certain men who, with distorted suppositions, falsify the right doctrine concerning the incarnation of the Lord, I beseech them, through your love, to refrain from that absurd notion which some are reported to us to hold: that God Himself was turned into flesh, and did not assume the lump of Adam through holy Mary, but that He Himself, in His own Godhead, was changed into the material nature.

Now to refute this absurdity is altogether easy. But since the blasphemy carries its plainness in itself, I think that for one who fears the Lord even the bare reminder suffices. For if He was turned, then He was also altered. But far be it from us either to say or to think this, since God said, "I am, and I am not altered." Again, how did the benefit of the incarnation pass over to us, if our body, joined to the Godhead, did not become superior to the dominion of death? For He did not, by being turned, take to Himself His own body, which He would have taken on by His divine nature being thickened. And how was the incomprehensible Godhead circumscribed within the small bulk of a body, if the whole nature of the Only-begotten was turned?

But I think that no one who has a mind and possesses the fear of God suffers from this sickness. Yet since report came to me that some of those with your love are in this weakness of reasoning, I thought it necessary not to make my greeting bare, but to have in our letter something of such a kind as can build up the souls of those who fear the Lord. These things, then, we exhort: that you obtain correction in the manner of the Church, and that you keep yourselves from communion with the heretics, knowing that to be indifferent in these matters takes away our boldness before Christ.
To the Westerners

May the Lord our God, on whom we have set our hope, grant to each of you grace to attain the hope set before us, as great as the joy with which you have filled our hearts — both by the letter which you sent us through our most beloved fellow-presbyters, and by the fellow-feeling you showed us in our sorrows, as men clothed with bowels of compassion, according to what the aforesaid reported to us. For even though our wounds remain the same, yet it brings us some ease to have physicians ready, able, if they find the occasion, to bring a swift healing of our pains. Therefore again, through these beloved men, we both greet and exhort you: if the Lord grants you leave to come to us, do not shrink from visiting us. For the visiting of the sick is one of the greatest commandments. But if the good God and wise steward of our life reserves this grace for another time, then write to us whatever it befits you to write, for the consolation of the afflicted and the correction of the broken. For many are now the breakings of the Church, and great is our affliction over them; and there is no expectation of help from any other quarter, unless the Lord, through you who genuinely serve Him, sends out the healing.

Now the bold and shameless heresy of the Arians, having openly broken away from the body of the Church, abides in its own error, and harms us little, because their impiety is manifest to all. But those who have put on the skin of the sheep and present a gentle and mild appearance, while inwardly they tear without sparing the flocks of Christ, and — because they set out from among us — easily cast harm upon the simpler folk, these are the grievous ones, hard to guard against. These we ask your exactness to make publicly known to all the Churches throughout the East, so that either, walking uprightly, they may genuinely be with us, or, remaining in their perversity, may keep the harm to themselves alone, unable through unguarded communion to impart their own disease to those who draw near. And it is necessary to mention them by name, so that you yourselves may recognize those who work disturbances among us, and may make it clear to our Churches. For a word from us is suspect to the many, as though perhaps we had chosen this pettiness toward them out of certain private quarrels; but you, the further removed you are from them, so much the more credit do you have among the peoples — besides that the grace of God assists you in your care for the oppressed. And if more of you together decree the same things in agreement, it is plain that the multitude of those who decree will establish for all an unquestionable acceptance of the decree.

There is, then, one among those who contrive much grief for us: Eustathius, the man from Sebasteia in Lesser Armenia. He, long ago made a disciple of Arius — and that at the time when Arius was at his height in Alexandria, composing his wicked blasphemies against the Only-begotten — followed that man and was numbered among his most genuine disciples. When he returned to his own country, he gave to the most blessed bishop Hermogenes of Caesarea, who was judging him for his false doctrine, a confession of sound faith. And having thus received ordination from him, after that man's falling asleep he ran to Eusebius in Constantinople, who himself no less than any espoused the impious doctrine of Arius. Then, driven from there for whatever reason, he came and again made his defence to those in his own country, concealing his impious mind, while putting forward a certain correctness of phrasing. And having obtained the episcopate however he did, he is at once found to have written an anathema of the consubstantial in the assembly held by them at Ancyra. And going thence to Seleucia, he did, with those of his own opinion, the things that all know. And in Constantinople he again agreed to what was put forward by the heretics. And thus, driven from the episcopate because he had earlier been deposed at Melitene, he devised the journey to you as his road to restoration. And what was put to him by the most blessed bishop Liberius, and what he himself agreed to, we do not know, except that he brought back a letter restoring him, which, having shown it to the synod at Tyana, he was restored to his place. This man now ravages that very faith on which he was received, and is in company with those who anathematize the consubstantial, and is a leader of the heresy of the Pneumatomachi. Since, then, the power of doing wrong to the Churches has come to him from your quarter, and he uses the boldness given him by you for the overthrow of the many, it is necessary that the correction too come from your quarter, and that letters be sent to the Churches, telling on what terms he was received, and how, now changed, he annuls the grace given him through the fathers of that time.

Second after him is Apollinaris, who himself also grieves the Churches not a little. For having, through his facility in writing, a tongue sufficient for every subject, he has filled the world with his treatises, disregarding the charge which says, "Take heed to make many books"; for in the multitude, plainly, many things are also done amiss. For how is it possible, out of much speaking, to escape sin? His writings on theology, then, have their construction not from scriptural proofs but from human premises; and there are also his writings on the resurrection, composed in a mythical, or rather Judaic, manner, in which he says that we shall again turn back to the legal worship, and shall again be circumcised, and keep the sabbath, and abstain from foods, and offer sacrifices to God, and worship in Jerusalem at the temple, and in short shall become Jews instead of Christians. What could be more laughable than these things, or rather more alien to the evangelical doctrine? Then his writings on the incarnation too have made such a disturbance for the brotherhood that few of those who have read them still preserve the ancient stamp of true religion; but the many, attending to his innovations, have been turned aside to inquiries and contentious inventions of these unprofitable phrases.

As for Paulinus — whether he has anything blameworthy concerning his ordination, you yourselves can say; but he grieves us by being attached to the doctrines of Marcellus, and by admitting without discrimination into his communion those who follow that man. And you know, most honoured brethren, that the doctrine of Marcellus involves the setting aside of all our hope, since it neither confesses a Son in His own hypostasis, but says that He was brought forth and again returned into the source from which He came forth, nor admits that the Paraclete subsists in His own person; so that one would not err in declaring his heresy altogether alien to Christianity, and calling it a corrupted Judaism. We ask that the care of these matters be undertaken by you. And it could be done, if you would deign to write to all the Churches throughout the East, that those who corrupt these things, if they correct themselves, should be in communion, but if they wish contentiously to persist in their innovations, should be separated from. And that we ought to have sat in council with your wisdom and taken up these matters in common deliberation, we ourselves are not unaware; but since the occasion does not permit it, and to delay is harmful, the harm from these men having taken root, we have of necessity sent the brethren, that whatever escaped the instruction of the letter, they, supplying it of themselves, may rouse your reverence to provide the help sought for by the Churches of God.
To Barses, Bishop of Edessa, in Exile

To the truly most beloved of God, and worthy of all reverence and honour, Bishop Barses, Basil sends greeting in the Lord. As our most genuine brethren, the company of Domninus, were coming to your reverence, we gladly took the occasion for a letter, and we greet you through it, praying to the holy God that you may be kept in this life until such time as we are counted worthy to see you and to enjoy the graces that are in you. Only pray, I beseech you, that the Lord may not deliver us up utterly to the enemies of the cross of Christ, but may keep His own Churches until the time of peace, which the just Judge Himself knows when He will grant. For He will grant it, and will not forsake us altogether. But as He fixed for the Israelites the seventy years for their sins as the sentence of captivity, so perhaps the Mighty One, having delivered us up for some appointed time, will at length call us back and restore us to the peace we had from the beginning — unless, indeed, the apostasy is somewhere near, and the things now happening are the prelude to the entrance of the Antichrist. But if that be so, pray that the Good One may either turn aside the afflictions or preserve us unfallen through the afflictions. We greet, through you, all the company counted worthy to be with your reverence. All who are with us greet your reverence. May you, strong and of good cheer in the Lord, and praying earnestly for me, be kept for the Church of God by the grace of the Holy One.
To Eulogius, Alexander, and Harpocration, Bishops of Egypt in Exile

In all things we find great the management of the good God concerning His Churches, so that even the things that seem to be grievous, and that do not in every way fall out according to our wish, are themselves dispensed for the benefit of the many, in the wisdom of God that is hard to discern and in the unsearchable judgments of His righteousness. For behold, the Lord, having raised up your love from the places of Egypt, and brought it into the midst of Palestine, has there established it, in imitation of Israel of old, whom, leading through captivity into the land of the Assyrians, He used to quench the idolatry there through the coming of the saints. And now therefore we find ourselves reasoning thus: that the Lord, setting forth your contest on behalf of true religion, has through exile opened for you the arena of the blessed struggles, and to those who meet with your good purpose has bestowed plain examples leading to salvation. Since, then, by the grace of God we have learned the rightness of your faith, and have learned your diligence concerning the brotherhood — and that not carelessly nor negligently do you provide what is for the common good and necessary to salvation, but, if there is anything to be done for the building up of the Churches, you choose to do it — we judged it right to become partakers of your good portion and to join ourselves through this letter to your reverence. For which cause we have sent also our most beloved son and fellow-deacon Elpidius, both to carry the letter and to be able, of himself, to report to you whatever may escape the instruction of the writing.

And what especially strengthened us toward the desire of union with you was the report of your zeal for the rightness of true religion: that the firmness of your heart was not carried away either by the multitude of treatises or by the variety of sophistries; but you recognized those who innovate against the apostolic doctrines, and did not consent to keep silence over the harm wrought by them. For indeed we found great grief among all who hold fast to the peace of the Lord at the manifold innovations of Apollinaris of Laodicea, who has grieved us the more, in that he seemed at first to be from among us. For to suffer something from an open enemy, even if it exceed in painfulness, is in a way bearable to the one oppressed, as it is written, "If an enemy had reproached me, I would have borne it"; but to experience some harm from one of the same soul and household, this is altogether hard to bear, and admits of no consolation. For the one whom we expected to have as a fellow-shield-bearer of the truth, this man we now find in many ways hindering those being saved, by dragging their mind about and tearing it away from the straightness of the doctrines. For what bold and hot deed was not done by him? What innovation, fraught with danger, was not devised by him in words? Has not every Church been divided against itself — and especially those governed by the orthodox, men being sent by him to split them and to set up some private conventicle of their own? Is not the great mystery of true religion made a laughing-stock, when bishops go about without people or clergy, bearing a bare name, achieving nothing toward the advancement of the Gospel of peace and salvation? Are not his words about God full of impious doctrines, the old impiety of the vain-minded Sabellius now renewed by him in his treatises? For if the things which the people of Sebasteia circulate are not forged by enemies, but are truly his own writings, he has left no excess of impiety untried, saying that the Father and the Son and the Spirit are the same, and other dark impieties, which we did not even consent to admit to our hearing, praying to have no portion with those who utter such phrases. Is not the doctrine of the incarnation confounded by him? Has not the saving dispensation of our Lord become doubtful to the many because of his turbid and dark inquiries about the incarnation? To gather all these and to bring them to refutation would need much time and discourse. And as for the place of the promises, who has so obscured and darkened it as this man's myth-making? For the blessed hope, laid up for those who have lived their lives according to the Gospel of Christ, he has dared to expound so basely and abjectly as to turn aside into old wives' fables and Judaic tales. He promises afresh the renewal of the temple, and the observance of the legal worship, and again a typical high priest after the true High Priest, and a sacrifice for sins after the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world; and partial baptisms after the one baptism, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling the Church, which through faith in Christ has no spot or wrinkle or any such thing; and a cleansing of leprosy after the impassibility of the resurrection; and an offering of jealousy, when men neither marry nor are given in marriage; loaves of the presence after the Bread from heaven; lamps burning after the true Light; and in short, if now the law of the commandments has been abolished in doctrines, it is plain that then the doctrines of Christ will be annulled in the legal commandments.

At these things shame and confusion have covered our faces, and a heavy grief has filled our hearts. Therefore we beseech you, as skilled physicians taught to instruct in meekness those who oppose, to try to bring him back to the good order of the Church, and to persuade him to despise the loquacity of his treatises — for he has confirmed the saying of the proverb, that "out of much speaking it is impossible to escape sin" — and firmly to set before him the doctrines of orthodoxy, that his amendment may become manifest and his repentance be made known to his brethren.

It is reasonable also to remind your reverence concerning the affairs of Marcellus, that you may decree nothing about them inconsiderately or rashly. But since that man went out of the Church on account of impious doctrines, it is necessary that those who follow him, having anathematized that heresy, should thus be received into communion, so that those joined to us through you may be received by the whole brotherhood. For at present no slight grief has seized the many, on hearing that, when they came to your honour, you both received them and shared with them the communion of the Church. And yet you ought to have known that, by the grace of God, you are not alone even in the East, but have many of your own portion, who defend the orthodoxy of the fathers, who at Nicaea set forth the pious doctrine of the faith; and all those of the West are in agreement both with you and with us. The tome of whose faith we have received and have it among us, following their sound teaching. All, then, who are in the same union with you ought to have been fully assured, so that the things done might be the more confirmed in the consent of the more numerous, and the peace might not be torn apart in the reception of some while others stood off. So then it would have befitted you to deliberate firmly and gently about matters that concern all the Churches throughout the world. For not the one who quickly decrees something is praiseworthy, but the one who fixes each thing solidly and unshakeably, so that his judgment, examined even in the time afterward, may appear the more approved — such a one is acceptable both with God and with men, as managing his affairs with discernment.

These things, all that the converse through a letter allowed us, we have spoken to your reverence. And may the Lord grant that we too may one day come together with one another, so that, having ordered all things with you for the perfecting of the Churches of God, we may with you receive the reward prepared by the just Judge for the faithful and prudent stewards. But for the present, deign to send us the terms on which you received the followers of Marcellus, knowing this: that even if you altogether secure your own position, you ought not to entrust so great a matter to yourselves alone, but it is necessary that those in the West and those throughout the East who are in communion should be joint voters with you in their restoration.
To Peter, Bishop of Alexandria

You rebuked me well, and as befits a spiritual brother taught true love by the Lord, in that we do not make all things, both small and greater, clear to you. For it belongs both to you to care for our affairs, and to us to refer ours to your love. But know, our most honoured and most beloved brother, that the continuousness of our afflictions, and this great turmoil that now shakes the Churches, makes us find nothing of what happens strange. For as those whose ears are deafened in the foundries become inured to the noises, so we, by the frequency of the dreadful tidings, have at last grown accustomed to keep our heart untroubled and undismayed before what is contrary to reason. The things, then, contrived from of old by the Arians against the Church, even if they are many and great and noised abroad over all the world, are nevertheless bearable to us, because they come from open enemies and foes of the word of truth; whom we marvel at when they do not do their usual things, not when they venture something great and audacious against true religion. But the things done by those of the same soul and the same faith grieve and trouble us. Yet even these, because they are many and continually fall upon our ears, do not appear extraordinary. Hence we were neither moved at the disorderly things done lately, nor did we trouble your ears — knowing, on the one hand, that report would of itself carry what was done, and, on the other, waiting for others to become the messengers of these sorrows; and then, not judging it reasonable that you should be vexed at such things, as though aggrieved at having been overlooked. To the very men, however, who did these things we wrote what befitted, exhorting them, since the brethren there suffered some dissension, not to fall away from love, but to await the correction from those able to heal the faults in the manner of the Church. And since you did this, being moved well and fittingly, we praised you, and gave thanks to the Lord that there is a remnant of the ancient good order preserved in you, and that the Church has not lost its own strength in our persecution. For the canons were not persecuted along with us. Often, then, troubled by the Galatians, I was never able to answer them, awaiting your decisions. And now, if the Lord grants it, and they are willing to bear with us, we hope to bring the people to the Church, so that we ourselves may not be reproached for having gone over to the Marcellians, but that they may become members of the body of the Church of Christ, so that the wicked blame, spread abroad from the heresy, may be made to vanish in our reception of them, and that we may not be put to shame as having joined ourselves to them.

Brother Dorotheus grieved us, as you yourself wrote, by not having conversed in all things gently and meekly with your good order. And this I reckon to the difficulty of the times. For we seem, because of our sins, to prosper in nothing, if even the most diligent of the brethren are not found gentle, nor fit for their ministries, by not accomplishing everything according to our mind. He, on his return, recounted to us the discussions he had with your honour in the presence of the most revered bishop Damasus, and he grieved us by saying that our most God-beloved brethren and fellow-ministers, Meletius and Eusebius, were reckoned together with the Arian-maddened. Even if nothing else established their orthodoxy, at least the war waged against them by the Arians furnishes no small proof of their rightness to those who reason fairly. And your reverence ought to be joined to them in love also by the fellowship of sufferings for Christ. But be persuaded of this, most truly honoured one, that there is no word of orthodoxy which was not proclaimed with all boldness by these men, with God as witness and ourselves as hearers. With whom we would not have received communion even for an hour, had we found them limping concerning the faith. But, if you please, let us leave the past, and give to what follows some peaceful beginning. For we all need one another, according to the fellowship of the members, and especially now, when the Churches of the East look toward us, and will take your concord as an occasion for support and steadfastness; but if they perceive that you are in some suspicion toward one another, they will be weakened and will let their hands fall, so as not to lift them against the enemies of the faith.
To Barses, Bishop of Edessa, in Exile

For the sake of the disposition I have toward your godliness, I longed to come myself and in my own person to embrace your true love, and to glorify the Lord who has been magnified in you, and has made your honoured old age conspicuous to all who throughout the world fear Him. But since a grievous weakness of the body wears me down, and an unspeakable care of the Churches lies upon me, and I am not my own master to travel where I wish and to meet with those I desire, I give rest by this letter to the longing I have for the enjoyment of the good things in you, and I beseech your unsurpassed reverence to pray for me and for the Church, that the Lord may grant us to pass without stumbling the sorrowful days, or hours, of our sojourning here; and may He grant us also to see the peace of His Churches, and to hear concerning the rest of your fellow-ministers and fellow-combatants the things we pray for, and concerning you yourself the things which the peoples under you seek night and day from the Lord of righteousness.

Know that often we did not write — not as often as we ought — yet we did write to your godliness. And perhaps the brethren entrusted with the ministry of the letters were unable to preserve our greetings. But now, since we have come upon some of our own people travelling to your honour, we have eagerly put the letters into their hands, and we have sent certain things, which deign to receive from our lowliness without disdain, and to bless us, in imitation of the patriarch Isaac. And if in anything, as men preoccupied and having our mind plunged beneath a multitude of cares, we have overlooked what was fitting, do not reckon it to us, nor be grieved; but imitate your own perfection in all things, that we too may enjoy your virtue as do all the rest. Strong and of good cheer in the Lord, and praying earnestly for me, may you be granted to me and to the Church of God.
To Eusebius, in Exile

The Lord has shown in our case too that He does not forsake His holy ones, having sheltered the life of your holiness with His great and mighty hand. For we count this nearly equal to the holy man's remaining unharmed in the belly of the sea-monster, and to those who fear the Lord dwelling unharmed in a raging fire — seeing that He has preserved your godliness unharmed, though the war, as I hear, was poured round you on every side. And may the mighty God preserve, for the time to come, that much-prayed-for sight for us, if we still live, or at least for the others, who await your return as their own salvation. For I am persuaded that the Lover of mankind, giving heed to the tears of the Churches and to the groans with which all groan over you, will keep you in this life until He grants the favour to those who beseech Him night and day.

Now of the things done against you up to the coming of our beloved brother Libanius, the fellow-deacon, we were sufficiently informed through him as he passed by; but of the things from that time on we need to learn. For we hear that in the meantime greater and harsher sufferings have come about in those regions; which we would learn, if it be possible, the sooner — but if not, then at least through the most reverent brother Paul, our fellow-presbyter, on his return — that, as we pray, your life is kept unharmed and unmolested. But because we have heard that all the roads are full of brigands and deserters, we were afraid to put anything into the hands of the brother, lest we become to him too a cause of death. But if the Lord grants a moderate calm — for we hear of the passing of the army — we shall be eager to send out one of our own people, to visit you and to report to us each of the things among you.
A Letter of Consolation to the Wife of Arinthaeus the General

It would have been fitting, and owed to your disposition, that we ourselves should be present and share in what is taking place. For so we should both have soothed our own grief and have rendered to your dignity the due of consolation. But since my body no longer endures the longer journeys, we have come to converse by letter, that we may not seem altogether estranged from what has happened.

Who, then, did not groan over that man? And who is so stony of heart as not to shed a warm tear for him? But me he filled with an especial dejection, when I reckon both the man's own honours toward me and his common patronage of the Churches of God. Yet nevertheless we reasoned that, being a man and having performed in this life the services laid upon him, he has at the fitting times been taken back again by God, who orders our affairs. We beseech your wisdom, considering these things, to be gentle over what has happened, and, so far as may be, to bear the misfortune moderately. Time, indeed, is sufficient to soften your heart and to give passage to reflection; but nevertheless your exceeding love of your husband, and your kindness toward all, make us afraid lest you give yourself over as a prey to grief, having received, through the simplicity of your character, a deep wound of sorrow. Always, indeed, the teaching of the Scriptures is useful, but most of all in such times. Remember, then, the sentence of our Creator, by which all of us who have sprung from the earth return again to earth; and none is so great as to be found superior to dissolution.

Noble, then, and great was that admirable man, and matching the strength of his body with the virtue of his soul — I too say it — having indeed no excess in either direction; but nevertheless a man, and he has died, as Adam, as Abel, as Noah, as Abraham, as Moses, as any you might name of those who shared the same nature. Let us not, then, because we have been deprived of him, be indignant, but, because at the first we lived together with him, let us give thanks to Him who joined us. For to be bereft of a husband is common to you with other women; but for such a partnership I do not think any other of women can boast equal honour. For truly our Creator fashioned that man as a single example of human nature, so that all eyes were turned toward him, every tongue recounted his deeds; but painters and sculptors fell short of his worth, and historians, recounting his brave deeds in the wars, fall into the incredibility of fables. Hence the many could not even endure to believe report when it carried round that sorrowful tidings, nor to accept at all that Arinthaeus had died. But nevertheless he has suffered what shall befall heaven and sun and earth.

He has departed, having ended his course brilliantly, not bowed down by old age, not having let fall any of his splendour; great in the present life, and great in the life to come; in no way harmed, by his present brilliance, with respect to the glory that is hoped for, because he washed away every stain of the soul, at the very departure from this life, by the laver of regeneration. And that you yourself became to him the procurer and helper of these things gives you the greatest consolation. And transfer your soul from the present to the care of the things to come, so that you may be counted worthy, through good works, to attain a place of rest like to his. Spare your aged mother, spare your young daughter, to whom you alone are left for consolation. Become an example of courage to the rest of the women; and so measure your grief that you neither cast it out of your heart nor be swallowed up by your sorrow. In all things look toward the great reward of endurance, promised by our Lord Jesus Christ in the recompense for the lives we have lived.
Without Address, Concerning an Abduction

I am greatly grieved that I do not find you, in the face of forbidden deeds, either indignant or able to reckon that this abduction now committed is against life itself and against human living a lawless act and a tyranny, an outrage against the free. For I know that, if you all held such a mind, nothing would have hindered, long ago, this evil custom from being driven out of our country. Take up, then, for the present the zeal of a Christian, and be moved in a manner worthy of the wrong. And the girl, wherever you find her, take her away with all energy and restore her to her parents; and that man himself banish from the prayers, and make him an outcast; and those who joined in the deed with him, according to the proclamation already issued by us, banish, with all their households, from the prayers for three years. And the village that received the abducted girl, and kept her, or fought in defence of her, this too put outside the prayers, all together; that all may learn to drive off the abductor as a serpent, as some other wild beast, regarding him as a common enemy, and so to stand up for the wronged.
To his Friend Eusebius, a Letter of Recommendation for Cyriacus the Presbyter

When, immediately and close upon your departure, I arrived at the city, how dejected I was at having missed you — what need is there even to say it, to a man who needs no telling, but knows by experience, through having suffered the like? For how much would it have been worth to me to see Eusebius, the best of men in every way, and to embrace him, and to return again in memory to our youth, and to be reminded of those days, in which we had one chamber, one hearth, the same tutor, and leisure and study, and luxury and want, and everything was ours in common, shared equally with one another! How great a worth do you suppose I set on recovering all these things in memory through meeting you, and, scraping off this heavy old age, seeming to have become young again out of an old man? But the enjoyment of those things escaped me; yet to see your eloquence by letter, and to console myself in such manner as I can, I was not deprived of, through my meeting with the most reverend Cyriacus, the fellow-presbyter — whom I am ashamed to recommend to you and to make your friend through myself, lest I should seem to be doing something officious in bringing to you what is already your own and peculiar to you. But since I must be both a witness of the truth, and bestow upon those spiritually joined to me the greatest of the things I possess, I judge the soundness of this man with regard to the priesthood to be manifest to you also, and I too confirm it, knowing against him no injury from those who lay hands on all, who do not fear the Lord. And yet, even if something had been done by them, the man was not on that account unworthy; for the enemies of the Lord rather confirm the rank of those whom they attack than take away anything of the grace belonging to them from the Spirit. But, as I said, nothing was even devised against the man. As, then, a presbyter unmolested, joined to us, and worthy of all reverence, so deign to look upon him, both benefiting yourself and showing favour to us.
To Sophronius the Master

Actiacus the deacon reported to me that certain men grieved you against us, slandering us as not being well disposed toward your dignity. For my part, I did not wonder if there are flatterers attending upon so great a man. For somehow these servile attentions are wont to grow up alongside great powers — men who, because they lack any good of their own by which they might be known, commend themselves out of the evils of others. And almost as rust is a corruption of the grain arising in the grain itself, so flattery, creeping in under the guise of friendship, is a ruin of friendship. I did not wonder, then, as I said, if some, like drones about the hives, so buzz about your brilliant and admirable household.

But this seemed to me astonishing and altogether contrary to reason: that you, a man most conspicuous for the weight of your character, should bear to lend them both your ears and to admit a slander against me — me who, having loved many from my earliest age to this old age, know that I have preferred none to the friendship of your perfection. For even if reason had not persuaded me to love you, being such as you are, the familiarity from boyhood would have sufficed to bind me to your soul. And you know how much custom avails toward friendship. But if I show nothing worthy of this purpose, forgive my weakness. For neither will you yourself seek from me a deed for the proof of goodwill, but plainly a purpose that joins in praying the best things for you. For may your affairs never come to this, that you should need the benefit of men so small as I am.

How then was I likely to say or do anything contrary to you in the affairs concerning Memnonius? For these things the deacon reported to me. And how did I set the wealth of Hymetius as more to be preferred than your friendship — the friendship of a man who so squanders his substance? But none of these things is true: neither has anything been said by me, nor done, in opposition. But perhaps this gave occasion to those who tell falsehoods, the thing said by me to certain of those making the disturbance: that "If the man has resolved beforehand to bring his own purpose to action, then whether you make a disturbance or not, the things sought will assuredly come to pass no less, whether you speak or are silent; but if he changes his mind, do not drag down the most revered name of our friend, nor, under the pretext, forsooth, of zeal for your patron, procure for yourselves some gain from this, out of the fear and threat you hold over men." But to that very man who was drawing up the will, neither through myself nor through another did I utter anything, small or great, about this matter.

And you ought not to disbelieve these things, unless you consider me altogether desperate, and to despise the great sin of lying. But do you yourself altogether lay aside even the suspicion in this matter, and henceforth make my disposition toward you higher than all slander, imitating Alexander, who, having received a letter against his physician as plotting against him, since it happened that at that very time he had taken a medicine to drink, was so far from believing the slanderer that at one and the same moment he read the letter and drank the medicine. For I do not deign to set myself as less honoured than any of those known to me in friendship, in that I have never been caught offending in friendship, and have besides received from my God the commandment of love, of which I am a debtor not only according to the common nature of men, but because I also recognize you in particular as a benefactor of myself and of my country.
Without Address, Concerning Hera

Being exactly persuaded that you love our honour so well as to reckon what concerns us as your own, I commend to your surpassing nobility our most reverend brother Hera — whom we call our brother not according to any mere custom, but according to the most exact disposition of friendship, which admits of no excess — and I beseech you both to look upon him as one of your own, and to grant him such patronage as is in your power, in whatever he may need of your magnanimity; so that I may have this benefit also to number among the many good things I have already obtained from you.
To Himerius the Master

The friendship and familiarity I have with our most reverend brother Hera — that it took its beginning from very boyhood, and has remained with me, by the grace of God, until old age — you yourself know better than anyone. For it was almost out of that friendship that the Lord bestowed on us the love of your great nobility, from the time when he procured for us our acquaintance with one another. Since, then, he stands in need of your patronage, I beseech and earnestly entreat you, both showing favour to your ancient disposition toward us and giving heed to the necessity that has now seized him, so to make his affairs your own that he may need no other patronage, but may return to us having accomplished everything according to our prayers; so that to the many benefits we have received from you we may have this also to number — than which we could find none greater for ourselves, nor one more closely concerning us, to make our own.
Without Address, Concerning Hera

You have anticipated our entreaties by your disposition toward our most reverend brother Hera, and you have proved to him better than our prayer, both by the exceeding honours you have shown him and by your patronage on each occasion. Nevertheless we too, since we cannot bear in silence what concerns him, beseech your unsurpassed honour to add, for our sake as well, to your zeal for the man, and to send him back to his country superior to the malice of his enemies; since at present he is not out of range of the darts of envy, many attempting to assail the quiet inoffensiveness of his life. Against whom we shall find one unbreakable security, if you yourself would be willing to hold your hand over the man.
To Harmatius the Great

Even the common law of all mankind makes those advanced in age into common fathers, and our own law, which belongs to Christians, sets us elders in the rank of parents to those of such years. So do not think me presumptuous, or meddling beyond what is fitting, if I am here interceding with you on behalf of your own son. His obedience in other matters I think it right that you should require of him, for he is answerable in body both to the law of nature and to that civil law under which we live our common life. But his soul, since he came possessing it from a more divine source, it is fitting to regard as subject to another, and to hold that it owes to God debts that are the oldest of all debts. Since, then, he has chosen the God of us Christians, the true God, in preference to the many gods worshipped among you through material symbols, you should not be displeased with him, but should rather admire the nobility of his soul, in that he has set it above both fear and filial service to be joined to God through true knowledge and a life of virtue. Nature herself, then, and the gentleness and mildness of your character in all things, will not permit you to feel grief over him even for a little while. And surely you will not slight our intercession either—or rather the intercession of your own city, made through us, who out of our affection for you and our prayer for every good thing on your behalf, suppose that you yourself too will be received as a Christian. So joyful did the report make them, falling suddenly upon the city.
To Maximus the Scholar
