The good and excellent Theotecnus has reported to me concerning your dignity of character, and has stirred in me a longing for your company, vividly sketching in words the stamp of your soul; and he so kindled my affection for you that, were I not weighed down by old age, and held fast by my long-familiar infirmity, and fettered by countless cares of the Church, nothing would have kept me from coming to you in person. For it is truly no small gain, when a man has passed from a great house and an illustrious family to the life of the Gospel, to bridle his youth by reason, to make the passions of the flesh slaves to reason, and to practise the humility that a Christian owes, thinking of himself as is fitting—whence he sprang and whither he is going. For the thought of our nature checks what is inflamed in the soul, banishes all arrogance and self-will, and, in a word, makes a man a disciple of the Lord, who said: Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart. For in truth, dearest of my children, the only good worth all our zeal and worthy of praise is the good that endures; and this is the honour that comes from God.

These human things are dimmer than a shadow and more deceptive than dreams. For youth fades more swiftly than the flowers of spring, and the bloom of the body withers away by sickness or by time. Wealth is faithless, glory easily overturned, and the labours spent upon the arts are bounded together with this present time. Even what all men pursue so eagerly—eloquence—has its charm only as far as the hearing. But the practice of virtue is a precious possession for the one who has it, and the sweetest of sights for those who meet with it. By caring for these things you will make yourself worthy of the good things laid up in the promises of the Lord.

In what way you might come to take up these noble things, and how you might preserve what you have gained, would take longer to say than the present impulse of my letter allows. Yet it occurred to me to address even these few words to you, prompted by what I heard from our brother Theotecnus—whom I always pray may speak the truth, but most of all in what he says about you, that the Lord may be the more glorified in you, since from an alien root you bring forth the precious fruits of godliness in abundance.
To Valerianus

I longed to see your nobility even while I was in Orphanene. For I expected that you, living at Korsagaina, would not hesitate to cross over to us at Attagaina, where we were holding the synod. But when I missed that meeting, I longed to see you on the mountain; for there again Euesus, being near, raised my hope of meeting you. And when I missed you on both occasions, I have come to writing, that you may think me worthy to be visited by you—at once doing what is fitting, as a younger man visiting an elder, and at the same time receiving through our meeting some counsel from us, since you have business with certain persons in Caesarea that needs our mediation toward a settlement. If, then, it is not burdensome, do not shrink from coming to us.
To Modestus the Prefect

Though there be many who bring you letters from us, your Honour, yet because of the surpassing measure of the honour you show toward us, I judge that the multitude of letters causes no trouble to your great mind. For this reason I have gladly given this letter also to this brother, knowing that he himself will obtain all that he seeks, and that we shall be counted among your benefactors, in furnishing to your good purpose occasions for kindness.

The matter in which he needs your protection he will himself state, if you will deign to look upon him with a kindly glance and give him the courage to find his voice before your great and extraordinary authority. We for our part present our own concern through this letter: that we hold whatever is done for him to be our own gain, and this especially because, having set out from Tyana on this very account, he has come to us, expecting to win some great advantage if he might put forward our letter in place of a suppliant's branch. Therefore, that he himself may not fall short of his hopes, that we may enjoy our accustomed honour, and that your zeal for good works may be fulfilled in this present case as well, we ask that he be received kindly and be numbered among those most intimate with you.
To Modestus the Prefect

Though it be a bold thing to bring petitions by letter to so great a man, yet the honour you have long shown toward us takes away the timidity from our heart, and we take courage to write on behalf of men who are indeed our own kindred by birth, but worthy of honour through the graciousness of their character. Now the man who delivers this letter of ours stands to me in the rank of a son. Since, then, he needs only your goodwill for what he seeks to be granted him, deign to receive my letter, which the aforesaid man holds out to you in place of a suppliant's branch, and to grant him an occasion to set forth his own affairs and to speak with those who are able to help him, so that by your command he may speedily obtain what he seeks, and I in turn may have ground for pride that there has been given to me, by the grace of God, such a protector—one who regards those connected with me as his own suppliants and refugees.
To Modestus the Prefect

I remember your great honour, in that, among your other gifts to me, you gave me also the boldness to write to your great mind. I make use, then, of the gift, and enjoy your most humane favour, at once gladdening myself by conversing with so great a man, and at the same time giving your magnanimity an occasion to dignify us with your replies. And since I once entreated your clemency on behalf of our companion Helladius the magistrate—that, being released from the charge of the assessment, he might be allowed to labour in the affairs of our country—and was thought worthy of a gracious nod of assent, I renew the same intercession, and beseech you that an order be sent down to the governor of the province to relieve him of the trouble.
To a Bishop

When uncalled you complain, and when called you do not obey. From this second course it is plain that you employed your former plea to no purpose; for, in all likelihood, you would not have come even then, had you been called. Heed, then, those who call you now, and do not again prove yourself ungracious, knowing that to add a charge to a charge confirms the first and makes the second accusation more credible than the former. I always urge you to bear with us; but if you will not bear with us, still it is not right to slight the martyrs, in commemoration of whom you are summoned. Grant, then, this favour—first to both, but if that does not seem good to you, at least to the more honoured of the two.
To Eleuthera

A suitable day for the synod we hope to find after the meetings that are to be appointed by us in the mountain country; but apart from the service of the synod no other occasion for a meeting appears to us, unless indeed the Lord should arrange something beyond our hopes. You ought to judge this from your own affairs. For if so great a crowd of cares besets your nobility, who have but one household to manage, how many occupations do you suppose we have each day?

Your dream, I think, points to something more complete: that you ought to take some care for the contemplation of the soul, and to tend those eyes by which God is naturally seen. And having the comfort that comes from the divine Scriptures, you will need neither us nor anyone else in order to discern what is needful, since you possess in the Holy Spirit a counsel and guidance sufficient to lead you to what is profitable.
Concerning Monks, to a Tax-Assessor

I think that some rule has already prevailed with your Honour concerning monks, such that we have no need to ask any special favour on their behalf, but that it is enough for them if they enjoy the common humanity shown to all. Nevertheless, judging it incumbent upon me also to take what care I can for such men, I write to your perfect discernment to ask that those who long ago renounced the world, and have so mortified their own bodies that they can furnish nothing useful to the public treasury either from money or from bodily service, be released from the tax-payments. For if indeed they live according to their profession, they have neither money nor bodies, having parted with the one for fellowship with the needy, and having worn out the other in fasting and prayer. And I know that you will hold men who have so lived in the highest reverence, and will wish to gain for yourself powerful helpers, men able by their Gospel manner of life to move the Lord on your behalf.
Without superscription, on the administration of the Church

The man who has charge of the Church and holds in hand the management of its possessions is himself the one delivering this letter to you—the beloved son So-and-so. Deign to grant him freedom of speech concerning the matters he reports to your good order, and to give heed to the things he affirms, so that from now at least the Church may be able to recover itself and be freed from this many-headed hydra. For such is the nature of the property of the poor that we are always seeking someone to take it over, since the Church spends more upon it than it has any profit from the possessions.
To a Registrar

Since certain men who do evil were caught at this synod, stealing—against the commandment of the Lord—the cheap garments of poor men, whom they ought rather to have clothed than stripped, those who have charge of the good order of the Church arrested them; and thinking that the receiving of such persons concerns you, as one who manages public affairs, I have written to you, making it known that the sins committed in the churches ought to receive from us the correction that befits them, and that judges should not be troubled about these matters. For this reason I have ordered that the stolen goods, which the document deposited with you sets forth, together with the inventory made in the presence of all who were there, be received: some to be kept in store for those who are to come, and some to be distributed to those present; and that the men themselves be turned back to amendment in the discipline and admonition of the Lord, whom I hope, in the name of God, to make better for the future. For what the blows of the law-courts do not accomplish, this we have often known the dread judgements of the Lord to bring about. But if it seems good to you to refer these matters also to the count, we have such confidence in the justice of the cause and in the man's uprightness that we leave you free to do as you wish.
Without superscription, on church-advocates

The case of this man seems hard to handle. For we do not know what to do with a character so versatile and, as one may conjecture from what is seen, so past all hope. When summoned to judgement, he does not obey; and if he does appear, he uses such an abundance of words and oaths that we are glad to be quickly rid of him. I have often seen him even turn the charges back upon his accusers. In short, no nature among all that feed upon the earth is so manifold and so apt for moulding into wickedness as that of this man, as one may judge of him from even a little experience. Why, then, do you ask me, and do not rather persuade yourselves to endure the wrongs you suffer from him as a kind of God-sent visitation? But that you may not be defiled by sharing in his sins, let him with his whole household be cut off from the prayers, and from the rest of fellowship with the clergy. Perhaps, becoming an object of caution to all, he will be brought to shame.
Without superscription, on church-advocates

Those whom the common penalties do not bring to their senses, and whom exclusion from the prayers does not lead to repentance, must of necessity be made subject to the canons given by the Lord. For it is written: If your brother sins, reprove him between you and him alone; if he will not hear you, take another with you; and if he will not hear even so, tell it to the Church; and if he refuses to hear the Church also, let him be to you henceforth as a heathen and a tax-collector. This is just what has happened in his case. Once he was charged; before one and then a second witness he was convicted; a third time before the Church. Since, then, we have testified to him, and he has not accepted it, let him henceforth be cast out by public proclamation. And let it be announced to the whole village that he is to be admitted to no fellowship in the common dealings of life, so that, from our refusal to mix with him, he may become wholly the prey of the devil.
Without superscription, concerning a woman who was wronged

Judging it an equal fault both to leave sinners unpunished and to exceed due measure in the punishment, I have imposed upon this man the penalty that falls to me to impose, expelling him from the fellowship of the Church; and I have urged those who were wronged not to avenge themselves, but to leave the requital to the Lord—so that, if our instructions are of any use, I might then have been heeded, my word carrying far more weight than any letter could ever avail to enforce.

But since I heard words of great gravity, I kept silent at the time, and now too I do not think it fitting for me to speak about the same matters. "For I," she says, "have set at naught a husband, and the bearing of children, and a life of my own, that I might attain this one thing—to be well thought of by God and to be held worthy of the better repute among men. Yet a man, bred from childhood in the corruption of households, forcing his way in once with his habitual shamelessness, fell upon our house, and became known to us only to the extent of a bare acquaintance; and out of ignorance of his ways and a certain ill-instructed modesty I plainly was ashamed to drive him off. He has gone to such a length of impiety and outrage as to fill the whole city with his slanders against me, and to brand me with a public placard set up at the doors of the church. And when for this he met with some indignation from the laws, returning again he renewed his slanders. Once more the marketplace is full of his abuse of me, the gymnasia, the theatres, the houses of those who, through likeness of life, receive him. Nor has it even been granted me to be known for the better things, in which I was held in honour, but rather for the most shameful, because through his licentious spirit I have become notorious among all.

At this," she says, "some take pleasure in the slanders, because men by nature delight in abuse; others say they are grieved, but do not share my pain; others are persuaded that the slanders are true; others are in doubt, swayed by the multitude of his oaths. But there is no one who shares my pain. Now indeed I have felt my desolation, and I lament my own self, having no brother, no friend, no kinsman, no slave, no free man—no human being at all—to share my pain. And, it seems, I find myself alone more pitiable than the city, in which there is so great a scarcity of those who hate wickedness, who do not consider that the wantonness done to one another, going round in a circle, will one day overtake themselves as well."

These things, and others still more piercing, she went through to me with countless tears, and departed, not even leaving me free from her reproaches—that, when I ought to feel a father's pain with her, I am indifferent to so great an evil and play the philosopher amid the sufferings of another. For you do not bid me overlook the remission of money, nor to share in bodily toils, but to suffer loss in reputation itself, the harm of which becomes a common loss to the clergy.

After these words, decide yourself, my admirable friend, what you would now have me say to her, holding as you do such a judgement of your own: not to hand wrongdoers over to the magistrates, yet not to rescue them either when they have been handed over—men of whom it was long ago foretold by the Apostle that the ruler is to be feared for the evil deed: "For he does not," he says, "bear the sword in vain." As, then, to hand a man over is not humane, so to rescue him is to foster his wantonness. Perhaps there might be some postponement of the proceedings until our own arrival; and then we shall show that we are of no use, since there are none who obey us.
To Nectarius

Many blessings be upon those who move your Honour to keep up this continual converse with us by letter. For do not think that we say such things out of mere custom; rather, it is from genuine affection that we set the highest value on your voice. For what could be more precious to me than Nectarius—who from childhood was known to us by his fairest qualities, and who has now run up, through virtue of every kind, to such a height of distinction? So that to me the dearest of all my friends is the one who brings me your letters.

But concerning the choice of those who are to be set over the company: if I do anything to gratify men, or yielding to entreaties, or giving way to fear, may I never do such things. For I shall be no steward, but a huckster, bartering the gift of God for human friendships. But if the votes that men cast are given on the strength of an outward appearance, of which they are able to bear witness in whatever they testify, while the judgements as to who are the more suitable are entrusted by our humble selves to Him who knows the hidden things of hearts, then perhaps it is altogether better, having deposited one's testimony, to stand aside from all zeal and partisanship—as though the persons testified to were one's own—and to pray to God that what is profitable may not escape us. For thus we shall no longer blame any man for the outcome, whichever way it falls, but shall render to God the thanks for what comes to pass. And yet, if these things are done after the manner of men, they are not really done at all, but are an imitation, and fall very far short of the truth.

Consider, too, that no small danger lies close at hand for the man who strives by every means to make his own opinion prevail—lest we ever draw upon ourselves a share in the sins committed. For many sins might be committed, even by those one would never have expected, through the frailty of human nature. Again, when in private we have often given our friends the best advice, and yet seem unpersuasive to those who consult us, we are not angry; but in matters that are not the counsel of men but the judgement of God, shall we be vexed if even the judgements of God are not preferred to ours? If, then, the office is given by men, why should it be sought from us, and not rather a man take it for himself? But if it is given by the Lord, it befits us to pray, not to be vexed; and in our prayer not to ask our own will, but to leave it to God, who dispenses what is profitable. And may the holy God lead away every trial of grievous affairs from your house, and measure out to you yourself and to all who belong to you a life free from sickness and harm, in all prosperity.
To Timothy, country-bishop

To write all that I think I see to be neither suited to the measure of a letter nor otherwise befitting the kind of address I owe you; and yet to pass over it in silence is for me well-nigh impossible, since my heart is inflamed with a just anger against you. I shall therefore take a middle course, writing some things and leaving others out. For I wish to take you to task, if it be permitted, with the frankness of a friend speaking to an equal.

If you are that Timothy whom from childhood we knew to apply himself with such intensity to uprightness and the disciplined life that he was even charged with going to excess in these things—are you now standing aside from considering by every means what one must do to be made near to God, and looking instead to what So-and-so thinks of you? Have you made your life hang upon the opinion of others, and are you taking thought how not to be useless to friends nor a laughing-stock to enemies, fearing the shame that comes from the many as though it were some dreadful thing—and do you not perceive that, all the while you wear yourself out over these matters, you are unawares neglecting the life that ought to come first? For that it is not possible to prevail in both at once—the affairs of this world and the manner of life according to God—the divine Scriptures are full of what they have taught us; and nature herself, too, is full of such examples. For in the working of the mind it is wholly impossible to think two thoughts at the same moment; and in the perceptions of the senses it is impossible to receive and to distinguish at the same time two voices falling together upon the ears, even though two passages of hearing are open to us. And the eyes, unless both are directed toward some one of the visible things, cannot perform their office accurately. So much for what comes from nature; but to set forth for you the lessons from the Scriptures is no less absurd than, as the saying goes, to carry an owl to Athens.

Why, then, do we mix things that will not mix—the tumults of civic life and the practice of godliness—instead of withdrawing from the tumults, and from having troubles and giving them to others, and becoming our own masters, and confirming by our deeds the aim of godliness which we long ago set before ourselves, and showing those who wish to harass us that it does not lie with them to grieve us whenever they please? And this will come to pass once we have shown ourselves free of every handhold. So much, then, for this. May it be granted us one day to come together in the same place and to take more careful counsel about what is profitable to our souls, that we may not be caught up in care for vain things when the necessary departure comes upon us.

I was greatly delighted with the things your love sent, which were of their own nature most pleasant; but the addition of the sender made the pleasure many times greater. As for the wax and the lozenges from Pontus, accept them gladly when we send them; for at present we had none to hand.
To Palladius

The holy God has fulfilled half of our desire, by arranging the meeting with our most decorous sister, your wife. And He is able to grant what remains as well, that, having seen your nobility also, we may render to God perfect thanks. For we are in great longing, especially now, when we have heard that you have been honoured with the great honour, the immortal garment, which, enwrapping our humanity, has done away with the death that is in the flesh, and the mortal has been swallowed up in the garment of incorruption.

Since, then, the Lord has made you His own through grace, and has estranged you from all sin, and has opened to you the kingdom of heaven, and has shown you the ways that lead to the blessedness there, we exhort you—a man so far surpassing the rest in good sense—to receive the grace with reflection, and to become a faithful guardian of the treasure, keeping with all care the watch over the royal deposit, so that, having preserved the seal inviolate, you may stand before the Lord shining in the splendour of the saints, having put no spot or wrinkle upon the pure garment of incorruption, but preserving holiness in all your members, as one who has put on Christ. For "as many of you," he says, "as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ." Let all your members, then, be holy, so that they may be fit to be covered by the holy and shining robe.
To Julian

How has your body fared in this time between? Have you fully recovered the use of your hand? And how stand the rest of the affairs of your life? Do they go on according to your wish, as we pray they may, and as is owed to your purpose of life? For where the mind is prone to change, in such men it is not surprising that life too should be without order; but where the purpose is fixed, ever standing firm and the same, it follows for such men that they lead their life in harmony with that purpose. For indeed it is not granted to the helmsman to make a calm whenever he wishes, but for us to make our own life waveless is altogether easy, if we silence the tumults that rise up against us from within, out of the passions, and set our mind higher than the things that fall upon us from without. For neither losses, nor sicknesses, nor the other hardships of life will touch the earnest man, so long as he keeps his mind trading with God, and looking off toward what is to come, and lightly and trimly rising above the storm that surges up from the ground. Since those who are firmly held fast by the cares of life, like fat-fleshed birds that bear their wings in vain, are dragged along somewhere down below with the grazing herds.

But we have been permitted by our affairs to see you only as much as those who pass one another on the open sea. Yet, since from the claw one may know the whole lion, we think that from this brief experience we have come to know you well enough. Hence we make much of the fact that you hold our affairs in some account, and that we are not absent from your mind, but are continually present with you through memory. And the proof of memory is to write; the more continually you do this, the more you will gratify us.
To Festus and Magnus

It is fitting, no doubt, for fathers to take forethought for their own children, for farmers to care for their plants and seeds, and for teachers to be concerned for their pupils, especially when through natural aptitude these give promise of better hopes for themselves. For the farmer rejoices in his toil when his ears of grain swell or his plants grow; pupils too gladden their teachers, and children their fathers—the one advancing toward virtue, the other toward growth. But we have over you a care so much the greater, and a hope so much the better, as godliness is better than every art, and better than all living things and fruits together; and this godliness, rooted and nourished by us in your souls while they are still tender and pure, we pray to see advance to perfect maturity and to fruits in season, your own love of learning lending its aid to our prayers. For know well that both our goodwill toward you and the cooperation of God lie stored up in your own purposes; and when these are directed aright toward what is needful, God, called upon as a fellow-worker, will be present even uncalled, and every man who loves God will come of his own accord to teach. For the eagerness of those able to teach something useful is invincible, when the souls of the learners are kept clean of all resistance.

Nor, indeed, does separation of body hinder this, since the One who fashioned us, out of the abundance of His wisdom and love for mankind, did not confine our understanding within the bounds of the body, nor the power of words to the tongue, but gave something more, even from time, to those able to help—so that they can pass on their teaching not only to those far separated in space, but indeed to those born very long after. And experience confirms this saying for us, since those who lived many years before teach the young, their teaching being preserved in writing; and we, though so far separated in body, are ever together in mind, and converse with ease, our teaching hindered neither by land nor by sea—if you have any care for your own souls.
To Monks

I think that by the grace of God you need no other exhortation, after the words we spoke to you in person, urging you all to take up the common life together in imitation of the apostolic manner of living—which indeed you received as a good teaching, and for which you gave thanks to the Lord. Since, then, what we spoke were not mere words, but teachings that ought to issue in deeds, for the benefit of you who accept them, for the repose of us who proposed the counsel, and for the glory and praise of Christ, whose name is called upon us—for this reason I have sent our most beloved brother, that he may both make known the willing, rouse the sluggish, and bring to light for us any who hold out against us.

For great is my desire both to see you gathered together, and to hear concerning you that you do not love the unwitnessed life, but rather that you all accept being guardians of one another's strictness and witnesses of what is rightly done. For thus each one will receive in full both the reward for himself and that for his brother's progress; and this it befits you to furnish to one another in word and deed, through continual converse and exhortation. And above all we urge you to remember the faith of the fathers, and not to be shaken by those who attempt to lead you about in your quietude—knowing that neither strictness of life by itself, unless it be enlightened by faith in God, is profitable, nor a right confession, if it be without a share in good works, will be able to present us to the Lord; but both must go together, that the man of God may be complete, and that our life may not be lame for want of the one. For it is faith that saves us, as the Apostle says, working through love.
To Eleuthera

Reckoning your disposition toward us, and recognizing the zeal you have for the work of the Lord, we took courage as with a daughter the other day, and used the mules at greater length; and though we used them sparingly, as being our own, we yet prolonged their service. These things, then, had to be written to your dignity, that you may know that what was done is a proof of our trust.

At the same time we also remind your good order through this letter to remember the Lord, and, keeping ever before your eyes the departure from this world, to order your life with a view to your defence before the Judge who cannot be deceived, that you may have boldness in your good works before Him who is to reveal the hidden things of our hearts on the day of His visitation.

Your most noble daughter we greet through you; and I urge that she pass her time in the study of the oracles of the Lord, so that her soul may be nourished by good teaching, and her mind may advance toward growth and greatness even more than her body does by nature.
To Eleuthera

Judging it altogether incumbent upon me—both because of the age of an old man and because of the genuineness of my spiritual affection—to visit your incomparable nobility even in bodily presence, and, when you are absent, not to fall away from you but to make up the lack by letters, now that I have found a suitable bearer of letters to your dignity, I greet you through her, urging you above all on to the work of the Lord, that the holy God, bringing you honourably through the days of your sojourning in all godliness and dignity, may render you worthy also of the good things to come.

And next I also commend to you the aforesaid daughter, that you may so receive her as my daughter and your own sister, and that, in whatever she shares with your seemly and pure soul, you may make it your own concern and take her part—so that, having first your reward from the Lord, you may then also give rest to us, who in the heart of Christ are filling up toward you the measure of love.
Without superscription, to a devout man

That you deign to use us as counsellors in all things and as sharers in your concerns, you do in a manner befitting your own perfection; and may God reward you both for your love toward us and for your care in the conduct of life. But that this delusion has touched you I was amazed, and that you have believed some irrational power to reside in water, and that with no testimony to confirm the report. For there is no one of those who went there who received, whether less or more, into his body any of the good things he had hoped for. Unless, indeed, some relief came to someone of itself, of the kind that naturally befalls men in their sleep or while they are engaged in other things in the course of life. But the one who does away with love persuades the simpler sort to reckon these chance occurrences to the nature of the water. And that our word is true, you may be taught from the very experience itself.
To a Tax-Assessor

You wrote, to one who knew it already, that you are reluctant toward the management of public affairs. For there is an old saying, that those who lay claim to virtue do not take up offices with pleasure. For what is proper to physicians, this I see belongs to rulers also. They look upon dreadful things, they meet with unpleasant ones, and over the misfortunes of others they reap griefs of their own—those, at least, who are truly rulers. Whereas all that part of mankind which is given to trade, and looks to money, and is excited about this kind of glory, counts it the greatest of goods to take up some position of power, from which they will be able to do good to friends, to take vengeance on enemies, and to win for themselves the things they crave. But you are not such a man—how could you be?—you who, when civic power so great was within your reach, withdrew willingly, and when it was in your hands to rule a city as one household, chose instead the untroubled and quiet life, counting it of more worth to have no business and to give none to others than is the price at which the rest are esteemed for their harshness.

But since the Lord has willed that the country of the Iborites should not fall under hucksters of men, nor that the assessment should be like a market of slaves, but that each be registered as is just, take up the matter—even though otherwise burdensome—as one that can yet procure for you good repute with God. And neither cower before power, nor despise poverty, but offer to those you administer a judgement more unswerving than any balance. For thus your zeal for justice will become manifest to those who have trusted you, and they will admire you above the rest. Or even if it should escape their notice, it will not escape our God, who has set before us great rewards for good works.
To the father of a deceased scholar, a letter of consolation

Since the Lord has set us in the second rank of fathers to Christians, entrusting to us the forming, through godliness, of His children who have believed in Him, the suffering that has befallen your blessed son we have reckoned to be our own as well; and we have groaned over the untimeliness of his departure, feeling compassion above all for you, and considering how great will be the weight of grief for a father by nature, when even in us, who are made his own by the commandment, so great a dejection of heart has arisen. For over him there was no need either to suffer or to utter anything mournful; but pitiable are those who have been disappointed of their hopes in him. And truly they are worthy of many tears and groans, who, having sent forth a son in the very flower of his age to the training of eloquence, receive him back in silence, keeping this long and dreaded silence. But these things, as men, at once stirred us, and we poured out a hasty tear and let go an unschooled groan from the midst of the heart, the suffering suddenly, like some cloud, enveloping our reason. But when we came to ourselves, and looked with the eye of the soul toward the nature of human things, we made our defence to the Lord for the way our soul, swept along, had been affected toward what had happened, and we admonished ourselves to bear these things with measure, since they were allotted to the life of men by the ancient decree of God.

A son is gone, leading the very prime of his age, distinguished in the companies of his fellows, dear to his teachers, able from a bare meeting to draw even the most savage into goodwill, quick in his studies, gentle in character, composed beyond his years; and one who said more than this would still say less than the truth. Yet, after all, he was a man born of a man. What, then, did it befit the father of such a son to consider? What else than to remember his own father, that he is dead? What wonder, then, that one born of a mortal should become the father of a mortal?

But that it was before his time, and before he had his fill of life, and before he came to the measure of full age, and was made known among men, and left a succession to his line—these are not, as I persuade myself, an increase of the grief, but a consolation for what has happened. The dispensation of God ought to be received with thanks, in that He did not leave orphan children upon the earth, in that He did not leave a wife a widow, given over to a long affliction, or to live with another man and neglect her former children. And as for the fact that the boy's life was not prolonged in this world, who is so ungracious as not to consider this the greatest of goods? For a longer sojourn here is an occasion of more evils. He did no evil; he wove no guile against his neighbour; he came under no necessity to mingle with the brotherhoods of those who do wickedly; he was not entangled in the evils of the marketplace; he endured no compulsion to sin—no falsehood, no ingratitude, no greed, no love of pleasure, none of the passions of the flesh that naturally arise in ill-bred souls. He departed with his soul branded by no stain, but withdrew pure to the better lot. It was not the earth that hid the beloved, but heaven that received him. God, who orders our affairs, who appoints to each the boundaries of his times, who led him into this life, He Himself also removed him. We have, in the excesses of our misfortunes, a school in that renowned utterance of great Job: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it seemed good to the Lord, so also has it come to pass. Blessed be the name of the Lord for ever."
To Maximus, a letter of consolation

How we were affected when we heard of your affliction, no words of ours could suffice to convey with any vividness. At one moment we reckon the loss that the whole company of the devout has suffered, having lost the patroness of its own order; at another we consider into what dejection the brightness of your dignity has fallen. When we behold in our mind a household that all men counted blessed brought to its knees, and a married life grown together in perfect harmony dissolved more swiftly than a dream, how should we not be bowed in soul, even were we made of adamant?

For our part, from our very first conversation a certain intimacy arose toward your venerable self, and we were so won to you by your virtue that at every hour we had your affairs upon our lips. And when we came also into familiar acquaintance with that blessed soul, we were truly persuaded that the saying of the Proverb was confirmed in your case, that a wife is fitted to her husband by God—so suited were you to each other in character, each one showing forth in himself, as in a mirror, the disposition of the other. And though a man should say much, he would not attain even to the smallest fraction of her worth.

But what must one feel in the face of a law of God that has long prevailed: that the one who has come into being should in due season depart again, and that every soul, having rendered to life what is needful, should then be released from the bonds of the body?

We are neither the first to suffer this, my admirable friend, nor the only ones; but what our parents have known by experience, and our grandparents, and all our forebears above us in the line, that too we have come to know by experience. The present life is full of such examples. But you, who so surpass the rest in virtue, ought, even in the midst of your sufferings, to keep the greatness of your soul unhumbled—not chafing at the present loss, but grateful to the Giver for the gift that was yours from the beginning. For to die is common to all who share the same nature, but to have lived with a good wife has fallen to only the few who are counted blessed in this life. Indeed, the very fact of bearing the separation with grief is no small one of God's gifts, to those who reckon it with right judgment; for we have known many who received the dissolution of an ill-matched marriage as the laying down of a burden.

Look up to the heaven and the sun, and survey the whole creation round about, and see that these things, great and many as they are, will a little while hence appear no more. And from all this draw this conclusion: that, being a part of a creation that dies, we have received what falls to us from our common nature. For marriage itself is a consolation for dying. Since it was not possible to remain forever, the Creator devised, by the succession of the race, what suffices for the continuance of life. And if we grieve because she set out before us, let us not begrudge her that she was not filled up to the full with the troubles of life, but that, by a kind of grace, like the bloom of flowers, she left us while we still longed for her. Above all, let the doctrine of the resurrection bring comfort to your soul, since you are a Christian and carry your life through in the hope of the good things to come.

Thus, then, it is fitting to think of her as having gone before along a road which we too shall have to travel; and if she has gone before us, that is no cause for lamentation. For a little later our own case may perhaps be the more pitiable, if, being stretched out to greater length, we become liable to greater punishments. Let our reason, then, shake off the weight of grief, and take up instead the care for how we ought henceforth to be well-pleasing to the Lord.
To the wife of Brison, a letter of consolation

How greatly we groaned at the news of the affliction touching Brison, the best of men—what need is there even to speak of it? For surely no one has a heart so stony that, having come to know that man and then heard that he had been suddenly snatched away from among the living, he would not have reckoned the loss of him a common loss to life itself. And in us the grief was at once succeeded by concern for you, when we reflected that, if to those far removed from his intimacy the event was so heavy and hard to bear, how natural it was that your soul should be afflicted by the blow—a soul by nature so kind, and so ready for fellow-feeling through the gentleness of its disposition, and so subject to the suffering that you feel, as it were, a being cut in two at the separation from your spouse. For if in truth, according to the word of the Lord, they are no longer two but one flesh, plainly such a parting is no less painful than if half of our own body were torn away.

But the griefs are of this kind, and greater than these; what then is the consolation for what has happened? First, the law laid down for us by God, which has prevailed from the beginning: that whoever has come into being must in due season depart from life. If, then, human affairs have been so ordered from Adam down to us, let us not be vexed at the common laws of our nature, but accept the dispensation of God concerning us—who ordained that this noble and unconquered soul should depart from life not with the body wasted by disease nor withered by time, but should lay down its life at the height of its prime and in the splendour of its achievements in war. So that we ought not to be vexed because we have been parted from such a man, but rather, because we were counted worthy of life together with such a man, let us give thanks to the Lord—a man whose loss almost the whole Roman dominion felt, whom the emperor recalled, whom the soldiers lamented, and whom those of the highest rank mourned as a true son.

Since, then, he has left you the memory of his own virtue, consider that you have in it a sufficient consolation for your grief. And next, I would have you know this also: that whoever has not sunk under his afflictions, but has borne up the weight of grief through hope in God, has from God a great recompense for his endurance. For we have not been allowed to grieve over those who have fallen asleep as the outsiders do, by the law the Apostle has laid down for us. Let your children too be as living images, consoling you for the absence of the one you long for. So let the occupation of rearing your children draw your soul away from its sorrows; and in taking thought for how you may pass the time that remains to you in a way well-pleasing to the Lord, you will devise a good occupation for your reflections. For the preparation of our defence before our Lord Jesus Christ, and the earnestness to be found numbered among those who love him, is enough to overshadow grief, so that we are not swallowed up by it. May the Lord grant to your heart the comfort that comes from his good Spirit, so that we too, hearing what concerns you, may be relieved, and that you may be a good example to all of your own age and station of the life lived according to virtue.
To the Count of the Privy Purse

The people of this estate have, I think, by a false slander, persuaded your honour to impose on these men a tax upon their mares. Since, then, what is being done is unjust, and on that account ought to be displeasing to your honour, and is grievous to us as well, on account of the intimacy we have with those who have been wronged, we have made haste to entreat your goodness not to allow the harassment to go forward against those who are attempting to do this wrong.
To Aburgius
This is the man on whose behalf I spoke to you before, through the deacon. Since, then, he has come bearing this letter from us, may he go away with what he wishes from you.
Without address, on virtuous men

So-and-so is already known to you, as the man's own accounts make plain. For on every occasion his tongue is full of you: in the remembrance of the orthodox, in the hospitality shown to ascetics, in every virtue, the man sets you first. And if anyone makes mention of teachers, he will not endure to put others before you; if of champions of true religion, men able to refute the plausibility of heresy, he would not choose to reckon another ahead of you, testifying that in all things your virtue is unconquerable and unrivalled. And it costs him no great effort to persuade us when he says these things; for he recounts to our ears greater things of men he knows than one might be thought to be reporting with exaggeration.

This man, then, on returning to you, asked for a letter—not that he might commend himself to you through us, but that he might do me a kindness, by furnishing an occasion to greet my beloved ones; and may the Lord reward him for his good intention. And do you also, by your prayers and by your good disposition toward all, apportion to him what favour you can. Let us know, too, how the affairs of the churches stand.
To the Governor of Sebaste

I perceive that your honour gladly receives our letters, and I know the reason. Being a lover of the good and ready for acts of kindness, since each time we furnish you with some matter sufficient to engage the nobility of your purpose, you hasten to our letters as to so many occasions for good works. There comes, then, yet another occasion able to receive the marks of your readiness in all things, and bringing with it, at the same time, a herald of your good deeds.

For certain men have set out from Alexandria, fittingly, on a necessary errand—one owed, as is common to the whole nature of mankind, to the departed. They need your protection, so that you may grant them, by an official decree, leave to move the body of their kinsman, who died here in Sebaste during the army's encampment; and further, that what help is possible may be furnished to them from the public post, so that they may find through your nobility some relief from their long wandering. That this kindness will reach as far as great Alexandria, and will be a service to those there, the wonder of your honour will be made plain to your good sense, even if I do not say it. And we, in addition to the many favours we have already received, shall reckon this one too among them.
Without address

Contentious natures often thrust aside even good counsels, and judge a thing fine and useful not by what seems so to everyone else, even when it is profitable, but by what pleases themselves alone, even when it is harmful. The cause is folly and a perversity of character that pays no heed to the advice of others, but trusts only its own opinions and the reasonings that occur to it. And the reasonings that occur are those in which they take pleasure, and they take pleasure in what they wish. But the man who thinks that what he wishes is profitable is no sure judge of what is just; he is like the blind being led by the blind. Hence he readily stumbles into losses, and has experience for his teacher of what is to his advantage.

This is the very fate that the man here joined in dispute is now enduring. For when he ought to have entrusted the case to mutual friends—indeed, after having been judged often before, by many who cared for justice and truth—he has now run off to the magistrates and the verdict of the law courts, and chooses, after losing much, to gain a little. But judgments before magistrates do not bring even victory without loss.

Be a helper, then, dear friend—best of all to both parties to the suit, for that is the godly course—by preventing the approach to the magistrate, and by becoming their judge in his stead. But if the other party will not obey and contends against the verdict, then take the side of the one who is wronged, and add the weight of your support to the man who seeks to obtain his rights.
Without address, concerning patronage

While your honour was present with the brethren, I spoke on behalf of the men from the estate of Caprales, and brought them before your gentleness, entreating you—keeping before your eyes the recompense that comes from the Lord—to be their protector, as men poor and burdened in every way. And now once more, through this letter, I renew the same request, praying to the holy God that the eminence you possess and the splendour of your life may be preserved and brought to yet greater things, so that, from greater power, you may have it in your hands to confer richer benefits upon us. For that our one prayer is for the welfare of your whole house, I believe you are persuaded.
Without address, concerning a man in need

I thoroughly disapproved when this brother grew anxious about the registration of his estate, seeing that he has already received the exemption he needs from his very poverty. For from a life of plenty he has now been reduced—the Lord having so ordered it for the good of his soul—to the utmost poverty, so that he scarcely has even his daily food in sufficiency, and is master of not a single slave, out of the many he formerly held under his own authority. To this man only his body is left, and that too feeble and aged, as you yourself can see, and three children, an addition to the cares of a poor man.

That he had no need of our intercession, having in his poverty enough to move compassion through the kindliness of your character, I knew well. But since those who make requests are hard to satisfy, I was afraid that something owed to him might be left wanting, and so I have written, knowing that the day on which he first sees your dignity will become for him the beginning of a happy life for the time thereafter, and will give some better change to his affairs.
Without address, on behalf of kinsmen

It was a thing greatly desired by me to meet with your learnedness, for many reasons: first, to enjoy the good qualities in you after so long an interval of time between; and next, to entreat you also on behalf of the people of Ariarathia. To them, long afflicted, the Lord has given a worthy consolation, in granting them the oversight of your uprightness. There is, besides, yet another matter that lies very heavily upon my kinsmen, and is almost the most critical part of the distress at Ariarathia; and this too I beg may, as far as possible, be remedied by your goodness, so that it may henceforth be made bearable for those who own the property.
To a leading citizen

Many letters to your honour are made for us by those who do not heed our assurances, but seek something private and special in their own affairs. For long ago we testified to them that you would be so common and equal a guardian of justice to us that no one would seek anything more in the way of kindness, unless he were to go beyond all bounds in greed. Nevertheless, to satisfy this man, we have given him the letter, commending the man to you and entreating you both to look upon him favourably, and—because his house has in time been worn down by public services—to deem him worthy of such relief as may be possible.
To an assessor of the census

You know the benefits and the harms that come to men from the census-assessments. So pardon this man, who has taken much pains to suffer no harm, and be willing to assist him, as far as you can, toward what is just.
To an assessor of the census

It is not possible to see God's dispensations from afar; rather, through faintheartedness, we men look only to what is at our feet, and often, even when we are being led to a good outcome, we are vexed—the Master, who governs all things in his own wisdom, bearing with our ignorance. For you remember, no doubt, how much we then chafed at the charge laid upon us, and how many friends we took to ourselves in order, through them, to thrust away the imposition. For that is what we called the matter.

But now you see how things stand at present. For God has given you an occasion to bring the nobility of your character into the open, and to leave for all your life thereafter the grounds of a good remembrance. For whatever these assessments may be, of such a kind, too, are the remembrances of them naturally preserved by those who come after. And since not even the Galatians, had they prayed for it, could have obtained a more humane disposition, I am fully persuaded. And I have cause to count happy not only the Galatians for your oversight, but also myself. For I too have a house in Galatia—and, with God's help, the most splendid of houses—on whose behalf, if I should obtain some help from you (and I shall obtain it, so long as friendship keeps its own power), I shall acknowledge a great debt of thanks to God.

If, then, my friendship counts for anything with your honour, be entreated to furnish some acknowledged benefit, for our sake, to the house of that most admirable magistrate, our friend Sulpicius—so as to take off something from the present assessment: best of all an amount considerable and worthy of your magnanimity (and I will add, of our intercession on behalf of those who love you); but if not, then as much as the times allow and the nature of the affairs admits. In any case, take off something, and do not leave it as it stands, so that we, out of the countless benefits we have from that good magistrate, may repay this one favour through your dignity.
Without address, concerning a servant

And how was I to overlook so fitting an occasion for a letter, and not greet your honour, when this man was coming to you? He would have been able, of himself, to tell you our news and to fulfil the office of a letter; but he wished also to become the bearer of a letter, because he loves us greatly and is attached to us with his whole soul. In every way he wishes both to carry back your words and to be of service to you.

We have given him, then, this letter, by which, first, we pray for you all good things—both those that this life holds and all those that are laid up and kept in store, the blessedness promised in the promises; and next, we entreat the holy God that a second meeting with you may be granted to us, while we are still upon the earth. That you will, for our sake, multiply your love toward the aforesaid brother, I do not doubt. So be entreated to give him proof of it in deed.
Without address, on behalf of a kinswoman

Being fully persuaded that I shall in no way fail in whatever I ask of your honour with justice on my side, I came eagerly to give this letter to this most decorous woman, who has the care of orphans and keeps a household harder to manage than some many-headed hydra. And on top of all this, there is besides between us a tie of kinship. Therefore we entreat your nobility—both honouring us and preserving the honour owed to the grandfather of the orphans—to furnish some help, so as to make their property bearable to them henceforth.
Without address, on behalf of a man in distress

Though fully persuaded that those who come to your goodness have no need of letters—since you do more, out of the nobility of your character, than anyone could urge you toward the good by entreaty—nevertheless, because of my exceeding care for this son of mine, I have been moved to write to your pure and guileless soul, commending the man to you, and entreating you, in whatever ways may be possible, to furnish him for the matters before him such aid as lies within your power. And that he will need no other protector, once you have deigned to use, with all the power the Lord has given you, his protection on his behalf, I know full well.
Without address, on behalf of a man in need

The scarcity of replies from your quarter makes our letters to your honour scarce. For we take it as a sign that our letter is a trouble to your honour, when we receive no answers to what we write from time to time. Yet again, the thought of the multitude of affairs about you shifts us to another mind, and we make allowance for one who, having so much in hand, forgets us—of whom, even were there full leisure and quiet, it would not, given the lowliness of our life, be easy to remember.

May the Holy One, then, both bring you to a greater eminence and preserve you in your present splendour by his own grace. As for us, we answer every occasion with letters—and not least the present one, on account of this man, whom we commend to you, and ask that he may be given some sense of the service rendered by our letters.
Of Basil, without address, on behalf of a fellow countryman

Those who have come from our native land are commended to you by the very claim of that land—if indeed it is so, since by the kindness of your character you bring under your own care all who in any way stand in need of some support. Receive, then, the man who puts this letter into your decorous hands, the son of this person, both as a fellow countryman and as one needing support and as commended to you by us; and out of all these claims let this one thing be his, to obtain from you such help as may be possible for the matters before him. And it is plain that the recompense for good works comes not from us, who are little, but from the Lord, who rewards good intentions.
Likewise, on behalf of a stranger

Hard upon your departure there came to us this son, the one who delivers this letter to you, in need—as a man living in a foreign land—of all the consolation that Christians owe to strangers. The matter itself he will recount to you more clearly; the help you yourself will furnish, such as lies in your power and is needful for the business before him. If, then, the governor is present, you will yourself, of course, introduce him to the governor; otherwise you will provide him what he is bent upon through the men of the city council. For it is no small care of mine that he should return having accomplished everything according to his wish.
Without address, by way of greeting

It has been long since we were able to greet your honour, because the man who brings back our answers spent much time in our country and fell in with men and affairs of a most troublesome kind. For a whole year he was kept away from his homeland. Drawn on by men's deceits and proposals of settlement, in the belief that, if he could master the present mischief against him, he would come out ahead in everything, he perceived only late the sum of his loss, his discernment being stolen away by the deceit that worked upon him little by little.

Since, then, he is now returning, delivered both from the hardships of the climate and from the wickedness of those men, we greet you through him, entreating you to remember us in your prayers (for we have great need of the help that comes from prayers); and at the same time we make known to you that those who were left answerable for the discharge of the debt by the blessed bishop—who in his will made mention both of the debt itself, and of the source from which it ought to be paid, and through whom—have disregarded our friendly reminders and are waiting for the constraints of the courts. For this reason our companion has returned with nothing accomplished, and asked that these very facts be testified to him by us, so that he might incur no charge of idleness or negligence before your honour. So much for this. As for the affairs of the churches—whether they have been permitted to remain in their present state, or whether they have fallen to the worse, or what hope there is of a change for the better—deign to make it known to us through one of the true brethren.
To Thekla

This past year a heavy frost fell upon our country and cut off the buds of the vines, which were already opening toward their travail. Those that remained, being barren, made our cups dry and waterless. Why, then, have I been moved to recite to you, as in a tragedy, the barrenness of the plants? That you yourself may become for us, in the words of Solomon, a vine in bloom, a fruitful tendril—not putting forth a cluster of grapes, but pressing out from the clusters their dew for the thirsty. And who are the thirsty? Those who are walling round the enclosure of the community. Since I am unable to give these men the mountain liquor to drink, I have had recourse to your richly clustered right hand, that you may bid your own streams flow down to us from your river, river-like. For if you do this quickly, you will both relieve the dry mouths of many, and gladden first of all, as much as may be, the Atticizing beggar that I am.
Without address, to a friend, in fellow-feeling

On receiving the letter of your honour I was glad, as was natural, and gave thanks to the Lord, and was eager to answer, if anyone in good time had reminded me about a reply. For the matter that you laid upon us was only in time coming to a settlement, and it was not possible to answer anything with assurance before the end of it. This is the cause of our silence—certainly not negligence, nor ignorance of what is fitting. For even had we been altogether negligent, we should surely have been at pains to keep our shortcomings out of your honour's sight. But as it is, we cannot forget you, not even for the briefest moment (one would sooner be ignorant of one's own self); rather, whether we write or not, we carry you about set firmly in our hearts, and we bear the long parting of the winter so ill that we pray—if it is not possible for you yourself, on account of the engagements we hear of, to leave the country folk—that some occasion may arise for us to come to those parts and to enjoy the true steadiness of your character and your decorum. In any case, you will surely be eager to keep the saving day of the Pascha with us, together with your most decorous wife, whom too we greet through you, and whom we entreat to join in helping us, to hasten you toward us.
To Philagrius Arcenus

Thanks be to the holy God—for I could not say that I am thankful to those who have wronged you, because they have become for me the occasion of a letter; but the Lord, who confers benefits upon us from every side, knows how, often, even through griefs to fulfil our consolations. Hence he has made the senseless conduct of those who have run away from you into an occasion of gladness for us as well.

But do you write to us on every occasion, writing such things as these—proceeding so from a kindly mind, and so from a tongue refined. For even if we deny that we lay claim to the charm in your diction, still we are somehow by nature enchanted by it, and you who are graceful in speech lead us along, as men lead bees by the striking of cymbals. Send us, then, many letters, and as long as may be; for brevity is no virtue in a letter—no more than it is in a man.

Write to us, too, of how things stand with your house, and how your own body fares in health, and whether the affairs of the churches are at peace; for you care for these things also, and do well to do so. And indeed, if there is any power in you to labour together for the peace and union of those who are divided, do not decline it.

The good Cyriacus first applied himself to the task, and then delivered to us your letter; and for the remnants of the matter he found us joining in to do what was in our power. For we have written to the country bishop of those parts, who, if he carries out any of what was charged, will himself make the affairs known.
To Pasinicus the physician

It is a proof that you do not hold us as a thing of no account, that you greet us at once, so to speak, from the very doors of the entrance. Now, to meet with a friendly letter is itself a thing worth being eager for; but if what is written also accomplishes a need in matters of the greatest importance, it plainly becomes worth far more.

Know well, then, that Patricius, that man best in all things, carries upon his lips so many drugs of persuasion that—not only because you have written, but even were he to get hold of some Sauromatian or Scythian—he could easily persuade them of whatever he might wish. Yet those words of cheerfulness are not from the heart. For this is a posture long practised: men who, as far as words go, profess to be obliging and, supposedly, without affectation, and ready to entrust the matters concerning them to any court; but when they come to the business itself—may you not chance to be there.

But let these things be said by me to you, so that you yourself may know it, and—the man being in any case not easily led—you may further be persuaded, of your own accord, not to attend to the fair appearance of his words, but to wait for the proofs that come from the facts.
To Magninianus

Even the letter of your dignity would have sufficed to work in us every gladness. But as it is, the most decorous of women, Icelium, our common daughter, by delivering your letter increased that gladness more than twofold—not only because she is a living image of your nobility, but because she displays, of herself, every care for virtue. So that, having first received her gladly for your sake, we afterwards, on her return, counted you blessed for her sake, since the rewards of such child-rearing await you from the Master, God. But may we one day see you yourself too, and enjoy the good qualities in you, with no sickness, nor any other difficulty, hindering our meeting.

Without title, by way of admonition The holy God has given us a most fitting occasion in our affairs by making known to us this brother, the man whom, on our return to your Honour, we have employed as the bearer of this written conversation of ours; and we pray to God that, as you advance to ever greater distinction and renown, you may adorn both us and the whole of our homeland by your own virtue. We urge you, throughout your whole life, to remember the God who created you and bestowed honour upon you, so that, in addition to the splendour of this present life, you may further be counted worthy of the glory of heaven, for the sake of which we must do all things, we who direct our lives toward that blessed hope.

Without title, by way of encouragement For the honour you showed us while we were present, and for thinking us worthy to be remembered now that we are absent (for the report of it has reached us), may a recompense come to you from the good Master; and may we see you, on the great day of the righteous judgement of our God, held in good esteem for your good works, so that, just as you have been counted worthy of distinction here, so also you may enjoy honour in the presence of the King of heaven. We urge you, then, first of all to extend your unfailing zeal to the Church of God, and after that to increase your goodwill toward us as well, counting us worthy of all remembrance and protection, and to dignify us with letters; so that, having proof that we are not a burden to you when we write, we may take courage to address your magnanimity more frequently.

To Hyperechius I both greet your Honour and pray that good things may be yours; and I disclose my own affairs to you, who are altogether eager to know how we are faring, namely that I am doing nothing better than my usual state. For I spare you the more dismal news, so as not to grieve too greatly one who joins us in praying for the best.

To Phalerius I took very great delight in the river-fish, though I bore them a grudge for the flight they took when they ran for shelter from the cold. But your letters are more precious to us than fish. So write rather than send. And if it is more agreeable to you to keep silent, still, at the very least, do not cease to pray on our behalf.

Without title That I love you, learn from the letters I send. That you hate me, I have come to know from your silences. Yet write, for the future at least, with reed and ink and a brief sheet of paper, loving those who love you.

Without title It is pointless to write twice about the same matter. For either the affair admits by its nature of no correction, and those who come to us trouble us in vain, or else those who receive the letters disregard us, and so we are foolish to write to men who hold us in contempt. Since, then, you have already received a letter on this same subject, and we have now been compelled to write a second time, either set the matter right, if it is in your power, or make known to us the reason why what was enjoined has long gone undone.

Another, without title Speech is the one sign of being alive. How then could you be reckoned to exist above the earth, when you never utter a word? Come, drive away your silence by writing to us and showing us that you are indeed alive.

To a secretary Words are winged by nature. For this reason they require signs, so that the writer may catch their speed as they take flight. You, then, my boy, make your strokes complete, and place the points correctly in their proper places. For by a small error much of the sense is corrupted, whereas by the writer's care what is spoken is set down aright.

To a calligrapher Write straight, and keep to the lines correctly; and let your hand neither rise up toward the heights nor be carried down the precipices. Do not force the reed to walk crookedly, like Aesop's crab, but go straight ahead, as though walking along a carpenter's rule, which everywhere preserves the level and removes all that is uneven. For the crooked is unseemly, but the straight is a delight to those who behold it, not allowing the eyes of the readers to nod up and down, as the well-sweeps do. Something of this sort befell me too when I came upon your writing. For since the lines lay like the rungs of a ladder, whenever it was necessary to pass from one to another, I had to set myself straight again at the end of the line I was approaching. And since the sequence nowhere appeared, I had to run back again and search out the order, retracing my steps and following along the furrow, as they say Theseus followed the thread of Ariadne. Write straight, then, and do not lead the mind astray by the slanting and crooked character of what is written.

Basil to Libanius I am ashamed to bring the Cappadocians to you one by one, instead of persuading all who are of an age to lay claim to learning and education and to make use of you as their teacher in the discipline. But since it is impossible to succeed with all at once, when each chooses what suits himself, we send on to you those who are persuaded from time to time, conferring upon them as great a favour as do those who guide the thirsty to the springs. The young man who comes to you now will, a little later, be sought after for his own sake, once he has become known to you. For the present he is known through his father, who has won among us a great name for uprightness of life and for ability in public affairs, and who is bound to me as well in the closest friendship. In requital of this friendship I grant to his son this favour, making him known to you, a thing well worth praying for in the eyes of those who know how to judge a man's virtue.

Libanius to Basil After a long time a young Cappadocian has come to us. Here is one gain: that he is a Cappadocian. But more, this Cappadocian is of the first rank. Here is a second gain. But more, he brings us a letter from the admirable Basil. And what could anyone call greater than this? For the man whom you suppose to have forgotten you—I held him in respect even long ago, when he was young, seeing him vie with old men in temperance, and that too in that city which teems with pleasures, and already possessing a great share of eloquence. And when you thought you ought to see Athens as well, and were persuading Celsus to go, I rejoiced with Celsus for being so attached to your soul. And when you had come home again and were keeping to your homeland, I said to myself: "What is Basil now doing for us, and to what kind of life has he set out? Does he turn to the law courts, emulating the orators of old? Or does he make orators of the sons of prosperous fathers?" But when certain men came reporting that you were walking a far better road than these, and were considering how you might become more a friend to God than gather up gold, I counted you happy, and the Cappadocians too: you, for wishing to be such a man, and them, for being able to display such a citizen. That famous Firmus, I well know, has continued to prevail everywhere; for from this comes his power in words. But though he has enjoyed much praise, I do not know that he ever enjoyed any so great as I have now heard in your letter. For your saying that no one could surpass that man's reputation—how great a thing must this be reckoned for him, coming from you who say it? You seem to me, moreover, to have sent these men off before you had seen Firminus; for otherwise your letter could not have failed to contain him. And what is Firminus now doing, or what does he intend? Is he still amid longings for marriage, or have those long since ceased, while the council weighs heavy upon him, and there is every necessity that he remain? Or what hopes are there that he will once more be a sharer in eloquence? Let him answer us something, and may it be something good; but if it should also bring some grief, it will at least release us from gazing toward the gates. And if Firminus were now at Athens, what would your councillors do? Would they send the Salaminia after him? You see that I am insulted by your fellow-citizens, and that alone. Yet I for my part will not cease to love and praise the Cappadocians; but I pray that they may become better disposed toward me, and if they remain as they are, I shall bear it. Firminus stayed with us four months, and not a single day did he idle away. How much he has amassed, you yourself will learn, and perhaps you will not find fault. But to make it possible for him to come here again, what ally must I call upon besides? For if the councillors are right-minded, and it would befit educated men, they will do him honour by the second sort, since by the first they gave him pain.

Basil to Libanius See, here comes yet another Cappadocian to you, a son of mine, and he too; for this habit in which we now live makes them all sons to us. So in this respect at least he would be a brother to the one who came before, and worthy of the same zeal both from me, his father, and from you, his teacher—if indeed those who come from us can have any advantage at all. And I say this, not as though your eloquence would not grant something more to the old companions, but because your benefit lies open to all in ungrudging abundance. It would be enough for the young man, before he has been tested by time, to be ranked among your own household; and may you send him back to us worthy both of our prayers and of the reputation you hold in eloquence. He brings with him also a youth of the same age, who shares an equal zeal for eloquence, himself too of noble birth and a member of our household; and we are confident that he will be in no way inferior, even though in wealth he falls far short of the rest.

Libanius to Basil I know that you will write this often—"See, here comes yet another Cappadocian to you." For many, I suppose, you will send, always and everywhere employing your praises of me, and by this very means stirring up both fathers and sons. But what happened in the matter of your fine letter, it would not be fine to pass over in silence. There were seated beside me not a few of those who have held office, and among them the wholly excellent Alypius, cousin of the famous Hierocles. So when the bearers handed over the letter, having gone through it all in silence, "We are defeated," I said, smiling and rejoicing at once. "And what victory have you been defeated in?" they asked; "and how is it you feel no pain at being defeated?" "In beauty of letters," I said, "I am beaten; Basil has won. And the man is my friend, and for that reason I rejoice." When I had said this, they wished to learn the victory from the letter itself. And Alypius read it aloud, while those present listened. And the verdict was given, that I had told no lie. And the reader went out holding the letter, to show it, I suppose, to others as well, and only with difficulty gave it back. Write, then, the like, and conquer; for that is to conquer me. And you conjecture rightly in this too, that what comes from us is not measured by money; rather, for one who cannot give, it is enough to be willing to receive. For if I perceive someone in poverty who is in love with eloquence, he comes before the rich. And yet such were not the teachers we ourselves experienced; but nothing will prevent us from being better at least in this respect. Let no poor man, then, hesitate to make his way here, if he possesses that one thing only—the knowledge of how to labour.

Basil to Libanius What would a sophist not say—and such a sophist as you, for whom it is acknowledged to be the very mark of the art both to make great things small whenever he wishes, and to invest small things with greatness? Just such a thing you have displayed in our case. For that squalid letter of mine—as you who revel in eloquence would call it—which was in no way more tolerable than this one you now hold in your hands, you raised so high by your discourse as to feign yourself defeated by it, and to yield to us the first prize in writing; doing the same as fathers do in their games, when by their own victories they let their children plume themselves, neither harming themselves at all, and nourishing the children's love of honour. And in truth the speech, in its play toward us, held untold delight: like some Polydamas or Milo declining the contest of pancratium or wrestling against me; for though I searched much, I found no sample of any weakness—so that those who seek out the extravagances of eloquence admire you more here for your power, in being able to come down to play with us, than if you had brought the barbarian sailing his fleet above Athos. But we, my admirable friend, keep company with Moses and Elijah and men so blessed as these, who tell us their own affairs in the barbarian tongue; and we utter what comes from them, with a true meaning but an unlettered diction, as these very lines make plain. For if we had learned anything from you, we have forgotten it through the lapse of time.
